SENATE RESOLUTION 239 

[Submitted by Mr. Millikin] 

IN THE SENATE OF THE UNITED STATES, 

April 28 (legislative day, April 14), 1954.

Resolved, That the United States Tariff Commission Report on the Investigation of the Lead and Zinc Industries, conducted under section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930, pursuant to a resolution by the Committee on Finance, be printed as a Senate document. 

Attest: 

J. MARK TRICE, Secretary. 

II

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

Acknowledgment is made of important aid given in the preparation of this report by several Government agencies: The United States 

Bureau of Mines of the Department of the Interior provided extensive statistical and technical information that greatly assisted the Commission in conducting and completing this investigation. The Bureau of the Census of the Department of Commerce furnished statistics on international trade, and the United States Geological Survey of the Department of the Interior supplied data on ore reserves in the United States and foreign countries. The Interstate Commerce Commission, the Federal Maritime Board, and the Government of Mexico furnished information on transportation charges for rail and water movement of ores, concentrates, and metals. The Office of Defense 

Mobilization supplied information on strategic stockpiling, and the General Services Administration, on Government contracts for the purchase of lead and zinc in the United States and foreign countries. 

The Bureau of Labor Statistics of the Department of Labor furnished statistical material on employment, hourly earnings, wage rates, and wholesale commodity prices, and the Department of the Treasury supplied information on mine taxation.

Grateful acknowledgment is also made to the many persons and concerns throughout the lead and zinc industries who aided in the preparation of this report. To a large extent the completeness of the 

Commission's investigation directly reflects the cooperation of many individuals and mining, smelting, and importing concerns that supplied detailed information on their operations in the United States and foreign countries. Valuable information was also supplied by representatives of trade associations in the domestic lead and zinc industries. The Commission notes especially the cooperation of those producers of lead and zinc in foreign countries who furnished statistical data covering their operations on the same basis as the data furnished by domestic producers.

The Honorable EUGENE D. MILLIKIN, Chairman, Committee on Finance, United States Senate. 

DEAR SENATOR MILLIKIN: I am transmitting herewith 18 copies of the Tariff Commission's report of its investigation, made under the provisions of section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, of the lead and zinc industries.

This investigation and report were made pursuant to a resolution by the Committee on Finance of the United States Senate dated July 27, 1953, and a resolution by the Committee on Ways and Means of the 

United States House of Representatives dated July 29, 1953. 

Sincerely yours,

EDGAR B. BROSSARD, Chairman.

PART I INTRODUCTION, SUMMARY, AND CONCLUSIONS 

46566-54-

I. INTRODUCTION OCCASION FOR INVESTIGATION 

In each year since our entry into World War II, United States imports of unmanufactured lead and zinc for consumption have been very much larger than in immediate prewar years, or in any earlier years. Initially this expansion of imports was stimulated by greatly increased United States requirements for these metals for various wartime uses, but imports have remained large in all postwar years and have continued to supply a substantial part of domestic requirements. 

Among the conditions contributing to continued high-level demand and imports in postwar years were the durable-goods boom and high industrial activity generally; inventory replenishment following wartime depletion of stocks; heavy defense demands arising from hostilities in Korea; and Government purchases for stockpiling. During the postwar period of high demand, domestic production did not expand sufficiently to meet increased United States requirements, and net imports of lead and zinc were approximately equal to one-third of domestic consumption. These greatly increased imports included large quantities of lead and zinc that in prewar years would normally have been marketed in other countries, principally those of Western Europe.

In 1939 for unmanufactured zinc, and in 1943 for unmanufactured lead, the rates of duty, which are specific, were reduced for the first time pursuant to trade agreements. The rates now in effect represent a reduction of 60 percent for zinc, and of 50 percent for lead, from the statutory rates in the Tariff Act of 1930. Since the prices of these metals have increased substantially since 1939, the relative decreases in the ad valorem equivalents of the current rates in comparison with the ad valorem equivalents of the statutory rates in prewar years have greatly exceeded the reductions in the specific rates of duty. 

In the postwar period substantial imports entered free of duty for the account of the United States Government, and during part of this period the duties on lead and zinc were temporarily suspended, prices were under Government regulation with different ceiling prices for metal of domestic and foreign origin, and the United States had difficulty in meeting its greatly expanded requirements with the quantities that foreign suppliers were able or willing to make available. In the inventory-readjustment period that extended from the middle of 1949 to the middle of 1950 there were strong indications of weakness in the domestic lead and zinc markets as sales fell off, producers' stocks increased, and prices declined, but demand strengthened and prices increased sharply following the start of hostilities in Korea. As late as the first part of 1952 there was concern whether the United States could obtain adequate supplies of foreign lead and zinc, and on February 11, 1952, legislation was approved temporarily suspending the 3

2 import duties on these metals (Public Laws 257 and 258, 82d Cong.).¹

Soon thereafter the prices of both lead and zinc started to decline. 

Acting on reports from the Tariff Commission that the prices of lead and zinc had fallen below the minimum specified in these laws (18 cents per pound for each metal), the President proclaimed the revocation of the suspension of import duties, effective for lead on 

June 26, 1952, and for zinc on July 24, 1952.

Notwithstanding the reimposition of import duties in mid-1952, prices for both lead and zinc have continued generally downward, and present base quotations (March 10, 1954) are 13 cents and 9.75 cents per pound for lead and zinc, respectively. These prices represent reductions of 32 percent for lead and 50 percent for zinc from the prices in effect on January 1, 1952. Meanwhile, important items of cost-such as wage rates and prices of machinery and supplies-which had increased substantially since World War II, have not decreased. 

The progressive deterioration in the position of the domestic lead and zinc industries since mid-1952 has been marked also by the following developments: Imports of lead and zinc were extraordinarily large in 1952 and also in 1953; the strike in the United States steel industry in 1952 reduced domestic demand for the largest use of zinc (galvanizing); the British Government decided to dispose of surplus Government-owned lead and zinc stocks on a market that was already weakening; private trading in lead and zinc on the London Metal 

Exchange, which had been suspended in 1939, was resumed (on 

October 1, 1952, for lead and on January 2, 1953, for zinc), and there were rapid reductions in the prices of these metals on the London market; the cessation of hostilities in Korea increased the possibility of reduced United States demand for defense needs; and uncertainties regarding the business outlook developed, which, with ample supplies of lead and zinc available, encouraged reductions in consumers' inventories and price concessions by sellers to obtain purchase commitments. In the face of these conditions there has been a decline in domestic mine production of both metals, accompanied by mine closures and reduced employment.

The developments described above have caused widespread apprehension on the part of domestic lead- and zinc-mining and smelting interests, as well as on the part of persons and groups whose welfare is related to the economic well-being of the areas in which lead and zinc ores are mined. In consequence, numerous proposals have been made to increase the duties on unmanufactured lead and zinc, to restrict imports by other methods, and to provide other forms of direct and indirect aid. Over the past 2 years the problems of the domestic lead and zinc industries have been reviewed extensively before various committees of the Congress. In that period, 2 Federal commissions and 1 Federal board 3 have also issued reports concerned with certain aspects of these problems, as well as with other questions of trade and resource policy. The views and recommendations given

in these reports, as well as those presented in testimony before congressional committees, differ widely with reference to remedial action that would be in the best interests of the domestic lead and zinc industries, of consumers who require additional supplies to meet expanded use of these metals, of national-defense needs, and of the requirements of an integrated national trade policy. 

In view of the widespread repercussions which any significant alteration in the tariff treatment applicable to unmanufactured lead and zinc would have on domestic interests mining and processing these products and on the consuming public, as well as on this country's foreign-trade relations, the United States Senate Committee on Finance in a resolution dated July 27, 1953, and the Committee on Ways and Means of the House of Representatives in a resolution dated July 29, 1953, directed the Tariff Commission to make a thorough study of all factors bearing on the domestic lead and zinc situation, and to report the result of its investigation to each committee on or before March 31, 1954.4 This report is made in response to both resolutions, the texts of which are practically identical. The resolution of the Senate Finance Committee-the first received by the 

Commission-reads as follows: 

Resolved, That the Tariff Commission is hereby directed pursuant to section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (19 U. S. C. 1332), to make a thorough investigation of the domestic lead and zinc industries, including the effect of the imports of lead and zinc on the livelihood of American workers, and to report the results of its investigation to the Senate Finance Committee on or before March 

31, 1954.

SEC. 2. Such investigation shall be made after due notice and opportunity for hearing is given to interested parties. The report of the Commission shall set forth the facts so determined relative to the production, trade, and consumption of lead and zinc in the United States, and shall take into account all relevant factors affecting the domestic economy, including the interests of consumers, processors, and producers. Such report also shall contain a statement of findings as to the effect upon the competitive position of the domestic lead and zinc industries of the present tariff status of imported lead and zinc, so as to assist the Congress in determining what changes, if any, should be made in that status. 

On July 29, 1953, in response to the above-mentioned resolutions of the Senate Finance Committee and the House Ways and Means 

Committee, the Tariff Commission instituted a general investigation of the lead and zinc industries. Public notice of the investigation was given by posting a copy of the notice at the office of the Commission in Washington, D. C., and at its New York City office, and by publication in the Federal Register (18 F. R. 4529) and in the 

August 6, 1953, issue of Treasury Decisions. A public hearing was ordered for November 3, 1953, with respect to lead, and for November 5, 1953, with respect to zinc, public notice of which was given in the same manner (18 F. R. 4529; Treasury Decisions issue of Aug. 6, 1953).

On September 14, 1953, an application was filed with the Tariff Commission for escape-clause action under section 7 of the Trade Agreements Extension Act of 1951 covering articles provided for in paragraphs 72, 77, 391, 392, 393, and 394 of the Tariff Act of 1930. 

Paragraphs 72, 391, and 392 provide for lead ores, unmanufactured lead metal, and certain other lead-bearing articles. Paragraphs 77, 393, and 394 provide for zinc ores, unmanufactured zinc metal, and certain other zinc-bearing articles. In terms of volume and value 

4 The date for submittal of the Tariff Commission's report was subsequently changed to April 20, 1954.

of imports, by far the most important articles provided for in these paragraphs are lead and zinc ores and unmanufactured lead and zinc metals. The existing rates of duty on all the articles covered by the paragraphs mentioned reflect trade-agreement concessions granted by the United States in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade 

The Tariff Commission instituted an escape-clause investigation under section 7 on September 16, 1953. Public notice of this investigation was given in the usual manner (18 F. R. 5673; Treasury Decisions issue of Sept. 24, 1953), and a public hearing was ordered on

November 3, 1953, with respect to lead, and on November 5, 1953, with respect to zinc, this hearing to be conducted concurrently with the hearing previously ordered for the general investigation of the lead and zinc industries under section 332. The concurrent public hearings for both investigations were held from November 3 to 6, inclusive, 1953, in the Tariff Commission hearing room in Washington, D. C., at which all interested parties were given opportunity to appear and to be heard. The escape-clause investigation is in process of completion.

In addition to the information obtained at the public hearing bearing: on the general investigation under section 332, the Commission used information obtained from its files and from other official sources, and that obtained through field work by members of the Commission's: staff and through questionnaires sent to importers and to operators of domestic and foreign mines, mills, and smelting and refining plants. 

Domestic concerns also supplied information covering their operations: (conducted directly, or by subsidiary or affiliated concerns) in foreign countries, and certain important foreign lead and zinc producers not affiliated with domestic concerns cooperated by supplying the Commission with information comparable with that supplied by domestic producers.

The Commission devoted major attention in this investigation to developments affecting the mining and milling of lead and zinc ores as separate from developments affecting the smelting and refining of lead and zinc. For all segments of the domestic lead and zinc industries taken together, mines and mills provide the major part of the employment, account for the principal part of the total cost of producing lead and zinc, and are most affected by weaknesses in the markets for these metals.

Imports of unmanufactured lead are primarily in the form of pigs and bars, dutiable under paragraph 392, and of lead in ores, dutiable under paragraph 391. Imports of unmanufactured zinc are primarily in the form of zinc in ores, dutiable under paragraph 393, and of zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs, dutiable under paragraph 394. Imports of the following lead- and zinc-bearing articles, for which the rates of duty are related to the rates on unmanufactured lead and zinc, are relatively small: Imports of lead articles other than unmanufactured lead under paragraph 392; imports of lead pigments under paragraph 72; imports of zinc articles other than unmanufactured zinc under paragraph 394; and imports of zinc pigments and compounds under paragraph 77. 

Since most of these articles have advanced at least through the first stages of manufacture, and since the small imports could not be of material significance in connection with the current problems of the lead and zinc industries, they are not included in this investigation.

However, if the Congress should change the tariff status of imports of unmanufactured lead and zinc, it might wish to consider the need for compensatory changes in the duties applicable to imports of such articles. 

PRODUCTION ACTIVITIES COVERED AND MAJOR PRODUCTS. 

For the purpose of this investigation, the lead and zinc industries are viewed broadly as constituting a series of production operations which begin with activities directed toward the production of ore and which terminate with the output of metal. The usual production pattern is for ores to be mined, milled (concentrated), shipped to a smelter, and reduced to metal. However, the sequence of production operations may not always be direct or the same in all instances, for not all ores are smelted into metal nor is all metal produced from newly mined ores.

For example, some ores are normally diverted for direct processing (without smelting) into pigments and chemicals, and materials other than ores (scrap, dross, metal dust, skimmings, etc.) enter the production sequence at the smelter level and are reduced to metal.

Unmanufactured lead and zinc are overwhelmingly the major products of the United States lead and zinc industries. In finished form unmanufactured lead and zinc are metals ready for fabrication; they are usually in the form of pigs, slabs, blocks, or bars. The finished metals, in turn, are obtained by producing or collecting and by processing a variety of materials including ores, scrap, flue dust, and others, and there are intermediate steps in the production and processing operations. A study of all unmanufactured lead or zine appropriately includes, in addition to finished metal, all crude materials irrespective of source, ores diverted for direct processing into pigments and chemicals, and materials in intermediate stages of production or processing. The basic statistics given throughout this report are oriented to facts that bear on the production and processing of these materials, and on the trade in them. 

As used in this report, the term "unmanufactured lead" covers lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes, all of which are dutiable under paragraph 391 of the Tariff Act of 1930; it also covers lead bullion or base bullion, lead pigs and bars, lead dross, reclaimed lead, scrap lead, type metal, antimonial lead, antimonial scrap lead, and alloys or combinations of lead not specially provided for, all of which are dutiable under paragraph 392. The term does not cover additional lead-bearing articles dutiable under paragraph 392, or lead-bearing articles dutiable under other paragraphs of the tariff act. 

Similarly, as used in this report, the term "unmanufactured zinc" covers zinc-bearing ores dutiable under paragraph 393; it also covers zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs, and zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings, all of which are dutiable under paragraph 394. The term does not cover additional zinc-bearing articles dutiable under paragraph 394, or zinc-bearing articles dutiable under other paragraphs of the tariff act. 

MAJOR INDUSTRY DIVISIONS AND RELATIONSHIPS 

There are two major divisions or branches in the United States lead and zinc industries, respectively. One division consists of activities directed toward the exploration and development of ore bodies, and

8. 

toward the mining and milling (concentration) of ore. These operations are relatively numerous, and are carried on in a large number of mining districts distributed among many States. In 1952 lead and zinc ores were mined at about 900 mines distributed over 23 States and Alaska, although the bulk of the newly mined production of each metal comes from a limited number of areas. 

The second major division or branch in each industry consists of smelters and refineries that process the ores and concentrates and produce metal in finished form. The number of primary smelters and refineries (those that process ores and concentrates and refine the resulting metal) is small compared with the number of mines and mills; in 1952 lead concentrates or lead bullion were smelted or refined at 13 plants, and zinc concentrates were smelted or refined at 18 plants. 

In addition to mines and primary smelters and refineries, there are over 200 concerns engaged in recovering lead metal from scrap lead and 9 smelters that produce secondary slab zinc; secondary zinc is also recovered, either as slab zinc or in alloys of zinc, at other secondary-metal plants.

Whereas the location of mining and milling operations is determined by nature at sites where ores of commercial grade occur-primary smelters and refineries are situated on the basis of many economic factors which include availability of ores, fuel, power, labor, and access to principal markets. Since mining operations are broadly distributed, distances from mines to smelters vary widely and they may be considerable. Moreover, smelters use different fuels and processes in carrying on their operations and some smelters may be better adapted than others for the reduction of certain ores. 

It may thus be advantageous in certain instances to ship ores to more distant smelters that are adapted for their treatment, rather than to send them to less distant smelters that are not so well adapted. Plants that process lead and zinc scrap are generally located in, or near, the heavily industrialized and populated areas of the country where supplies of scrap are abundant. 

The smelting of lead and zinc is largely conducted separately, at different plants situated at different locations. Thus there is a clear-cut division between the smelting branches of the two industries. 

MINE PRODUCTION OF LEAD AND ZINC INTERRELATED 

In contrast with the definitive separation of the lead and zinc industries at the smelter level, mine production of ores of the two metals in the United States is closely interrelated. This is because lead and zinc concentrates are frequently obtained from the same ores, although the proportion of each metal present may differ greatly from district to district and even from mine to mine in the same district. There are some important exceptions to this generalization; for example, lead ores, nearly free of zinc, are mined in Southeastern Missouri, in certain districts of Utah, and at some mines in other districts; also, certain zinc ores mined in the Eastern States are free of lead. However, in most mining districts the two metals are associated to some degree in the same ore, and in many mining districts in the Western States they occur with gold, silver, copper, and sometimes with other metal. Regardless of which of the two metals may be dominant in such complex ores, mills which concentrate them normally produce both lead concentrates and zinc concentrates.

Owing to the extensive occurrence of lead and zinc in the same ores it is virtually impossible to classify individual mines producing lead and zinc into two separate groups representing (1) lead mines which belong in the lead industry, and (2) zinc mines which belong in the zinc industry. It is possible, however, on the basis of available information to determine approximately what types of mines are dominantly the source of lead and what types are dominantly the source of zinc. Such information was developed as a result of the 

1939 census of mineral industries and is given in table S-1. Since the results reflect principally physical and geological features of leadand zinc-mining operations that have not changed materially, they are reasonably representative of present conditions.

The census figures indicate that in 1939 approximately 75 percent of the lead output came from operations of which lead was the principal product, 15 percent from mines of which zinc was the principal product, 5 percent from mines of which silver was the principal product, and the remaining 5 percent from mines of which gold, copper, and other metals were the principal products. In the same year about 82 per cent of the zinc came from mines of which zinc was the principal product, about 12 percent from mines of which lead was the principal product, and about 5 percent from mines of which copper was the principal product. The proportion of the zinc output accounted for by silver, gold, and other metal mines was very small (about 1 percent). 

Thus, it would appear that economic changes affecting principally lead would have their greatest impact upon mines that produce threefourths of the Nation's newly mined lead. Economic changes affecting zinc would have their greatest impact upon mines accounting for about four-fifths of the Nation's production of newly mined zinc. 

At the same time it is noted that most of the zinc produced at mines of which that metal is not the principal product comes from lead mines, and that most of the lead produced at mines of which that metal is not the principal product comes from zinc mines. Moreover, there are many individual mines where the ores yield approximately the same, or not greatly different, quantities of the two metals. Thus, many zinc producers have an important interest in developments affecting the market for lead, and many lead producers in developments affecting the market for zinc, depending upon conditions at their individual operations. In several Western districts many lead and zinc producers also have an important interest in economic developments affecting silver and gold.

Insofar as figures are available and it has been possible to do so, the information obtained in this investigation is presented for lead and

zinc separately. However, for some aspects of these industries, particularly with reference to mining and milling, the information available to the Commission covered operations that produced both lead and zinc and is necessarily so presented. 

POSITION OF THE UNITED STATES IN WORLD PRODUCTION, CON- SUMPTION, AND TRADE 

The United States is the first-ranking country in the world as a producer and as a consumer of both lead and zinc. None of the other principal lead- and zinc-producing countries, with the exception of the Soviet Union, are among the major consumers of these metals. Also, since the beginning of World War II the United States has been by far the largest importer of lead and zinc.

As lead and zinc are frequently obtained from the same ores, the countries which are the principal world sources of lead ores and concentrates the United States, Mexico, Australia, Canada, the Soviet Union, and Peru-are also the major producers of zinc ores and concentrates. However, there is a difference in the position of the producing countries with respect to the output of lead and zinc ores and the output of smelted lead and zinc metal. Whereas the principal ore-producing countries smelt all or a large part of their lead-ore output, the major part of the zinc concentrates is smelted close to the main consuming centers. 

Another feature of the world situation with reference to lead and zinc is that the consumption of these metals is concentrated in the highly industrialized countries, whereas most of the mine production comes from countries (except the United States, Canada, and the Soviet Union) that generally are not regarded as heavily industrialized. As a result there is an extensive international trade reflecting the movement of lead and zinc from the principal producing to the principal consuming areas. Although exact figures are not available, indications are that from 60 to 70 percent of world supplies of lead and zinc ordinarily cross international borders at least once either as ore or as metal.

The situation since the war has been influenced by factors which, while not altering the broad features set forth above, have materially changed the position of the United States. These are (1) a general upward trend in the foreign production of primary lead and zinc in late postwar years accompanied by decreased United States primary-lead production and only moderately increased primary-zinc production, (2) a very great expansion of United States requirements for both lead and zinc, which have been much larger than domestic production, and (3) the shipment to the United States of a large part of the exportable surpluses of foreign producing countries, since demand outside the United States has decreased substantially for lead and has increased only slightly for zinc. Attributable mainly to these factors, the position of the United States has changed from one of relatively minor importance in the international movement of lead and zinc during immediate prewar years to one of very great current importance in this trade.

The figures which are available for comparisons regarding lead and zinc on a world basis cover the production and consumption of primary lead and zinc only. These data exclude secondary metal, which is

much more important in the United States than in other countries, and hence they represent substantial understatement of total United States production and consumption. Despite these limitations, the available data are useful to illustrate broad features of the world lead and zinc industries, and they are summarized briefly below. 

It should be noted that figures for the Soviet Union are estimated, and they are largely excluded from this discussion, since that country has little import or export trade in lead and zinc.

Most of the world's supply of lead ore is produced by 5 countriesthe United States, Mexico, Australia, Canada, and Peru-which together in 1952 accounted for about 59 percent of total production (see table S-2); in the same year these countries produced 60 percent of the world's smelter output. With the exception of the United States, however, none of these countries are large consumers of lead. Compared with an aggregate share of about 40 percent and 36 percent, respectively, of world mine and primary-smelter production of lead, Mexico, Australia, Canada, and Peru together accounted in 1952 for only about 6 percent of world consumption. By way of contrast, the United States-for which output represented about 19 percent and 24 percent, respectively, of world mine and smelter production in 1952 accounted for about 45 percent of the world consumption of primary lead in that year.

The principal lead-consuming countries outside the United States (and excluding the Soviet Union) are Western Germany, the United Kingdom, and France. None of these countries is an important producer of lead, although in 1952 the lead content of mine output in

POSITION WITH REFERENCE TO ZINC 

In considering world sources of primary zinc, a distinction must be made between the countries that are major producers of zinc ores and those that are major producers of zinc metal. This is because most zinc ores are smelted in countries other than those where the ores are mined. Although all principal zinc-ore-producing countries have zinc-smelting facilities, only in the United States is the smelter ca-pacity sufficiently large to treat the entire domestic mine output. 

On the other hand, some countries that mine little or no zinc ores have smelters that treat substantial quantities of such ores. 

The principal countries producing zinc ore are the United States, Canada, Mexico, Australia, and Peru. (See table S-3.) In 1952 these countries together accounted for about 59 percent of world mine production; the United States alone accounted for 24 percent of the total. Except for the United States, where total smelter capacity greatly exceeds domestic mine production, these countries smelt only a part, and mostly a relatively small part, of their mine output. Mexico, Australia, and Peru send much the larger part of their ore production abroad for smelting, and a substantial, although smaller, propor-tion of Canada's mine output is processed elsewhere.

The countries that predominate in the production of primary zinc metal are the United States, Canada, Belgium, and Western Germany.

These countries, except Canada, derive a considerable part of their primary-smelter output from imported ores and concentrates. Canada smelts largely domestically mined ores. The production of primary zinc metal in Belgium is exclusively derived from imported ores and concentrates. In 1952 the 4 major zinc-smelting countries mentioned above accounted for about 62 percent of the world output of primary zinc metal, but they produced only 40 percent of the world output of zinc ores and concentrates. The United States produced 37 percent of world smelter production and 24 percent of world mine output. 

The United States is by far the world's largest consumer of primary zinc, accounting in 1952 for 39 percent of world consumption. Other important consuming countries (excluding the Soviet Union) are the 

United Kingdom, Western Germany, France, and Belgium, but the aggregate quantity used by these 4 countries (24.9 percent of world output) was much less than United States consumption. As was true for the lead-consuming countries, the major zinc-consuming countries (excluding the Soviet Union) import a considerable part of their zinc supply as ores or metal. 

II. SUMMARY UNITED STATES FOREIGN TRADE AND TARIFFS, PRODUCTION, EMPLOYMENT, CONSUMPTION, AND STOCKS FOREIGN TRADE IN LEAD, AND LEAD TARIFFS 

The international trade of the United States in unmanufactured lead since World War II has been confined almost wholly to imports, the nature and extent of which are discussed in subsequent sections of this report. The postwar export trade has been of minor, and almost negligible, significance. (See table L-6 in pt. II.) For a long period prior to World War II the United States had been generally a net importer of lead; the excess of imports over exports, however, was very small.

Over the past 5 years, 5 countries have supplied about 85 percent of the total lead entering the United States for consumption. These are Mexico (the chief source), Canada (including Newfoundland),

Australia, Peru, and Yugoslavia. Over three-fourths of the imports have been in the form of pigs and bars, less than one-fifth in the form of lead ores and concentrates, and the small remainder in other forms (reclaimed lead, scrap lead, and lead dross, etc.). 

United States rates of duty applicable to unmanufactured lead 

Lead bullion or base bullion, lead pigs or bars, lead dross, reclaimed lead, scrap lead, type metal, antimonial lead, antimonial scrap lead, and alloys or combinations of lead not specially provided for were originally dutiable at 2% cents per pound of lead content under the Tariff Act of 1930. In 1943, pursuant to the trade agreement with 

Mexico, the rate was reduced to 16 cents per pound of lead content. 

When that agreement was terminated, the rate was restored on 

January 1, 1951, to 2% cents per pound of lead content. Effective

June 6, 1951, pursuant to concessions granted in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT-Torquay), the rate was reduced to 1. cents per pound of lead content, the rate now in effect.

Lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes of all kinds were originally dutiable at 12½ cents per pound of lead content under the Tariff Act of 1930. In 1943, pursuant to the trade agreement with Mexico, the rate was reduced to three-quarters of a cent per pound of lead content. When that agreement was terminated, the rate was restored on January 1, 1951, to 1½ cents per pound of lead content. Effective

June 6, 1951, pursuant to concessions granted in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT-Torquay), the rate was reduced to three-quarters of a cent per pound of lead content, the rate now in effect.

During World War II the bulk of the greatly expanded imports were entered free of duty for the account of the United States Government, and a substantial part of the imports since the war have also entered free of duty. Import duties on unmanufactured lead were suspended from June 20, 1948, to June 30, 1949, inclusive (Public 

Law 725, 80th Cong.), and again from February 12, 1952, to June 

25, 1952, inclusive (Public Law 257, 82d Cong.). The duty on lead scrap was suspended by a series of public laws for virtually the entire period from March 14, 1942, to June 30, 1952. Lead imports in postwar years also entered free of duty for United States Government account, and to a lesser extent for smelting, refining, and export, and as a product of the Philippine Republic (in accordance with the 

Philippine Trade Act of 1946). Of the total imports for consumption of unmanufactured lead during the period 1946 through September 

1953, 44.6 percent entered free of duty.

Differential between the rates of duty on ores and lead metal.-The rate of duty currently applicable on lead in lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes (three-quarters of a cent per pound of lead content) is equal to about 71 percent of the current rate of duty on lead in pigs and bars and on other forms of unmanufactured lead metal (16 cents per pound of lead content). This relationship between the two current rates of duty is the same as that between the rates provided for in the Tariff Act of 1930. The 1930 rate of duty on lead in lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes (1½ cents per pound of lead content) was also 71 percent of the duty on lead in lead pigs and bars (2% cents per pound of lead content). Both the rates of duty on lead-bearing ores and those on lead pigs and bars have been reduced 50 percent since 1930.

The differential between the rates of duty on lead in ores and those on refined lead metal (71 percent) is more than sufficient to compensate for metallurgical losses in converting the ore to refined lead metal (lead pigs and bars). Although the 1930 and current rates of duty on lead in ores are 71 percent of the rates of duty on lead pigs and bars, about 97.6 percent of the total lead content of ores and concentrates imported into the United States during 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953 was recoverable (taking into account the quantities of lead in ores imported by the various lead smelters and their approximate metal recoveries). Of the total difference of 0.3125 cent between the current rate of duty on lead in lead pigs and bars (1.0625 cents) and that on lead in lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes (0.75 cent), only 0.0255 cent represents compensation for metal lost in smelting operations, and the remainder, 0.287 cent, is the element in the differential which is protective of processing operations.

Although about 97.6 percent of the lead contained in imported lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes is probably recovered in current smelting and refining processes, a smaller percentage, probably no more than about 96 percent, was recovered by lead smelters and refineries in 1930. The increased recoveries reflect improvements in metallurgical processes that have reduced losses in smelting and refining. The element of protection of lead smelting and refining is slightly greater under the present duties and at the present rate of recovery of pig lead from lead ores (97.6 percent) than it would be if the percentage of recovery had remained the same as in 1930 (96 percent). On the basis of the 1930 recovery rate and the present duties, the element of protection of the smelting and refining process would have been 0.270 cent per pound instead of the 0.287 cent it is now.

FOREIGN TRADE IN ZINC, AND ZINC TARIFFS 

The international trade of the United States in unmanufactured zinc since World War II has consisted principally of imports, which are reviewed in later sections of this report. In this period exports of zinc ore and concentrates have been negligible, but moderate quantities of slab zinc-produced by domestic smelters largely from imported ores have been exported. In the prewar period until the latter part of the 1930's the United States was generally self-sufficient with regard to zinc supplies, and exports exceeded imports, usually by a small margin. This trade balance shifted in 1937 and average annual net imports for 1937-39 were 39,000 tons. (See table Z-10 in pt. III.) 

United States imports of unmanufactured zinc come principally from Mexico, Canada, and Peru. During the past 2 years these 

3 countries have accounted for about 80 percent of total imports for consumption. Of the quantity imported since World War II, about 

70 percent has been ores and concentrates, 29 percent has been zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs, and the remaining 1 percent has been other materials (scrap, skimmings, and dross). 

United States rates of duty applicable to unmanufactured zinc.-Zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs were originally dutiable at 14 cents per pound under the Tariff Act of 1930. In 1939, pursuant to the trade agreement with Canada, the rate was reduced to 1% cents per pound. In 

1943, pursuant to the trade agreement with Mexico, the rate was further reduced to seven-eighths cent per pound, and a similar concession was provided in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT—Geneva), effective January 1, 1948. On June 6, 1951, pursuant to a concession in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT-Torquay) the rate was reduced to seven-tenths cent per pound, the rate now in effect.

Zinc scrap, zinc dross, and zinc skimmings were originally dutiable at 1½ cents per pound (not on zinc content as for ores) under the Tariff Act of 1930. In 1943, pursuant to the trade agreement with 

Mexico, the rate was reduced to three-fourths cent per pound. A similar concession was provided in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT-Geneva), effective January 1, 1948, and the rate pursuant to this concession is the rate now in effect. 

Zinc-bearing ores were originally dutiable at 1½ cents per pound of zinc content under the Tariff Act of 1930. In 1939, pursuant to the trade agreement with Canada, the rate was reduced to 1% cents per

pound of zinc content. In 1943, pursuant to the trade agreement with 

Mexico, the rate was reduced to three-fourths cent per pound of zinc content, and a similar concession was provided in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT-Geneva), effective January 1, 1948. On June 6, 1951, pursuant to a concession in the General 

Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT-Torquay), the rate was reduced to six-tenths cent per pound of zinc content, the rate now in effect.

Most of the greatly expanded imports during World War II entered free of duty for the account of the United States Government, and after the war certain imports continued to enter free of duty. For the years 1946-51 duty-free imports represented 22 percent of total imports; of imports entering duty-free in this period somewhat more than one-fourth represented imports for Government account, the remainder being principally imports for smelting, refining, and export, and to a smaller extent zinc scrap. The duty on zinc scrap was suspended by a series of public laws for virtually the entire period from March 14, 1942, to June 30, 1953. Import duties on all forms of unmanufactured zinc were suspended from February 12, 1952, to July 23, 1952, inclusive (Public Law 258, 82d Cong.), and during 

1952 about 86 percent of total imports of unmanufactured zinc entered free of duty. Of the total imports for consumption of unmanufactured zinc during the period 1946 through September 1953, 33 percent entered free of duty.

Differential between the rates of duty on ores and zinc metal.-The rate of duty currently applicable on zinc-bearing ores (six-tenths cent per pound on the zinc content) is equal to about 86 percent of the current rate of duty on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs (seven-tenths cent per pound gross weight). This differential between the two current rates of duty is proportionate to that provided in the Tariff Act of 1930, in which the rate of duty on zinc-bearing ores (1½ cents per pound on the zinc content) was also equal to about 86 percent of the duty on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs (1% cents per pound). The difference in the bases on which the duties are applicable (the duty on zinc ores being on zinc content and the duty on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs being on gross weight) are not important with reference to the differential between the duties, since zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs are virtually pure zinc.

At the time of the enactment of the Tariff Act of 1930, the differential of 86 percent approximately compensated for metallurgical losses incurred by zinc smelters and refineries in the United States in converting ore to slab zinc. Thus, there was no element of protection for zinc smelting and refining operations at that time. By comparison, data obtained by the Tariff Commission in this investigation show that the average recovery by the 16 zinc smelters and refineries in the United States which used imported zinc ores in 1952 and the first 3 quarters of 1953 was about 91 percent of the zinc content of ores processed. This higher average recovery of zinc contained in ores processed reflects increased efficiency in smelting and refining at individual operations in the United States over the past two decades, as well as an increase in the proportion of total slab-zinc output produced by electrolytic zinc plants, which on the average recover a larger 5 All but 2 of the 18 zinc smelters and refineries in the United States reported importing zinc ores.

proportion of the zinc content of materials processed than that recovered by other plants. Thus zinc smelters and refineries now have an element of protection which they did not have in 1930. 

Rate of duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings.-The rates of duty originally provided for under the Tariff Act of 1930 on (1) zincbearing ores, and (2) zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings were both 1%2 cents per pound, but the rate on ores was applicable to zinc content and the rate on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings was applicable to gross weight. The 1930 rate on scrap, dross, and skimmings was about 86 percent of the rate (14 cents per pound) on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs. Since 1930, the rate on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings which continues applicable to the gross weight of these articles has been reduced 50 percent, whereas the duties on zincbearing ores and on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs have been reduced 60 percent. As a consequence, the rate of duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings is now three-fourths cent per pound while the rate of duty on zinc in blocks, pigs, and slabs is seven-tenths cent per pound. 

Whereas zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs are virtually pure zinc, not all the gross weight of zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings represents recoverable zinc metal. Nevertheless, the present duty on the gross weight of zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings is about 7 percent higher than that on zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs, and the latter are the more advanced products.

The materials classifiable as zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings vary widely in zinc content. For example, it is estimated that the zinc content of zinc skimmings may be either 50 or 75 percent, depending on the type of skimmings; that of zinc dross, from 90 to 95 percent; and that of miscellaneous zinc scrap, from 90 to 99 percent. The proportion of the zinc content of each of these materials that is economically recoverable in processing is also different. For these reasons no specific rate of duty per pound of gross weight on imports of zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings could be established which would have a uniform relationship to the recoverable zinc content of these materials, or to the present duties on zinc metal and zinc ores. It is noted that a rate of duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings that would be applicable on the basis of zinc content, and that would be related to the duties either on zinc ore or on zinc metal, would reduce possible inequality in the tariff structure. 

INTERNATIONAL OBLIGATIONS OF THE UNITED STATES WITH REGARD TO LEAD AND ZINC TARIFFS 

As previously mentioned, the present rates of duty applicable to lead and zinc ores and metal are now the subject of tariff commitments under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). 

Any changes in the tariff treatment of imports now subject to these commitments would contravene international obligations of the United States unless made consistently with the provisions of the agreement. Of the contracting parties to GATT, Canada, Peru, and Australia would probably be the countries principally concerned. 

Although the United States has no specific obligations to Mexico or Yugoslavia with respect to the tariff treatment applicable to United States imports of lead and zinc ores and metal, these countries would also have an important interest in such a matter. 46566-54-

With regard to changes in tariff treatment that might be made pursuant to the provisions of GATT, possible action is not limited to that taken under the standard "escape clause" of the agreement (art. XIX). For example, article XXI of GATT provides that any contracting party may takeany action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests * * * taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations.

If during an emergency in international relations the United States were to impose on imports of lead and zinc additional restrictions that it declared to be necessary for the protection of its essential security interests, such restrictions would not be contrary to the provisions of GATT.

As noted above, under this general exception in the GATT, the United States would be free, in time of war or other emergency in international relations, to impose on imports of lead and zinc any restrictions that it considered necessary for the protection of its essential security interests. The exception appears in article XXI of the GATT, which provides in pertinent part that— Nothing in this agreement shall be construed *** to prevent any contracting party from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests *** taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations. [Emphasis supplied.]

Accordingly, if legislation imposing increased import restrictions on lead and zinc contained a recital to the effect that an emergency in international relations exists and that the imposition of the import restrictions provided for in the legislation is necessary for the protection of the essential security interests of the United States, the restrictions imposed by such legislation would not be inconsistent with United States commitments in the GATT. It would seem necessary that such a recital would have to be predicated, of course, upon a determination made in good faith that the additional import restrictions on lead and zinc were necessary to protect the essential security interests of the United States and upon the existence of an emergency in international relations such as is contemplated by article XXI.® • Commissioner Edminster wishes to add the following observations:

Whether Congress could, "in good faith," take such action in conformity with the provisions of art. XXI would, of course, be for the Congress to determine. Apart from any question as to the existence of an "emergency in international relations" within the meaning of art. XXI, the basic issue in such a determination would appear to be: (1) Whether the national security would be best served by the imposition of such import restrictions on lead and zinc, on the ground that such action is required in order to prevent such a deterioration of conditions in the industry as would create an undue hazard with respect to access to essential supplies in time of war; or (2) Whether, on the contrary, the national security would be best served by avoidance of such restrictions (or if such restrictions be regarded as necessary, the exercise of due restraint with respect to their severity and duration), in view of the extent to which the United States has come to rely upon imports to meet the normal increase in its peacetime requirements, of our greatly increased dependence on imports in time of war (as in World War II), and of the fact that such imports are available from already well-developed, economical, and nearby sources of supply on the North American Continent. 

In any case, should the Congress take such action, "good faith" in the matter would require that it recognize (1) that the other contracting parties to the GATT would carefully scrutinize any such action; (2) that, if satisfied that the action was not justified, they might invoke the "Nullification or Impairment" clause (art. XXIII); and (3) that this might lead to retaliatory action and possibly to complete withdrawal from the agreement.

Commissioner Ryder concurs in the above statement of Commissioner Edminster. In addition, he wishes to state that he doubts whether, as a matter of international comity, it would be advisable to invoke art. XXI merely through a "recital" in a preamble to legislation increasing import restrictions on one commodity or a group of related commodities. He feels that the GATT exception in question might well be interpreted as contemplating that it could be invoked only during an emergency in international relations which had previously been declared to exist by formal proclamation of the President or by appropriate legislative action such as a congressional joint resolution.

UNITED STATES PRODUCTION OF LEAD AND ZINC 

The lead and zinc industries have long been important in the 

Nation's economy. Lead was probably the first nonferrous metal produced domestically in quantity, the first authentic record of production being the mining and smelting of lead ores at Falling Creek, Va., in 1621. In 1881 the United States became the world's leading lead producer. The zinc industry developed more slowly, the first smelter production being in 1858 at South Bethlehem, Pa., and it was not until 1909 that the United States firmly took first-rank position in world production. Since the particular years in which the United States attained the rank of leading world producer, it has not relinquished this position with respect to either metal. 

Prior to World War I almost the entire United States supply of lead and zinc consisted of metal derived from domestically mined ores. However, with the expansion of industrialization, and the increased use of lead and zinc in machinery and equipment, in manufacture, and in a multitude of products necessary to everyday life, scrap lead and zinc have become increasingly important sources contributing to the supplies of these metals obtained entirely from domestic sources. Thus, total production of lead and zinc derived entirely from domestic sources includes both the metal obtained from domestic ores and the metal obtained from domestic old scrap.7 

Metal obtained from ores is known as primary metal, and that derived from scrap as secondary metal.

ORGANIZATION OF THE DOMESTIC LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES 

Corporate structure generally follows the main divisions of activity in the United States lead and zinc industries, although the larger concerns are integrated and operate mines as well as smelters and refineries.

Whereas the number of mining companies (as well as the number of mines) is relatively large, a substantial part of the mine production of both lead and zinc comes from operations controlled by a relatively small number of concerns. In 1952, for example, the 10 companies which were the largest producers of lead ore accounted for close to 65 percent of the total domestic mine output of lead. In the same year the 10 companies that were the largest producers of zinc ore accounted for about 62 percent of the total mine output of zinc. 

Seven of the companies in each of these two groups are the same, and these 7 accounted for 55 percent of the United States lead mine output, 51 percent of the zinc mine output, and 52 percent of the mine production of lead and zinc combined. 

Most of the concerns that are the largest producers of lead and zinc ores also smelt and refine these metals. United States companies engaged in the primary smelting and refining of lead and zinc in 1952 also produced 56 percent of the country's mine output of lead and 55 percent of the zinc mined in that year." 'As used in this report, the term "scrap" refers to old scrap, such as wornout and discarded articles whose useful life in present form has terminated and from which the contained lead and zinc is recovered as a net addition to the domestic supply of these metals. The term does not include what is known in the trade as "plant scrap," "current scrap," or "runaround scrap," which refer to scrap wastes resulting from current manufacturing processes. These wastes are also processed for the recovery of contained metals, but they represent a rapidly revolving stock of metal which is an adjunct to manufacturing operations, and which does not constitute a net addition to domestic supply.

! 

The number of companies engaged in the smelting and refining of primary lead and zinc in the United States is relatively small, and the number of smelters and refineries they operate is not large. 

There are 6 companies operating 13 primary lead smelters and refineries, which have a total capacity of 870,000 short tons of refined lead. About 86 percent of this total capacity is accounted for by 

3 companies, of which 1 alone accounts for about 63 percent. 

There are 12 concerns engaged in primary zinc smelting and refining. These companies operate 18 primary zinc smelters and refineries with a total capacity of about 1,014,000 short tons of refined zinc. The 4 largest concerns account for about 55 percent of the total capacity for zinc smelting and refining, and the largest single producer accounts for 24 percent. 

Four concerns have interests in both lead and zinc smelting and refining. These 4 concerns have 6 operations in lead smelting and refining, and 6 operations in zinc smelting and refining. The operations of the 4 concerns taken jointly in 1952 accounted for 91 percent of total shipments of refined lead by primary refineries, and 48 percent of total shipments of slab zinc by primary processors. 

The activities of some of the large concerns engaged in the primary smelting and refining of lead and zinc also include secondary smelting and fabricating operations. Some of the companies produce metals other than lead and zinc and some of them are engaged in mining and processing operations in foreign countries.

As noted above, most of the concerns that operate primary lead and zinc smelters and refineries own important mining properties, but they do not confine their processing operations to treatment of their own ores. Such companies, in addition to processing ores from their own properties, also usually process purchased ore, as well as ore owned by others, on a toll or custom basis. There are also some companies engaged in the smelting and refining of primary lead and zinc that own no domestic mines, and that process entirely, or mainly, ores and concentrates purchased outright or treated on a toll or custom basis.

Although some secondary lead and zinc is recovered at primary smelters and refineries, most of the scrap lead and zinc is processed at secondary-metal plants. Complete information is not available on the number of companies engaged in the recovery of secondary lead and zinc, or on the number and capacity of the plants these concerns operate. The capacity of all secondary-lead plants is known to be large, since the annual production of secondary lead now exceeds primary production from domestic ores. The capacity of plants processing secondary zinc, which is less important in relation to primary production than secondary lead, is known to be much smaller than that of plants processing secondary lead. It is estimated that there are probably between 200 and 300 companies, operating between 300 and 400 plants, that process scrap lead and zinc in the United States. 

However, the bulk of the total output of both secondary lead and zinc is accounted for by a relatively small number of concerns. The 18 largest companies processing scrap lead ordinarily account for over 90 percent of the total domestic secondary-lead output; 12 concerns account for the bulk of the production of secondary zinc metal. 

Most secondary-metal plants do not confine their operations to the recovery of any one metal; such plants usually process and produce a wide variety of different metals and alloys.

NUMBER AND TYPES OF PRODUCTION OPERATIONS 

The production of primary lead or zinc metal requires mining crude 'ore, milling the ore to produce concentrates, and processing the concentrates by smelting and refining to produce refined metal. Some of the ores or concentrates, especially of zinc, are used directly in making pigments and chemicals. Lead concentrates from the complex ores of the Western States usually contain values in other metals, and are first smelted to produce lead or base bullion, which must be refined to produce commercial grades of unmanufactured lead. Some plants processing concentrates from complex ores combine the smelting and refining operations in the same plant; other plants conduct only one of these operations, either smelting the ores to produce lead bullion or refining lead bullion to produce refined lead. Concentrates from the West Central States are relatively free of impurities and values in other metals, and smelting and refining operations are usually combined in the plants processing such concentrates. Refined zinc (slab zinc) is produced from zinc concentrates by electrolysis at electrolytic plants, or by distillation processes at plants known as zinc smelters.

In the production of secondary lead or zinc, the mining and milling functions are supplanted by scrap collecting, sorting, and segregation. 

Also, the smelting and refining processes are usually conducted in the same plants. As previously mentioned, secondary smelters and refiners generally smelt and refine several kinds of nonferrous scrap metals and a large part of their production is in the form of metal alloys.

The number of mines producing crude ores is relatively large, and the number of mills engaged in concentrating such ores is very much smaller. The number of primary lead and zinc smelters and refineries is small. Complete information on plants smelting and refining secondary lead and zinc is not available, but the number is known to be fairly large, and the number of scrap-metal dealers is very large. 

Information obtained in the investigation on the number of production operations active in 1952 is summarized as follows. There were 

912 lead- and zinc-mining operations, counting all operations regardless of size of output, of which 242 accounted for 95.5 percent of the total mine output of lead plus zinc. The lead and zinc ores from these mines were concentrated by some 120 mills. Lead concentrates or lead bullion (from both domestic and foreign sources) and zinc concentrates (from both domestic and foreign sources) were smelted or refined in 31 smelters and refineries, as noted in the preceding section of this report. The primary lead and zinc refineries also processed some lead and zinc scrap, but the bulk of the lead and zinc scrap was smelted and refined by several hundred widely scattered secondarymetal plants. Information is not available on the number of individuals, junk dealers, and concerns engaged in the gathering and assembly of scrap lead and zinc-usually in conjunction with other scrap metals-but the number is at least several thousand. 

TREND OF LEAD PRODUCTION AND RELATION TO CONSUMPTION 

Total production of unmanufactured lead from domestic sources has increased over the past decade and a half, and annual output in postwar years has been substantially higher than that during the 1930's. In 5 out of the last 8 years (1946-53) annual production has

exceeded 800,000 tons, which is larger than output in any year during 1943-45. In comparison with a yearly average of 637,000 tons for 

1937-39, annual total production for 1951-53 averaged 782,000 tons, 23 percent over the earlier period. Over the last 5 years (1949-53) annual production has ranged from a low of 715,000 tons to a high of 859,000 tons, the average for this period being 796,000 tons. (See table S-4.)

Total production of lead from domestic sources in postwar years reached a peak in 1950, when output was 859,000 tons. Since that year the trend of production has been downward, the decreases being moderate in 1951 and 1952 and much more pronounced in 1953. 

Moreover, the figures on quarterly production for 1952 and 1953 indicate that during this period the rate of output was declining almost continuously from quarter to quarter. Production decreased from 217,000 tons in the first quarter of 1952 to 194,000 tons in the last quarter; output declined in the first 3 quarters of 1953 and was 

173,000 tons in the last 2 quarters, the lowest quarterly rate of production in the 2 years.

Statistics on United States lead production are compared with data on domestic consumption in table S-4. The figures on consumption used for this purpose represent consumption reported by manufacturers who use lead in their products. The data on reported consumption do not include changes in United States Government or private stocks. The figures on reported consumption would differ from those on supply obtained by adding domestic production to net imports. In some postwar years the supply (production plus net imports) differs substantially from the reported consumption, 'owing chiefly to additions to, or withdrawals from, the United States Government stockpile, and to changes in private stocks.

Although average domestic lead production in the postwar period has been higher than that in immediate prewar years, domestic production has been much smaller in relation to consumption than it was previously. Whereas in prewar years domestic production was approximately equal to domestic consumption, in postwar years domestic production on the average has been equivalent to about 70 percent of consumption. Since, as was noted above, postwar output has been relatively high, this change in the position of domestic production in relation to consumption is attributable to a substantial increase in the level of consumption-the increase being largely supplied by imports. 

Importance of secondary lead

Although total domestic production has been well sustained in postwar years, there have been important changes in the pattern of production sources. In comparison with prewar years, for example, mine output has declined actually and in relation to total domestic production. For 1937-39 average annual mine output was 416,000 tons, or 

65 percent of domestic production; for 1951-53 the average was 

371,000 tons, or 47 percent of production. In 7 of the last 8 years (1946-53) mine output has not been as large as the average for 1937-39, and in 6 years in this period mine output has represented less than one-half of total domestic production. 

On the other hand, domestic production from old scrap has increased both absolutely and relatively. For 1937-39 the average annual recovery of secondary lead from old scrap was 221,000 tons, or 35 percent of total domestic production. For 1951-53 the average annual recovery from old scrap was 411,000 tons, or 53 percent of total domestic production. In 6 of the last 8 years (1946-53) secondary lead has accounted for more than half of total domestic production, and the quantity recovered from old scrap in 1951-53 increased 86 percent over the quantity recovered in 1937-39.

The increasing importance of secondary lead as a source of domestic supply grows out of the fact that most lead is used for products from which a large proportion of the contained lead can be salvaged when the useful lives of these articles terminate. About three-fourths of all lead is used for such articles as storage batteries, cable coverings, type metal, etc., and the remainder goes into dissipating uses such as tetraethyl lead, pigments, etc. Taking account of all the uses of lead, it is estimated that for each 100 pounds of new lead put into use, approximately 60 pounds is ultimately recovered as secondary lead from old scrap. With a steady long-term growth in the Nation's stock of leadcontaining products, there has been a long-term upward trend in the quantity of secondary lead recovered. In comparison with the United 

States, other countries do not use such large quantities of lead for storage batteries, cable coverings, and other articles from which secondary recovery is high, and secondary lead is of considerably less importance to them. It is estimated that the recovery of secondary lead from storage batteries is 85 percent; from cable coverings, 90 percent; from bearing metal, 60 percent; from type metal, 90 percent; and from other articles (excluding those which represent dissipating uses), 32 percent. The duration of the useful life of lead-containing articles varies widely. Storage batteries usually have an average life of 2 years or less; cable coverings last about 20 years; and type metal may be reprocessed in a few months.

TREND OF ZINC PRODUCTION AND RELATION TO CONSUMPTION 

In no year since World War II has the production of unmanufactured zinc from domestic sources been as large as during 1941-44, when output in each year exeeded 800,000 tons. Nevertheless postwar production has been at a higher average level than that in immediate prewar years. Over the last 8 years (1946-53) annual production has ranged from a low of 601,000 tons in 1953 to a high of 749,000 tons in 1951, the average for the period being 688,000 tons. In comparison with a yearly average of 616,000 tons for 1937-39, annual total production for 1951-53 averaged 697,000 tons, 13 percent over the earlier period (see table S-5).

Postwar total production of zinc from domestic sources reached a peak in 1951, when output was 749,000 tons. Output then showed a small decrease in 1952, and a very pronounced decrease to the lowest production in a decade in 1953. Statistics on quarterly production for 1952 and 1953 indicate that there has been a strong and almost continuous downward trend in quarterly production over the 2 years. 

Production in the last quarter of 1953 was 128,000 tons, or about 36 percent less than the 200,000 tons produced in the first quarter of 1952. 

Since the war, mine output has accounted for about 90 percent of total domestic production. Although the production of secondary zinc from old scrap has increased since the late 1930's, it is not likely to be in the near future a major source of domestic zinc. 

Statistics on United States zinc production are compared with data. on domestic consumption in table S-5. The figures on consumption used for this purpose represent consumption reported by manufacturers who use zinc in their products. The data on reported consumption do not include changes in United States Government or private stocks. The figures on reported consumption would differ from those on supply obtained by adding domestic production to net

imports. In some postwar years the supply (production plus net imports) differs substantially from the reported consumption, owing chiefly to additions to, or withdrawals from, the United States Government stockpile, and to changes in private stocks. 

Although postwar total domestic zinc production has exceeded that in immediate prewar years, domestic production has been much smaller in relation to consumption than it was previously. In 1937-39, domestic production was equal to 93 percent of consumption, although prior to 1937 the ratio was usually about 100 percent. By way of contrast with the prewar situation, for the aggregate period 1946-53 domestic output was equivalent to 67 percent of consumption. Since total domestic output has been relatively well sustained, this change in the position of domestic production in relation to consumption is attributable to a significant increase in the level of consumptionthe increase being largely supplied by imports. 

PRICES OF LEAD AND ZINC 

Most of the domestically produced lead is sold at prices based on quotations in the New York and St. Louis markets. The New York quotation, which is for Common lead, currently exceeds the St. Louis price by about 0.2 cent a pound. Since in the United States the bulk of the lead is sold at the New York price, it is used in this report for the purpose of indicating price changes and trends. Market prices for Common lead at New York, beginning with 1948, are shown in table L-7. 

East St. Louis, Ill., has been traditionally the price-basing point for zinc in the United States. The standard quotation is for Prime 

Western zinc, which is the least pure (98.32 percent zinc) of the 6 market grades of slab zinc and which has the largest use. Prices for the other 5 market grades are integrated with the f. o. b. East St. 

Louis quotation for Prime Western zinc and usually command established premiums over this price. Premiums for other grades over 

Prime Western zinc currently quoted in the East St. Louis market are as follows: Selected, 0.10 cent; Brass Special, 0.25 cent; Intermediate, 0.5 cent; High Grade (delivered), 1.35 cents; and Special High Grade (delivered), 1.50 cents. The 2 grades with the maximum premiums (High Grade and Special High Grade) are sold on a delivered-price basis, whereas the other 3 grades with smaller premiums have usually been sold on the basis of f. o. b. East St. Louis. Beginning on July 16, 1953, several major sellers of zinc offered Prime Western zinc on a delivered-price basis. The delivered price (east of the Continental 

Divide) ranged from one-fourth to one-half cent per pound above the East St. Louis price. In August 1953, one major seller announced it would continue to price Prime Western f. o. b. St. Louis, but would absorb freight charges in excess of 50 cents per hundredweight. In 

September 1953 sellers of zinc generally returned to the practice of pricing Prime Western zinc on the basis of f. o. b. East St. Louis, although the practice of absorbing freight charges in excess of one-half cent per pound was widespread. Since September 1953, price quotations for the four market grades of zinc other than High Grade and

Special High Grade, which continued to be quoted on a delivered basis, have been on both an f. o. b. East St. Louis and a delivered-price basis. The delivered price for each of the four grades at centers

where freight from East St. Louis exceeds 0.50 cent a pound is 0.50 cent per pound higher than the f. o. b. East St. Louis price. The changes in market prices for Prime Western zinc at East St. Louis beginning with 1948 are shown in table Z-7 in part III. 

In general, prices of both lead and zinc are sensitive to short-term market influences, and in recent years there has been more shortterm instability in prices of zinc than in prices of lead. Excluding 

1951 when price control restrained price changes that might have taken place in an open market, in the period 1948-53 the highest price for zinc in any year was never less than 30 percent greater than the lowest price for the same year, and for the years 1948-50 this difference ranged from 67 to 79 percent. Making the same comparison with reference to the prices of lead, in no year was the highest price for lead less than 21 percent greater than the lowest price for the same year, and for the years 1948-50 this difference ranged from 43 to 63 percent. It is noteworthy that even though the years used in the foregoing comparisons were periods of very high aggregate demand for both metals, they were characterized by wide short-term fluctuations in lead and zinc prices. 

Postwar prices of lead

Owing to the frequent and often wide short-term fluctuations in the currently quoted prices for both lead and zinc, mentioned above, substantive changes in general price levels are more effectively indicated by comparisons of average yearly prices. Such average prices are used in the following discussion, supplemented by a review of current prices from January 1952 to the present (March 10, 1954), which period is of special interest in this investigation. 

Following the termination of price control in 1946, under which the final ceiling price for lead was 8.25 cents per pound, the price increased rapidly, and for 1947 the yearly average market price per pound was 14.7 cents. For 1948, when there was a strong demand, the average was 18 cents per pound, but for 1949-when the price declined from 

21.5 cents (the postwar high) in January to 12 cents in Decemberthe average was 15.4 cents. Prices weakened further in the first half of 1950 to 10.5 cents on March 14, but advanced rapidly after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea to 17 cents on October 31, and the yearly average was 13.3 cents. On January 26, 1951, lead was placed under price control and prices for almost the entire year reflected allowable ceiling prices (the ceiling price was 17 cents through October 1 and 19 cents per pound thereafter); the average yearly price was 17.5 cents per pound.

During the first 4 months of 1952 lead continued to be sold at the ceiling price of 19 cents, but there was a series of declines that began at the end of April and the average price for the month of May fell to 15.7 cents. Prices continued downward and reached the low for the year, 13.5 cents, on October 22, 1952. A considerable part of the decline came after the resumption on October 1 of private trading on the London Metal Exchange, which had been suspended for 13 years. 

Lead prices on the London Exchange declined owing in part to the sale by the British Government of some of its surplus stock of lead. 

In the last 2 months of 1952, prices were above the low October price of 13.5 cents per pound, and the monthly average for December was 

14.1 cents, compared with the average of 19 cents for January. The yearly average price for 1952 was 16.5 cents.

For 1953 the average yearly price of lead was 13.5 cents per pound.

The market price decreased from 144 cents at the beginning of the year to a low of 12 cents in April, and it was 13.5 cents at the end of 

December. The recent price changes have generally followed changes in price quotations on the London Metal Exchange. The cost of transportation and insurance from the United Kingdom to New York plus the United States import duty of 16 cents amounts to a little less than 2 cents per pound. On January 18, 1954, the New York price of lead, which had been
