Postwar prices of zinc

After the termination of price control in 1946, under which the final ceiling price for zinc was 9.25 cents per pound, the price of zinc advanced quickly to 10.5 cents, which was also the average price for 

1947. A generally strong zinc market, in which the price advanced to 17.5 cents per pound, prevailed in 1948, and the average price for the year was 13.6 cents. In 1949, however, the market weakened significantly, as reflected by the price of 9 cents per pound in June, and the average for the year was 12.1 cents. Zinc prices continued weak in the first half of 1950, but increased sharply after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea, and the yearly average was 13.9 cents. On 

January 26, 1951, zinc was placed under price control, and prices for virtually the entire year reflected allowable ceiling prices (the ceiling price was 17.5 cents through October 1 and 19.5 cents per pound thereafter, which was the postwar high); the average yearly price was 18 cents.

In 1952 the price of zinc_first dropped below the ceiling price of 

19.5 cents, to 17.5 cents on June 2, and there were 29 additional price changes by the end of October, when the price was 12.5 cents, which was also the year-end price. The price decline in June coincided with the 2-month strike, which began on June 2, in the United States steel industry. When the steel strike was called, it became apparent that the demand for zinc for galvanizing-which normally accounts for one-third of total zinc consumption would be drastically reduced. 

For 1952 the average yearly price of zinc was 16.2 cents.

For 1953 the average yearly price was 10.9 cents per pound. During the year the price declined from 12.8 cents in January to 10 cents in December. United States zinc prices weakened following the resumption on January 2 of private trading in zinc on the London Metal Exchange, which had been suspended since 1939, and the sale by the British Government of some of its surplus stock of zinc. The cost to purchasers of transporting Prime Western zinc from 

East St. Louis to New York, under the sellers' present practice of absorbing freight charges in excess of 0.5 cent, is 0.5 cent per pound. (The actual charge for freight and insurance from East St. Louis to 

New York was 0.83 cent per pound in September 1953, of which the shipper absorbed 0.33 cent.) The cost of transportation and insurance from the United Kingdom to New York of slightly less than 0.8 cent per pound plus the United States import duty of 0.7 cent per pound amounts to slightly less than 12 cents. 

Information is not available on the quantity of zinc sold on the London market at the quoted London price for importation into the United States. Similarly, information is not available on the quantity of domestic zinc sold at the quoted East St. Louis price. Both domestic and imported zinc are usually sold on the basis of individual contracts or transactions, the terms of which are subject to negotiation. 

Although the London price is an important factor that would be considered by participants to a transaction for the sale of foreign zinc for importation into the United States, it is not necessarily the determining factor. Hence, the landed duty-paid value of imports might be more or less than the quoted London price plus transportation, insurance, and duty. Similarly, the delivered price of domestic zinc might be more or less than the quoted East St. Louis price plus the applicable transportation and handling charges. Under conditions when the general prospect is for an increase in prices, it can be expected that buyers will attempt to negotiate firm prices in contracts for future delivery, whereas sellers will attempt to negotiate terms under which future deliveries would be made on the basis of quoted prices applicable at the time of delivery. Conversely, when the general prospect is for a decrease in prices, it can be expected that sellers would favor con-

tracts for future delivery on the basis of firm prices, and buyers would seek terms under which deliveries would be made on the basis of quoted prices applicable at the time of delivery. Since substantial quantities of slab zinc are sold under contracts that contain different price provisions, it is probable that there is considerable variation between the highest and lowest prices actually paid by purchasers for slab zinc delivered at a given time. It is also probable that there are considerable differences between some of the prices actually paid at a given time and the standard price quotations for either domestic or foreign slab zinc at the same time. 

On January 18, 1954, the East St. Louis price of Prime Western. zinc declined from 10 to 92 cents. On February 15 there was another reduction to 9% cents, but on March 10 the price increased to 94 cents.. 

Thus, between the first quarter of 1952 and March 10, 1954, the price of zinc declined 50 percent. 

Prices of ores and concentrates

Many mining concerns and mills sell lead and zinc ores and concentrates as end products. The sale of these materials usually takes place on the basis of negotiation and agreement between buyer and seller, most frequently under a contract called a schedule. Such a contract usually states all conditions of settlement, such as metal to be paid for, the basic smelting charge, penalties for impurities and grades of ore lower than a certain standard, premiums for grades of ore higher than standard, the rate of payment, and other conditions of sale. For small shipments of ores and concentrates, smelting concerns frequently maintain a public or open schedule. Unless the shipper has a separate contract, he is paid according to this schedule. 

The price paid for the ores and concentrates is usually based upon the market price of refined metal when the ore is received.

Prices paid for ores and concentrates vary widely depending on the characteristics of particular materials, such as metal content, metal yield, cost of processing, penalties for impurities and substandard ores, premiums for grades of ore higher than a certain standard, and on other factors. The prices paid are also influenced by practices usually followed within certain local areas, as well as policies that vary with individual companies.

The most useful measure of the price a mine actually receives for ores and concentrates is the net mine or mill realization for these products. This net realization can thus be related to the market prices for refined lead and zinc to determine the proportion of the market prices received by the mine or mill for each metal. Such information is given in a later section of this report in connection with the discussion of operating and financial data for mines and mills.

The tabulation indicates that although the indexes of lead and zinc prices have generally followed the broad trends of the other indexes, there have been periods when the movements of the price indexes for lead and zinc have been different than those of the indexes of other prices. Also, the indexes of lead and zinc prices show more frequent and extensive short-term fluctuations than the other price indexes. 

All of the price indexes in the tabulation are much higher for 1953 than for 1939, indicating substantial price increases between these years. The largest gain has been in the price index for lead, which in 1953 showed an increase of about 167 percent over 1939, compared with increases of 113 percent for zinc, 105 percent for iron and steel, 102 percent for all metals and metal products, and 120 percent for all commodities.

The index of lead prices reached its highest point in 1948 (112.6), declined in both 1949 and 1950, increased in 1951, and declined again thereafter and was 84.2 in 1953. The index for zinc, which was about the same as that for lead in 1948, increased to a high of 149.0 in 1951, and thereafter declined to 89.9 in 1953. Between 1951 and 1953 the price index of zinc declined 39.7 percent and the price index of lead, 22.9 percent.

In contrast with the pronounced downward movement in the indexes of lead and zinc prices from 1951 to 1953, the other price indexes have either risen or shown little change. For example, over the same period the wholesale-price index for iron and steel increased 6.6 percent, the price index for all metals and metal products increased 3.3 percent, and the price index for all commodities decreased by 4.1 percent. 

EMPLOYMENT IN THE PRIMARY LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES 

Data on trends in employment in the primary lead and zinc industries, published regularly by the United States Bureau of Mines and the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, are summarized in subsequent statistical tables of this report (see appendix tables 8, 37, and 61). In this investigation the collection of employment statistics has been confined largely to new information for the primary lead and zinc industries for the years 1952 and 1953. No employment data were obtained covering the collection and processing of scrap lead and zinc, owing to the limitation of time and to technical difficulties in obtaining accurate information. 

The employment data presented below are based on reports received by the Tariff Commission from the companies engaged in the mining, milling, and primary smelting and refining of lead and zinc. The reports received cover all domestic primary lead and zinc smelters and refineries. They also cover lead and zinc mines that in 1952

accounted for 92 percent of the domestic mine output of lead and 93 percent of the domestic mine output of zinc. 

The reports for mines and mills were classified to give separate results for operations producing principally lead and principally zinc. 

These two major groups were further subdivided to show operations "predominantly" or "chiefly" lead or zinc. Operations were classified as "predominantly" lead or zinc when the gross market value (at average 1952 prices) of the recoverable lead or zinc content of the ores produced was 75 percent or more of the total gross market value of all recoverable metals contained. All other operations were classified as "chiefly" lead or zinc when the gross market value of the recoverable lead or zinc content of the ores produced was greater than the gross market value of the recoverable content of any other single metal. 

For the purpose of this discussion, "principally lead" refers to the aggregate of operations that are predominantly or chiefly lead operations, and "principally zinc" refers to the aggregate of operations that are predominantly or chiefly zinc operations. 

The reports for lead and zinc smelters were classified to give separate results for plants processing mostly domestic materials, and for plants processing mostly foreign materials.

As noted above, data on employment were obtained for all domestic primary lead and zinc smelters and refineries, and the employment figures for mines and mills cover operations that accounted for 92 percent of the domestic mine output of lead and 93 percent of the domestic mine output of zinc. The reports received by the Commission indicated an average of 40,046 employees for 1952. For operations that did not supply employment figures to the Commission, employment is estimated at 1,697. Thus the indicated total employment in 1952 (employment for reported operations plus estimated employment for unreported operations) amounted to 41,743. Table S-6 shows that total reported monthly employment in the primary lead and zinc industries declined from 43,022 employees in January 1952 to 34,549 in October 1953, a reduction of 8,473 em-

ployees, or 19.7 percent. The rate of decline in total employment over the first 10 months of 1953 was nearly twice the rate during entire 1952. From January to December 1952 employment decreased 6.7 percent; from January to October 1953 the decrease was 13.0 percent. 

The figures for 1953 also indicate that employment declined each month for the 10 months covered. Seasonal factors would not materially affect the employment trends discussed above. 

Virtually all of the drop in total employment in the primary lead and zinc industries was accounted for by declines in employment in mining and milling rather than in processing. The number of employees at lead and zinc smelters and refineries in October 1953 was 17,155, compared with 17,423 in January 1952, or a decrease of only 1.5 percent. On the other hand, the number of employees at lead and zinc mines and mills declined from 25,599 in January 1952 to 17,394 in October 1953, a decrease of 32.1 percent, which was substantially greater than the relative decline in total employment (19.7 percent) previously noted. Over the same period employment at lead smelters and refineries increased 4.0 percent, and at zinc smelters and refineries it decreased 3.5 percent.

The information collected by the Commission does not go beyond October 1953, but there is substantive evidence that there have been further declines in total employment. Statistics on employment at lead and zinc mines, published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which show the same relative decline in employment from January 1952 to October 1953 as the Tariff Commission's survey, indicate that there were about 500 fewer employees at lead and zinc mines in December 1953 (the latest month for which data are available) than in October. Since October 1953 the Commission has received reports. of closures of several mines and of one large zinc smelter, and of cutbacks in employment by reason of reduced scale of operations at mines and smelters. Both mining and processing concerns have also announced reductions in the length of the workweek. Information is inadequate for a full appraisal of these developments and of their net effect on employment, but information obtained from trade and other sources since October 1953 indicates that there has been a further substantial decline in employment in the domestic lead and zinc industries.

From January 1952 to October 1953, the number of employees at mines and mills producing principally zinc declined from 15,681 to 

9,794, a decrease of 37.6 percent. Making the same comparison for mines and mills producing principally lead, the number of employees declined from 8,126 to 6,382, a decrease of 21.5 percent. As noted previously, although the declines of employment at lead and zinc mines in 1952 were significant, they were substantially larger over the first 

10 months of 1953.

Among the major areas and States mining lead and zinc, the decline in employment has been most severe in the Tri-State region (Oklahoma, Kansas, and southwest Missouri) and the Western States, and least severe in Southeastern Missouri and the Eastern States (New York, New Jersey, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and Virginia).

From January 1952 to October 1953 employment in the Tri-State region declined 63.8 percent, and that in the Western States 38.6 percent. Over the same period employment in Southeastern Missouri and the Eastern States declined 4.5 percent and 5.0 percent, respectively. The Tri-State region is mainly a producer of zinc; the complex ores of the Western States yield substantial quantities of both lead and zinc; Southeastern Missouri is almost entirely a producer of lead; and the Eastern States are almost entirely producers of zinc. 

For the four States which are the largest lead and zinc producers in the Western States group, between January 1952 and October 1953 employment decreased 38.7 percent in Utah, 34.0 percent in Colorado, 30.3 percent in Montana, and 26.9 percent in Idaho. For other Western States, the relative decreases in employment over the same period were as follows: California, 39.7 percent; Nevada, 57.0 percent; New 

Mexico, 87.6 percent; and Washington, 35.9 percent. (See appendix table 62.)

Employment at plants processing domestic and foreign ores During the period for which employment data were available from the Commission's questionnaires, employment at smelters and refineries processing mostly imported materials showed either smaller relative decreases or larger relative increases than employment at plants processing mostly domestic materials (see table S-8). From 

January 1952 to October 1953, employment at zinc smelters and refineries processing mostly imported materials decreased 0.8 percent, compared with a decline of 4.2 percent in employment at zinc plants processing mostly domestic materials. Over the same period employment at lead plants processing mostly imported materials increased 5.8 percent, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent in employment at lead plants processing mostly domestic materials. 

AVERAGE HOURLY EARNINGS 

Information obtained in this investigation indicates that hourly earnings of employees at lead and zinc mines and mills in 1952 averaged $1.95, compared with $0.62 in 1939. The 1952 figures were collected. on the same basis as those in the census for 1939 and are comparable with the figures for that year. No information was collected for the period beyond 1952, but statistics on hourly earnings published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics indicate that the average for December 1953 (the latest available figure) was $0.03 per hour above the averagefor 1952.

Average hourly earnings in 1952 were lowest for the Eastern States ($1.69) and the Tri-State region ($1.76); they were highest for the 

Western States as a group ($2.02), Southeastern Missouri ($1.98), and the North Central States ($1.97). For individual Western States average hourly earnings ranged from $1.83 in Nevada to $2.13 in both 

Idaho and Montana.

Figures on average hourly earnings in other types of mineral production, compiled by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, indicate that the average hourly earnings obtained in this investigation for lead and zinc mines and mills for 1952 ($1.95) were somewhat higher than the average for copper mines and mills ($1.88), and lower than the averages for bituminous coal mines ($2.29) and crude petroleum and natural gas production ($2.09).

No complete information was collected in the investigation on hourly earnings of employees at lead and zinc smelters and refineries.

However, annual and monthly statistics on average hourly earnings of workers at copper, lead, and zinc smelters and refineries are published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. These figures show that average hourly earnings in 1952 were $1.80, and that in 1953 the monthly average increased from $1.87 in January to $1.92 in 

December.

DOMESTIC MINES AND MILLS 

Information on trends in mine output, on production in principal mining regions and districts, on geographic distribution of mines and mills, and on the number and size of mining operations, and additional facts regarding the mining and milling of lead and zinc ores are assembled and reviewed in other sections of this report. A summary of available information on domestic reserves of lead and zinc ores is also given in a later section of this report. 

To supplement the information referred to above on mines and mills, the Tariff Commission undertook a canvass of domestic lead and zinc mines for the purpose of obtaining current financial and operating data. The Commission's questionnaire called for information on total sales, principal operating expenses, and profit or loss before and after income taxes, for operations engaged in mining, milling, and producing_ores or concentrates valued chiefly for their lead or zinc content. The data were requested for 1939, 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953.

Very few companies could report data for 1939 and only a limited number reported data on income taxes paid and net profit or loss after income taxes. Some large concerns with integrated operations extending into lead and zinc mining, smelting, refining, and fabricating, and in some cases covering other metals and activities in foreign countries as well as the United States, could not report financial data in the segregated manner called for, especially with respect to income taxes allocable to various production operations. Some other concerns submitted reports in which certain information, and particularly that on income taxes, was estimated. Since, owing to the early date set for the completion of this investigation, it was not possible to conduct extensive work to correct incomplete and inadequate returns, the financial information presented in this report excludes data on income taxes. Also the information tabulated with regard to profitand-loss experience represents a smaller number of returns than the information with regard to principal operating expenses and mine and mill value of products.

PROFIT-AND-LOSS EXPERIENCE 

Data on the profit-and-loss experience of lead and zinc mines and mills for 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953 are given in table S-9. 

The Commission did not undertake a detailed accounting study of the records of reporting concerns with regard to the information furnished on sales income and profit-and-loss experience. The companies were asked to report data summarized from their audited profit-andloss statements; some check on the accuracy of the data reported was afforded by information given in other parts of the questionnaires, and some obviously incorrect reports were rejected as a result. By and large, however, the information was tabulated as reported.

The available statistics on net sales and profit-and-loss experience are summarized from 95 reports covering 185 mines and 67 mills, which in 1952 accounted for 79 percent (282,876 tons) of the domestic mine output of lead and 56 percent (354,087 tons) of the domestic mine output of zinc. This is a substantially smaller number of reports than the 211 reports from which salient operating data for 1952 are tabulated (discussed in a later section of this report), and which in that year covered operations that accounted for 92 and 93 percent, respectively, of the domestic mine output of lead and zinc. Although the total domestic mine output of zinc is larger than that of lead, the

95 reports from which profit-and-loss data are tabulated cover less zinc production than lead production. With regard to the geographic coverage of the available profit-and-loss information, the States east of the Mississippi River, and Colorado, California, and Montana are poorly represented. The ratio of the principal operating expenses (wages and salaries, materials and supplies, fuels, and purchased electricity) to mine or mill value of products was 66.7 percent for all operations covered by the 95 reports, and 68.8 percent for all operations covered by the 211 reports. With a more favorable ratio of principal operating expenses to mine value, the information from the 95 reports probably represents somewhat better performance profitwise than would be obtained if profit information were available for the 211 reports.

For lead and zinc mines and mills taken together, over the period. covered by the figures there has been a very large decrease in operating profit before income taxes (hereafter referred to as net operating profit) and a much smaller decrease in net sales. Net sales, which increased in 

1952 in comparison with 1950, were about $66 million in the first half of 1953; assuming that the same level of sales was maintained for the last half of the year, total net sales for 1953 would have been about $133 million, a decline of about 14 percent from the sales of $154 million in 1950. Although net sales were 18 percent higher in 1952 than in 1950, net operating profit decreased about 17 percent between these years (from $36.4 million to $30.4 million). Net operating profit for the first half of 1953 was $3.5 million, and if the same profit was obtained during the last half of the year, total net operating profit for 1953 would have been about 80 percent less than in 1950. The ratio of net operating profit to net sales declined from 23.6 percent in 

1950 to 5.3 percent in the first half of 1953, a decrease of about 78 percent. 11 Although over the period covered by the profit data the profit-andloss position has become much less favorable both for operations classified as principally lead and for those classified as principally zinc,10 the shrinkage in profits has been greatest for principally zinc operations. These operations had a higher ratio of net operating profit to sales (25.8 percent) in 1950 than principally lead operations (20.7 percent), and in 1952 the ratios for the 2 types of operations were not far apart (17.9 percent for principally lead and 16 percent for principally zinc). However, in the first half of 1953 the ratio was only 3.3 percent for principally zinc operations, compared with a ratio of 7.9 percent for principally lead operations.12 The ratio of net operating profit to net sales in the first half of 1953 for principally zinc operations was 87 percent below the ratio for 1950; in a like comparison for principally lead operations, the ratio of net operating profit to net sales in the first half of 1953 represented a decline of 62 percent. 

10 The method used in classifying financial data by type of operation is the same as that previously used in classifying employment data, and is explained in the preceding section on employment in the primary lead and zinc industries. 

11 The average price in 1950 was 13.3 cents per pound for lead and 13.9 cents per pound for zinc. 

12 The average price in the first half of 1953 was 13.3 cents per pound for lead and 11.4 cents per pound for zinc.

There are considerable differences between the profit-and-loss experience of the two subclassifications ("predominantly" and chiefly" lead or zinc) that, respectively, comprise the classifications "principally lead operations" and "principally zinc operations." The ratio of net operating profit to sales for operations classified as predominantly lead, which accounted for 33 percent of the domestic mine output of lead in 1952, was 25.2 percent in 1950, 22.2 percent in 

1952, and 15.8 percent in the first half of 1953. On the other hand, the like ratio for operations classified as chiefly lead, which accounted for 22 percent of the domestic mine output of lead in 1952, was 15.8 percent in 1950 and 13.8 percent in 1952, and there was a ratio of net operating loss to net sales of 1.1 percent in the first half of 1953. The ratio of net operating profit to sales for predominantly zinc operations, which accounted for 28 percent of the domestic mine output of zinc in 1952, declined from 28 percent in 1950 to 12.8 percent in the first half of 1953. The like ratio for chiefly zinc operations, which accounted for 20 percent of domestic mine output of zinc in 1952, was 24.1 percent in 1950, but in the first half of 1953 there was a ratio of net operating loss to sales of 7 percent. 

Of the four subclassifications, operations classified as chiefly zinc have shown the greatest deterioration in profit-and-loss position. 

Operations classified as chiefly lead have made the second poorest showing. On the other hand, although profits for predominantly lead operations and predominantly zinc operations have declined significantly, the ratios of net operating profit to sales for these 2 groups in the first half of 1953 (15.8 percent for predominantly lead operations, and 12.8 percent for predominantly zinc operations) were still considerably above levels at which losses would be incurred. 

The relative profitability of each of the 4 classifications of operations does not depend, as might appear at first glance, upon the fact that the 2 most profitable groups work richer ore deposits than the 2 least profitable groups. On the contrary, the two most profitable classifications (predominantly lead and predominantly zinc) work deposits for which the average value of all products per ton of crude ore mined is less than the average value of all products obtained per ton of crude ore by the two least profitable classifications (chiefly lead and chiefly zinc). For example, in 1952 the average value of all products obtained per ton of crude ore was $6.13 for operations classified as predominantly lead, $7.95 for predominantly zinc operations, $19.45 for chiefly lead operations, and $14.10 for chiefly zinc operations (see table LZ-4 of this report). On the other hand, average total principal operating expenses (salaries and wages, cost of supplies and materials, fuels, and purchased electric energy) are relatively greater for the 

2 least profitable classifications of operations than for the 2 most profitable. For 1952 these average total expenses per ton of crude ore mined were $4.04 for predominantly lead operations, $4.98 for predominantly zinc, $13.22 for chiefly lead, and $11.01 for chiefly zinc. 

The ratio of total principal operating expenses to mine value of all products was 65.9 percent for predominantly lead operations, 62.7 percent for predominantly zinc, 68 percent for chiefly lead, and 78 percent for chiefly zinc. Thus, operations classified as predominantly

lead and predominantly zinc had more favorable ratios of total principal operating expenses to mine value of all products than the other two classifications, and this undoubtedly had significant bearing on the greater relative profitability of the former. 

For each period covered by the available information (1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953) there was a very wide disparity in the profit-and-loss experience reflected by the individual reports. For 

1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953 there were, respectively, 60, 57, and 51 reports showing a net operating profit; for the same periods, respectively, there were 35, 38, and 44 reports showing a net operating loss. There were also very great differences among the reports that showed either a net operating profit or a net operating loss. For reports showing either a profit or a loss the gradation in experience ranged from very small net operating profits or losses to very large net operating profits or losses. Over the entire period covered by the available data, the number of reports with high profit ratios has declined and the number with high loss ratios has increased. In 

1950 there were 34 reports in which the ratio of net operating profit before income taxes to net sales was 20 percent or more; in the first half of 1953 there were only 9 reports in this classification. On the other hand, in 1950 there were 18 reports in which the ratio of net operating loss to net sales was 20 percent or more; in the first half of 

1953 there were 30 reports in this classification. 

The Tariff Commission obtained no financial data for the period after July 1, 1953. As noted previously, however, prices of both lead and zinc are currently (March 10, 1954) lower than they were in the first half of 1953. The two largest factors in operating expenses are costs of labor and supplies and materials. Hourly wage rates for lead and zinc miners were slightly higher at the end of 1953 than at the beginning of the year, and there has been no indication that prices of supplies and materials have declined. 

RELATION OF MINE VALUE OF PRODUCTS TO MARKET VALUE 

A larger number of companies supplied adequate information on mine or mill value of products and principal operating expenses than on profits. The Commission received reports covering 313 lead and zinc mines and 113 mills which accounted for an estimated 92 percent of the recoverable lead and 93 percent of the recoverable zinc produced in 1952 by all operations in the United States producing ores or concentrates valued chiefly for their content of lead plus zinc. The mine value of the ores (and tailings) produced by these operations plus the value added in milling (value of the concentrates produced minus the value of ores and tailings milled) in 1952 aggregated $225,384,000. (See table S-10.) This represented 67.7 percent of the gross market value of the recoverable metals produced from the ores mined (and old tailings reclaimed) at average market prices prevailing in 1952.

This ratio was 7 percent higher than the 63.3 percent which the mine or mill value was of gross market value of products in 1939, as reported by the mineral census for that year.

For principally lead operations, mine or mill value of products in 1952 was $78,137,000, which represented 76.1 percent of the gross market value of recoverable metals contained in ores and concentrates produced. For principally zinc operations, the mine or mill value was $147,247,000, which was 63.9 percent of the gross market value of products. For operations classified as predominantly lead, chiefly lead, predominantly zinc, and chiefly zinc, the ratios of mine or mill value to gross market value were 85.7, 69.1, 64.9, and 62.8 percent, respectively.

If mine or mill value of all products is apportioned among the individual recoverable metals contained in the ores mined and tailings reclaimed according to their gross market value (the quantity of each recoverable metal multiplied by its average market price) and the total mine or mill value of each metal thus obtained is divided by the units of recoverable metal contained in the ores and tailings reclaimed, approximate unit values at the mines or mills are indicated. Such unit values are not precise because the recoverable contents of the ores produced are not necessarily the contents paid for, and because this method of computation apportions the smelting charge paid by the mines in proportion to the market value of each metal whereas the cost of smelting zinc is higher than the cost of smelting lead. 

The unit values thus computed tend to overstate the average mine or mill value of a pound of zinc and to understate the average mine or mill value of a pound of lead. Nevertheless, the computation provides an approximate indication of the unit values of lead and zinc at the mine or mill stage of production, and provides a basis for relating these values to refinery and delivered values.

SALIENT OPERATING DATA 

Supplementing the information discussed above, the Tariff Commission obtained significant additional operating data for lead and zinc mining and milling. This material was derived from the questionnaires previously referred to which cover 313 lead and zinc mines and 113 mills. In addition to other information, detailed data were obtained on the following principal expenses: Salaries and wages, supplies and materials, fuels, and purchased electric energy. Selected operating data for 1952, classified by types of mining operations and by producing regions, are given in table S-10. 

For the operations covered by this table, which accounted for most of the United States mine production of both lead and zinc, zinc was the most important metal produced; output in 1952 was 596,000 tons with a gross market value of $193 million. Lead production was 

346,000 tons with a gross market value of $114 million. Other metals produced, at gross market values, were silver worth $15 million, copper worth $6 million, and gold valued at $4.5 million. 

Principal operating expenses

Total principal operating expenses in 1952 amounted to $155 million. Expenditures for salaries and wages were $99.7 million; supplies and materials, $46.6 million; fuels, $1.2 million; and purchased electric energy, $7.7 million. Wages and salaries represented 

44.2 percent of the mine value of all products; supplies and materials, 20.7 percent; fuels, 0.5 percent; and purchased electric energy, 3.4 percent.

The mine or mill value of all products (ores and concentrates from crude ores mined and old tailings reclaimed) produced by lead and zinc mines per ton of crude ore mined (excluding tailings) amounted to $3.84 in 1939 and $9.83 in 1952an increase of 156 percent. 

Principal expenses per ton of crude ore mined, comprising salaries and wages paid to all employees, cost of supplies and materials, fuels, and purchased electricity, amounted to $2.46 in 1939 and $6.77 in 

1952an increase of 175 percent. These principal expenses were equal to 64 percent of total value of products at mines or mills in 1939 and 69 percent of the total value of products at mines or mills in 1952.

Between 1939 and 1952 expenses for wages and salaries per ton of crude ore mined increased 182 percent and expenses for supplies and materials, 214 percent. Expenses for wages and salaries were equal to 40 percent of the total value of products at mines and mills in 1939 and 44.2 percent of such value in 1952. Corresponding ratios to mine or mill value of products for the cost of supplies and materials were 17 percent in 1939 and 20.7 percent in 1952. The cost of fuels is relatively minor compared with that of other products. The cost of purchased electric energy per ton of crude ore mined is more important than that of fuels but still relatively small. The 50-percent increase between 1939 and 1952 in the cost of electric energy per ton of ore mined, despite a reduction in the cost of electricity per kilowatthour, indicates that much more electricity was used at mines per ton of ore in 1952 than in 1939. 

Differences among major producing regions.-The statistics in table 

S-10 are classified to show separately operating data for principal producing regions and States. 

Properties in the Western States are the most important in number of operations and in production of both lead and zinc, as well as of all other metals recovered. In 1952 they accounted for 55.9 percent of the zinc, and 56.2 percent of the lead, produced by the 313 mines for which data were available. The ratio of mine or mill value of products to gross market value of recoverable metals produced was 64 percent, or 5.5 percent less than the average of 67.7 percent for all States. Total principal expenses in the Western States represented 

73.9 percent of mine or mill value of products, which was considerably above the United States average (68.8 percent of mine or mill value of products). This was largely attributable to higher expenses for wages and salaries, which represented 50 percent of the mine value of products for this region, compared with 44.2 percent for all areas combined. 46566-54-

Operations located in the West Central States, which include those in Southeastern Missouri and the Tri-State area (Oklahoma, Kansas, southwest Missouri), are second in importance in production of lead and third in production of zinc. The mine and mill value of all products for the region totaled $61 million in 1952. In the same year the properties in this region accounted for 41.5 percent of the lead, and 15 percent of the zinc, produced by all operations. 

The ratio of principal expenses to mine or mill value of products for the West Central States was 66.6 percent, or 3.2 percent less than the ratio for all operations. Salaries and wages represented the principal expense, which was 38.7 percent of the mine and mill value of all products for the area. This ratio was 12.4 percent less than the corresponding ratio for the United States. 

Lead and zinc operations in the area east of the Mississippi River include those in northern Illinois, Wisconsin, New York, New Jersey,

Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and Virginia. In 1952 this region ranked second in the production of zinc (173,500 tons), but the output of lead was relatively unimportant (8,000 tons). Mine or mill value of all products in that year was $38 million. The ratio of principal expenses to mine or mill value of products was 55.5 percent, or 19.3 percent less than the average for all operations. For this area the ratios of expenses for salaries and wages, and for supplies. and materials, to mine and mill value of all products are less than the corresponding ratios for the two other major regions reviewed, and for the United States.

Principally lead and principally zinc operations. Of the total 1952 mine or mill value of all ores and concentrates produced, operations classified as principally lead producers accounted for 34.7 percent ($78.1 million) and those classified as principally zinc producers, 65.3 percent ($147.2 million). Of total lead production of all operations (346,359 short tons), principally lead producers accounted for 64.8 percent (224,471 short tons) and principally zinc producers for 35.2 percent (121,888 short tons). Principally lead producers accounted for only 9.7 percent (57,723 short tons) of the total zinc output of all operations (596,185 short tons), while principally zinc producers accounted for 90.3 percent (538,462 short tons). Lesser quantities of gold, silver, and copper were produced by both groups of operations.

DOMESTIC PRIMARY LEAD AND ZINC SMELTERS AND REFINERIES UTILIZATION OF CAPACITY AND USE OF DOMESTIC ANd foreign MATERIALS 

Total primary smelting and refining capacity in the United States for both lead and zinc has long been considerably larger than was necessary for the processing of domestic mine production only. Many smelters and refineries-especially since the war-have utilized imported ores and concentrates to maintain operation of at least part of their capacity; some plants process foreign materials mainly, and some almost exclusively.

Relative to domestic mine output, the aggregate primary refining capacity is larger for lead than for zinc, although the present refining capacity of United States lead plants is about 17 percent less than it was before the war, whereas that of zinc plants is about 20 percent greater. Table S-11 compares production of primary lead and zinc. metal from foreign and domestic materials with total United States smelting and refining capacity for the years 1948 to 1952, the last year for which complete information is available. The figures available on smelter capacity are necessarily approximations, and this should be borne in mind in their use and interpretation.

As reported by the industry, United States primary lead smelting and refining plants in 1952 had an aggregate capacity of 870,000 tons of refined lead a year. This was more than double the recoverable lead content of domestic mine output in that year. This excess of lead smelting and refining capacity over domestic mine production has been substantially the same in all postwar years. During the period 1948-52 the capacity of United States plants for smelting and refining lead was on the average 116 percent greater than domestic mine production.

United States lead smelting and refining capacity has also been considerably larger than domestic production of refined lead by primary plants, notwithstanding that such production includes not only the product of domestic mines but also substantial quantities of lead metal derived from foreign ores and base bullion. Production of refined lead in 1952, which was 530,000 tons, required the utilization of only 61 percent of the existing capacity of domestic primary smelters and refineries. During 1948-52, utilization of the domestic lead smelting and refining capacity has ranged from about 56 to 66 percent annually, and has averaged 61 percent. For the same period, lead metal produced from domestic materials utilized on the average 51 percent of the domestic smelting and refining capacity, and lead metal derived from foreign materials utilized 10 percent. 

The capacity of United States primary zinc smelting and refining facilities has increased during and since the war. For 1952 the industry reported that smelting and refining plants were capable of producing 1,014,000 tons of zinc metal a year; capacity of this magnitude was about 52 percent greater than domestic mine output in the same year. For the period 1948-52 the average annual capacity of zinc smelters and refineries has been about 55 percent larger than average annual domestic mine production in the same period. 

As was true of United States lead capacity, United States primary zinc smelting and refining capacity is also larger than the domestic production of zinc metal. However, the proportion of the domestic smelting and refining capacity that is being utilized is much greater for zinc than for lead, mainly because of the large quantities of foreign zinc ores and concentrates that are regularly processed in this country. 

The production of zinc metal in 1952 (923,000 tons) was equal to 91 percent of the reported capacity of primary zinc smelters and refineries. During 1948-52, utilization of the domestic zinc smelting and refining capacity has ranged between 84 percent and 91 percent annually, and has averaged 88 percent. For the same period the production of zinc metal from domestic materials accounted on the average for the utilization of about 61 percent of total capacity; zinc metal produced from foreign material accounted for about 27 percent. 

PROFIT-AND-LOSS EXPERIENCE OF ZINC SMELTERS AND REFINERIES 

The Commission obtained financial data from primary zinc smelters and refineries by questionnaire, but has made no verification or accounting examination of such data. The information obtained covered 12 smelters and refineries that in 1952 accounted for 72.4 percent of the total primary zinc shipped by domestic plants. Adequate financial data were not available for six domestic primary zinc

er smelters and refineries which accounted for the remainder of the 1952 shipments. The figures obtained include net sales and net operating profit before income taxes, for 1950, 1952, and the first 6 months of 1953; they are summarized in table S-12. The information is classified to show financial experience for the aggregate of all operations for which data were available, and also to show experience for "operations smelting mostly domestic materials" and "operations smelting mostly foreign materials."

With regard to the 6 plants that did not furnish information on sales and profits, 2 were located in Texas and 1 each in Illinois, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia. Of these 6, 3 were vertical-retort plants, 2 were the horizontal-retort type, and 1 was an electrolytic plant. Plants for which profit data were available included 7 horizontal-retort plants, 4 electrolytic plants, and 1 vertical-retort plant. Of the unreported plants, 5 smelted mostly domestic materials, and 1 smelted mostly foreign materials. Average annual production per plant in 1952 for the unreported plants was substantially below the average for plants for which profit data were available.

Over the period covered by the available information, there was a substantial increase in the rate of net sales of the reporting plants. 

Net sales of $202 million in 1952 were 17 percent above 1950 sales ($173 million), and net sales in the first half of 1953 were at an annual rate of $229 million. In contrast with sales, net operating profit before income taxes has decreased substantially. Net operating profit in 1952 ($25.3 million), despite the larger sales in that year, was 6 percent below net operating profit in 1950 ($26.9 million). 

Net operating profit for the first half of 1953 was $7.1 million, and

if the same profit was obtained during the last half of the year, total net operating profit for 1953 would have been about 47 percent less than that in 1950. The ratio of net operating profit to net sales declined from 15.5 percent in 1950 to 4.9 percent in the first half of 

1953, a decrease of about 68 percent. 

Over the period covered by the profit data, the profit-and-loss position has become much less favorable for operations classified as smelting mostly domestic materials than for operations classified as smelting mostly foreign materials. Of the 12 plants covered by the tabulation, 4 operations were in the last-named group. In 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953, these operations accounted for 30.5 percent, 33.2 percent, and 21.4 percent, respectively, of the total net sales of all 12 operations.

Net operating profit for the 8 operations smelting mostly domestic materials was $15 million in 1952, or about 16 percent below net operating profit in 1950 ($18 million). Net operating profit in the first half of 1953 was $3.2 million, and if the same rate was maintained for the last half of the year, total net operating profit for 1953 would have been about 64 percent less than that in 1950. The ratio of net operating profit to net sales was 2.8 percent in the first half of 1953, or a decrease of about 81 percent from the ratio for 1950 (14.9 percent). 

In comparison with the experience of operations smelting mostly domestic materials, the profit position of operations smelting mostly foreign materials has been relatively favorable. Net operating profit for these operations in 1952 ($10.3 million) was about 15 percent greater than that in 1950 ($8.9 million), whereas profits of plants smelting mostly domestic materials decreased over the same period. 

Net operating profit in the first half of 1953 was $3.9 million, and if the same rate was maintained for the last half of the year, total net operating profit for 1953 would have been $7.8 million, or only 12 percent below the 1950 profit. The ratio of net operating profit to net sales for this group in 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953 was 

16.9 percent, 15.3 percent, and 12.6 percent, respectively.

Of the 12 plants for which profit-and-loss data were available, 1 showed a net operating loss in each of the 3 periods for which information was obtained, and 2 other plants had net operating deficits. in the first half of 1953. For the 11 plants that showed a net operating profit in 1950 and 1952, the ratio of net operating profit to net sales for individual plants ranged from 4.7 percent to 30.6 percent in 1950, and from 0.2 percent to 26.3 percent in 1952. For the 9 plants that showed a net operating profit in the first half of 1953, the ratio of net operating profit to net sales for individual plants ranged from a minute fraction of 1 percent to 19.8 percent.

PROFIT-AND-LOSS EXPERIENCE OF LEAD SMELTERS AND REFINERIES 

The Tariff Commission obtained, by questionnaire, data on profitand-loss experience for 1950, 1952, and January-June 1953, from five plants engaged in the primary smelting and refining of lead. Of the 

5 plants reporting, 3 were combined smelter and refinery operations, 1 was a smelter, and 1 was a refinery. Shipments of refined lead from the five plants for which financial data were available represented about one-third of the total refined lead shipped by all domestic primary lead smelters and refineries in 1952. Adequate financial

1 data were not available for the remaining 6 primary lead smelters and 4 primary lead refineries that were in operation in 1952, and these smelters and refineries accounted for most of the domestic production of refined lead. Operations for which financial data were not available include those of the two largest and most important domestic concerns engaged in primary lead smelting and refining. 

The financial data obtained, which are presented in table S-13, can be regarded as reflecting the aggregate experience of the plants that reported. Owing to the small coverage, however, the data cannot be regarded as reflecting the aggregate financial experience of the domestic primary lead smelting and refining industry. For this reason, the information in table S-13 is not comparable with the information on financial experience in zinc smelting and refining presented previously (table S-12), which represents a larger coverage of primary zinc smelters and refineries.

Net sales of the 5 plants for which financial data were received were about $56.5 million in 1952, an increase of about 3 percent over sales in 1950. Net sales for January through June 1953 were at an annual rate of about $48 million, or about 13 percent less than 1950 sales. 

Actual net operating profit before income taxes in 1952 was 39 percent lower than in 1950; on the basis of data reported for the first half of 1953, net operating profit before income taxes for all of 1953 is estimated at less than half the figure for the preceding year. The ratios of net operating profit before income taxes to net sales for 1950, 1952, and 1953 (January-June) were 5.9, 3.5, and 1.8 percent, respectively. The ratio for the first half of 1953 was 69 percent lower than the ratio for 1950. There was a similar downward trend in the ratio of final net profit before income taxes (which includes income from sources other than the smelting and refining of lead, minus expenses incurred in connection with other income) to net sales, but the decline was greater. The ratio of final net profit before income taxes for the first half of 1953 (1.3 percent) was 79 percent lower than the ratio for 1950 (6.1 percent).

The figures on reported consumption accurately indicate changes in the quantities of lead and zinc used by manufacturers, but they do not reflect the extent to which demand was influenced by changes in United States Government stocks and in private stocks. Also, the figures on reported consumption differ from those on supply, obtained by adding domestic production to net imports. In some postwar years the supply (production plus net imports) differs substantially from the reported consumption, owing chiefly to additions to, or withdrawals from, the United States Government stockpile, and to changes in private stocks.

RECENT CHANGES IN TOTAL CONSUMPTION AND NET IMPORTS OF LEAD 

Total domestic consumption of unmanufactured lead, as shown in table S-14, rose sharply during World War II, and has continued at a high level throughout postwar years. Domestic lead consumption for all postwar years (1946-53) averaged over 1,100,000 tons annually, compared with an average of about 600,000 tons in immediate prewar years. For 1946-50 the annual average was 1,092,000 tons. 

1951-53 average annual consumption was 1,164,000 tons, 84 percent above the annual average of 631,000 for 1937-39. In each of the past 

4 years (1950-53) annual consumption was well in excess of 1,100,000 tons. For

As total consumption has risen, net imports have also risen, and there has been a very large increase in the ratio of net imports to domestic production. As was noted previously, prior to World War 

II the United States had long been a small net importer of lead; the average annual net imports for 1937-39 were only 2,000 tons, equivalent to less than 1 percent of production. On the other hand, net imports for 1946-50 averaged 331,000 tons annually, and the ratio of net imports to production for this period was 41 percent. For 

1951-53, net imports averaged 439,000 tons annually and were equal to 56 percent of production. During postwar years net imports of lead were highest in 1950 (560,000 tons), 1952 (640,000 tons), and 1953 (451,000 tons), and for these years, respectively, imports were equal to 65, 80, and 63 percent of domestic production. 

RECENT CHANGES IN TOTAL CONSUMPTION AND NET IMPORTS OF ZINC 

As was true of domestic lead consumption, total domestic consumption of unmanufactured zinc increased greatly during World War II, and has continued at a high level since the war. Domestic zinc consumption for all postwar years (1946-53) averaged over 1 million tons annually, compared with a yearly average of somewhat more than 600,000 tons for the last half of the 1930's. For 1946-50 the annual average was 991,000 tons. For 1951-53, annual average consumption was 1,107,000 tons, 67 percent above the annual average of 664,000 tons for 1937-39. In the period since the war, the years of highest consumption were 1950 (1,149,000 tons), 1951 (1,126,000 tons), and 

1953 (1,172,000 tons).

For a long time preceding World War II the United States was generally independent of foreign zinc supplies. During most of that time exports exceeded imports, usually by a small margin, but the foreign-trade balance in zinc shifted in the midthirties, and in the year just prior to the war the United States was a small net importer of zinc. For the years 1937-39 net imports averaged 39,000 tons annually and were equal to about 6 percent of domestic production. 

As the total consumption of zinc has risen, net imports have also risen, and there has been a large increase in the ratio of net imports to domestic production. For 1946-50, net imports averaged 280,000 tons annually, and the ratio of net imports to production for this period was 41 percent. For 1951-53, net imports averaged 534,000 tons yearly and were equal to 77 percent of domestic production. Net imports in 1952 (637,000 tons) and 1953 (676,000 tons) were much larger than those in any other postwar years, and were equal to 86 and 113 percent of domestic production, respectively.

With reference to both lead and zinc, it is noted that the term "domestic metal" means metal produced by domestic lead and zinc smelters and refineries. As was noted previously, domestic primary smelters and refineries use both domestic and foreign ores to produce refined metal, and thus "domestic metal" does not mean metal produced entirely from domestic raw materials. Moreover, primary smelters and refineries normally produce small quantities of slab zinc and lead from secondary materials (in 1952 they produced 19,000 tons of secondary slab zinc, and 38,000 tons of secondary refined lead and antimonial lead) and such secondary metal is included in the shipments they reported. As noted above, information on the distribution of shipments of the slab zinc and the refined lead and antimonial lead which was produced by secondary smelters is not available.

Principal consuming areas On the basis of information supplied to the Commission, the most important consuming areas for refined and antimonial lead are those designated as Middle Atlantic (New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Delaware), East North Central (Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Wisconsin), and West South Central (Louisiana, Oklahoma, Texas,

Arkansas). In 1952, aggregate shipments of domestic and foreign lead to these areas were 34, 30, and 13 percent, respectively, of the shipments of refined and antimonial lead (both domestic and foreign) reported to the Commission. Comparatively much smaller quantities were reported as shipped to the consuming areas ranking next to the first three, which were the South Atlantic, Pacific, New England, and 

West North Central areas. 

Two consuming areas were by far the largest recipients of the shipments of domestic and foreign slab zinc reported to the Commission. 

In 1952 the East North Central area accounted for 51 percent of aggregate reported shipments, and the Middle Atlantic area for 22 percent. In contrast with the large-volume shipments to the two major consuming areas, substantially smaller aggregate quantities of slab zinc were reported as shipped to the next-ranking areas. These areas were New England, South Atlantic, East South Central, West North 

Central, and Pacific.

Shipments of domestic and foreign metal to consuming areas The reported information on shipments is classified in table S-15 to show separately shipments of domestic metal, and shipments of foreign metal, for each consuming area and for the United States. As mentioned above, the reported data on zinc represent a very high proportion of both total imports and total domestic shipments and thus closely reflect the actual national distribution of slab zinc in 1952. 

Owing to the much smaller coverage of the data reported on shipments of both domestic and foreign lead, the figures on shipments of lead do not fully reflect the national distribution of that metal in 1952. 

However, it is possible on the basis of other available data to compute figures on approximate total shipments of domestic and foreign lead which reflect the pattern of national distribution more fully than those given in table S-15. For example, if the figure on reported total shipments of domestic lead (460,250 tons) is adjusted to take account of

for

Comparatively small quantities of foreign slab zinc were reported shipped to other consuming areas. Although foreign slab zinc competes with domestic slab zinc, it is noted that most of the unmanufactured zinc imported into the United States is in the form of ores and concentrates and not in the form of slab zinc.

The information on net selling values reported by domestic producers and importers covered total sales of all market grades of lead and zinc without differentiation of sales values for the separate grades of metal. In this connection it is noted that antimonial lead and 

Corroding grade lead command price premiums over Common lead, and that five market grades of zinc (Special High Grade, High Grade, Intermediate, Brass Special, and Selected) command price premiums over Prime Western zinc. To an important degree, average delivered values for lead and zinc, both domestic and foreign, for particular consuming areas would be affected by the specific market grades of metal shipped to the areas. Since no information is available on values of shipments by market grades, it is not possible to determine whether, or to what degree, the average delivered values for consuming areas, or for foreign and domestic metal, do or do not represent values for comparable proportions of the different market grades of lead and zinc. Indeed, it would be fortuitous if the product mix of shipments into one consuming area were closely comparable with the product mix of shipments to other individual consuming areas, or if the product mix of foreign shipments to an area were comparable with the product mix of domestic shipments to the same area. 

Disparities in the size of shipments to consuming areas, and in the size of shipments of domestic and foreign metal to each area, are additional factors that should be taken into account in appraising the figures on average delivered values. A large total shipment of either foreign or domestic metal to an area is likely to include a variety of market grades. On the other hand, a comparatively small shipment might represent mainly a single grade of metal, or might reflect special conditions of use or sale. The available figures on average delivered values are probably most representative when comparisons are made between large-volume shipments of domestic metal and large-volume shipments of foreign metal, but the observations made. above should also be considered in connection with such comparisons. 

Average values of lead. Compared with an average New York price of 16.467 cents per pound for Common lead in 1952, the average delivered value of all grades of refined lead and antimonial lead shipped from domestic refineries in 1952, as reported to the Commission, was 16.46 cents per pound. The average delivered value for all imported lead was 16.03 cents per pound.

For domestic lead the average delivered value in consuming areas ranged from a low of 16.28 cents per pound for shipments to the East 

North Central States, to a high of 16.92 cents per pound for shipments to the New England States. For imported metal, the average delivered value in consuming areas ranged from a low of 14.43 cents per pound in New England to a high of 16.59 cents per pound in the 

Middle Atlantic region.

The qualifications which have been noted previously with regard to the quantity data on shipments of domestic and foreign lead to consuming areas are also applicable to the information on average delivered market values of lead.

Average values of slab zinc.-During 1952 the average delivered value of all reported shipments of domestic slab zinc was 17.35 cents per pound, and the average delivered value of all reported shipments of imported slab zinc was 16.33 cents per pound. In 1952 the average market price of Prime Western zinc (f. o. b. East St. Louis) was 16.215 cents per pound.

ad des and ■d. de. ed ar of De at 5, The average delivered value of shipments of domestic zinc in the various consuming areas ranged from a low of 16.14 cents per pound in the West South Central States to a high of 17.76 cents per pound in the Pacific States. For shipments of imported metal to domestic consuming areas, the average delivered value ranged from 13.56 cents per pound in New England to 18.22 cents per pound in the West 

North Central States. As was previously noted, most of the unmanufactured zinc imported into the United States is not in the form of slab zinc, but in the form of ores. 

COMPETITION OF LEAD AND ZINC WITH OTHER MATERIALS 

Future United States needs for lead and zinc will be influenced by trends in their utilization for certain purposes, and by the possibility that other materials might be substituted to a greater or less degree for lead and zinc in certain important uses. Detailed information on the quantities of lead and zinc used for various purposes is given in later chapters of this report, and the following comments are confined to a brief review of factors bearing on the substitution of other materials for lead and zinc.

Lead and zinc are normally the lowest priced nonferrous metals, by weight, and a substantial part of the demand for them derives from this fact. Where nonferrous metal is used, and where lead or zinc are technically suitable for the purpose, management would not ordinarily select a more expensive metal unless there were other factors than cost governing the choice. Some significant factors governing a decision whether to substitute other materials for lead or zinc, aside from availability of the substitute materials, would be the additional cost of converting existing manufacturing facilities for the use of other materials, the technical suitability of the substitute materials under consideration, and the possible resistance of customers to new materials with which they have not had long and extensive experience.

Lead is strongly entrenched in most of its major uses because of its high suitability in these particular applications. Even in its major uses, however, lead is not free from the competition of other materials, or from the influence of technological changes that might make the use of lead less necessary than it now is. Among materials currently being substituted for two important uses of lead are plastics, aluminum, and combinations of plastics and aluminum in certain types of cable sheathing, and nickel and cadmium in storage batteries. The use of plastics and aluminum for cable covering is a relatively recent development, and its effect upon the domestic consumption of lead cannot be adequately appraised at this time. Nickel-cadmium batteries require the use of materials that in recent years have been in shorter supply than lead; such batteries have comparatively high initial cost, but they are smaller in size and have very much longer life than the conventional lead battery. A substantial number of nickel-cadmium batteries have been produced for military use, but this type of battery has not yet been widely distributed in the civilian market. The most widely used antiknock additive in gasoline is tetraethyl lead, which has become the second largest use of lead. It appears likely that the upward trend in the use of tetraethyl lead will continue, but the quantity required will probably be influenced by 46566-54-6

increased production of higher octane motor fuel by catalytic cracking and re-forming processes. Among other applications of lead, the use of lead in paints has decreased in favor of titanium and other pigments; plastics and other metals have replaced lead to some extent in construction; and new packaging methods and the use of aluminum foil have restricted the use of lead foil to specialized purposes. The use of lead in insecticides meets competition from chemical insecticides that do not contain lead. Lead is increasingly used as a protective shield against dangerous radiation from radioactive substances. 

In permanent installations handling dangerous radioactive substances, concrete (including special concrete mixtures) is also used as a shield against radiation, and in special instances high-density tungsten-copper alloys are used as shields, although they are much more expensive than lead.

The most important material competing with zinc is aluminum, and this competition is significant with regard to the largest uses of zincgalvanizing and diecasting. Products of aluminum sheet may be substituted for galvanized products, and there was a notable expansion in the market for aluminum-sheet products during those postwar periods when there were zinc and steel shortages. Aluminum is also highly competitive with zinc in the manufacture of die castings. Since aluminum has a greater volume per pound than zinc, comparative costs of the two metals for the manufacture of die castings must be considered in terms of costs per unit of volume. In order that the cost of zinc will not be disadvantageous on a volumetric basis as compared with the cost of aluminum, producers of zinc try to keep the price of their product below the level where the use of aluminum for die castings would encroach on the use of zinc. In 1951 the National Security 

Resources Board reported that a differential of at least 3 cents per pound between the prices of zinc and aluminum would probably be required to achieve this result. With regard to other uses of zinc, zinc pigments compete with titanium and other pigments, and there is the possibility of increased substitution of magnesium for rolled zinc, which is used largely for dry-cell batteries and engraving plates. 

STOCKS OF LEAD AND ZINC 

Information on consumers' and producers' stocks of lead and zinc is available from official and private sources. Monthly figures on consumers' stocks of both of these metals are published by the United States Bureau of Mines. October 1953 is the latest month for which figures are available on consumers' stocks of lead, whereas December 1953 is the latest month for which figures are available on consumers' stocks of zinc. The information is obtained by canvassing a limited list of consumers of lead and zinc, and is incomplete to the extent that certain smaller consumers are not covered and that some large consumers might not be included in the surveys. However, the figures reflect the bulk of consumers' inventories, and are useful as indicators of trends in consumers' stocks generally.

Monthly figures on producers' stocks of lead are reported by the American Bureau of Metal Statistics, and monthly data on producers' stocks of slab zinc by the American Zinc Institute. For lead this information is available throughout 1953, and for slab zinc through February 1, 1954.

The term "producers' stocks" means stocks held by smelters and refineries. For lead the available figures include lead metal and alloys, ores, and materials in transit and in process. The figures for zinc represent slab zinc only; information on actual quantities of zinc ores and concentrates held by smelters and refineries is confidential, but permission was granted the Tariff Commission to publish such data in terms of index numbers' which reflect changes in these stocks. The figures on producers' stocks of both lead and zinc probably exclude ores and concentrates at mines and mills where such materials are not owned by, or held in storage for the account of, smelters and refineries, but the extent to which these materials are excluded from, or included in, the available figures on producers' stocks is not fully clear. 

Detailed information on producers' and consumers' stocks is assembled in appendix A (see tables 1 and 7 for lead, tables 31 and 36 for zinc). Salient changes in the figures on stocks since the beginning of 

1952 are discussed below.

PRODUCERS' AND CONSUMERS' STOCKS OF LEAD 

Over the period 1952-53 the quantity of lead held by producers expanded from 124,000 tons on January 1, 1952, to 196,000 tons at the end of 1953, a gain of 72,000 tons, or 58 percent. Most of this increase occurred during 1953, when stocks increased 47,000 tons, whereas the gain in stocks during 1952 was 26,000 tons. The size of stocks at the end of 1953 (196,000 tons) was only slightly below that at the end of 1949 (202,000 tons), when producers' inventories were at a postwar high.

The growth in total stocks in the hands of producers was largely attributable to increased holdings of refined lead; stocks of refined lead rose from 18,000 tons to 65,000 tons, or by 47,000 tons, during the 2-year period. Most of the remaining gain in total producers' stocks was accounted for by the increase of 17,000 tons in stocks of base bullion, from 31,000 tons at the beginning of 1952 to 48,000 tons at the end of 1953.

Consumers' stocks of lead increased from 103,000 tons at the beginning of 1952 to 122,000 tons at the end of the year, or about 18 percent. Figures on consumers' stocks in 1953 are available for 

January through October; in this period stocks reached a high of 

137,000 tons in July, after which they declined in each subsequent month to 115,000 tons in October. The decrease in consumers' stocks after July was attributable mainly to uncertainties over the business outlook, and to the reluctance of consumers to maintain or increase inventories when the price of lead was declining.

Information on the total quantity of lead held in the strategic stockpile by the Government is "classified" information and cannot be published. On November 6, 1953, however, the Office of Defense 

Mobilization informed the Tariff Commission that "the current stockpile objective for lead has been completed," and that information could be published on acquisitions in 1952 and during the first half of 1953. A total of 226,000 tons of lead was acquired for the strategic stockpile during 1952, and acquisition during the first half of 1953 amounted to 69,000 tons. Some additional quantities of foreign lead are expected to be delivered to the stockpile. These include 8,700 tons to be delivered by February 23, 1955, under existing contracts

with foreign suppliers, and undetermined quantities to be delivered under development contracts of the former Economic Cooperation Administration or its successor agencies. The quantities to be delivered under the development contracts are not firm, since they are based on market prices prevailing at the time of delivery. 

PRODUCERS' AND CONSUMERS' STOCKS OF ZINC 

In 1952, producers' stocks of slab zinc increased from 22,000 tons in January (stocks had remained at an abnormally low level since the outbreak of hostilities in Korea) to 87,000 tons at the end of December. 

During 1953 there was a rapid expansion in stocks, which reached a postwar high of 181,000 tons at the end of December. During January 1954 producers' stocks of slab zinc increased further, and reached 199,000 tons at the end of the month. 

As noted above, information on the actual quantities of producers' stocks of zinc in ores and concentrates is confidential, but the Tariff Commission is able to indicate the trend of such stocks in terms of index numbers. Total stocks of zinc in ores and concentrates were at the lowest level of the postwar period late in 1951, following the outbreak of hostilities in Korea. The index published by the Commission uses the level of stocks on January 1, 1952, as the base period (January 1, 1952=100). The index of total stocks of ores and concentrates in the hands of producers increased from 100 on January 

1, 1952, to 154.7 on December 31, 1953. Information available to the Commission also permits the computation of separate indexes for stocks of ores and concentrates of domestic origin and for those of foreign origin. Using the same base period (January 1, 1952=100), the index of stocks of ores and concentrates of domestic origin was 

40.2 percent higher on December 31, 1953, than on January 1, 1952.

A much greater expansion was shown in stocks of ores and concentrates of foreign origin, and over the same period the index of these stocks increased 75.6 percent.

Stocks of slab zinc held by consumers increased from 50,000 tons at the beginning of 1952 to 93,000 tons at the beginning of 1953, or by about 85 percent during the 12-month period. Consumers' inventories of zinc rose from 93,000 tons on January 1, 1953, to 108,000 tons at the beginning of August 1953; they declined each month thereafter, and amounted to 86,000 tons on December 1, 1953. 

Information was available to the Tariff Commission on acquisitions of zinc for the strategic stockpile during 1952 and the first half of 1953, with the same privilege of publication as was granted with reference to the information on lead. On November 6, 1953, the Office of 

Defense Mobilization informed the Tariff Commission that "the current stockpile objective for zinc is completely on hand or on order.” 

Acquisitions for the stockpile were 27,000 tons in 1952, and 25,000 tons in the first half of 1953. At the end of 1953 existing contracts with foreign suppliers called for the delivery of approximately 20,000 tons of zinc by December 31, 1956. Additional quantities of zinc are expected to be delivered under development contracts of the Economic Cooperation Administration or its successor agencies, but the quantities to be delivered are not fixed, since they are based on market prices prevailing at time of delivery.
