Financial data for foreign producers

Important Canadian and Mexican producers of lead and zinc cooperated in the Commission's investigation by supplying financial and operating data on the same questionnaire forms that were used in canvassing domestic mining and milling companies. Reports received for Canada covered 4 mines and 3 mills that in 1952 accounted for 80 percent and 61 percent, respectively, of total Canadian mine production of lead and zinc. Reports received for Mexico covered 15 mines and 12 mills that in 1952 accounted for 28 percent and 45 percent, respectively, of Mexico's mine production of lead and zinc. 

The data were supplied on a confidential basis and were carefully considered by the Commission in the preparation of this report. 

Although the information obtained from foreign producers is not available for publication, the following general observations can be made.

A comparative analysis of the data reported for the three countries indicates that average labor costs per ton of ore mined and milled are highest in Canada and lowest in the United States. The value of products obtained from crude ores mined, however, is very much greater in Canada and Mexico than in the United States, owing both to the higher recoverable content of lead and zinc and to the higher recoverable content of gold, silver, and copper. Hence, despite higher average labor costs per ton of crude ore mined in those two countries, their average labor cost per dollor's worth of mine or mill product is less than in the United States.

Average hourly earnings reported for workers at Canadian mines. and mills were only slightly less than the United States average. 

Average hourly earnings for Mexican workers were very much less than average hourly earnings either in the United States or in Canada. 

The ratio of net operating profit before income taxes to net sales was much higher for the reporting Canadian producers than for United States producers for all years covered by the survey (1950, 1952, January-June 1953). This ratio was much higher for reporting 

Mexican producers than for United States producers for 1950; for 

1952 the ratios were nearly the same, and for the first half of 1953 the ratio was substantially lower for the reporting Mexican concerns than for United States producers.

An outstanding difference between the cost of lead and zinc mining and milling in the United States and Canada on the one hand, and that in Mexico, on the other, is in the element of taxes other than income taxes. In Mexico such taxes per ton of crude ore mined, as

tec the 52 of 18 te reported to the Tariff Commission, were much higher than in Canada and very much higher than in the United States. A review of taxes paid by the Mexican lead- and zinc-mining industry constitutes an appendix of this report.

MEXICO'S PRODUCTION, CONSUMPTION, AND TRADE 

Production and trade in lead

Mexico's postwar mine production of lead has averaged approximately 235,000 tons annually, or about 90 percent of the average annual output of 265,000 tons during 1937-39. From 1948, when it amounted to 213,000 tons, production in Mexico increased to 271,000 tons in 1952, or about 30 percent during the 5 years. In the first 

9 months of 1953, however, mine output declined to an annual rate of 246,000 tons. Virtually all of the crude ore mined in Mexico is smelted in that country, chiefly by American-owned companies. In the period 1946-52, Mexico accounted for about 14 percent of the total world mine and primary smelter output of lead; in both of these categories, it ranks second only to the United States as a world producer.

Consumption of lead in Mexico averaged about 10,000 tons per year during 1946-52 and was equivalent to only 4 percent of Mexico's mine output, leaving a large annual surplus available for export. 

From 1948 through 1952, Mexican shipments of unmanufactured lead to foreign countries averaged about 230,000 tons annually. The 

United States was the principal foreign outlet, and the United Kingdom and Belgium were the other major foreign markets. During the 

5-year period 1948-52, United States imports from Mexico for consumption averaged about 150,000 tons per year and were equivalent to nearly 60 percent of that country's total lead mine output. United 

States imports from Mexico increased from 120,000 tons in 1948 to about 230,000 tons in 1950, but declined sharply to 50,000 tons in 1951, when Mexico diverted lead shipments to European markets. 

In 1952 imports from Mexico increased to 210,000 tons, and in 1953 they amounted to 138,000 tons. In the period 1948 through 

1953 Mexico accounted for 33 percent of total United States imports of unmanufactured lead from all sources. 

Production and trade in zinc

Mexico's mine production of zinc increased steadily from about 150,000 tons in 1946 to 250,000 tons in 1952, or about 65 percent during the 7-year period. For the first 10 months of 1953, Mexican mine output was an an annual rate of 220,000 tons. During 1946-52, average output was nearly 210,000 tons a year, or approximately 25 percent higher than the average 1937-39 level of 170,000 tons. 

Primary smelter production of zinc in Mexico has averaged 60,000 tons per year since 1946, or about 30 percent of Mexico's postwar mine output. Thus, most of Mexico's zinc ores and concentrates are exported. Mexican zinc consumption has averaged about 10,000 tons annually since 1946, and was equivalent to 4 percent of mine output 

The United States is the principal market for Mexico's zinc exports, and the United Kingdom and Belgium are the other major foreign

outlets. Imports of unmanufactured zinc into the United States from Mexico averaged 160,000 tons per year in 1948-52, or nearly 75 percent of Mexican mine production. Imports increased from 115,000 tons in 1948 to nearly 300,000 tons in 1952, or nearly 160 percent during the 5-year period, In 1953, entries into the United States from Mexico decreased and amounted to 175,000 tons. Mexico accounted for 36 percent of total United States imports of unmanufactured zinc from all sources during the period 1948 through 1953. 

CANADA'S PRODUCTION, CONSUMPTION, AND TRADE 

Production and trade in lead

In the immediate prewar period (1937-39) Canada's mine output of lead averaged about 240,000 tons annually. During 1946-52, mine production averaged 170,000 tons, and was approximately 30 percent below the 1937-39 level. Mine production declined from 205,000 tons in 1946 to a postwar low of 158,000 tons in 1951, but it increased to 165,000 tons in 1952. In the first 10 months of 1953, Canada's mine output of lead was at an annual rate of about 190,000 tons. 

In both the prewar and postwar periods, Canada accounted for approximately 10 percent of the total world mine output of lead and ranked fourth as a world producer, after the United States, Mexico, and Australia.

Primary smelter production of lead in Canada averaged about 160,000 tons per year in 1946-52, and was equivalent to 95 percent of Canadian mine output of lead. During this 7-year period, Canada accounted for about 10 percent of the total world smelter output. 

Consumption of lead in Canada was at a fairly stable rate of about 60,000 tons per year during 1946-52, and was equivalent to about 

35 percent of Canada's average postwar mine output. The quantity of lead available for export from Canada consists of lead from domestic ores and lead obtained from concentrates imported from South America and the United States. Canadian total exports averaged 

130,000 tons during 1948–52; exports increased steadily from 120,000 tons in 1948 to about 155,000 tons in 1952, or approximately 30 percent during this 5-year period.

The United States is the principal foreign market for Canadian lead; the United Kingdom and Belgium are the other major foreign outlets. From 1948 to 1952, United States imports of unmanufactured lead from Canada averaged approximately 90,000 tons yearly and were equal to 56 percent of Canada's lead mine output in these years. In 1953, imports of lead from Canada amounted to 62,000 tons, compared with imports of 120,000 tons in 1952. From 1948 through 1953, Canada supplied 20 percent of total United States imports of unmanufactured lead from all sources. 

Production and trade in zinc

Canada's mine and primary smelter output of zinc have both increased steadily during the postwar period. Mine production rose from about 250,000 tons in 1947 to an annual rate of approximately 400,000 tons during the first 10 months of 1953. During the 7-year period 1946-52, mine output averaged 300,000 tons per year and was about 15 percent greater than the annual average of 260,000 tons for 1937-39. Primary smelter production was at an average annual rate

te en te of 200,000 tons during 1946-52, and was equivalent to about 66 percent of Canada's postwar mine production. Smelter output increased steadily from 180,000 tons in 1947 to 220,000 tons in 1952, or about 

25 percent during the 6-year period.

Consumption of zinc in Canada was at a relatively stable rate of 50,000 tons per year during 1946-52, and during these years was equivalent to about 17 percent of Canada's mine output. 

The quantity of zinc available for export from Canada consists of zinc from domestic ores and zinc obtained from concentrates imported from South America and the United States. From 1948 through 

1952, Canadian total exports of unmanufactured zinc were at an average annual rate of nearly 290,000 tons. The United States is 

Canada's principal foreign market for zinc, and the United Kingdom and Belgium are other major outlets. United States imports of unmanufactured zinc from Canada increased from 120,000 tons in 1948 to 250,000 tons in 1952. In 1953 imports of unmanufactured zinc from Canada were 280,000 tons. In the 5-year period 1948–52, United States imports from Canada averaged 175,000 tons per year and were equivalent to about 55 percent of Canada's mine production of zinc. During the 6-year period 1948-53, Canada accounted for 

42 percent of total United States imports of unmanufactured zinc from all sources.

PERU'S PRODUCTION, CONSUMPTION, AND TRADE 

Production and trade in lead

Mine output of lead in Peru averaged about 70,000 tons per year during 1946-52, which was about one-third greater than the annual average of 55,000 tons for 1937-39. Peru's mine production increased substantially from about 50,000 tons in 1946 to 108,000 tons in 1952, and in the 1946-52 period it accounted for about 4 percent of the total world mine output of lead. Primary smelter output has been maintained at a rate of about 40,000 tons annually since 1946, a substantial increase over the average of about 25,000 tons for 1937-39. 

Consumption of lead in Peru is negligible, and virtually all the lead output is exported. The United States is the principal market, and during 1948-52 United States imports of unmanufactured lead from Peru accounted for about 61 percent of that country's mine production. 

With the exception of 1951, United States imports of lead from Peru have increased each year, from about 30,000 tons in 1948 to 74,000 tons in 1952. In 1953, imports amounted to 73,000 tons. Shipments from Peru accounted for 12 percent of total United States imports of lead for consumption from all sources during 1948–53. 

Production and trade in zinc

Peruvian mine production of zinc averaged about 90,000 tons annually in 1946-52, and for these years was equivalent to about 4 percent of total world mine output. Mine output expanded from 

64,000 tons in 1947 to about 135,000 tons in 1952, an increase of about 110 percent in the 6-year period. Since 1946, primary zinc smelter production has been maintained at an annual rate of about 2,000 tons per year.

Peru's consumption of zinc is very small and most of the output is exported. United States imports from Peru averaged about 30,000 tons annually during 1948-53. Imports from Peru amounted to

55,000 tons in 1952, and in 1953 they increased to 77,000 tons, a postwar high.

Peru accounted for 7 percent of total United States imports of unmanufactured zinc from all sources during the 6-year period 194853. For the years 1948-52, United States imports from Peru were equivalent to about 25 percent of that country's mine production of zinc.

AUSTRALIA'S PRODUCTION, CONSUMPTION, AND TRADE 

During the 7-year period 1946-52, mine production of lead in Australia averaged about 240,000 tons annually and was equivalent to 14 percent of total world mine output. Although postwar mine output has been about 20 percent below the 1937-39 average of 300,000 tons, it increased about 30 percent from 206,000 tons in 1946 to an annual rate of 273,000 tons during the first 10 months of 1953. Primary smelter output of lead in Australia was at an average annual rate of 180,000 tons for 1946-52, and was equivalent to 11 percent of total world smelter production in this period. 

The consumption of lead in Australia and New Zealand combined has been at an annual rate of about 50,000 tons since 1946, and has been about 20 percent of Australia's postwar mine output. Hence, a large surplus has been available for export, and during the 5-year period 1948-52 Australia's exports of lead averaged 185,000 tons annually. The United Kingdom is the principal foreign market, and the United States the second most important foreign outlet. 

From 1948 through 1952 United States imports of unmanufactured lead from Australia averaged 45,000 tons annually, and were equivalent to about 18 percent of Australia's mine output. In most postwar years United States imports from Australia ranged between 16,000 tons and 40,000 tons; they reached a postwar high of 98,000 tons in 

1952, and in 1953 they amounted to 77,000 tons. Since 1948, Australia has accounted for about 12 percent of total United States imports of unmanufactured lead.

Australia is a major world producer of zinc as well as lead, but United States imports of zinc from Australia have not been large in postwar years. Imports have, however, increased from 2,500 tons in 1951 to an annual rate of about 13,000 tons during the first 9 months of 1953.

YUGOSLAVIA'S PRODUCTION, CONSUMPTION, AND TRADE 

Mine output of lead in Yugoslavia expanded from 50,000 tons in 1946 to 87,000 tons in 1952, an increase of nearly 75 percent over the 7-year period. Over the same years mine output averaged 75,000 tons annually, compared with an annual average of 82,000 tons for 

1937-39. Postwar lead smelter production has averaged about 60,000 tons yearly. Consumption, which amounts to about 6,000 tons per year, is equivalent to about 8 percent of Yugoslavia's mine output of lead, and the surplus available for export is substantial. 

United States imports of unmanufactured lead from Yugoslavia were negligible in 1947, but they increased substantially in subsequent years and were about 55,000 tons in 1952. In 1953 imports amounted to 52,000 tons. Imports from Yugoslavia accounted for 8 percent of total United States imports of unmanufactured lead from all sources during 1948-53. In the 5-year period 1948-52 United States im-

ports from Yugoslavia represented 39 percent of that country's mine output of lead.

Yugoslavia produces somewhat less zinc than lead, and has never been a large source of United States imports of zinc. In 1953, however, imports of zinc from Yugoslavia increased greatly and during the first 9 months of that year they were at an annual rate of 16,000 tons.

III. CONCLUSIONS 

1. The situation in the lead- and zinc-mining industries of the world changed greatly during and since World War II. A decided change has taken place in the United States trade in comparison with prewar years. Four notable changes are (1) a very great expansion of United States consumption of both lead and zinc, which has become much larger than domestic production; (2) a general upward trend of foreign primary lead and zinc production, especially in late postwar years, accompanied by somewhat decreased (11 percent) United States primary lead production and only moderately increased primary zinc production; (3) a substantial decrease in the demand for primary lead, and only a slight increase in the demand for zinc, outside the United States; and (4) the movement to the United States of a large part of the exportable surpluses of foreign producing countries. 

Owing mainly to these developments, the position of the United States has changed from one of relatively minor importance in the international movement of lead and zinc during immediate prewar years to one that, by reason of greatly increased imports of these products, is now of great importance in international trade. 

2. Since the end of World War II the domestic lead and zinc industries have been affected by a series of rapidly changing developments. After the termination of price controls in 1946, demand increased owing to depleted stocks and prices rose, and the markets for both metals continued generally strong through 1948. From the middle of 1949 to the middle of 1950, sales of domestic lead and zinc fell off, producers' stocks increased, and prices declined. Demand strengthened and prices increased sharply beginning in June 1950 following the start of hostilities in Korea. On January 26, 1951, ceiling prices were placed by the Government on both lead and zinc, and the effective prices for almost the entire year were the allowable ceiling prices. At the beginning they were fixed at 17 cents per pound for lead and 17.5 cents per pound for zinc; on October 2 they were increased to 19 cents for lead and 19.5 cents for zinc, which were also the ceiling prices at the end of the year. Demand during this period, which was affected by war-scare buying, generally exceeded available supply. As late as the first part of 1952 there was concern whether the United States could obtain adequate supplies of foreign lead and zinc, and on February 11, 1952, legislation was approved temporarily suspending the import duties on these metals. Soon thereafter the prices of both lead and zinc declined and the suspension of the import duties was revoked, effective for lead on June 26, 1952, and for zinc on July 24, 1952.

Notwithstanding the reimposition of duties in mid-1952, prices for both lead and zinc continued generally downward, and present base quotations (March 10, 1954) are 13 cents per pound and 9.75 cents per pound for lead and zinc, respectively. These prices represent

reductions of 17 percent for lead and of 39 percent for zinc from the average prices for these metals in 1950-52 (15.754 cents per pound for lead and 16.027 cents per pound for zine). Meanwhile, important items of cost-such as wage rates and prices of machinery and supplies have remained practically unchanged. 

Since the beginning of 1952 the position of the domestic lead and zinc industries has also been affected by the following developments: 

Imports of lead and zinc were unusually large in 1952, especially during the period when duties were suspended, and also in 1953, when large inventories were built up; the strike in the United States steel industry in 1952 reduced domestic demand for the largest use of zinc (galvanizing); the British Government decided to dispose of surplus 

Government-owned lead and zinc stocks on a market that was already weakening; private trading in lead and zinc on the London Metal 

Exchange, which had been suspended in 1939, was resumed on October 1, 1952, for lead, and on January 2, 1953, for zinc, and both lead and zinc prices fell rapidly on the London market; the cessation of hostilities in Korea in July 1953 increased the possibility of reduced United States demand for defense needs; and uncertainties regarding the business outlook developed, which, with ample supplies of lead and zinc available, encouraged reductions in excessive consumers' inventories and price concessions by sellers to obtain purchase commitments. In the face of these conditions domestic mine production of both metals has declined sharply, many mines have been forced to close, and employment has been greatly reduced. 

3. One of the most significant changes in the United States lead and zinc industries has been the very substantial expansion in domestic consumption (exclusive of stockpile requirements) of these metals. 

Domestic consumption of both lead and zinc in postwar years has been greatly in excess of production of these metals from domestic materials.

Domestic consumption of unmanufactured lead rose sharply during World War II, and has continued at a high level throughout the postwar years. In 1946-53 it averaged over 1,100,000 tons annually, compared with an average of about 600,000 tons in immediate prewar years. For 1951-53 average annual consumption was 1,164,000 tons, an increase of 84 percent over the annual average of 631,000 tons for 1937-39. In the years 1952 and 1953, which are of particular interest in this investigation, annual consumption was well in excess of 1,100,000 tons. In 1953 consumption was 1,177,000 tons. 

As was true of lead, domestic consumption of unmanufactured zinc increased greatly during World War II, and has continued at a high level since the war. In 1946-53 it averaged over 1 million tons annually, compared with a yearly average of somewhat more than 600,000 tons for the last half of the 1930's. For 1951-53 average annual consumption was 1,107,000 tons, an increase of 67 percent over the annual average of 664,000 tons for 1937-39. In 1953 consumption was 1,172,000 tons.

The figures on consumption, given above, represent actual consumption reported by manufacturers who use these metals in their products. 

These figures on reported consumption of lead and zinc would differ from apparent consumption as measured by the sum of reported domestic production and imports minus exports, mainly because of changes in stocks, both those held privately and by the Government.

80 In recent years changes in stocks have been of considerable importance particularly because of the buildup of strategic stockpiles of lead and zinc. For years in which stocks of lead and zinc in this country increase, apparent consumption data overstate actual consumption, and vice versa. 

4. By comparison with those in any other peacetime years, imports of lead and zinc have been very high in all postwar years, and they were at record levels in 1952 and 1953. 

Prior to World War II the United States had long been a small net importer of lead, and average annual net imports for 1937-39 were only 2,000 tons. On the other hand, for 1946-53 net imports averaged 

372,000 tons annually, and for 1951-53 the average was 439,000 tons. 

Net imports in 1952 (640,000 tons) were the highest in any postwar year, and net imports in 1953 (431,000 tons) were exceeded only by the net imports in 1952 and in 1950 (560,000 tons). 

For a long time preceding World War II the United States was generally independent of foreign zinc supplies. During most of that time exports exceeded imports, usually by a small margin, but the foreign-trade balance in zinc shifted in the mid-1930's, and in the years just prior to the war the United States was a small net importer of zinc. For the years 1937-39 net imports averaged 39,000 tons annually. As was true of lead imports, imports of zinc have greatly increased in the postwar period. For 1946-53 net imports averaged 

375,000 tons annually, and for 1951-53 the average was 534,000 tons. 

Net imports in 1952 (637,000 tons) and in 1953 (676,000 tons) were the largest on record and were much larger than in other postwar years. 

Most of the imports of unmanufactured lead are in the form of pigs and bars. Since World War II over three-fourths of the imports have been in this form, less than one-fifth in the form of ores and concentrates, and the small remainder in other forms. 

Most of the imports of unmanufactured zinc are in the form of ores and concentrates. For all postwar years about 70 percent of the imports have been in this form, 29 percent have been zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs, and the remainder have been in other forms. 

5. A substantial part of postwar imports of both lead and zinc have entered free of duty. Import duties on unmanufactured lead were suspended from June 20, 1948, to June 30, 1949, inclusive (Public Law 

725, 80th Cong.), and again from February 12, 1952, to June 25, 1952, inclusive (Public Law 257, 82d Cong.). The duty on lead scrap was suspended by a series of public laws for virtually the entire period from March 14, 1942, to June 30, 1952. Lead imports in postwar years also entered free of duty for United States Government account, and to a lesser extent for smelting, refining, and export, and as a product of the Philippine Republic (in accordance with the Philippine Trade Act of 1946). Of the total imports for consumption of unmanufactured lead during the period 1946 through September 1953, 44.6 percent entered free of duty. There was also 104,312 tons of imported dutiable lead that was exported in manufactured articles with benefit of drawback of 99 percent of the import duty paid on their lead content.

For the years 1946-51 duty-free imports of zinc represented 22 percent of total imports; of imports entering duty-free in this period somewhat more than one-fourth represented imports for Government account, the remainder being principally imports for smelting, refining,

and export, and to a smaller extent imports of zinc scrap free of duty. 

The duty on zinc scrap was suspended by a series of public laws for virtually the entire period from March 14, 1942, to June 30, 1953. 

Import duties on all forms of unmanufactured zinc were suspended from February 12, 1952, to July 23, 1952 (Public Law 258, 82d Cong.), and during 1952 about 86 percent of total imports of unmanufactured zinc entered free of duty. Of the total imports for consumption of unmanufactured zinc during the period 1946 through September 1953, 33 percent entered free of duty. There was also 101,697 tons of imported dutiable zinc that was exported in fabricated articles with. benefit of drawback of 99 percent of the import duty paid on their zinc content. 

6. The total United States output of unmanufactured lead from domestic materials has increased over the past decade and a half, and during the last 8 years (1946-53) averaged 789,000 tons, or about 19 percent higher than the yearly average of 637,000 tons during 1937–39. 

Total United States production from domestic materials reached a postwar peak of 859,000 tons in 1950. Since that year, the trend of total production has been downward, with decreases moderate in 1951 and 1952, and much more pronounced in 1953. From 1950 to 

1952 total output declined from 859,000 tons to 802,000 tons, or about 7 percent over this period. 

In 1953 total production dropped sharply to 713,000 tons, which was 17 percent below the 1950 level. Moreover, quarterly data indicate that the rate of output was declining almost continuously during 1952 and 1953. Between the first and last quarters of 1952, mine output declined 8 percent, compared with a decline of 15 percent between the first and last quarters of 1953. Production from old scrap declined 

13 percent between the first and last quarters of 1952, but was maintained at a fairly stable level throughout 1953. Information from trade and other sources indicates that since the end of 1953 there has been a further substantial decline in mine output. 

Although total domestic production from domestic materials has been well sustained in postwar years, there have been significant changes in the proportions derived from domestic ores and from old scrap. Mine output has averaged 383,000 tons per year since 1946, or about 9 percent below the 1937-39 annual average of 416,000 tons, whereas production from old scrap has increased substantially from an average of 221,000 tons for 1937-39, to an average annual rate of 406,000 tons in 1946-53. Thus, mine output in the postwar era has declined in terms of absolute quantity, as well as in relation to total domestic output from domestic materials. Before the war (1937–39) mine output accounted for 65 percent of total production from domestic sources, whereas in the 8-year period 1946-53 it accounted for 48.5 percent of total domestic production. In 7 of the last 8 years (1946-53) mine output has not been as large as the average for 1937-39, and in 6 years in this period it has represented less than one-half of total domestic production. By way of contrast, production from old scrap accounted for 35 percent of total domestic output in the years 1937-39 and for 51.5 percent of the total during 1946-53. 

7. Total United States output of unmanufactured zinc from domes tic sources since the end of World War II has been moderately higherthan that in the late 1930's. During the last 8 years (1946-53).

19 ni -1 production averaged 688,000 tons annually, which was about 11 percent higher than the yearly average of 616,000 tons for 1937-39. 

The recovery of zinc from old scrap is not a major source of supply, and although it has increased since the late 1930's, it accounts for only about 10 percent of total zinc production from domestic materials. 

Total production of zinc from domestic sources, which is mainly mine production, reached a postwar peak of 749,000 tons in 1951. 

Output declined to 741,000 tons in 1952, and in 1953 it dropped sharply to 601,000 tons, or about 20 percent below the 1951 level. 

As was true for lead, for zinc the quarterly data indicate that output declined almost continuously in 1952 and 1953. Between the first and last quarters of 1952, zinc production from domestic materials declined 14 percent, compared with a much sharper drop of 26 percent between the first and last quarters of 1953. Information from trade and other sources indicates that since the end of 1953 there has been a further substantial decline. 

8. Monthly employment data were obtained by the Tariff Commission for the period January 1952 through October 1953 for all domestic primary lead and zinc smelters and refineries, and for lead and zinc mines and mills that in 1952 accounted for 92 percent of the domestic mine output of lead and 93 percent of the mine output of zinc. The reported employment figures for mines and mills were adjusted to include estimated employment for unreported operations. 

Total employment in the lead and zinc industries, adjusted as indicated above, declined from 43,022 in January 1952 to 34,549 in 

October 1953, a decrease of 8,473 employees, or 19.7 percent, during this period. The decline over the first 10 months of 1953, 13.0 percent, was nearly twice the decline during the entire year 1952, which was 6.7 percent. Seasonal factors would not materially affect the employment trends that have been noted. 

No extensive statistics on employment were obtained beyond October 1953, the closing date for responding to the Tariff Commission questionnaire. Since October the Commission has been advised of mine closures as well as of the closure of one large zinc smelter. There have also been reported cutbacks in employment by reason of reduced scale of operations at some mines and smelters. The information obtained from trade and other sources since October 1953 indicates that there has been a further substantial decline in employment in the domestic lead and zinc industries.

Virtually all of the decline in total employment revealed by the Commission's figures was attributable to decreases in employment at mines and mills, whereas employment at smelters and refineries was maintained at a relatively stable level. For example, employment at lead and zinc mines and mills declined from 25,599 in January 1952 to 17,394 in October 1953. The decline of 8,205 in mine and mill employment was approximately the same as the reduction in the total number of employees. Thus while from January 1952 to October 

1953 employment at mines and mills declined 32.1 percent, employment at primary smelters and refineries declined only 1.5 percent. 

It is not possible to adjust the detailed information reported on regional employment and employment at different types of operations to take account of unreported mines and mills. The reported employment figures indicate that the decline in employment at mines and mills that are engaged principally in the production of zinc was

more severe than the decline in employment at those operations producing principally lead. For mining and milling operations classified as principally zinc producers, employment declined by 

5,887, or 37.6 percent, compared with a decline of 1,744 employees, or 21.5 percent, at operations classified as principally lead.

Among the major mining areas of the United States, the regions affected most seriously by the decline in employment were the Tri- State district (Oklahoma, Kansas, and southwest Missouri), and the Western States. For these areas, the declines in employment amounted to 63.8 percent and 38.6 percent, respectively, compared with declines of only 4.5 percent in Southeastern Missouri and 5.0 percent in the Eastern States. The Tri-State region is mainly a producer of zinc, while the Western States produce complex ores yielding substantial quantities of both lead and zinc. Southeastern 

Missouri is almost entirely a producer of lead, and the Eastern States are almost entirely producers of zinc.

Although total employment at smelters and refineries declined 1.5 percent during the period covered, this decline was attributable solely to the drop in employment at primary zinc smelters and refineries, which declined from 12,936 in January 1952 to 12,489 in October 1953, or 3.4 percent. In the same period employment at primary lead smelters and refineries increased from 4,487 in January 

1952 to 4,666 in October 1953, or 3.8 percent.

The data also indicate that employment at the smelters and refineries processing mostly imported materials was better sustained than employment at plants processing mostly domestic materials. 

From January 1952 to October 1953 employment at zinc smelters processing mostly imported materials decreased 0.8 percent, compared with a decline of 4.2 percent at plants processing domestic materials. 

Over the same period, employment in lead plants processing mostly imported materials increased 5.8 percent, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent at plants processing mostly domestic materials. 

9. The Commission obtained financial and operating data from domestic lead and zinc mines and mills by questionnaire, but has made no verification or accounting examination of such data. The data obtained on the profit-and-loss experience of lead and zinc mines and mills for 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953 indicate that over this period there was a very large decrease in net operating profit before income taxes (subsequently referred to as net operating profit). The data available are for 185 mines and 67 mills, which in 1952 accounted for 79 percent of the domestic mine output of lead and 56 percent of the domestic mine output of zinc, and which cover operations in all important States except New Jersey.

For lead and zinc mines and mills taken together, net operating profit decreased about 17 percent from 1950 to 1952 (from $36.4 million to $30.4 million). Net operating profit in the first half of 

1953 was $3.5 million, and if the same profit was obtained during the last half of the year, total net operating profit for 1953 would have been about 80 percent less than that in 1950. The ratio of net operating profit to net sales declined from 23.6 percent in 1950 to 5.3 percent in the first half of 1953, a decrease of about 78 percent.

Operations classified as principally zinc showed a much greater shrinkage in profits than those classified as principally lead.¹³ Principally zinc operations had a higher ratio of net operating profit to sales (25.8 percent) in 1950 than principally lead operations (20.7 percent), and in 1952 the ratios for the two types of operations were not far apart (17.9 percent for principally lead and 16.0 percent for principally zinc). However, in the first half of 1953 the ratio was only 3.3 percent for principally zinc operations, compared with a ratio of 7.9 percent for principally lead operations. The ratio of net operating profit to net sales in the first half of 1953 for principally zinc operations was 87 percent below the ratio for 1950; for principally lead operations, the ratio of net operating profit to net sales in the first half of 1953 represented a decline of 62 percent. 

There are considerable differences among the profit-and-loss experiences of each of the two subclassifications ("predominantly" and "chiefly" lead or zinc), that, respectively, comprise the classifications "principally lead operations" and "principally zinc operations." The ratio of net operating profit to sales for operations classified as predominantly lead, which accounted for 31 percent of the domestic mine output of lead in 1952, was 25.2 percent in 1950, 22.2 percent in 1952, and 15.8 percent in the first half of 1953. On the other hand, the like ratio for operations classified as chiefly lead, which accounted for 23 percent of the domestic mine output of lead in 1952, was 15.8 percent in 1950 and 13.8 percent in 1952, and there was a ratio of net operating loss to net sales of 1.1 percent in the first half of 1953. The ratio of net operating profit to sales for predominantly zinc operations, which accounted for 28 percent of the domestic mine output of zinc in 1952, declined from 28 percent in 1950 to 12.8 percent in the first half of 

1953. The like ratio for chiefly zinc operations, which accounted for 

21 percent of domestic mine output of zinc in 1952, was 24.1 percent in 1950, but in the first half of 1953 there was a ratio of net operating loss to sales of 7.0 percent.

Of the subclassifications, operations classified as chiefly zinc have shown the greatest deterioration in profit-and-loss position. Operations classified as chiefly lead have made the second poorest showing. 

On the other hand, although profits for predominantly lead operations and predominantly zinc operations have declined significantly, the ratios of net operating profit to sales for these two groups in the first half of 1953 (15.8 percent for predominantly lead operations, and 12.8 percent for predominantly zinc operations) were still considerably above levels at which losses would be incurred.

12. Operating data obtained by the Commission for 1952 are comparable with information available for 1939 and indicate that between these years total principal operating expenses (wages and salaries, materials and supplies, fuels, and purchased electric energy) of domestic lead and zinc mines and mills increased much more than the mine or mill value of products.

The average mine or mill value of all products per ton of crude ore mined was $3.84 in 1939 and $9.83 in 1952, an increase of 156 percent.

For the same years average total principal operating expenses per ton of crude ore mined were $2.46 and $6.77, respectively, an increase of 

175 percent. The particular principal operating expenses that have shown the largest increases are wages and salaries, and supplies and materials. Comparing 1952 with 1939, wages and salaries increased 

182 percent, and supplies and materials 214 percent. 

13. Wages and salaries are by far the largest item of expense at 

United States lead and zinc mines. In 1952, expenditures for wages and salaries were $99,667,000, or 64 percent of total principal operating expenses (wages and salaries, supplies and materials, fuels, and purchased electric energy). The second largest item of principal operating expenses was supplies and materials, for which expenditures were $46,642,000. Aggregate expenses for wages and salaries and for materials and supplies were $146,309,000, or 94 percent of total principal operating expenses. 

14. The mine or mill value of all products of the operations reporting (which in 1952 accounted for 92 percent of the domestic mine. output of lead and 93 percent of the domestic mine output of zinc) was $225,384,000 in 1952, or 67.7 percent of the gross market value of all products.

For principally lead operations, mine or mill value of products in 1952 was $78,137,000, which represented 76.1 percent of the gross market value of all recoverable metals contained in the ores produced. 

For principally zinc operations, the mine or mill value was $147,247,- 

000, which was 63.9 percent of the gross market value of all recoverable metals contained in the ores produced. For operations classified as predominantly lead, chiefly lead, predominantly zinc, and chiefly zinc, the ratios of mine or mill value to gross market value were 85.7 percent, 69.1 percent, 64.9 percent, and 62.8 percent, respectively.

On the basis of information obtained in the Commission's survey it is possible to compute approximate unit values per pound of lead and zinc at mines or mills in 1952, and to compare these mine or mill unit values with average delivered unit values. The approximate mine or mill unit values in 1952, so computed, were 11.1 cents per pound for lead and 11 cents per pound for zinc. For lead the computed mine unit value was 67.3 percent of the delivered unit value of refined lead (16.5 cents per pound), and for zinc the computed mine unit value was 63.6 percent of the delivered unit value of refined zinc (17.3 cents per pound). Thus, under the conditions that prevailed in 

1952 a 1-cent increase in the delivered unit value of lead per pound would have been reflected by an additional return of 0.673 cent per pound at the mine or mill level; a 1-cent increase in the delivered unit value of zinc per pound would have been reflected by an additional return of 0.636 cent per pound at the mine or mill level. Conversely, a reduction of 1 cent per pound in the prices of these metals would have reduced the mine or mill returns by corresponding amounts. 

15. The rates of duty under the Tariff Act of 1930 (1) on zinc bearing ores and (2) on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings were both 1½ cents per pound, but the rate on ores was applicable to zinc content and the rate on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings was applicable to gross weight. Since 1930, the rate on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings which continues applicable to the gross weight of these articles-has been reduced 50 percent, whereas the duties on zinc-

bearing ores and on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs have been reduced 60 percent. As a consequence, the rate of duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings is now three-fourths cent per pound while the rate of duty on zinc in blocks, pigs, and slabs is seven-tenths cent per pound. 

Whereas zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs are virtually pure zinc, not all the gross weight of zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings represents recoverable zinc metal. Nevertheless, the present duty on the gross weight of zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings is about 7 percent higher than that on zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs, and the latter are the more advanced products.

The materials classifiable as zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings vary widely in zinc content, and the proportion of the zinc content of the different materials that is economically recoverable also varies. For this reason no specific rate of duty per pound of gross weight on imports of zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings could be established which would have a uniform relationship to the recoverable zinc content of these materials, or to the present duties on zinc metal and zinc ores. 

16. United States "domestic exports" of unmanufactured lead and zinc consist largely of metal produced in the United States from imported crude materials, and of relatively small quantities of ores and concentrates produced in the United States and shipped to Canada for processing. Of the small United States exports of unmanufactured lead, which during 1948-53 averaged 4,000 tons a year, about 15 percent consisted of lead metal produced from imported materials entered under bond for smelting or refining and export, and 16 percent represented lead ores and concentrates shipped to Canada. During the same period, exports of unmanufactured zinc averaged 46,000 tons a year, of which three-fourths was zinc metal produced from material entered under bond for smelting or refining and export, and 7 percent represented zinc ores and concentrates shipped to Canada. 

The trade in lead and zinc ores and concentrates entering under bond for processing and export is of long standing, and has been more important for zinc than for lead. Lead and zinc ores and concentrates treated in bonded smelters and refineries and the derived metal reexported (without payment of duty) do not compete with the products of domestic mines. These imports, however, do add to the volume of material smelted and refined by United States plants. During the period 1948-53 the smelting and refining of foreign ores and concentrates under bond utilized on the average about 4 percent of the capacity of domestic primary zinc smelters, but less than 1 percent of the capacity of domestic primary lead plants. 

The exportation of lead and zinc ores and concentrates to Canada largely reflects a situation that exists in the State of Washington close to the Canadian border. Because of their location near the 

Canadian smelter at Trail, British Columbia, some domestic mines in this area ship ores and concentrates to this smelter rather than to smelters in Idaho and Montana, where the bulk of the Washington mine output has been traditionally shipped. 

17. The principal sources of United States imports of lead are 

Mexico, Canada, Australia, Peru, and Yugoslavia. During the period 

1948-53 these five countries supplied about 85 percent of total United States imports for consumption of unmanufactured lead from all sources. Three of these countries-Mexico, Canada, and Peru-are

also the major sources of United States imports of unmanufactured zinc. From 1948 through 1953 these three countries supplied about 

85 percent of total United States imports for consumption of unmanufactured zinc.

The United States market is of very great importance to the principal foreign supplying countries. During the period 1948-52 

United States imports from Mexico represented 60 percent of the lead mine output and 74 percent of the zinc mine output of that country. For the same period imports from Canada represented 56 percent of the lead mine output and 55 percent of the zinc mine output of Canada; for Peru the comparable percentages were 61 percent for lead and 25 percent for zinc. Although Australia and Yugoslavia have not been major United States suppliers of zinc, United States imports of lead from these countries during 1948-52 represented 18 percent of the lead mine output of Australia, and 39 percent of the lead mine output of Yugoslavia. 

18. It has not been possible to make a complete survey of the interests of United States concerns in operations producing lead and zinc in foreign countries, but available data indicate that a large part of United States imports of lead and zinc from some foreign countries is accounted for by companies in which United States corporations have a substantial financial interest. 

In Mexico virtually all the smelting and refining of lead and zinc is done by companies in which United States concerns have a major interest, and it is estimated that in 1952 more than one-half of total United States imports of lead from Mexico (which consist mostly of pigs and bars) and almost two-fifths of total zinc imports (mostly in ores) from that country were produced in Mexico by companies in which United States concerns have a major interest. 

Of total United States imports of lead and zinc from Canada, probably less than one-fifth come from operations owned by United 

States companies. by In Peru, virtually all smelting and refining of lead and zinc is done a United States concern, and a substantial part of Peru's mine output of lead and most of its mine output of zinc are produced by this company. In Argentina, the bulk of the mine output of lead and zinc is produced by a subsidiary of a United States corporation. 

United States producers have a major interest in operations in South-West Africa that probably accounted for most of the United States imports of lead and zinc from that territory in 1952, and United States companies also have a substantial interest in mines that are principal producers of lead and zinc in French Morocco. 

In Australia, United States corporations have interests in 4 operations that are large producers of lead and zinc in that country; these 4 operations supply an undetermined part of total United States imports of lead and zinc from Australia. A United States company also has an interest in the lead and zinc producing operations in Guatemala that probably accounted for most United States imports from that country in 1952. 

19. Information obtained by the Commission on the distribution of lead and zinc metal to consuming areas indicates that the most important domestic markets for lead are in the Middle Atlantic 

States, East North Central States, and West South Central States.

By far the largest domestic markets for slab zinc are the East North 

Central States and the Middle Atlantic States. 

Available information on the shipments of domestic and foreign lead to domestic consuming areas is incomplete in several important respects, particularly with regard to shipments of domestic secondary lead, which are very important. The information that is available indicates that the largest quantities of foreign lead went to the three most important domestic lead-consuming areas named above. The available information on the distribution of domestic and foreign slab zinc is much more complete than the information for lead. The important Middle Atlantic and East North Central States together received 83 percent of the shipments of foreign slab zinc in 1952 that were reported to the Commission. 

20. Data on production and consumption of lead and zinc before and after World War II indicate a changing situation in countries outside the United States that has had an important bearing on the United States position as a market for these products. 

In the period before the war, the supply and demand for both lead and zinc in foreign countries tended to be roughly in balance, and the United States, which did not rely extensively on foreign sources during this period, was generally only a small net importer of these products. 

In the postwar period, however, there have been large exportable surpluses of both commodities in countries outside of the United States, due chiefly to the failure of consumption in those countries to keep pace with the increasing level of production. In contrast, the 

United States has become a large net importer of these products. 

Since 1946, the mine output of lead in foreign countries has increased steadily in each year, and during 1950-53 it was at about the level of the average during 1937-39. On the other hand, foreign consumption of lead since the end of the war has been substantially below the prewar level, and in most years there has been a large excess of production over consumption; moreover, this surplus has increased nearly every year since 1946. For zinc, postwar mine output in foreign countries has been substantially higher than the prewar output, and has increased continuously since 1946. Although foreign zinc consumption has also increased somewhat, it has failed to keep pace with the rising level of foreign output, and the excess of foreign zinc production over consumption has been increasing. A great part of this excess production in foreign countries has been exported to the 

United States. 

21. The Commission obtained, by questionnaire, financial and operating data from important Canadian and Mexican producers of lead and zinc in the same manner that it obtained similar information from domestic concerns, but made no verification or accounting examination of the records of reporting concerns. Reports received for Canada covered operations that in 1952 accounted for 80 percent and 61 percent, respectively, of total Canadian mine production of lead and zinc; reports received from Mexico covered operations that in 1952 accounted for 28 percent and 45 percent, respectively, of Mexican mine production of lead and zinc. The information obtained from foreign producers cannot be published without revealing the operations of individual concerns, but such data made available to the Commission point to some general observations.

The information available to the Commission indicates that total principal operating expenses, as well as expenses for wages and salaries, are lower per ton of crude ore mined in the United States than in Canada and Mexico. This appears to be the case even though average hourly earnings of workers are much lower for operations in Mexico than for those in either Canada or the United States, and are slightly lower for those in Canada than for those in the United States. The data also indicate that taxes other than income taxes per ton of crude ore mined in Mexico were much higher than those in Canada and very much higher than those in the United States. 

However, when allowance is made for the differences in the average value of the ores mined in the three countries, as affected by differences in the yield of metals obtained from them, the situation with respect to the foregoing comparison of costs is quite different. Notwithstanding apparently higher operating expenses, and higher expenses for salaries and wages, per ton of crude ore mined in Canada and Mexico than in the United States, these expenses are lower per unit of recoverable metal in Mexico and Canada than in the United States. This helps to explain why, despite higher expenses per ton of ore mined in Canada and Mexico than in the United States, the ratio of net operating profit before income taxes to net sales, as indicated by the data, has in general been more favorable for Canadian and Mexican producers than for United States producers. This ratio was much higher for the reporting 

Canadian producers than for United States producers for all years covered by the survey (1950, 1952, January-June 1953). For reporting Mexican producers it was much higher than for United States producers in 1950, and in 1952 the ratios were nearly the same, but in the first half of 1953 the ratio was substantially lower for the reporting Mexican concerns than for United States producers. 

22. The extent to which the domestic lead and zinc industries encounter competition from imports is different for the mining and milling segments of these industries than for smelters and refineries. 

As far as domestic mines and mills are concerned, imports whether in the form of ores and concentrates or in the form of metal compete with their operations. Under normal conditions of supply and trade, imports of both ores and metal tend to have the net effect of reducing the demand for domestically produced ores.

For domestic lead and zinc smelters and refineries, on the other hand, imported ores and concentrates which they process provide an additional source of income for them and supplement their supply of raw materials. A substantial part of the zinc metal produced in the 

United States, as well as a smaller proportion of the lead metal produced domestically, is derived from imported ores. For the 5 years 

1948-52 lead metal derived from imported crude materials utilized 10 percent of the domestic lead smelting and refining capacity. Since the average utilization of total capacity for this period was only 61 percent, foreign materials accounted for about one-sixth of domestic lead smelting and refining in 1948-52. For the same period zinc metal derived from imported ores utilized 27 percent of domestic zinc smelting and refining capacity. The availability of the imported ores and concentrates to the domestic lead and zinc smelters and refineries using such materials has made it possible for them to maintain or to substantially increase the level of their activity.

23. The future demand for imports of lead and zinc will be determined by certain economic factors that cannot be fully and clearly foreseen at present. Important among these economic considerations are (1) defense requirements for these metals; (2) the volume of 

United States demand for peacetime products into which lead and zinc enter; (3) the degree of competition from other materials encountered by these two metals in their major uses; (4) the quantities of lead and zinc available from domestic sources; and (5) the quantities of foreign lead and zinc available at prices that permit their being marketed in the United States.

Future needs for lead and zinc for defense purposes cannot be foreseen; however, in the light of existing international conditions, it would appear that defense requirements for lead and zinc are more likely to continue large, or possibly to increase, than they are to diminish.

With regard to the other economic factors that will significantly influence the future volume of lead and zinc imports, it is possible to make certain general comments. A major feature of the lead and zinc industries since World War II has been the high level of domestic consumption of these metals compared with prewar years. Although to a considerable extent this increased demand is attributable to requirements under the defense program, it is to a much larger extent due to the high level of industrial activity in the United States and to the high demand for goods generally. Over the past decade the growth in population has augmented the demand for lead and zinc in a wide variety of producers' and consumers' goods. For example, the consumption of lead in storage batteries and tetraethyl lead (the two most important uses of lead) has greatly expanded, and the consumption of zinc in galvanizing and diecasting (the two most important uses of that metal) has also expanded notably. In addition, both lead and zinc have generally held their markets for other important uses, and in most instances have increased them substantially. 

Thus, if there is no prolonged economic recession, there is a strong probability that the per capita domestic consumption of lead and zinc will continue at a high level in the future. 

The extent to which future domestic requirements for lead and zinc can be met from domestic sources will depend on the production of newly mined ores as well as on the recovery of these metals from secondary sources. In the case of zinc, production from old scrap is not a major factor with reference to total zinc production; generally this source represents about 10 percent of total domestic output. 

Since World War II the quantity of zinc recovered from old scrap has averaged 70,000 tons annually, and it will probably continue at about this level for some years to come. The output of secondary lead, however, is larger than the production of lead from ores, and production from this source has been generally increasing, owing to the long-term growth in the Nation's stock of lead-containing articles from which secondary lead is recoverable. On the average, the recovery of secondary lead over the next decade will tend to increase. 

The probable level of future domestic mine production of lead and zinc poses difficult questions on which mining engineers and geologists have long held conflicting opinions. The rapid changes that have taken place since the war with regard to costs, prices, and other conditions of production-and that are still in process-make it even more difficult to obtain agreement on this matter among those who

are most familiar with these industries. The Commission can make no contribution that would aid in the resolution of this complex question. The actual production as distinct from possible production would be influenced by many factors, including price levels, production costs, and United States Government policies affecting the domestic lead and zinc industries.

The extent to which foreign lead and zinc will seek United States markets in the future through active price competition with domestic lead and zinc is a question which cannot be determined at present. In comparison with consumption in prewar years, the postwar consumption of lead outside the United States has been substantially reduced and that of zinc has increased only slightly. It is not known, moreover, when and to what extent foreign consumption will expand in the future. Meanwhile, there has been a general upward trend of foreign lead and zinc production in late postwar years, and a large part of the excess foreign production has moved to the United States market. 

If foreign requirements should increase under continuing peace and the progress of economic rehabilitation and development, then the principal foreign producing countries could market outside the United States a larger proportion of their exportable surpluses of lead and zinc than has been so marketed in recent years. In this connection it should be noted that Canada, Mexico, Australia, Peru, and Yugoslavia do not have large home markets for lead and zinc and that most of their output is exported. 

24. The Commission does not undertake in this report to Congress to pass upon the question as to whether or to what extent tariffs or quotas should be imposed upon lead and zinc. This is a matter of public policy which is for the Congress to decide. 

The resolutions of the congressional committees, in response to which this report has been prepared, request the Commission to state its "findings as to the effect upon the competitive position of the domestic lead and zinc industries of the present tariff status of imported lead and zinc, so as to assist the Congress in determining what changes, if any, should be made in that tariff status." The Commission has done this in considerable detail in the main body of this report. 

The facts in this report show that, under the present tariff status, imports of lead and zinc are restricted only slightly. During the past decade a substantial part of the imports have been exempt from duty. 

Present rates of duty, therefore, are having only slight effect upon the competitive position of the several factors of the domestic lead and zinc industries.

It is not possible in this brief summary to restate in adequate detail satisfactory conclusions on the minute effects of the present rates of duty on imports of these metals and their influence on the various. factors in those industries without numerous qualifications involving theoretical conjectures and suppositions. Consequently no attempt is made here to restate the many facts as to the separate and specific effects of the present tariff status of these metals on the miners, smelters, refiners, and on the fabricators of these metals, that are more fully set forth in the main body of this report.¹4 

14 Commissioners Edminster and Ryder are of the view that the committee resolutions to which this report is in response, as well as the facts contained in the report, require a more comprehensive statement of conclusions regarding the competitive impact of imports upon the several interests mentioned in the resolutions than is here included under numbered conclusion 24. They are also of the view that a statement should be made of the perspective in which the current situation with respect to lead and zinc should be considered in making policy decisions regarding them. Supplementary statements containing their respective comments appear on pages 91 and 95.

25. The existing rates of duty on all the lead and zinc articles covered by this investigation are reduced rates made effective pursuant to concessions granted by the United States in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). So long as these concessions remain in force, the enactment of legislation imposing increased import restrictions on these articles would be inconsistent with international commitments of the United States. (For exception, see conclusion 

No. 26.)

Under certain circumstances which are specified in the "escape clause" (art. XIX) of the GATT and section 7 of the Trade Agreements Extension Act of 1951, and subject to the limitations imposed upon him by section 350 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, the President could impose increased import restrictions on the articles in question. If it was determined that the articles were, as a result in whole or in part of the duty reflecting the concessions, being imported in such increased quantities as to cause or threaten serious injury to the domestic industry producing like or directly competitive products, the President, acting under the escape clause, could withdraw or modify the concessions to the extent and for such time as might be necessary to prevent or remedy such injury. 

Withdrawal of the concessions by the President would result in the reestablishment of the rates originally enacted for the products in the Tariff Act of 1930. On the other hand, as a result of appropriate modification of the concessions by the President, the rates could be increased up to 50 percent higher than the rates "existing on January 1, 1945," and/or quantitative limitations on imports could be established. 

26. As noted in the preceding conclusion, the present rates of duty applicable to lead and zinc ores and metal are now the subject of tariff commitments under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). Any changes in the tariff treatment of imports now subject to these commitments would contravene international obligations of the United States unless made consistently with the provisions of the agreement. Of the contracting parties to GATT, Canada, Peru, and 

Australia would probably be the countries principally concerned. 

Although the United States has no specific obligations to Mexico or Yugoslavia with respect to the tariff treatment applicable to United States imports of lead and zinc ores and metal, these countries would also have an important interest in such a matter. 

With regard to changes in tariff treatment that might be made pursuant to the provisions of GATT, possible action is not limited to that taken under the standard escape clause of the agreement (art. 

XIX). For example, article XXI of GATT provides that any contracting party may takeany action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests * * * taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations.

If during an emergency in international relations the United States were to impose on imports of lead and zinc additional restrictions that it declared to be necessary for the protection of its essential security interests, such restrictions would not be contrary to the provisions of GATT.

As noted above, under this general exception in the GATT, the United States would be free, in time of war or other emergency in

international relations, to impose on imports of lead and zinc any restrictions that it considered necessary for the protection of its essential security interests. The exception appears in article XXI of the GATT, which provides in pertinent part that- Nothing in this agreement shall be construed *** to prevent any contracting party from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests *** taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations. [Emphasis supplied.]

Accordingly, if legislation imposing increased import restrictions on lead and zinc contained a recital to the effect that an emergency in international relations exists and that the imposition of the import restrictions provided for in the legislation is necessary for the protection of the essential security interests of the United States, the restrictions imposed by such legislation would not be inconsistent with United States commitments in the GATT. It would seem necessary that such a recital would have to be predicated, of course, upon a determination made in good faith that the additional import restrictions on lead and zinc were necessary to protect the essential security interests of the United States and upon the existence of an emergency in international relations such as is contemplated by article XXI.16

STATEMENT OF COMMISSIONER EDMINSTER 

The resolutions to which this report responds definitely contemplate a discussion of the matters hereinafter set forth, in requiring the Commission to state such conclusions as it may be able to formulate with respect to the effect upon the competitive position of the domestic lead and zinc industries (including workers in these industries), and upon processors and consumers, of the present tariff status of lead and zinc. Such a discussion, however, is appropriate to, and should be a part of, the report irrespective of whether the language of the resolutions requires its inclusion. The committees concerned should not be deprived, on purely legalistic grounds, of information pertinent to the subject matter of the resolutions. 

The tariff status of lead and zinc is one which, while impeding to some extent the flow of imports into the United States, has not during the postwar period (even while the duties were not temporarily suspended) greatly restricted the quantities imported. Thus, in essence, 15 Commissioner Edminster wishes to add the following observations:

Whether Congress could, "in good faith," take such action in conformity with the provisions of art. 

XXI would, of course, be for the Congress to determine. Apart from any question as to the existence of an "emergency in international relations" within the meaning of art. XXI, the basic issue in such a determination would appear to be: (1) Whether the national security would be best served by the imposition of such import restrictions on lead and zinc, on the ground that such action is required in order to prevent such a deterioration of conditions in the industry as would create an undue hazard with respect to access to essential supplies in time of war; or (2) Whether, on the contrary, the national security would be best served by avoidance of such restrictions (or if such restrictions be regarded as necessary, the exercise of due restraint with respect to their severity and duration), in view of the extent to which the United States has come to rely upon imports to meet the normal increase in its peacetime requirements, of our greatly increased dependence on imports in time of war (as in World War II), and of the fact that such imports are available from already well-developed, economical, and nearby sources of supply on the North American Continent. 

In any case, should the Congress take such action, "good faith" in the matter would require that it recognize (1) that the other contracting parties to the GÃÅTT would carefully scrutinize any such action; (2) that, if satisfied that the action was not justified, they might invoke the "Nullification or Impairment" clause (art.
