He feels that the GATT exception in question might well be interpreted as contemplating that it could be invoked only during an emergency in international relations which had previously been declared to exist by formal proclamation of the President or by appropriate legislative action such as a congressional joint resolution. !

the conclusions contemplated in the committee resolutions relate to the impact upon the domestic producers, processors, and consumers of a tariff status or level which does not at present greatly restrict the volume of imports; or, conversely, the likely impact upon these several interests of a change in the tariff status of lead and zinc designed to reduce the quantities imported. The effects of the present tariff status of lead and zinc upon these several interests can most conveniently be set forth by considering what would be the nature of the impact upon these interests of a substantially more restrictive tariff treatment. Manifestly, the effects of the present tariff status of lead and zinc would be the obverse of what is hereinafter set forth. 

The status of the domestic industry engaged in mining and milling lead and zinc, of the processors (smelters and refiners), and of consuming industries using these metals, including the manner in which these several interests are affected by imports, is set forth in detail in the main body of this report. It is impossible to formulate, in brief compass, conclusions which are clear cut, precise, and free from qualifications and exceptions such as would be indicated by consulting the more detailed discussion or by more sustained analysis. that will be attempted here, accordingly, is a more or less general statement regarding the interests of the various groups affected by the present tariff status of lead and zinc, and that would be affected by any change in that status. All

As to the domestic industry engaged in mining and milling lead and zinc, it is obvious that imports of lead and zinc must tend to reduce market outlets in the United States for domestic ores, and that the greater the volume of imports the more marked will be this tendency. It is equally obvious that such foreign competition tends to be more keenly felt when the market is weak and prices have declined (as is presently the situation) than when the reverse situation exists. It follows that any action by the Government to reduce substantially the quantities imported would, at least for the immediate future, tend to benefit the mining and milling segments of the industry, including the workers engaged therein, and that the more drastic the restriction of imports the greater the immediate benefit conferred. These simple facts require no elaboration. 

The effectiveness of such assistance to the mining industry, and particularly of this method of assistance, would not necessarily, however, be as great as might be supposed, and it is appropriate that the reasons for this be briefly indicated.

One factor to be borne in mind is that, inasmuch as the domestic price structure for these metals is tied to world prices, the imposition of import restrictions diverting from the United States market the considerable and increasing portions of the exportable surpluses of foreign countries which have been sold here in recent years would tend to depress the world prices of these metals and hence to limit the effectiveness of the import restrictions in raising prices in the United States. The extent to which the incidence of these restrictions would be absorbed by foreign producers would vary from time to time with fluctuations in actual marketing conditions. Another factor relates to the substitution of other metals or materials for these two metalsespecially for zinc-which occurs in connection with certain of their uses, particularly when market conditions are such as to afford strong

incentives for such substitution. If at a time when there is a buyers' market for these metals (i. e., when the demand is relatively weak), action is taken by the Government which substantially raises their prices relative to those of substitute metals or materials, the tendency to resort to substitutes is likely to be marked. On the other hand, when there is a sellers' market (i. e., when the demand is relatively strong), such substitution is less likely to occur or in any case is not likely to be greatly felt by the producers of lead and zinc. Significant also is the fact that when prices of these metals are high there is an added incentive to reclaim secondary lead and zinc. Finally, any additional restrictions on imports would tend to encourage the expansion of domestic operations and the working of ores the exploitation of which would not otherwise be economically feasible; in so doing it would contribute to a later condition where new marginal mines would have difficulties in maintaining operations even at the higher prices resulting from the increased restrictions. 

As to the impact upon lead and zinc processors of additional restrictions on imports of these metals, such restrictions, insofar as they would result in a reduction in the total United States consumption of primary lead and zinc, would tend to reduce the aggregate total of smelting and refining (whether of domestic or imported ore) in the United States. This would be especially true of zinc, since nearly four-fifths of the zinc consumed in the United States is smelted in the United States, whether from domestic or from imported ore. It would be less true of lead, the imports of which enter chiefly as metal rather than ore and hence are not smelted in the United States. 

Assuming that the additional import restrictions on lead and zinc were applied uniformly to imports whether in the form of ore or in the form of metal, such restrictions would thus tend to curb the domestic smelting of foreign zinc ores to a greater extent than the 贰 ​domestic smelting of lead ores.

The overall extent to which consumption of lead and zinc, and hence total smelting activity, in the United States would be reduced by the additional restrictions would, of course, depend in part upon the severity of the restrictions. But it would also depend upon the extent to which domestic production of lead and zinc ores responded to the stimulus of reduced competition from imports and higher prices obtainable for the domestic ores. Part of the reduction in the supplies of these metals resulting from the reduction in imports would, of course, be offset by increases in domestic production, so that the amounts excluded from the United States market in consequence of the additional import restrictions would not represent the amounts by which the supplies available for domestic consumption would be reduced.

There is nothing, however, in the present condition or in the recent experience of the lead and zinc industries which would justify the belief that the increases in domestic production which would result from any drastic restriction of imports would be anything like sufficient to compensate for the quantity of imports thus excluded. The simple fact that these industries now seek action to restrict imports as a means of obtaining higher prices and thus of maintaining present operating capacity on a more profitable (or less unprofitable) basis raises an initial doubt regarding the extent to which the production increases would offset the import decreases. Postwar experience

reinforces this view; the high level of prices of these metals which prevailed throughout most of the postwar period did not, in fact, call forth the additional domestic production needed to meet our greatly increased peacetime requirements of these metals, and imports have made up the difference. Pertinent in this connection are the comments contained in the second paragraph of Commissioner Ryder's statement, which follows.

In short, additional and drastic restrictions on imports would be certain to result in reduced consumption of primary lead and zinc in the United States, and in all probability the reduction would tend to be large rather than small. This, in turn, would mean a very considerably reduced total of smelting operations in the United States. 

Within the processing branch of the industry, moreover, the impact of the additional restrictions on imports of lead and zinc would not be evenly distributed. Those domestic smelters that rely on foreign sources for most, or a substantial part, of their ores would be placed at a competitive disadvantage in comparison with those that obtain most, or all, of their supplies of ore from domestic sources. Smelters that are now favorably situated for the processing chiefly of imported ore would be handicapped and would presumably undergo some, and perhaps a severe, curtailment of their operations. On the other hand, those smelters situated more advantageously for the processing of domestic ores would tend to be benefited, insofar as any increase in domestic production of lead and zinc resulting from the additional import restrictions would result in an increase in their smelting operations.

Additional import restrictions on lead and zinc would, as already explained, be beneficial to the domestic lead- and zinc-mining industries and this would, of course, include the investors in these industries. Such restrictions would, however, affect adversely the interests of United States investors in lead- and zinc-mining operations in foreign countries by narrowing the export outlets for these metals, or by making returns from shipments to the United States less profitable. 

To some extent the interests of these investors in foreign mining operations are similar to those of investors in domestic smelters engaged in processing chiefly imported ores; indeed, in some cases these smelters of imported ores are owned by corporations which also own and operate foreign mining properties. In addition, however, there is ownership and operation of foreign mines by corporations which conduct both mining and smelting operations, and which do so both here and abroad. Also, some of these foreign investments involve corporations whose lead- and zinc-mining operations are conducted wholly or chiefly in foreign countries. Thus the situation varies greatly with respect to the extent to which the United States foreign investments are in corporations which are also engaged in mining and milling, or in smelting and refining, operations in the United States (or in both types of operations). But insofar as the income of the 

United States investors in lead- and zinc-mining operations in foreign countries is dependent upon the profitability of foreign operations, the interests of such investors, as stated, would tend to be adversely affected.

Finally, it remains to consider the impact which additional restrictions on imports of lead and zinc might be expected to have upon the industries in the United States which use these metals. The

t, те te answer to this question is clear: it is to the advantage of the industries which use these metals as raw materials to obtain them at as low a cost as possible; and since the purpose of the import restrictions would be to raise the prices of these metals in order to make domestic mining operations more remunerative, it follows that such action would tend to increase costs of production in the consuming industries. The extent to which it would do so would depend, of course, upon the severity of the import restrictions and the extent to which prices of these metals increased in consequence. 

Any such increase in costs to the users of these metals, like any other increase in costs, could not be regarded as advantageous to them. 

Generally speaking, it would tend to be to their disadvantage. To what extent it would be disadvantageous would depend upon (1) how successfully they could pass on to their customers this addition to their costs, without adversely affecting their volume of sales; or (2) how far they could avoid the burden of additional cost by greater use of substitute metals or materials. As to the first of these pointspassing on the additional cost to the consumer-not only would the extent to which this could be done vary with the nature of the demand for the particular product containing the lead or zinc, but it would also be affected by market conditions at any particular time. 

Ordinarily it would be more difficult to pass along to the customer the additional cost of the lead or zinc when the demand for the product containing the metal is weak than when the demand is strong. 

As to the second point-possible substitution of other metals or materials this too would vary with different uses, at different times, and also as between lead and zinc. As pointed out elsewhere in this report, the uses of lead are largely in those applications where it has high suitability, so that, in general, substitution of other metals or materials is less extensive for lead than for zinc; even so, the possibilities of substitution in certain uses (some of them fairly important) are considerable. For most of the uses of lead, however, the additional cost of lead resulting from higher lead prices could not readily be avoided by shifting to substitutes, and in the main it would be passed along to the consumer or absorbed by the manufacturer, or both. For zinc, the substitution of other metals or materials would tend to be more extensive. Particularly would this factor become operative if the price of zinc rose far out of line compared with its normal relationship to that of aluminum-a metal which competes with zinc in the largest uses of zinc, namely, in galvanizing and in diecasting. A considerable part of the additional cost of zinc to the consuming industries resulting from any substantial increase of zinc prices as compared with those of substitute materials (particularly aluminum) might, therefore, be avoided by increased use of substitutes. Any part of the additional cost not thus avoided would, of course, be passed on to the consumer or absorbed by the manufacturers, or both.

I concur in the statement, immediately below, by Commissioner Ryder.

STATEMENT OF COMMISSIONER RYDER 

Commissioner Ryder concurs with the foregoing statement of Commissioner Edminster. In addition, he wishes to make the following comment. This comment relates to the report as a whole, which contains authentic, exhaustive, and well-organized information regard-

ing current conditions in the lead and zinc industries of the United States. The purpose of this comment is to indicate the perspective in which the current situation in these industries should be considered by the Congress and the Executive in making policy decisions regarding lead and zinc.

In the report (sec. II of pt. I, subsection on production) it is noted that lead production in the area that now constitutes the United States dates back more than 300 years and that the domestic zinc industry is about a century old. The United States, moreover, has exploited its lead and zinc resources for a much longer period, and much more intensively, than have the countries which are the principal sources of United States imports. This difference between the older lead and zinc industries of the United States as compared with the newer lead and zinc industries of the principal supplying countries is a factor of major importance with regard to the competitive position of the United States New mineral industries tend to work the most easily discovered, most readily accessible, and richest deposits; also, they are usually capable of large and rapid expansion. Older mineral industries, on the other hand, work ores which, on the average, are less rich in metal content and more difficult and costly to extract than those formerly mined. Moreover, the ability of such industries to expand production substantially even under very favorable price conditions appears to be definitely limited. 

This difference between the lead and zinc industries of the United States and those of the countries which are the principal sources of its imports explains why the United States, even before World War II, had ceased to be a net exporter and had tended to become a net importer of both metals. It also explains why, as United States needs for lead and zinc expanded in the war and postwar periods, the older domestic lead and zinc industries, even with the stimulus of high prices, could not keep pace with the growth in demand, with the result that the United States had to draw increasingly upon the newer and more expansible industries in other countries for the needed supplies of lead and zinc. During most of the postwar period, the imports were, broadly speaking, supplementary to a domestic production which was much less than domestic needs. Since the cessation of hostilities in Korea, however, there has been a strong tendency for supply to exceed demand, for prices to decline, for imports to increase and to become more competitive, and for domestic production to decrease. This situation has brought into focus a major question of national policy. Briefly stated, this question is as follows: 

In view of the position of the United States in the production and consumption of lead and zinc, and especially in view of probable demand in the event of future emergencies, what should be the policy of the United States with respect to the competition between domestic production and imports? 

The question posed is similar to that coming to the fore with regard to many of our other extractive industries. For its resolution two diametrically opposed courses of action are urged. On the one hand, there is the view that imports should be severely restricted so that they may no longer be an important factor, and that-at whatever price level may result-the great bulk of domestic consumption and defense requirements should be supplied now and in the future from domestic sources.

On the other hand, there is the view that imports

should be encouraged through further reduction or removal of restrictions on imports; that in the interest of long-run defense needs domestic resources should be conserved and reliance placed upon imports for a large and increasing part of United States requirements for lead and zinc.

Between these sharply contrasting views, a third or intermediate position has been advanced in the effort to reconcile, so far as that can be done, the divergent interests of producers and consumers and to integrate these private interests with the overriding national interest. Pursuant to this intermediate view, action, on the one hand, would be directed toward maintaining substantial lead- and zinc-mining industries in the United States and affording them such assistance (in the form of import restriction or subsidization) as may be required to maintain production at levels that have prevailed generally in postwar years. On the other hand, action would also be directed to the maintenance of adequate imports of lead and zinc, and any stringent restrictions on imports would be avoided. Such a program would differ in results from a program involving stringent import restrictions and from a policy of entirely unrestricted imports in the following ways: (a) A program thus based would not, as would a program involving stringent import restrictions, tend to increase prices to such a degree as materially to discourage domestic lead and zinc consumption. (b) Under such a program the existing lead and zinc industries and the communities that are dependent on these industries would be protected to the extent necessary to prevent serious injury which might occur if domestic producers were required to submit to the impact of unrestricted imports without any form of governmental assistance. 

On the other hand, Government policy would not be such as would give rise to a rapid expansion of lead and zinc mining irrespective of costs. The purpose would be to maintain stability in the industry with a view to encouraging long-term orderly organization and development of the domestic lead and zinc industries. (c) The intermediate program would enable the United States to maintain its lead and zinc industries and, at the same time, would (1) permit the United States to maintain good relations with other lead- and zinc-mining countries, especially Canada and Mexico, and (2) encourage the maintenance of well-developed lead and zinc industries in those countries. The maintenance of Canada and Mexico as sources of supply is especially important since in the event of a serious national emergency we would again largely depend upon them to supply the increased United States requirements for lead and zinc. 46566-54- -8

CHAPTER I DESCRIPTION AND USES OF LEAD ARTICLES 

Lead is one of the most important basic metals in our industrial economy. It is used in the production of a wide variety of military and essential civilian products, and is included in the stockpiling program of the United States as a strategic and critical material. 

In 1953 the tonnage of lead consumed in the United States was about equal to that of zinc and was exceeded only by iron and steel, copper, and aluminum. The large consumption of lead is attributed both to its many useful physical and chemical properties and to its relative cheapness for many uses, in comparison with other materials. 

Lead, the softest and heaviest of all base metals, has a high boiling point and a low melting point. It is highly resistant to corrosion, especially from sulfuric acid. It has many useful alloying and chemical properties, and its impenetrability to shortwave radiation makes it invaluable for radiation shields (for X-ray equipment and, more recently, in atomic-energy applications). These properties of lead account not only for its most important uses but also for the relative ease of its recovery from ores and from scrap and for its easy workability.

In the United States in the past 5 years the use of lead in the form of chemical compounds (principally in storage-battery oxides, lead pigments, and tetraethyl lead for gasoline) somewhat exceeded its use in alloys (with antimony, tin, copper, bismuth, etc.), and the use of lead in alloys somewhat exceeded the use of unalloyed lead. 

Requirements in connection with transportation facilities accounted for close to half the total quantity of lead consumed, principally in lead-acid storage batteries (using both antimonial lead and lead oxides) and in gasoline. Large quantities of lead are also used for cable covering, solder, and rolled or extruded products like lead sheet and pipe, for lead calking, ammunition, bearing metals, type metals, brass, and bronze, and for many other uses. In fact, the uses of lead are so numerous and varied that changes in total consumption of lead are closely related to changes in the volume of industrial activity in general.

Lead articles covered in this investigation This investigation relates primarily to unmanufactured lead articles in various forms, especially to lead in lead-bearing ores and lead pigs and bars provided for in paragraphs 391 and 392, respectively, of the 

Tariff Act of 1930, as amended.

Consideration is also given, however, to related manufactured lead articles, such as lead pigments covered in paragraph 72 and some manufactured articles also covered in paragraph 392. 

Paragraph 72 covers lead pigments, including litharge, orange mineral, red lead, white lead, and all pigments containing lead, dry or in pulp, or ground in or mixed with oil or water, not specially 101

provided for. Of the pigments not listed by name, the more important are suboxide of lead and sublimed lead. The lead content, by weight, of these lead pigments, unmixed with oil or water, is 92.8 percent for litharge, 90.7 percent for red lead and orange mineral, 80.1 percent for white lead, 96.3 percent for suboxide of lead, and about 70-75 percent for sublimed lead. These lead pigments, except sublimed lead, are generally made directly from lead metal; sublimed lead is made directly from lead ores or concentrates. Litharge is used primarily in storage batteries and to a less extent in ceramics, chrome pigments, and varnish, as well as in oil refining, and for miscellaneous other purposes. Red lead is used chiefly in storage batteries and paints; white lead and sublimed lead, mostly in paints; and suboxides of lead, in storage batteries. 

Paragraph 391 covers lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes of all kinds. The most important item, from the standpoint of lead content imported, is lead-bearing ore, which comprises principally lead concentrates. Lead-ore deposits in the principal countries exporting lead-bearing ores to the United States contain from 4 to 12 percent lead. Most of the waste material is removed from the crude ore by concentration at the mines. In 1952 the lead-bearing ores and concentrates imported averaged about 55 percent lead, of which 96 to 98 percent was recoverable by smelting and refining. Flue dust and mattes are intermediate furnace products with varying percentages of lead. All of the materials covered in paragraph 391 require further treatment to recover the metal contained, although some ores or concentrates are used directly in making some lead pigments. 

Paragraph 392 covers several articles, including intermediate materials requiring further processing before use, refined metal, important alloys of lead, and lead fabricated forms. The most important item is lead pigs and bars. This is refined lead, usually in pigs or bars weighing about 100 pounds each. The great bulk of the refined lead imported into the United States is of Corroding grade, containing at least 99.94 percent lead, which today commands a premium of 

10 cent per pound over Common grade lead (at least 99.73 percent pure), the grade for which market prices are usually quoted. The purer grades of lead are required for use in contact with acids and for conversion into white lead of the requisite degree of whiteness. 

Lead or base bullion is the product of primary lead smelting; it contains about 97 to 99 percent lead in addition to silver, gold, and various impurities. Lead bullion is refined before use to recover the precious metals and remove the impurities.

Lead dross is an intermediate product of smelting, refining, or manufacturing processes and, like scrap lead and antimonial scrap lead, is further treated to recover its metal content. 

Type metal, as the name implies, is used in the printing trades; it is an alloy of lead, antimony (2 to 23 percent), and minor amounts of tin.

Antimonial lead generally contains 6 to 8 percent antimony. The antimony serves to impart stiffness and hardness to the alloy, which, for that reason, is often referred to as hard lead. 

All of the above-named articles in paragraphs 391 and 392 (not including babbitt metal and solder, or lead sheets, pipe, etc.), in addition to some miscellaneous alloys of lead, are referred to collectively in this report as "unmanufactured lead." In addition, para-

graph 392 covers babbitt metal (a tin-base or lead-base antifriction bearing metal), solder (usually a lead and tin alloy-with or without fluxing acid cores-used for joining metals at relatively low temperatures where it is not possible or practical to use other means of fastening), lead sheet and pipe (formed by rolling or extruding lead), lead shot (a granulated product usually obtained by dropping molten lead through a sieve into water), and lead wire and glazier's lead. The latter comprises rolled or extruded strips used for holding panes of glass together, particularly in art-glass windows. 

Relative importance of imports of lead articles Although the number of lead articles covered by paragraphs 72, 391, and 392 is large, only a few of the items account for the bulk of United States imports. In 1952 (see table L-1) lead pigs and bars accounted for 79.2 percent of the total value of all lead articles imported; leadbearing ores, for 16.0 percent; type metal and antimonial lead, for 2.0 percent; lead dross, reclaimed lead, and scrap lead, for 1.6 percent; and lead bullion, for 0.5 percent. None of the remaining items comprised as much as 0.5 percent of the total. The value of imports of lead pigments amounted to only 0.2 percent of the total value of all the lead articles considered, and that of babbitt metal and solder, to 0.4 percent; the value of imports of lead sheets, pipe, etc., was negligible. The relative importance of the lead articles imported in 1952 measured in terms of lead content is similar to their importance in terms of value. The group of articles termed "unmanufactured lead" accounted for over 99 percent of the total volume of imports. The lead articles in this group are the only ones the imports of which are large in proportion to the volume of United States production of comparable items.

Although the total volume of lead imports in 1952 was unusually high, as indicated later in this report, the great bulk of the imports have always been of unmanufactured lead. United States imports of lead pigments, babbitt metal and solder, and lead sheets, pipe, shot, etc., have usually been very small in comparison with imports of other lead articles and with United States production of these items. Exports of these articles have generally exceeded imports. (See tables 2, 3, and 4 in appendix.)

CHAPTER II TARIFF STATUS OF LEAD ARTICLES 

Rates of duty currently in effect United States rates of duty applicable since 1930 to imports of lead articles dutiable under paragraphs 72, 391, and 392 of the Tariff Act of 1930 are shown in table L-2. 

The rates of duty on the principal lead pigments-litharge, orange mineral, red lead, and white lead-are in cents per pound applied to their gross weights. The current rate of duty on litharge is 14 cents; on orange mineral, 2 cents; on red lead, 1% cents; and on white lead, 120 cents. These duties reflect reductions from the 1930 rates brought about by trade-agreement concessions amounting to 50 percent for litharge, 33% percent for orange mineral, 32 percent for red lead, and 58 percent for white lead.

The rates of duty on lead articles dutiable under paragraphs 391 and 392 are generally applied to the lead content of such articles. 

The duty on lead sheets, pipe, etc., is applied to their gross weight; however, metal other than lead (primarily antimony) comprises only a small percentage of their total weight. The rates of duty currently in effect are three-fourths of a cent per pound on the lead content of lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes, and 16 cents per pound on the lead content of lead bullion, lead pigs and bars, lead dross, reclaimed lead, scrap lead, type metal, antimonial lead, babbitt metal, solder, and miscellaneous alloys of lead. These rates of duty were made effective June 6, 1951, pursuant to concessions granted by the United States in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT); they are 50 percent below the statutory rates prescribed in the Tariff Act of 1930. The rates currently applicable are the same as those which were in effect from January 30, 1943, through December 31, 1950, pursuant to a trade agreement with Mexico; upon the termination of that agreement at the end of 1950 the rates had reverted to the statutory rates of 1930.

The current rate of duty on lead sheets, pipe, shot, glazier's lead, and lead wire is 1% cents per pound; this rate, made effective June 

6, 1951, pursuant to GATT, is 45 percent below the rate provided for in the Tariff Act of 1930.

Differential between the rates of duty on lead-bearing ores and lead pigs and bars. The rate of duty currently applicable on lead in leadbearing ores, flue dust, and mattes (three-fourths of a cent per pound on the lead content) is equal to about 71 percent of the current rate of duty on lead in lead pigs and bars (16 cents per pound on the lead content). Both the rates of duty on lead-bearing ores and those on lead pigs and bars have been reduced 50 percent since 1930.

The differential between the rates of duty on lead in ores and on lead metal (based on both the 1930 and the current rates) is more than sufficient to compensate for metallurgical losses in converting the ore to refined lead metal. Although the 1930 and current rates of duty on lead in ores are 71 percent of the rates of duty on lead pigs and bars, on the average about 97.6 percent of the total lead content of ores and concentrates imported into the United States during 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953 was recoverable. Although about 97.6 percent of the lead contained in imported lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes is probably recovered in current smelting and refining processes, a smaller percentage, probably no more than about 96 percent, was recovered by lead smelters and refineries in 1930. The increased recoveries reflect improvements in metallurgical processes resulting in smaller losses.

 shown in the above tabulation (as elsewhere in this report) include imports free of duty for smelting, refining, and export. A large part of the imports in prewar years were entered free of duty for smelting, refining, and export; such imports since the war have been very small. 

During World War II the bulk of the greatly expanded imports (over 90 percent of the total quantity in 1942 and 1943) were entered free of duty for United States Government use (for stockpiling and for distribution to consumers).

The Government continued to import lead free of duty during 1946, when 86 percent of the total quantity of imports were entered free of duty. More than 70 percent of the unmanufactured lead imported in 

1948, 1949, and 1952 were entered free of duty, primarily because of suspensions of duties. To encourage imports of lead, the Congress suspended import duties on unmanufactured lead from June 20, 1948, to June 30, 1949, inclusive (Public Law 725, 80th Cong.), and again from February 12, 1952, to June 25, 1952, inclusive (Public Law 257, 82d Cong.). The duty on lead scrap was suspended by a series of public laws for practically the entire period from March 14, 1942, to June 30, 1952. Lead imports in postwar years were also entered free of duty for United States Government use, and to a lesser extent for smelting, refining, and export, and as a product of the Republic of the Philippines (in accordance with the Philippine Trade Act of 1946). 

Of the total imports of unmanufactured lead in the postwar period 1946 through 1953, 43 percent entered free of duty. 

Trade-agreement commitments with respect to duties on lead The current rates of duty on all the lead articles covered in this investigation are reduced rates made effective by Presidential proclamations as a result of concessions granted by the United States in GATT. These trade-agreement concessions are subject to the escape clause of GATT, which permits the withdrawal or modification of trade-agreement concessions under the conditions specified in section 7 

of the Trade Agreements Extension Act of 1951 (Public Law 50, 1 Public Law 257 (82d Cong.) suspended the duties until March 31, 1953, but included a proviso for an earlier termination of the suspension when the average market price of lead shall have been below 18 cents a pound for a calendar month. The average price for May 1952 was below this average and the suspension was terminated on June 25, 1952, through the application of this proviso.

82d Cong.). Section 7 established procedures for invoking the escape clause of trade agreements whenever a product upon which a tradeagreement concession has been granted is, as a result, in whole or in part, of the duty or other customs treatment reflecting such concession, being imported into the United States in such increased quantities, either actual or relative, as to cause or threaten serious injury to the domestic industry producing like or directly competitive products.

Table L-4 shows the maximum rates of duty which could be imposed as the result of escape-clause action with respect to the lead articles and, for comparison, the rates of duty provided in the Tariff Act of 1930, as well as the current rates of duty. The maximum rates that could be imposed on unmanufactured lead articles such as lead-bearing ores, and lead pigs and bars, and on babbitt metal and solder would represent an increase of 140 percent over the current rates of duty. 

The maximum permissible increase in the rates of duty on red lead, orange mineral, suboxide of lead, and lead pigments not specially provided for, however, would result in rates of duty that would exceed the current rates of duty by smaller percentages (50-87% percent), and the maximum permissible increase in the rates of duty on litharge, white lead, and lead sheets, pipe, etc., would result in rates of duty that would exceed the current rates by larger percentages (170-200 percent).

As previously mentioned, the present rates of duty applicable to lead and zinc ores and metal are now the subject of tariff commitments under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). 

Any changes in the tariff treatment of imports now subject to these commitments would contravene international obligations of the United States unless made consistently with the provisions of the agreement. 

Of the contracting parties to GATT, Canada, Peru, and Australia would probably be the countries principally concerned. Although

26.2. E 

113 the United States has no specific obligations to Mexico or Yugoslavia with respect to the tariff treatment applicable to United States imports of lead and zinc ores and metal, these countries would also have an important interest in such a matter. 

With regard to changes in tariff treatment that might be made pursuant to the provisions of GATT, possible action is not limited to that taken under the standard "escape clause" of the agreement (art. XIX). For example, article XXI of GATT provides that any contracting party may take "any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests *** taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations." If during an emergency in international relations the United States were to impose on imports of lead and zinc additional restrictions that it declared to be necessary for the protection of its essential security interests, such restrictions would not be contrary to the provisions of GATT. 

As noted above, under this general exception in the GATT, the United States would be free, in time of war or other emergency in international relations, to impose on imports of lead and zinc any restrictions that it considered necessary for the protection of its essential security interests. The exception appears in article XXI of the 

GATT, which provides in pertinent part that— Nothing in this agreement shall be construed *** to prevent any contracting party from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests * * * taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations. [Emphasis supplied.]

Accordingly, if legislation imposing increased import restrictions on lead and zinc contained a recital to the effect that an emergency in international relations exists and that the imposition of the import restrictions provided for in the legislation is necessary for the protection of the essential security interests of the United States, the restrictions imposed by such legislation would not be inconsistent with United States commitments in the GATT. It would seem necessary that such a recital would have to be predicated, of course, upon a determination made in good faith that the additional import restrictions on lead and zinc were necessary to protect the essential security interests of the United States and upon the existence of an emergency in international relations such as is contemplated by article XXI.2 • Commissioner Edminster wishes to add the following observations:

Whether Congress could, "in good faith," take such action in conformity with the provisions of art. XXI would, of course, be for the Congress to determine. Apart from any question as to the existence of an "emergency in international relations" within the meaning of art. XXI, the basic issue in such a determination would appear to be: (1) Whether the national security would be best served by the imposition of such import restrictions on lead and zinc, on the ground that such action is required in order to prevent such a deterioration of con. ditions in the industry as would create an undue hazard with respect to access to essential supplies in time of war; or (2) Whether, on the contrary, the national security would be best served by avoidance of such restrictions (or if such restrictions be regarded as necessary, the exercise of due restraint with respect to their severity and duration), in view of the extent to which the United States has come to rely upon imports to meet the normal increase in its peacetime requirements, of our greatly increased dependence on imports in time of war (as in World War II), and of the fact that such imports are available from already welldeveloped, economical, and nearby sources of supply on the North American Continent. 

In any case, should the Congress take such action, "good faith" in the matter would require that it recognize (1) that the other contracting parties to the GATT would carefully scrutinize any such action; (2) that, if satisfied that the action was not justified, they might invoke the "Nullification or Impairment" clause (art. XXIII); and (3) that this might lead to retaliatory action and possibly to complete withdrawal from the agreement.

Commissioner Ryder concurs in the above statement of Commissioner Edminster. In addition, he wishes to state that he doubts whether, as a matter of international comity, it would be advisable to invoke art. XXI merely through a "recital" in a preamble to legislation increasing import restrictions on one commodity or a group of related commodities. He feels that the GATT exception in question might well be interpreted as contemplating that it could be invoked only during an emergency in international relations which had previously been declared to exist by formal proclamation of the President or by appropriate legislativo action such as a congressional joint resolution. 46566-54- -9

CHAPTER III UNITED STATES LEAD SUPPLY AND REQUIREMENTS 

General trend of production, foreign trade, and consumption since prewar years

The outstanding change in the United States position with respect to lead in recent years as compared with prewar years is the great increase in United States consumption of lead, accompanied by a marked decrease in the proportion supplied by domestic production and a marked increase in the proportion supplied by imports. Before 

World War II, the United States produced virtually all of the lead that it consumed. Most of the small imports, largely of lead-bearing ores, were entered free of duty for smelting, refining, and export. During 

World War II and in the postwar years the supply of lead from domestic sources was far below United States requirements for consumption, and strategic stockpiling and imports increased enormously, while exports became almost negligible. 

Of the total United States lead supply (production plus imports) in the prewar years 1937-39, about 61 percent came from primary domestic production (as measured by recoverable lead content of mine production), about 32 percent from secondary output from old scrap,* and 7 percent (mostly exported after treatment) from imports.5 In the last 5 years (1949-53) these sources accounted for 31 percent, 32 percent, and 37 percent, respectively, of the total supply (see table L-6).

United States production of lead (mine output plus recovery from old scrap) during the 5 years 1949-53 averaged 796,000 short tons per year (391,000 tons from mines and 405,000 tons from old scrap). 

This total production represents a 25-percent increase over the average for 1937-39. However, although total production increased 25 percent, average mine output of lead decreased 6 percent, whereas lead output from old scrap increased 83 percent. The quantity of lead recovered from old scrap in the United States exceeded mine output in each of the postwar years except 1949 and 1950. 

In contrast to the 25-percent increase in lead production, average annual consumption of lead in the United States during 1949-53 (1,138,000 tons, excluding lead withdrawn for the strategic stockpile) was 80 percent above the 1937-39 average, and imports, which averaged 462,000 tons per year during 1949-53, were practically a new source of lead supply for the United States. 

3 Primary domestic production may be measured also, with practically the same result, by adding to the quantity of refined lead produced from domestic ores and base bullion the lead content of antimonial lead produced from domestic ores and base bullion and the lead content of lead pigments produced directly from domestic ores and concentrates. 

4 In the 5-year period 1948-52 the quantity of lead recovered from old scrap constituted 87.2 percent of the total quantity of lead recovered from both old and new scrap. Lead recovered from new scrap is not included in this accounting of annual supply in order to avoid duplication. Such scrap consists of clippings and trimmings or of lead drosses or skimmings obtained in the process of fabricating or manufacturing lead articles. Annual figures on lead recovered from such scrap represent more or less duplication depending upon the number of times in the course of a year the same metal reappears as lead recovered from new scrap. 

Data on imports used throughout this report represent imports for consumption rather than general imports. The two measures do not give the same results in some periods. For definition of imports for consumption and general imports and for a comparison of monthly data for each in 1951, 1952, and 1953, see appendix table 14.

United States and world trends of production and consumption Available statistics on world production and consumption of primary lead (but not of secondary lead) afford comparison of the general trends of production and consumption of lead in the United States with those in the rest of the world (see appendix tables 20, 21, and 22). 

Average annual mine output of lead in the United States during 194852 was about 4 percent below the average for 1937-39. The annual average mine output of lead in the world outside the United States during 1948-52 was about 8 percent below the average for 1937-39. 

However, mine production in countries outside the United States, which had declined greatly after the cessation of hostilities in 1945, increased in each of the 5 years 1948-52, and in 1952 it reached a record total of 1,616,000 short tons, which exceeded the 1937-39 average by 7 percent. Mine output in the United States increased

from 390,000 tons in 1948 to 431,000 tons in 1950, but declined to 390,000 tons in 1952. In 1953 it declined further to 335,000 tons, while, according to such data as are available for some of the large foreign producing countries, world output outside the United States was at least as large in 1953 as in 1952. 

The trend of lead consumption in the United States contrasts sharply with that outside the United States. Whereas the average annual consumption of primary lead outside the United States during 1948–52 was 30 percent below the 1937-38 level (data for 1939 are not available), primary lead consumption in the United States rose 54 percent between the 2 periods. United States consumption of both primary and secondary lead between the 2 periods increased 84 percent. Comparable data on consumption of secondary lead outside the United States are not available, but it is known that the United States is by far the largest producer and consumer of secondary lead. 

Changes in supply and demand before 1952 United States supplies of lead increased rapidly during the first years of World War II, principally through increased imports. Beginning in 1940 the United States received large quantities of lead from countries, such as Mexico and Canada, that previously exported the bulk of their production to Europe. Normal trade with Europe had been disrupted by the war, and the United States Government purchased the newly available foreign supplies in anticipation of the expansion of war requirements, and in order to prevent lead from getting into unfriendly hands. Wartime imports of lead, mostly entered free of duty for Government account, reached a peak of 526,000 tons in 1942. The 

Government stockpile of lead, built up largely from purchases of foreign supplies, reached a total of 266,000 tons by April 1943. 

Lead supplies were also augmented in the early years of the war, with Government encouragement, by increased mine output, which rose to a peak of 496,000 tons in 1942, and by secondary production from old scrap, which was largest in 1941 (380,000 tons). In order to stimulate higher mine output, the Government adopted what is known as the premium price plan, under which mining concerns were paid premiums for above-quota production, in addition to the ceiling price of 6%½ cents a pound for Common lead, New York, fixed by the Government during the war period. This plan was put in effect on February 1, 1942, and was continued through June 30, 1947. Throughout the life of the plan, premium subsidies, averaging about 3% cents a pound, were paid on 42 percent of the lead produced by domestic mines. Under the plan, premium subsidies were paid for production from relatively high-cost operations, including some large producers as well as many whose output was small and erratic. 

Some of the mines the output of which was thus subsidized were old properties which had been idle for many years but which were revived under the encouragement of the premium subsidies. The principal purpose of the plan was to obtain production from submarginal ores known to exist in operating mines and in formerly productive but dormant or idle mines, as well as from the reworking of mine, tailing, and slag dumps.

Despite the efforts to increase production, mine output of lead declined after 1942. After 1941, production of lead from old scrap also 

U. S. Bureau of Mines, History of Premium Price Plan for Copper,, 'Lead, and Zinc, 1942-47, Information 

Circular 7536, January 1950.

f= declined sharply and remained at a relatively low level throughout the rest of the war years. Shortages of manpower, supplies, and equipment contributed to these declines. 

Lead consumption expanded during the war, despite use restrictions, to a peak of 1,119,000 tons in 1944, compared with the average annual consumption of 631,000 tons during 1937-39. Government regulations restricted the use of lead for nonessential uses but encouraged its substitution for metals, such as tin, brass, and zinc, that had more direct military application than lead. However, lead was employed in many military uses-such as in storage batteries and bearing metals used in motorized equipment, in lead paints for military structures, in construction of equipment for explosives plants, and in tetraethyl lead for high-octane gasoline-and in many other applications. It

Lead consumption in the United States, as used throughout this report, is "reported" consumption-that is, consumption as reported by individual consumers (and published by the American Bureau of Metal Statistics for the years up to and including 1947, and by the United States Bureau of Mines for the years beginning with 1948). does not include quantities going into Government or private stocks. 

Reported consumption differs from "supply" or "apparent" consumption, such as might be calculated by adding imports to production and subtracting exports. Reported consumption for a given year indicates the quantity of lead actually used by consumers in the United States in that year whether from that year's supply or from stocks accumulated in previous years. Apparent consumption, as noted above, indicates supply in a given year, made available from that year's domestic production and imports, for distribution in the United States for consumption or for Government or private stockpiling. 

The reduced production and curtailed imports after 1942, coupled with a high level of consumption, caused a severe shortage of lead toward the end of the war. The Government applied stringent end-use controls and drew upon its stockpile of lead to supply the essential needs of industry. Government stocks of lead, which amounted to 266,000 tons in April 1943, were reduced to 174,000 tons by the end of 1943, to 90,000 tons at the end of 1944, and to 68,700 tons by the end of 1945. Government stocks, which were imported free of duty, were distributed to industry at the ceiling price of 6% cents a pound, without any addition for the prevailing rate of import duty.

In 1946, the first postwar year and a period of general reconversion of industry to peacetime production, United States lead consumption, production, and imports all declined. Mine output, amounting to about 335,000 tons, was the lowest since 1935 and was exceeded for the first time by output of lead recovered from old scrap. The decline in mine production was a continuation of the reduction although at an accelerated rate that occurred in each year after 1942, and can be attributed in part to the shortages of manpower, equipment, supplies, and materials, and in part to the necessity of devoting more attention to mine development and exploration, work that was to a considerable extent suspended during the war. The progressive depletion during the war of developed ore bodies was also a factor contributing to the reduced output in 1946 and restraining the volume of production in subsequent years. United States lead imports in 

1946, amounting to 136,000 tons, were less than half the average

annual imports during the war. During 1946 the Government released to industry about 32,700 tons of its war-accumulated stocks of lead, mostly from foreign sources, so that United States consumption of imported lead in 1946 was larger than that indicated by the quantity actually imported during that year. The price ceiling on lead was increased on June 3, 1946, from 62 cents to 84 cents a pound. 

Price control expired at the end of June 1946; it was reestablished on 

July 25, 1946-reinstituting the ceiling of 84 cents a pound on leadand finally abandoned on November 9 of that year.

By 1947, reconversion of industry to peacetime production in the United States was largely completed. The demand for most manufactured products in which lead is used, swollen by the war-accumulated demand, was unusually high. Lead consumption in 1947 reached the unprecedented total of 1,172,000 tons, a figure considerably above that during any war year. The price of lead, no longer subject to Government control, rose to an average of 14.7 cents; moreover, as previously noted, while the premium price plan was still in effect during the first half of 1947, some mining concerns received premium subsidies. Lead production rose to a postwar peak of 828,800 tons-both as a result of a 15-percent increase in mine output and a record recovery of lead from old scrap. Lead imports in 1947 were about 66 percent higher than in 1946 and, in contrast to the imports in other years, were mostly dutiable. Government stocks of lead were reduced by 31,000 tons during 1947. 

The year 1948 was marked by unusually high lead prices which averaged about 18 cents a pound for the year as a whole. Lead consumption in that year, although somewhat lower than in 1947, was still higher than during any wartime year. The combined production from mines and old scrap in 1948 was only slightly below that of the previous year. Mine output of lead was partly retarded by work interruptions resulting from labor disputes, mostly in southeastern Missouri, as a result of which, according to trade reports, production was about 25,000 tons less than it would have been otherwise. In order to help relieve the lead shortage by encouraging imports of lead, Congress suspended import duties on unmanufactured lead from June 20, 1948, through June 30, 1949 (Public Law 

725, 80th Cong.). Lead imports in 1948, amounting to 332,000 tons, were 47 percent higher than those in the previous year. It should be noted, however, that about two-thirds of the lead imported during 1948 was imported during the last half of the year, when the import duties were suspended and lead prices were highest." 

During 1949 a rapid change occurred in the lead situation, from a condition of scarcity to one of abundance. This change was marked by sharp price declines beginning on March 8, 1949, when the New 

York price of Common lead dropped 2 cents from the peak of 21% cents that prevailed during the previous 4 months (see table L-7). 

The price continued to decline to a low point of 12 cents on May 26, rose to 15% cents on August 18, and resumed its downward trend thereafter; at the end of the year it was again 12 cents. At the time of the first sharp declines in the price of lead, trade reports attributed them mostly to the slackened demand for lead, especially demand Monthly data from January 1948 through the end of 1953 on lead production (mine output and lead recovered from old scrap), producers' and consumers' stocks, consumption, imports (dutiable and free of duty), exports, and average market prices in the United States are given in appendix table 1.

for automotive replacement batteries, in which about one-third of the lead is normally consumed. Battery replacements were below normal, owing to the unusually warm winter weather, but it was also apparent that much of the war-accumulated demand for lead had been satisfied and that manufacturers had built up unusually large inventories of lead metal. Moreover, the moderate business recession that developed in 1949 contributed to the slackened demand for lead.

NOTE. Price ceilings on sales of lead in the United States were imposed on Jan. 26, 1951; the price ceilings were increased by 2 cents a pound on Oct. 2, 1951, and, in order to prevent domestic buyers from buying lead at higher prices in foreign countries (previously permitted), the Office of Price Stabilization prohibited any person in the United States from receiving foreign lead at a delivered cost in excess of the ceiling price. All price ceilings on lead in the United States were removed by the Office of Price Stabilization on Feb. 12, 1953. 

Total United States lead consumption in 1949, amounting to 958,000 tons, was about 16 percent below the 1948 level. However, the reduction in the domestic demand for lead indicated by this decline was partly or wholly offset by 1949 transfers of undisclosed quantities of lead to the strategic stockpile. (Before 1949, additions of lead to the strategic stockpile were minor.) The lead-mining industry, with fewer work interruptions caused by labor disputes, produced about 20,000 tons more lead in 1949 than in the previous year, but lead recovery from old scrap declined by about 69,000 tons. United

States lead imports in 1949, amounting to 415,000 tons, were 25 percent above the level of imports in 1948 and higher than in any previous peacetime year. As in 1948, most of the lead imported during the year was imported in the half of the year when the lead import duties were suspended and when the lead prices were highest. 

Lead supplies expanded rapidly in the United States in 1950 despite the low market prices that prevailed in the first part of the year. 

Mine output increased to the highest level in postwar years, 431,000 tons, which was 5 percent above the level of the previous year; production of lead from old scrap rose by 18 percent over the preceding year, to 428,000 tons; and imports, amounting to 565,000 tons, were 36 percent above those in 1949 and at a higher level than in any previous year. Imports were unusually heavy toward the end of the year, when lead prices were rising sharply. Some of the increase in imports was due to anticipation of the 50-percent increase in import duties that became effective with the termination of the Mexican trade agreement at the end of the year. 

Lead consumption, which was relatively low near the end of 1949 and in the early months of 1950, rose rapidly after the outbreak of war in Korea in June 1950. As a result, consumption of lead in the 

United States in 1950 reached the record total of 1,238,000 tons-an increase of 29 percent over the amount consumed in 1949. The market price of lead, which had dropped to 10% cents a pound on

March 14, rose sharply thereafter, and was 17 cents a pound by the end of the year.

The period following the outbreak of hostilities in Korea in June 1950 and extending through the end of 1951 was one of severe lead shortages in the United States. Lead was needed in the United States and in foreign countries for rearmament and to meet the needs arising from the general expansion in industrial activity. Moreover, the demand for lead was increased by scare buying to build up consumers' stocks, which rose to unusually high levels near the beginning of 1951 (see appendix table 1). Producers' stocks, on the other hand, were curtailed. United States Government purchases of lead in the early part of the year for the strategic stockpile contributed to the intensity of lead demand. Purchases of large quantities of lead by the British 

Government toward the end of the year further aggravated the situation.

Contributing greatly to the United States lead shortage in 1951 was the 60-percent drop in imports. Domestic production declined slightly; a small increase in lead production from old scrap was more than offset by a 10-percent decline in mine output, attributed mostly to work stoppages owing to labor disputes. 

With the outbreak of the Korean war and developing metal shortages, the Government quickly established price, use, and allocation controls over lead and other metals. Government price controls were imposed on lead as on other nonferrous metals, beginning on January 26, 1951. From this date each seller of lead in the United States was prohibited from selling at a price that was higher than the highest price at which lead had been sold in the United States during the period from December 19, 1950, to January 25, 1951, inclusive. This resulted in a price ceiling of 17 cents a pound on domestic lead. At first imported lead, although paying a duty of 16 cents per pound, was sold at the same price. However, when, on January 1, 1951,

Di 

the import duty was increased to 2% cents a pound, the principal sellers of imported lead raised their price to 18%½ cents a pound and were readily able to sell considerable quantities at the increased price. When the import duty was again reduced, effective June 6, 1951, to the former rate of 16 cents a pound, there was no decline in the price at which foreign lead was sold in the United States. On 

October 2, 1951, the Office of Price Stabilization increased the price ceilings by 2 cents a pound and-in order to prevent buyers from buying lead at higher prices in foreign countries (previously permitted)-prohibited any person in the United States from receiving foreign lead at a delivered cost in excess of the ceiling price. Because of the strong demand for lead in relation to supply at this time, the ceiling prices were the prices at which lead was sold in the United States from the beginning of 1951 to the end of April 1952. 

The big drop in imports in 1951 is attributed principally to the fact that lead was selling in foreign markets at prices substantially above the ceiling prices at which it was permitted to be sold in the United States. As a result, foreign supplies, such as those from Mexico, ordinarily sent to the United States, were diverted to foreign markets. 

The disparity between the United States ceiling and foreign market prices appears to have been largest during the last half of 1951. The price of Mexican lead, f. a. s.8 gulf ports, regarded in the trade as the most representative foreign price at that time, was as much as 5½ cents above the United States ceiling price of 17 cents for domestic lead before October 2, 1951 (see table L-8). After the United States ceiling on the lead price was raised 2 cents a pound on October 2, 1951, the United States price was still as much as 3 cents below the price at which Mexican lead was being sold at gulf ports. (Freight and insurance costs for transporting lead from gulf ports to New York were about one-half cent a pound.)

In order to limit the use of the scarce supplies of lead to the most essential needs, the Government imposed lead-use restrictions, effective May 1, 1951. The slightly reduced consumption of lead in 1951 as compared with 1950 despite the large demand probably reflects the unavailability of sufficient lead supplies, as well as the use restrictions. 

On September 1, 1951, primary soft lead produced in the United

States was placed under allocation control, and on January 1, 1952, allocation control was extended to imported lead. 

Toward the end of 1951 the shortage of lead became so severe, aggravated by loss of production from mines and smelters because of labor disputes, that the President authorized the release of 30,000 tons to consumers from the strategic stockpile, and about 17,000 tons was released before the Government stopped further withdrawals.

NOTE.-Price ceilings on sales of lead in the United States were established by the Office of Price Stabiliza tion effective Jan. 26, 1951; price ceilings were increased 2 cents a pound on Oct. 2, 1951, on which date the 

Office of Price Stabilization also prohibited any person in the United States from receiving foreign lead at a delivered cost in excess of the ceiling price. All price ceilings on lead in the United States were removed on Feb. 12, 1953.

At the end of September 1953 freight and insurance cost of transporting lead from gulf ports to New York was about 0.5 cent a pound, and from London to New York, about 0.7 cent a pound. 

The prolonged fighting in Korea and the possibility that the war might spread and further aggravate the metal shortages led to a Government policy of active encouragement of production of lead and zinc and other critical metals, both in the United States and in foreign countries. In the United States the Government encouraged expansion of production facilities by allowing-for tax purposes-accelerated amortization of investments in such facilities, by making loans for expansion of production facilities, by sharing in the expense of lead and zinc exploration projects, and in a few cases by contracting for longterm purchase of lead and zinc at fixed prices. The United States assisted lead and zinc producers in 13 countries with both development loans and long-term contracts for purchases of lead and zinc at floor prices. These Government assistance projects and the stimulus provided to private investors by the high market prices resulted in the institution of many projects for the development and expansion of production facilities both in the United States and in foreign countries. (Table 69 in the appendix lists the major projects that have come to the attention of the Tariff Commission.) The long-term nature of some of the Government assistance projects, involving the purchase of metals at the relatively high prices prevailing in 1951 and providing

123 for deliveries extending into 1956 and 1959, suggests that the lead and zinc shortage was expected to last longer than it did. Such an expectation apparently prompted the British Government to make large metal purchases in 1951, and seems also to have induced some private domestic concerns to invest large sums in development projects the profitable operation of which would have required a market price of at least 18 cents a pound for lead or zinc.

Changes in supply and demand since the beginning of 1952 Mine

The year 1952, like 1949, was one of rapid transition from a period of severe scarcity to one of abundance of lead supplies. An increase in the volume of lead imports was the principal factor in the changed situation. Lead imports in 1952 rose to the record level of 644,000 tons, or 182 percent above the unusually low imports in 1951. output during 1952 was virtually at the same level as output in 1951, and production of lead from old scrap was 7 percent below that of the previous year. Outside the United States, lead consumption declined 

16 percent in 1952, while mine output rose 37 percent to a higher level than in any previous year.

Lead continued to be sold in the United States market at the permitted ceiling price of 19 cents a pound in the first 4 months of 1952. 

As previously indicated, lead import duties were suspended by Public Law 257, effective February 12, 1952. This law contained a proviso that if the average market price was below 18 cents a pound for any calendar month the suspension would be terminated. The average price for May 1952 (15.731 cents) was below 18 cents. Accordingly, as required by the law, the Tariff Commission notified the President of this fact on June 5 and the President signed an order that ended the duty suspension on June 26, 1952. About half the lead imported in 

1952 entered in the 5 months February through June, during most of which the import duty was suspended. 

Lead was the first of the major nonferrous metals to decline in price below established price ceilings. It dropped to 18 cents a pound on 

April 29, 1952, and continued to drop almost continuously until it reached the low point of 13½ cents a pound on October 22. 

Although the price of lead in the United States market remained at the price ceiling of 19 cents a pound during the first 4 months of 1952, the decline in prices of lead in foreign markets during this time indicated that world supplies were rapidly catching up with demand. 

The price of Mexican lead (free alongside ship, gulf ports) dropped from 212-22 cents a pound in November 1951 to 17%½ cents a pound by the end of April 1952. This latter price, after addition of the 

United States import duty (116 cents) and transportation and insurance costs (about one-half cent), was roughly equivalent to a dutypaid price in New York of 19 cents a pound. Thereafter, the downward trends of the New York price paralleled gulf port (free alongside ship) prices of lead.

The sharp drop in the price of lead in the United States beginning October 7, 1952, followed fairly closely the price drop in London with the resumption of private trading on the London Metal Exchange on October 1, which had been suspended for 13 years (see table L-8). The London price on October 1 dropped to 13% cents a pound, which, after the addition of the cost of transportation and insurance from London to New York and the United States import duty of 16 cents, was equivalent to a little more than 15 cents a

pound at a time when lead was selling in New York at 16 cents a pound. Late in October the London price dropped to about 10% cents a pound (more than 3 cents below the New York price) as the

British Government sold about 15,000 tons of its lead stock to consumers. The decline in the price of lead on the London Metal Exchange was arrested after October, as the British Government reduced its sales of the metal. At the beginning of November 1952 it was reported that of the lead stocks then held by the British Ministry of Materials, 9,000 tons would be set aside for sales for spot delivery at times when prompt deliveries were not available from normal trade sources. It was also reported that about 15,000 tons would be sold in the next 14 months on an average-price basis, and that much of the remainder would be retained for reserve stocks. (Official statistics on Government stocks held in the United Kingdom have not been available since the end of September 1952, when the quantity of such stocks amounted to about 107,400 short tons.) 

Perhaps the most outstanding feature of the lead situation in 1952 is the fact that while the market price of lead declined from an average of 19 cents a pound during the first 4 months of the year to an average of 14% cents during December, consumption of lead (1,130,- 000 tons) was at a relatively high level-only 5 percent below that of 1951. A little more than half of the total was consumed in the last half of the year. Moreover, a total of 226,000 tons of lead was acquired by the United States Government for the strategic stockpile; of this amount, 57,000 tons was acquired during the first half of 1952 and 169,000 tons during the last half of the year.10 It should be observed in this connection that 143,220 tons of lead pigs and bars were imported during 1952 free of duty for United States Government use (see appendix table 18).

Some of the increase in lead supplies in 1952 went to build up producers' and consumers' stocks.

1949 (see appendix table 7). Consumers' stocks decreased during the year, through December 1 by 7,000 tons (see appendix table 1). 

Recent price changes

The market price of lead in the United States continued to decline in 1953 from 14% cents per pound at the beginning of the year to a low point of 12 cents on April 20.12 The price then rose gradually and was 14 cents on July 23; on September 16 it declined to 13%2 cents, at which level it remained throughout the rest of the year. 

The price dropped a half cent to 13 cents a pound on January 18, 1954, and a month later, on February 18, it declined another half cent to 122 cents. On March 9, it increased to 124 cents, and on the next day, to 13 cents.

The recent declines in the market price of lead in the United States have generally followed decreases in price quotations on the London Metal Exchange. As previously indicated, the cost of transportation and insurance from London to New York plus the United States import duty of 16 cents amounts to a little less than 2 cents per pound. 

The total drop in the United States price of lead from 19 cents a pound in the first quarter of 1952 to 13 cents a pound on March 10, 1954, represents a decline of 32 percent. The average for January 

1954 was 30 percent below the average for the first quarter of 1952. 

Compared with this, the wholesale-price index of all commodities other than farm products and foods, as reported by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, rose from an average of 114.1 in the first quarter of 1952 to 114.5 in January 1954. 

Nature of available market price quotations

The market prices of lead in the United States referred to above are 

New York quotations for Common lead as reported by the Engineering and Mining Journal's E & MJ Metal and Mineral Markets.

They are based on actual first-hand sales of all grades of refined lead by major primary producers or their agents in the United States on a flat or fixed-price basis. (Sales on the basis of average prices over some stipulated period, or on the basis of the price prevailing on the date of shipment, are not included in compiling the market prices.) 

The E & MJ daily price quotations are weighted by the quantities of lead sold; the weekly, monthly, or annual averages are simple arithmetical averages of the weighted daily averages. 

The prices quoted for Common grade of lead reflect sales by producers on a flat-price basis of other grades of lead converted to Common grade equivalent. Sales of Corroding grade of lead, which commands a premium of one-tenth cent per pound over Common grade, are converted to the equivalent of Common grade by subtracting one-tenth cent from the price at which Corroding grade lead was sold. 

Of the total sales of refined lead (excluding antimonial lead) in the United States in the past 5 years (1949-53) by domestic producers and importers, only 20 percent was Common grade, and 69 percent comprised Corroding grade and 11 percent, Chemical grade. (See appendix table 6.)

Lead is generally sold delivered to the buyer, and the freight is usually paid by the seller, who seeks to reduce this cost as much as possible. Most United States consumers pay the New York_price. 

Important exceptions are: (1) Consumers in the vicinity of St. Louis,

Mo., Omaha, Nebr., and Joplin, Mo. (which are nearest the leadproducing center), who are charged the St. Louis price, which is 0.2 cent per pound below the New York price; (2) consumers in the

Chicago-Milwaukee area, who pay 0.15 cent per pound less than the

New York price; (3) consumers in New England, who are charged 

0.075 cent more than the New York price; and (4) consumers in 

California, who (since February 1, 1954) are charged 0.2 cent less than the New York price.

Antimonial lead, which usually contains about 8 percent antimony, commands a premium over unalloyed (soft) lead.¹4

Data for 1952 reported to the Tariff Commission by United States producers of refined lead and by importers, as summarized in table L-9, indicate the approximate distribution of domestic and imported lead metal by consuming areas, as well as the average delivered value of the metal and the cost of transporting it from shipping points within the United States. The tabulation is based on about 89 percent of all shipments from primary lead refineries in the United States and on about 50 percent of the total quantity of lead imports during 1952 including imports for Government use, or on about 69 percent of total imports excluding imports for Government account. Data include some shipments of antimonial lead.

As compared with an average New York price of Common lead of 16.467 cents per pound in 1952, the average delivered value of all grades of lead shipped from primary domestic producers was 16.46 cents, of which 0.39 cent was the average cost of transportation, insurance, and handling. The average delivered value of imported lead reported was 16.03 cents, including an average cost of about 

0.39 cent for delivering the metal from importers' distributing warehouses, or if consigned to consumers directly from foreign countries, from the United States points of entry.15

The delivered value of shipments to the Middle Atlantic States (where 27 percent of the total was shipped) averaged 16.44 cents a pound. The range of average delivered values of lead shipped by domestic producers to the nine geographic divisions for which data were summarized was very small-smaller than the range (0.24 to 0.90 cent) in the average costs per pound of transporting the lead.

CHAPTER IV UNITED STATES FOREIGN TRADE IN LEAD 

Trend of imports

The previous discussion of recent changes in United States imports of unmanufactured lead may be summarized as follows: Net imports (imports minus exports) were negligible in the years immediately preceding World War II. They became very large during the war and reached a wartime peak of 524,000 short tons in 1942. 

Net imports in the first postwar year, 1946, fell to 134,000 tons, but the consumption of imported lead in that year was considerably higher than that indicated by the volume of imports because part of the stocks of imported lead accumulated by the Government in the early war years were distributed to consumers during 1943-47. Net imports rose steadily in each successive postwar year until 1951-from 221,000 tons in 1947, to 331,000 tons in 1948, to 411,000 tons in 1949, and to 

560,000 tons in 1950. (See table L-10.)
