In 1951, when exports of countries normally supplying the United States were diverted to foreign countries where market prices were higher, net imports into the United States fell to 225,000 tons. But in 1952, net imports reached the record total of 640,000 tons. Net imports in 1953 amounted to 451,000 tons, of which 256,000 tons entered the United States in the first half of the year and 195,000 tons in the last half of the year. 

Taking into account the fact that some of the lead contained in lead-bearing ores imported is not recoverable, net imports of unmanufactured lead in 1949 were about equal to United States mine output of recoverable lead, and net imports of lead in all later years except 1951 exceeded domestic mine output by a substantial margin. 

Ratio of net imports to production United States net imports are compared with production (mine output plus production from old scrap) from prewar years through 

1953 in table L-10.

The ratio of net imports to production was less than 1 percent in the prewar years 1937-39, rose to 43.6 percent in 1943, and declined to 19.7 percent in 1946. The ratio rose steadily in the postwar years, with the exception of 1951, and reached a record peak of 79.8 percent in 1952. In 1951 the ratio dropped to 27.1 percent. The ratio for the second quarter of 1952, part of the period during which the import duties on lead were suspended, rose to 99.0 percent, and it was almost as high (95.4 percent) in the last quarter of 1952, when the import duties were applicable. The ratio of net imports to production averaged 63.1 percent in 1953 as a whole; it was higher than this in the first and second quarters of the year, 67.2 percent and 71.6 percent, respectively, and lower than the year's average in the third quarter (53.2 percent) and in the fourth quarter (59.5 percent).

United States imports, by kinds The great bulk of the unmanufactured lead imported into the United States is in the form of lead pigs and bars. Lead contained in lead-bearing ores, flue dust, and mattes is next in importance, although far below lead pigs and bars. Of the total imports of unmanufactured lead in the 6 years 1948-53, lead in pigs and bars constituted 76.5 percent; lead in ores, flue dust, and mattes, 17.5 percent; reclaimed lead, scrap lead, lead dross, and miscellaneous alloys other than antimonial lead, 3.4 percent; and lead in antimonial lead, 2.0 percent.

Imports of lead in the form of lead pigs and bars first became large during World War II; the small imports before the war consisted principally of lead-bearing ores and lead bullion entered free of duty for smelting, refining, and export. (See table L-11.) Since 1940 the bulk of United States imports of lead have been in the form of lead pigs and bars. From most countries the imports have been almost entirely in this form. Important exceptions, however, are the imports from Bolivia, Chile, Guatemala, and the Union of South Africa, from which lead imports are principally lead in lead-bearing ores. Imports of ore from Peru and Australia, although not in such large quantities as lead in pigs and bars from these countries, have been substantial. (See appendix table 17.) The unusually large imports of lead in lead-bearing ores, etc., in the last quarter of 1953, as shown in table

131 L, were almost entirely withdrawals for consumption from bonded warehouses rather than entries for immediate consumption. (See appendix table 14.)

Most of the imports of type metal and antimonial lead, as well as the bulk of the imports of reclaimed lead, scrap, dross, and miscellaneous lead alloys, come from Mexico.

Imports of lead in lead or base bullion have usually been very small since World War II; sporadic imports have come principally from 

Mexico or Australia.

The reports received cover about 53 percent of the total quantity of refined lead (and antimonial lead) imported in 1952 and 76 percent of the total quantity of metal imported during the first 9 months of 1953; the reports cover 73 percent and 86 percent, respectively, of total imports during these two periods excluding imports for United States Government use.

The reports from importers show that about 90 percent of the total quantity of lead metal imported during the period of 1% years was

Corroding grade. Most of the lead metal imported from each of the principal supplying countries was of this grade. Common grade lead, mostly from Mexico, accounted for 8 percent of the total; the remaining 2 percent was antimonial lead, imported from several countries.

The importers were requested to report the landed value of the metal imported exclusive of import duty. (The duty was suspended during part of 1952 and it was desirable to get the value of all imports on the same basis.) The average landed value, exclusive of import duty, of all grades of lead imported in 1952 was 15.3 cents a pound, and that of lead imported during the first 9 months of 1953, 12.0 cents. The import duty (116 cents per pound on the lead content) if applied to all of the imports would have raised these unit values to almost 16%

cents and 13 cents, respectively. The average New York market prices of Common lead were 16.467 cents during 1952 and 13.485 cents during the first 9 months of 1953. (An additional one-tenth cent a pound should be added for Corroding grade.)

The average landed value (exclusive of duty) of imports in 1952 was highest for antimonial lead, 16.0 cents a pound, and lowest for Common grade lead, 14.6 cents a pound. The average for Corroding grade lead imported in 1952 was 15.3 cents. The average landed value (exclusive of duty) of imports during the first 9 months of 1953 was 12.1 cents a pound for Corroding grade lead, 12.3 cents for Common grade lead, and 14.8 cents for antimonial lead.

The United States is the market in most years for most of the lead produced in Mexico, Canada, and Peru, and for a substantial part of the output of Australia and Yugoslavia. During the 5 years 1948-52 the quantity of unmanufactured lead imported from Mexico amounted to about 60 percent of Mexico's mine output, and that from Canada, to 56 percent of Canada's mine output. Imports from other countries during 1948-52 were equal to the following percentages of their mine production: 61 percent for Peru, 39 percent for Yugoslavia, 18 percent for Australia, and 50 percent for Bolivia.

Perhaps more than half the United States imports of unmanufactured lead are produced in foreign countries by companies controlled by United States concerns or by foreign companies in which United States corporations have a substantial financial interest. This is discussed more fully in part IV. Importers

Unmanufactured lead is imported into the United States by a relatively small number of importers. The great bulk of the lead in ores is imported by one large concern for smelting at two of the country's large lead smelters. Imports of refined lead and antimonial lead are also concentrated in the hands of a relatively small number of importers.

Imports of refined lead and antimonial lead in 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953 for which the Commission received reports from importers accounted for 77 percent of total imports, excluding those for United States Government use during this period. Of the imports so reported only 4 companies accounted for 98 percent of the total. 

United States exports 

United States exports of unmanufactured lead articles have been very small since the prewar years 1937-39, and exports of manufactured lead articles, though also small, have generally exceeded exports of lead in unmanufactured forms. The quantity and value of exports in 1952 of the lead articles covered in this investigation are compared with the quantity and value of production and imports of similar articles in table L-1. 

Exports of the unmanufactured lead articles were equal to only a fraction of 1 percent of domestic production in 1952; exports of lead pigments and babbitt metal and solder were similarly small, although exports of lead pigments exceeded imports. Exports of lead sheets, pipe, etc., in 1952, which greatly exceeded imports, amounted to only about 2 percent of United States production. The general relationship between the volume of exports and domestic production and imports noted above for 1952 for the various lead articles is also apparent for other years (see table L-6 for unmanufactured lead, and tables 2, 3, and 4 in the statistical appendix for lead pigments, babbitt metal and solder, and lead sheets, pipe, etc., respectively).

In recent years the United States exported unmanufactured lead mostly to Canada (principally in lead ores) and (in the form of lead pigs, bars, and anodes, type metal, and antimonial lead) to Brazil, other South American countries, and the Philippine Republic. The principal markets for the manufactured lead articles have been the 

Latin American countries.

Drawback of import duties on imported lead contained in manufactured articles exported from the United States Some imported lead on which duties were paid is included in articles manufactured in the United States for export. The duties paid on such lead may be claimed as a refund (drawback) to the extent of 99 percent of the duties paid when the articles are exported. CHAPTER V UNITED STATES CONSUMPTION OF LEAD 

The principal uses and properties of lead, the forms in which it is consumed, and the general trend of lead consumption in the United States compared with that in other countries were discussed briefly in chapters I and III of part II of this report. In this chapter the trends of lead consumption in the major uses are considered, as well as some of the factors affecting these trends, such as competition with substitute materials, and technological changes.

139

Much of the lead used in most applications is recovered as scrap. 

Principal dissipative uses of lead are in tetraethyl lead and lead pigments. It is estimated that about 85 percent of the lead in scrapped batteries is recovered. Much of the lead used in cable coverings, buildings (in lead sheet, pipes, etc.), bearings, type, brass, and other uses is also eventually recovered. Storage batteries last about 2 years and type metal is reused more frequently. In other important applications the use cycle of lead is much longer.

Because of lead's resistance to corrosion, relatively low melting point, and high recoverability, as well as the large quantity of lead in use especially in storage batteries, which have a comparatively short use cycle, the tonnage of lead recovered annually from old scrap in the United States is much larger in relation to newly mined metal than that of any other major nonferrous metal. Lead from used batteries is the source of most of the lead produced from old scrap in this country; the battery plates alone (probably with the yokes and clamps) account for nearly 60 percent of the lead recovered from old scrap.

Also closely related to the automobile use of lead is lead used for tetraethyl lead, an antiknock agent in gasoline. In the last 6 years, an average of 121,700 tons of lead or 11 percent of the total was consumed in tetraethyl lead manufacture. This use of lead, like that in batteries, is closely associated with the use of motor vehicles. Since the United States leads all countries in motor-vehicle traffic, this fact explains in large measure the relatively large quantity of lead consumed in the United States for this use compared with that so consumed in other countries.16 Data for the United Kingdom, for example, show that much more lead in that country is consumed for cable making and for lead sheet and pipe than for batteries or for tetraethyl lead.

The manufacture of cable covering required 144,700 tons of lead per year in the last 6 years. This use accounted for 13 percent of total consumption during the 6 years. Lead sheathing is used for all kinds of cable telephone, public utility, marine, and industrialalthough, as indicated later, it is meeting competition from substitute materials, especially for light-duty communication cable. Lead sheathing is pliable; easily reeled, joined, and repaired; highly resistant to corrosion and moisture penetration; and easily applied by extrusion over insulated conductors. Its great weight per unit of length retards its use in aerial cable as compared with underground installations. 

The fourth largest use of lead is in paint pigments, including red lead and litharge (except that used in batteries), white lead, pigment color, and miscellaneous compounds, as a group. Paint-pigment manufactures during the last 6 years consumed 132,900 tons of lead, or 12 percent of the total lead consumption. Litharge, other than for batteries, is used principally in the ceramics industry. Red lead is used primarily in paints as a rust-inhibiting primer coating on fabricated steel structures. White lead is consumed primarily in making white paint, especially for painting outside wooden surfaces. 

Lead used in construction, including calking lead, and lead in pipes, traps, bends, and sheets, as a group, accounted for 106,500 tons per year, or 9 percent of the total lead consumed during 1948-53. Calking 

16 Also, large-volume production and process improvements have permitted the price of tetraethyl lead to be reduced since 1939.

141 lead is used mostly in molten form but also in the form of lead wool for calking joints of cast-iron pipe, principally in municipal watersupply and sewage-disposal systems. The softness of lead permits some joint deformation resulting from ground movement or subsidence, and its low melting temperature facilitates its use for installation and repair of pipelines. Lead wool (loosely twisted strands of metallic lead), which requires no heat for calking, can be used for repairs of lines under water or where heat (as in the repair of gas lines) might be hazardous. Lead in pipes, traps, and bends is used for waste-disposal systems in building construction. Lead sheet is also used in buildings for flashings, gutters, and roofing, and in many applications where its use is desired to prevent moisture penetration, deaden sound, prevent vibration, or handle corrosive chemicals, especially sulfuric acid. The softness and pliability of lead facilitates its use for these purposes.

Of the remaining uses of lead, the most important in terms of quantities consumed in the United States in recent years are solder, ammunition, bearing metals, and type metal. In the last 6 years the annual consumption of lead for solder was 76,700 tons (7 percent of the total), for ammunition 38,700 tons (3 percent), for bearing metals 36,800 tons (3 percent), and for type metal 25,700 tons (2 percent).

Solder, usually an alloy of lead and tin, is used primarily in the canning industry (principally for soldering side seams of cans) and in the automobile industry (principally in the production of automobile radiators). Solder is also used extensively in joining metals in electrical appliances. The alloy of lead and tin in soft solder has a lower melting temperature than either pure lead or tin. The extensive use of soft solder is owing largely to this property as well as to the fact that soft solder of lead and tin adheres readily to other metal surfaces. The low melting temperature is important to prevent damage to the tin coating on cans. 

Lead in ammunition is used primarily in shot and bullet cores for use principally in small arms. Some chemical compounds of lead are also used in ammunition. Many desirable properties of lead contribute to its usefulness in ammunition, including its high density, low melting point, and proper surface tension essential for making spherical pellets for shot, and its softness, which permits easy forming of lead into bullet cores and also avoids abrasion of gun barrels. 

Bearing metal, also frequently called babbitt metal, is used to reduce friction between sliding metal surfaces. The great bulk of the leadbase bearing metal (about 14 percent tin, 8 percent antimony, and the rest lead) is used in railroad freight cars where the stationary bearing presses upon the revolving wheel axle. The lead-base bearing with the alloying elements in it has high resistance to compression, while its softness and plasticity reduce wear of the hard-to-replace axle or shaft. Worn bearings, which are bonded to harder bearing shells, are easily replaced, by melting and relining. 

Type metals, used for casting type for printing purposes, are leadbase alloys containing some antimony and tin (and for some purposes, also a little copper). They are used in linotype and similar typesetting machines, for casting stereotype plates (curved to fit the rolls of cylindrical printing presses), and for casting loose type. The combination of elements in the alloys permits them to be easily melted

at a practicable temperature, to have the great fluidity needed to bring out the fine details in type, to solidify almost instantly without shrinkage, and to remelt with low dross production.

Total consumption of lead in the United States in the prewar years. 

1937-39 was about 35 percent below the prewar peak consumption recorded in 1929. The quantity of lead consumed in 1953 was about 

21 percent larger than that consumed in 1929 and 87 percent larger than the average consumed in 1937-39.

Among the common uses of lead, the quantity consumed in 1953 for storage batteries, tetraethyl lead, calking, and solder was above the level of consumption for those uses in 1929 and 1937-39 by more-than-average percentages. Lead consumption for ammunition in 

1953 had increased above that in 1929 and the average for 1937-39, but by a much smaller percentage than that by which total consumption had increased between these periods for all uses combined. 

The consumption of lead in 1953 for white lead and for foil was far below the rate of consumption for these uses in either 1929 or 1937-39. 

Of the remaining uses, the consumption of lead for bearing metals and type metal declined between 1929 and 1937-39 and rose afterward to a higher level in 1953 than in 1929. The quantity of lead consumed in bearing metals in 1953 was 214 percent above the 1937-39 level but only 17 percent above that of 1929. The consumption of lead for type metal in 1953 was 85 percent above the average for the immediate prewar years and 47 percent above the 1929 consumption.

The quantity of lead consumed in cable covering and in lead sheet, pipe, and bends also declined between 1929 and 1937-39 and rose between 1937-39 and 1953, but the rise was not to so high a level as in 1929; the 1953 level of consumption for cable covering was 95 per-

cent above the 1937-39 average, while the quantity of lead consumed in 1953 for lead sheet, pipe, and bends was only 33 percent above the average for 1937-39. The consumption of lead in the manufacture of red lead and litharge increased over the entire period from 1929 to 1953, but the rise between 1929 and 1937-39 (163 percent) was much greater than the increase (51 percent) between 1937-39 and 1953. 

Some of the principal developments affecting the trends of lead consumption for individual uses are discussed in the following pages. 

Storage batteries.-The increased use of lead-acid batteries in the 

United States has paralleled the growth in the use of motor vehicles. 

Some improvements in battery design are being made that tend to reduce the lead content and prolong battery life. Also some automobiles have been equipped recently with 12-volt batteries instead of the usual 6-volt batteries; although the 12-volt batteries use about one-third more lead per battery, their life is longer so that this development may not result in an overall increase in lead consumption for batteries.

A new type of storage battery using nickel and cadmium has been announced recently by a United States manufacturer and may offer some competition for the lead-acid battery, provided sufficient quantities of nickel and cadmium are available to permit their large-scale manufacture. Over 500,000 units of this battery have been sold to the United States Armed Forces. It is claimed that this battery is one-third to one-half the size of lead-acid batteries, that it will last the life of the automobile, that it will give service at very low temperatures, and that it is very rugged, requires little care, and has other advantages. Its chief disadvantage is that its price may be 2 to 5 times that of a standard lead-acid battery."7 

Tetraethyl lead. The growth in the use of lead for this antiknock ingredient in gasoline (for motor vehicles and airplanes) is most conspicuous. This use of lead, unknown 30 years ago, accounted for the consumption of more lead in 1953 than any other single use except storage batteries. An important influence in this growth is the trend in recent years in the manufacture of automobile engines with higher compression ratios requiring gasoline (with higher octane number) possessing antiknock characteristics. Although no satisfactory substitute has been found for tetraethyl lead, the use of it may be retarded by improved refinery techniques making available higher octane fuel without tetraethyl lead and by technological developments reducing the need for high-octane gasoline, both by improved internal-combustion-engine design and by increased use of diesel engines in trucks and of turbojet engines in airplanes. 

Cable covering. Since 1937-39, the consumption of lead for cable sheathing has increased at a more rapid rate than total lead consumption, but the use of lead for this purpose is not now so great as it was in 1929. Lead sheathing is meeting strong competition, especially for low-voltage power cable and for some telephone cable, from plastics, aluminum, and combinations of plastics and aluminum. Also, the use of cable with thinner lead sheathing over polyethylene insulation tends to reduce consumption of lead per length of cable.

Aluminum sheathing has been introduced to a greater extent in Europe than in this country. Aluminum cable covering is stronger, 17 A new method of directly converting rays from radioactive atoms to electricity has been developed recently on an experimental basis. What this might lead to in the future use of lead in storage batteries is at least interesting to contemplate.

harder, and much lighter than lead (a given volume of lead weighs about 4.2 times as much as the same volume of aluminum). The light weight of aluminum is an important advantage for aerial cable suspended on poles. Also, a pound of aluminum at the price of 21% cents will cover with the same thickness of aluminum more than four times the length of cable that can be covered with a pound of lead at a price of 13 cents a pound. However, lead possesses certain properties, previously mentioned, which give lead sheathing inherent advantages over aluminum-among them the ease with which it can be fabricated, reeled, joined, and repaired. 

The growth in the use of lead in cable covering is also being retarded by the development since World War II of microwave long-distance communication systems that do not use cable. 

Calking lead. This use of lead is 1 of the 3 that have shown the most rapid growth since 1937-39. Competition from various nonmetallic jointing materials has not been sufficient to retard this growth.

Lead sheet, pipe, and bends.-The quantities of lead used in the form of sheet, pipe, and bends in buildings and construction, although one-third larger than in 1937-39, are substantially below the quantities consumed in these forms in the late 1920's. Lead for building construction has met with strong competition from cast iron, steel, copper, and brass, and more recently from aluminum and plastics. The use of sheet lead in chemical plants is meeting with competition from such materials as glass, ceramics, stainless steel, Monel metal, and reinforced plastics, and its use for this purpose may be retarded also because of development of chemical manufacturing processes that require less corrosion-resistant material of all kinds. 

Red lead and litharge.-Available statistics do not segregate the consumption of lead for red lead from the lead consumed in litharge.

The consumption of lead for red lead and for litharge other than that which is used in storage batteries has not increased since the late 

1930's as rapidly as total lead consumption. Red lead competes to some extent with zinc chromate. Litharge other than that used in batteries is used in ceramics (where it competes with lithium chemicals), for making lead arsenate (a use which has been seriously retarded by the advent of organic insecticides, such as DDT), and in treating gasolines to remove disagreeable odor (a use that is declining because of new processes).

White lead. The annual consumption of lead for making white lead for paint has declined since 1925-29 by more than 100,000 tons. 

White lead has met with serious competition from titanium dioxide pigments, which are cheaper. 

Solder. The use of lead for solder has increased since 1937-39 more rapidly than any other use except tetraethyl lead. Although the amount of solder used per tin can or per automobile radiator is being reduced by improvements in manufacture and design, the total consumption for this use is high because the number of tin cans and automobile radiators produced is large. 

Ammunition. The consumption of lead for ammunition is greatly affected by wars. The quantity so used during the war year 1943 amounted to 178,000 tons compared with only 43,800 tons in 1953. 

In peacetime, the nonmilitary use of lead for ammunition is greatly influenced by the amount of activity in hunting and target shooting.

Bearing metals. The use of lead for bearings has increased rapidly since 1937-39. Makers of ball and roller bearings have been making strenuous efforts to displace babbitt bearings and have succeeded in doing so in new railroad passenger cars. Only slight use has been made so far of ball or roller bearings in freight cars. Ball and roller bearings generate less friction and permit greater speeds a more important consideration for passenger cars than for freight cars. 

Recent reductions in the thickness of bearings have operated to curtail the consumption of lead per railroad car journal assembly. 

Type metal. The rate of increase in the annual consumption of lead for type métal since prewar years has been about the same as the rate of increase in total lead consumption. Lead-base type metal has many superior qualities, previously mentioned, that cannot be readily matched by substitute materials. Nevertheless some type metal has been supplanted by the use of magnesium, plastic, and rubber plates, and perhaps even more, by the development of new methods of printing and reproduction such as the photo-offset and varitype processes. 

Lead foil.-Lead foil is included in this discussion, despite the small quantity of lead consumed in its production in recent years, because it accounted for a large consumption of lead in the 1920's and it is thus a prime example of a use of lead that has been largely supplanted by a competing substitute. Before World War II almost all cigarettes in this country were wrapped in "tin" foil, which is lead foil with a flash of tin coating over it. The use of lead foil for cigarette packaging was prohibited by the Government during the war, and the production of lead foil was severely curtailed as a result. The use of lead foil remained low after the war, while that of aluminum, less expensive than lead foil, increased sharply.¹ 

Other uses, including new uses 18 

Consumption of lead in the "all other" use classification in 1953 (114,000 tons) was about 121 percent above the average for this group of uses in 1937-39 (51,500 tons). Data on consumption of lead in these uses in years before 1948 are not available. Statistics for the period since 1948 (see table L-14) indicate that these uses include principally lead for brass and bronze, miscellaneous pigments, casting metals, collapsible tubes, weights and ballast, miscellaneous chemicals, annealing, and "other uses, unclassified." Between 1948 and 1953 the consumption of lead remained nearly the same for brass and bronze and collapsible tubes; decreased for miscellaneous pigments and chemicals and annealing; and increased for casting metals, weights, and ballast, and "other uses, unclassified." The latter category, which accounted for about 16,000 tons of lead in 1953, probably includes some of the new uses of lead, which, as this figure indicates, do not yet account for much of the consumption of lead.

As noted in chapter I, part II, lead possesses the unique property of being impenetrable to atomic radiation. For this reason it is very valuable for shielding against the dangerous rays emitted by radioactive substances. No information is available on the quantity of lead consumed for this purpose. The unclassified uses mentioned above do not necessarily include lead used for such shielding, since 18 Although separate statistics on the consumption of lead for collapsible tubes are not available for the years before 1948, trade data indicate that lead for this purpose has also been largely displaced by aluminum. 46566-54- -11

this lead may be otherwise classified, for example, as "sheet lead." 

This country, it appears, is on the verge of a great transition from the production of atomic energy and products for defense purposes to the production of atomic energy and radioactive products for peacetime applications. Already thousands of shipments are being made of radioactive isotopes, many of which require shielding such as provided by lead. If mobile atomic powerplants are developed and used in large numbers, much lead may be needed to shield them. 

In recent years lead has been employed successfully as a stabilizer against heat and light in polyvinyl plastics. These plastics are used for insulation, floor and furniture coverings, shower curtains, and many other applications. Although lead constitutes only 1% to 2% percent of the weight of polyvinyls using lead stabilizers, the use of plastics is growing rapidly and the need for lead in their manufacture may grow likewise.

Lead imparts useful qualities to glass and has long been used in making leaded glass to obtain greater brilliance and facilitate glass cutting. Some of the characteristics of leaded glass-electrical resis tivity, greater density, and higher light dispersion are desired in the glass used for television picture tubes, which contain up to 30 percent lead by weight. The television industry is a rapidly growing one and hence probably a potential market for large quantities of lead compounds.

It is apparent that both economic and technologic developments profoundly affect the volume of lead consumed in its numerous and varied uses. Research and publicity regarding its useful properties and their applications, as compared with those of competing materials, are important in this connection.

CHAPTER I DESCRIPTION AND USES OF ZINC ARTICLES 

Zinc is one of the more common and widely used nonferrous metals and is consumed in large quantities in the manufacture of many kinds of metal products. In 1953 the consumption of zinc in the United 

States was only slightly smaller than that of lead, which was exceeded only by that of iron and steel, copper, and aluminum. 

The commercial importance of zinc is based largely upon its properties as a corrosion inhibitor, especially as a protective coating on steel in galvanized products, and upon its use in nonferrous alloys. Zinc is used in the production of an extremely wide variety of military and essential civilian products, and is included in the stockpiling program of the United States Government as a strategic and critical material. 

Most of the zinc consumed in the United States is in the form of slab zinc as recovered from ores by smelting or electrolytic refining and, to a relatively small extent, from scrap. Of the total quantity of zinc consumed in the United States during the period 1948-52, about 87 percent was consumed in the form of slab (including primary and secondary slab zinc) and 12 percent represented the zinc content of zinc pigments and salts produced from ore without its first being reduced to slab.

The largest use of zinc is normally in the galvanizing of iron or steel in order to increase resistance to corrosion. Zinc coating or galvanizing is applied to a great tonnage of steel products of many types and is the most economical means of corrosion protection available. 

The most pronounced development in recent years in the consumption of slab zinc has been its increased use in zinc-base alloys for die castings. Zinc-base alloys accounted for the second largest use of slab zinc in all postwar years. The automobile industry is the largest user of zinc-base alloys, principally for die-cast parts and assemblies for pumps, carburetors, radiator grills, and so forth. Zinc diecastings are used in a great variety of items such as vacuum cleaners, washing machines, gasoline pumps, recording machines, and hardware.

Brass products accounted for the third largest use of slab zinc in 1952. Brass finds a major wartime use in cartridge and shell casings and has a multitude of civilian uses. 

Rolled zinc, used for dry batteries, photoengraving plates, and other products, ranked fourth in importance in the utilization of slab zinc. 

In summary, of the total consumption of slab zinc (including zinc slab from secondary sources and imported slab zinc) in the United States in 1952, 44 percent was used by galvanizers, 28 percent in zinc-base alloys used predominantly in zinc die castings, 18 percent in brass products, 6 percent in rolled zinc, and the remaining 4 percent in miscellaneous other products, principally zinc oxide. 

Zinc articles covered in this investigation This investigation relates primarily to unmanufactured zinc articles in various forms, especially to zinc in zinc-bearing ores and zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs provided for in paragraphs 393 and 394, respectively, 149

.150

of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended. Consideration is also given, however, to related manufactured zinc articles such as lithopone and zinc oxide covered in paragraph 77 and some manufactured articles also covered in paragraph 394. 

Paragraph 77 covers lithopone and other combinations or mixtures of zinc sulfide and barium sulfate, and zinc oxide and leaded zinc oxide containing not over 25 percent lead. Lithopone, which is a white pigment made by coprecipitating barium sulfate and zinc sulfide, is used principally as an ingredient of interior paints and to a less extent as a filler in linoleum and textiles. It is also used as a filler in rubber goods and paper and in the manufacture of printing ink. Normal-strength lithopone, which accounts for the bulk of domestic production, contains about 20 percent zinc; high-strength lithopone may contain up to about 34 percent zinc. 

Zinc oxide is a white pigment used principally in the manufacture of rubber tires and other rubber products and of paints and enamels, as a filler in floor coverings and textiles, and in products of the ceramics industry. Zinc oxide covered by paragraph 77 may have a zinc content ranging from about 54 to 80 percent. Both lithopone and zinc oxide are manufactured from a variety of zinc-bearing materials, including ore, refined metal and secondary materials. The zinc contained in lithopone produced in the United States, however, in recent years was derived principally from secondary materials whereas that in zinc oxide came principally directly from ore (mostly domestic). 

Paragraph 393 covers zinc-bearing ores of all kinds, except pyrites containing not over 3 percent zinc. The most important imported zinc material, from the standpoint of zinc content, is zinc-bearing ore, which comprises chiefly zinc concentrates (most of the waste material having been removed from the crude ore at the mines and associated mills). Zinc-ore deposits in the principal countries exporting zincbearing ores to the United States contain from about 4 to 12 percent zinc. In 1952, according to reports from smelters who accounted for about 60 percent of the total receipts of zinc in ore in that year, the zinc-bearing ores and concentrates imported into the United States for smelting averaged about 55 percent zinc, of which close to 90 percent was recoverable by the smelters processing this foreign ore. 

Paragraph 394 covers zinc in blocks, pigs, or slabs, zinc dust, zinc sheets, and zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings. From the standpoint of imports, zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs are by far the most important of the items covered by this paragraph. 

Slab zinc generally contains from about 98 to 100 percent zinc and is generally produced and marketed in the United States in six standard grades as follows:

Most of the Special High Grade zinc consumed in the United States is used in the production of zinc die castings, the remainder being used by other industries, especially brass manufacture and electrogalvanizing. Other grades of zinc are generally not suitable for the

78 manufacture of zinc die castings. A large part of the imports of slab zinc in 1952 and January-September 1953 were of that grade. 

Regular High Grade zinc is consumed principally in the manufacture of brass and rolled zinc, and in electrogalvanizing. Intermediate,

Brass Special, and Selected zinc are consumed largely in the production of rolled zinc, in galvanizing, and in brass manufacture. Prime 

Western zinc is used very largely in galvanizing, and that grade supplies the great bulk of the zinc requirements of the galvanizing industry. Prime Western is the principal grade used in the hot-dip process; the higher grades used in galvanizing are used chiefly in the electrogalvanizing process. 

Zinc dust, containing from 85 to 98 percent zinc, is used in metal primers and other metal-protective paints, in sherardizing (a process for coating metal surfaces), as a deoxidizing agent in chemical manufacture, and for other purposes.

Zinc sheet, produced from slab zinc, is used for dry-cell battery containers, fruit-jar caps, photoengraving plates, and for other purposes.

Zinc scrap is derived from a variety of sources such as zinc clippings, engraving plates, discarded die castings, and dry-cell battery cases. 

Zinc dross is the sludge recovered from galvanizing pots, and skimmings are the impurities removed from the surface of the molten zinc during galvanizing operations. Secondary zinc metal is recovered by remelting and refining or by redistilling scrap, dross, and skimmings. 

Dross and skimmings are also used directly in the manufacture of pigments and zinc dust.

Of the above-named articles, zinc-bearing ores (in par. 393), zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs, and zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings (in par. 

394) are referred to collectively throughout this report as unmanufactured zinc.

Relative importance of imports of zinc articles Of all the articles covered by paragraphs 77, 393, and 394, unmanufactured zinc articles (zinc ore, zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs, and zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings) are by far the most important in terms of quantity and value of imports. In 1952 (see table Z-1) unmanufactured zinc articles accounted for 99.9 percent of the total value of imports of all zinc articles provided for in these paragraphs. Zincbearing ores accounted for 75.5 percent of the value of all zinc articles covered; zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs, for 24.0 percent; and zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings, for 0.4 percent. Imports of zinc oxide, lithopone, dust, and sheets combined accounted for only about 0.1 percent. 

Although imports of zinc articles other than unmanufactured zinc were greater during the period January-September 1953 than for the year 1952, such imports were still relatively very small, accounting for less than one-half of 1 percent of the total value of imports of all the zinc articles covered during the 1953 period. Similarly, imports of zinc articles other than unmanufactured zinc have generally been small in relation to domestic production of such articles. Moreover, exports of such articles have generally exceeded imports. (See appendix tables 32 and 33.)

The import duty now in effect on zinc-bearing ores and concentrates (dutiable under par. 393) is six-tenths cent per pound of zinc content, and that on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs (dutiable under par. 394) is seven-tenths cent per pound of gross weight. These rates (which are 

60 percent below the 1930 rates) were established under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) negotiated at Torquay, England, and became effective on June 6, 1951. The rates previously in effect, established under the trade agreement with Mexico, effective

January 30, 1943, were three-fourths cent per pound of zinc content of zinc-bearing ores and concentrates, and seven-eighths cent per pound of gross weight of zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs; these rates, 50 percent below the rates established under the Tariff Act of 1930, were bound in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade at Geneva in 1948, and thus they remained in force until June 6, 1951, even though the trade agreement with Mexico was terminated at the end of 1950. 

The import duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings, which was suspended until June 30, 1953, by Public Law 535 (82d Cong.), is three-fourths cent per pound of gross weight. This duty, which is 50 percent below the rate provided under the Tariff Act of 1930, was established by the trade agreement with Mexico and bound at Geneva in 1948.

The current rate of duty on zinc dust (dutiable under par. 394) is seven-tenths cent per pound of gross weight. This rate, which reflects a reduction of 60 percent from the 1930 rate, became effective June 6, 1951, pursuant to a concession in the GATT (Torquay). 

The current rate of duty on zinc sheets coated or plated with nickel or other metal (except gold, platinum, or silver), or solutions (dutiable under par. 394) is 1% cents per pound of gross weight. This rate, which reflects a reduction of 50 percent from the 1930 rate, became effective January 30, 1943, pursuant to the trade agreement with Mexico, and was bound at Geneva in 1948. 

The current rate of duty on other zinc sheets (dutiable under par. 

394) is 1 cent per pound of gross weight. This rate, which reflects a reduction of 50 percent from the 1930 rate, also became effective January 30, 1943, pursuant to the trade agreement with Mexico, and was bound at Geneva in 1948.

Differential between the rates of duty on zinc-bearing ores and zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs

The rate of duty currently applicable to zinc-bearing ores (six-tenths cent per pound on the zinc content) is equal to about 86 percent of the current rate of duty on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs (seven-tenths cent per pound). This differential between the two rates of duty is thus proportionate to that provided in the Tariff Act of 1930, in which the rate of duty on zinc-bearing ores (1½ cents per pound on the zinc content) was also equal to about 86 percent of the duty on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs (14 cents per pound).

This differential of 86 percent approximately compensated for metallurgical losses in converting ore to slab zinc and was about equal to the average percentage of zinc content recovered from ores processed by zinc smelters and refineries in the United States at the time of the enactment of the Tariff Act of 1930. In comparison, data obtained by the Tariff Commission in this investigation show that in 1952 and the first three quarters of 1953 the average recovery factor of the zinc smelters and refineries in the United States which consumed imported zinc ores was about 91 percent (taking into account the quantities of zinc in ores imported by the various zinc smelters and refineries and their approximate recovery experience). 

This higher recovery of zinc contained in ores processed reflects increased efficiency in smelting and refining at individual operations in the United States over the past two decades, as well as the substantial increase in the proportion of total slab-zinc output produced by electrolytic zinc plants, which on the average recover a larger

proportion of the zinc content of materials processed than is recovered by other plants. In addition to initial zinc-metal recoveries at smelters and refineries, it may be noted, there has been a substantial increase in the amount of zinc recovered in the United States from the residues of zinc smelters by treatment in Waelz kilns and from lead-smelter slag by treatment in slag-fuming plants. 

Rates of duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings The rates of duty originally provided for under the Tariff Act of 1930 on (1) zinc-bearing ores and (2) zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings were both 12 cents per pound, but the rate on ores was applicable to zinc content and the rate on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings was applicable to gross weight. The 1930 rate on scrap, dross, and skimmings was about 86 percent of the rate (14 cents per pound) on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs. Since 1930, the rate on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings which continues applicable to the gross weight of these articles has been reduced 50 percent, whereas the duties on zincbearing ores and on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs have been reduced 60 percent. As a result, the rate of duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings-which are crude raw materials-now exceeds that on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs by about 7 percent.

The import classification "zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings" includes articles that vary widely in zinc content. For example, it is estimated that the zinc content of zinc skimmings may be either about 50 or 75 percent (depending upon type of skimmings), while that of zinc dross may range from about 90 to 95 percent, and that of miscellaneous zinc scrap from 90 to 99 percent. The proportion of the zinc content of each of these materials recovered in processing also is different, and currently is understood to be about 85 to 90 percent for zinc skimmings, over 80 percent for zinc dross, and about 90 percent for miscellaneous zinc scrap. Information is not available on the relative change in metallurgical recovery of zinc from scrap between 1930 and the present time, but judging from the progress made in increasing recovery of zinc from ores, the percentage of recovery of zinc from scrap, dross, and skimmings has probably been upward, not downward. For these reasons no specific rate of duty per pound of gross weight on imports of zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings could be established which would have a uniform relationship to the recoverable zinc content of these materials, or to the present duties on zinc metal and zinc ores. It is noted that a rate of duty on zinc scrap, dross, and skimmings that would be applicable on the basis of zinc content, and that would be related to the duties either on zinc ore or on zinc metal, would reduce possible inequality in the tariff structure.

The average ad valorem equivalent of the 1930 rates of duty for all unmanufactured zinc articles is 67.2 percent, based on import values in 1939. The average ad valorem equivalent of the current (1954) rates of duty (which reflect trade concessions) is 8.2 percent, based on import values in the first 9 months of 1953. This reduction in the ad valorem equivalent of the duty is due to the fact that the foreign value of imports per pound of zinc increased 226 percent, while the specific rates of duty on zinc ores and on zinc blocks, pigs, or slabs decreased 60 percent. The ad valorem equivalents of the 1930 and the current rates of duty based on import values in 1952 are lower than those based on import values in the first 9 months of 1953 because unit import values were higher in 1952 than in 1953.

Of the total imports of unmanufactured zinc during the period 1937-39, only 8 percent (representing principally zinc ore for smelting, refining, and export) were free of duty. During World War II, however, when imports were greatly expanded, almost all of them (98 percent in 1943) entered free of duty, largely for United States Government use (for stockpiling and for distribution to consumers). 

During the postwar period 1946-51 duty-free imports declined considerably from the wartime level, but nonetheless accounted for 22 percent of total imports during those years. Of the total imports during this period, imports entered free for Government use accounted for about 5 percent, duty-free imports of ore for smelting, refining, and export accounted for 16 percent, and duty-free scrap for about 1 percent. The duty on zinc scrap was suspended by a series of public

laws for the greater part of the entire period from March 14, 1942, to June 30, 1953. To encourage imports of zinc, the import duties were suspended on zinc ore and slab zinc from February 12, 1952, to 

July 23, 1952 (Public Law 258, 82d Cong.).¹ During 1952, 86 percent of the total imports of unmanufactured zinc entered free of duty; the bulk of these imports consisted of zinc ore imported under the provisions of Public Law 258. In 1953 imports free of duty again declined sharply, accounting for only 6 percent of total imports of unmanufactured zinc during the year and consisting principally of imports free for Government use and for smelting, refining, and export. 

Detailed data on imports of unmanufactured zinc, by customs treatment, during 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953 are shown in appendix table 47.

Trade-agreement commitments with respect to duties on zinc The current rates of duty on all the zinc articles covered in this investigation are reduced rates made effective by Presidential proclamations as a result of concessions granted by the United States in GATT. These trade-agreement concessions are subject to the escape clause of GATT, which permits the withdrawal or modification of trade-agreement concessions under the conditions specified in section 

7 of the Trade Agreements Extension Act of 1951 (Public Law 50, 

82d Cong.). Section 7 established procedures for invoking the escape clause of trade agreements whenever a product upon which a tradeagreement concession has been granted is, as a result, in whole or in part, of the duty or other customs treatment reflecting such conces sion, being imported into the United States in such increased quantities, either actual or relative, as to cause or threaten serious injury to the domestic industry producing like or directly competitive products.

Table Z-4 shows the maximum rates of duty which could be imposed as the result of escape-clause action with respect to the zinc articles covered by the investigation, compared with the original rates of duty provided in the Tariff Act of 1930 and with the current rates. 

These maximum rates would represent increases of 200 percent over present rates for zinc ores, zinc slab, and zinc scrap (as well as all other zinc articles covered by pars. 393 and 394), as compared with a possible increase of 140 percent for lead-bearing ores and for lead bullion and lead pigs and bars. 

1 Public Law 258 (82d Cong.), which provided for the termination of the suspension with the close of

The average market price for the calendar month of June 1952 dropped below 18 cents and the suspension was terminated July 23, 1952.

In comparison with the 1930 rates, the maximum rates of duty possible for zinc-bearing ores and for zinc slab would represent increases of 20 percent, while that for zinc scrap would represent an increase of 50 percent.

With reference to the articles in paragraph 77, the maximum rate possible (based on a 50-percent increase in the rate of duty existing on January 1, 1945) on zinc oxide in any form of dry powder would represent an increase of 175 percent over the current rate; 2 that on zinc oxide ground or mixed with oil or water, an increase of 125 percent; that on lithopone containing less than 30 percent zinc sulfide, an increase of 157 percent; and that on lithopone containing 30 percent or more zinc sulfide, an increase of 200 percent.

The maximum rates possible as a result of escape-clause action (shown in table Z-4) represent the rates "existing on January 1, 1945" plus 50 percent of those rates. For the zinc articles in paragraph 77, the rates "existing on January 1, 1945" were the rates actually assessed on that date, but for the zinc articles in paragraphs 393 and 394 they were not the same. The actual rates assessed on the articles in paragraphs 393 and 394 were reduced emergency rates made effective pursuant to concessions granted in the trade agreement with Mexico. 

This agreement, however, provided for higher post-emergency rates, and it is these higher rates which, under the provisions of section 350 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, determine the rates "existing on January 1, 1945" for the purpose of computing the maximum rates possible under escape-clause action.

The ad valorem equivalent of the maximum rates possible for the unmanufactured zinc articles would average 24.7 percent, based on import values in the first 9 months of 

1953; the ad valorem equivalent of the 1930 rates of duty on these articles averaged 67.2 percent, based on import values in 1939. 

As previously mentioned, the present rates of duty applicable to lead and zinc ores and metal are now the subject of tariff commitments under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). Any changes in the tariff treatment of imports now subject to these commitments would contravene international obligations of the United States unless made consistently with the provisions of the agreement. 

Of the contracting parties to GATT, Canada, Peru, and Australia would probably be the countries principally concerned. Although the 

United States has no specific obligations to Mexico or Yugoslavia with respect to the tariff treatment applicable to United States imports of lead and zinc ores and metal, these countries would also have an important interest in such a matter. 

With regard to changes in tariff treatment that might be made pursuant to the provisions of GATT, possible action is not limited to that taken under the standard escape clause of the agreement (art. 

XIX). For example, article XXI of GATT provides that any contracting party may takeany action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests *** taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations.

If during an emergency in international relations the United States were to impose on imports of lead and zinc additional restrictions that it declared to be necessary for the protection of its essential security interests, such restrictions would not be contrary to the provisions of GATT.

As noted above, under this general exception in the GATT, the United States would be free, in time of war or other emergency in international relations, to impose on imports of lead and zinc any restrictions that it considered necessary for the protection of its essential security interests. The exception appears in article XXI of the 

GATT, which provides in pertinent part that— Nothing in this agreement shall be construed * * * to prevent any contracting party from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests *** taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations. [Emphasis supplied.] 46566-54 -12

Accordingly, if legislation imposing increased import restrictions on lead and zinc contained a recital to the effect that an emergency in international relations exists and that the imposition of the import restrictions provided for in the legislation is necessary for the protection of the essential security interests of the United States, the restrictions imposed by such legislation would not be inconsistent with United States commitments in the GATT. It would seem necessary that such a recital would have to be predicated, of course, upon a determination made in good faith that the additional import restrictions on lead and zinc were necessary to protect the essential security interests of the United States and upon the existence of an emergency in international relations such as is contemplated by article XXI.3 

CHAPTER III 

UNITED STATES ZINC SUPPLY AND REQUIREMENTS GENERAL TREND OF PRODUCTION, FOREIGN TRADE, AND CONSUMPTION SINCE PREWAR YEARS 

Preceding World War II the United States was generally independent of foreign zinc supplies. During most of that time exports exceeded imports, usually by a small margin, and it was not until 1935 that the foreign-trade balance in zinc changed. In the period 1937-39 annual United States supply of zinc (domestic production plus net imports) was about 655,000 tons, of which 616,000 tons, or 94 percent, were supplied from domestic sources (mine output plus secondary metal) and the balance represented net imports. However, a substantial part of the imports of zinc in prewar years was regularly manufactured into articles exported with drawback of duty. Thus, although on balance the United States imported more zinc than it exported as such in this period, little foreign zinc was actually retained in this country.

During the war domestic consumption of zinc increased greatly, and in 1943 amounted to a little over 1 million tons. Imports 5 of $ Commissioner Edminster wishes to add the following observations: Whether Congress could, "in good faith," take such action in conformity with the provisions of art. XXI would, of course, be for the 

Congress to determine. Apart from any question as to the existence of an "emergency in international relations" within the meaning of art. XXI, the basic issue in such a determination would appear to be: (1) Whether the national security would be best served by the imposition of such import restrictions on lead and zinc, on the ground that such action is required in order to prevent such a deterioration of conditions in the industry as would create an undue hazard with respect to access to essential supplies in time of war; or (2) Whether, on the contrary, the national security would be best served by avoidance of such restrictions (or if such restrictions be regarded as necessary, the exercise of due restraint with respect to their severity and duration), in view of the extent to which the United States has come to rely upon imports to meet the normal increase in its peacetime requirements, of our greatly increased dependence on imports in time of war (as in World War II), and of the fact that such imports are available from already welldeveloped, economical, and nearby sources of supply on the North American Continent. 

In any case, should the Congress take such action, "good faith" in the matter would require that it recognize (1) that the other contracting parties to the GATT would carefully scrutinize any such action; (2) that, if satisfied that the action was not justified, they might invoke the "Nullification or Impairment" clause (art. XXIII); and (3) that this might lead to retaliatory action and possibly to complete withdrawal from the agreement.

Commissioner Ryder concurs in the above statement of Commissioner Edminster. In addition, he wishes to state that he doubts whether, as a matter of international comity, it would be advisable to invoke art. XXI merely through a "recital" in a preamble to legislation increasing import restrictions on one commodity or a group of related commodities. He feels that the GATT exception in question might well be interpreted as contemplating that it could be invoked only during an emergency in international relations which had previously been declared to exist by formal proclamation of the President or by appropriate legislative action such as a congressional joint resolution. 

4 Net inports, that is, imports minus exports, are used in order that the supply figure represent supply available for distribution in the United States. 

Throughout this report data on imports represent imports for consumption rather than general imports. 

The 2 measures do not give the same results in some periods. For a definition of imports for consumption and general imports, and for a comparison of monthly data for each in 1951 and 1952, see appendix table 43.

zinc, which reached their wartime peak in 1943, were equivalent to over 80 percent of domestic mine output in that year. During the war, the increase in imports (most of which entered free of duty for United States Government use) was very much greater than that in domestic production, and for the first time a large proportion of United States requirements for zinc was supplied by foreign countries. 

This condition has continued throughout the postwar period. 

Domestic consumption of zinc has continued at very high levels in the postwar years; during the period 1949-53 it averaged 1,059,000 tons annually. Of the total United States zinc supply (production plus net imports) in this period, about 55 percent came from domestic mines (as measured by recoverable zinc content of ores and concentrates), about 6 percent represented the zinc content of old scrap processed,' and 39 percent represented net imports of unmanufactured zinc. In comparison, during the period 1937-39 domestic mine output accounted for 88 percent of the total United States supply of zinc, old scrap for 6 percent, and net im ports for 6 percent (see table Z-6). Domestic consumption, which averaged 664,000 short tons annually during 1937-39, increased to 1,001,000 tons in 1946. After declining to 826,000 tons in 1949, consumption increased again to 1,126,000 tons in 1951, was about 1,023,000 tons in 1952, and is estimated to have amounted to 1,172,000 tons in 1953, a quantity 76 percent above the prewar annual average. Average annual consumption of zinc in the United States in 1949-53 was 59 percent greater than the average for 1937-39.

United States mine production of zinc, which averaged 576,000 tons annually in 1937-39, reached a wartime peak of 768,000 tons in 1942, but declined to 575,000 tons in 1946. Mine production was at its highest postwar level in 1951, when output totaled 681,000 tons. 

In 1952, however, production declined to 666,000 tons, and in 1953 it declined further to 535,000 tons. Thus, whereas United States consumption of zinc was 76 percent larger in 1953 than in the immediate prewar years, domestic mine production was 7 percent smaller. 

During the 5-year period 1949-53 as a whole, annual average mine output was about 8 percent above the prewar average. 

In 1952 imports of zinc were for the first time in excess of the peak wartime imports in 1943. In 1952 and 1953, imports of zinc, also for the first time, exceeded domestic mine output of recoverable zinc. Average annual imports of zinc in 1949-53 were about 11 times as large as average imports in 1937-39. 

Exports of unmanufactured zinc have consisted very largely of slab zinc smelted from ore imported free of duty for smelting, refining, and export. Exports were at their highest postwar level in 1947, when they totaled 108,000 tons, equivalent to 17 percent of domestic mine production. Exports in 1953 declined to 22,000 tons, equivalent to about 4 percent of mine output.

Primary domestic production may be measured also, with practically the same result, by adding to the quantity of slab zinc produced from domestic ores the zinc content of zinc pigments and salts produced directly from domestic ores and concentrates. 

7 In the 5-year period 1948-52 about 77 percent of the recoverable zinc content of all scrap processed was derived from new scrap. In order to avoid duplication, zinc contained in new scrap is not included in this measure of annual supply. Such new scrap includes such items as clippings and zinc dross and skimmings obtained in the process of fabricating or manufacturing zinc products. Annual figures on recoverable zinc contained in such new scrap processed represent duplication depending upon the number of times the same metal reappears as zinc in scrap in the course of a year. A large part of the total zinc content of scrap processed annually in the United States is in brass and bronze, this form of recovery accounting for about 60 percent of the total recoverable zinc in scrap processed in 1952. Zinc recovered in all forms from all scrap processed in the United States in 1952 was equivalent to 34 percent of the total United States output of primary slab zinc in that year.

In summary the principal change in the zinc-supply situation of the United States since prewar years has been a change from selfsufficiency to dependence on foreign sources for a large part of the total supply. 

United States and world trends of production and consumption Available statistics on world production and consumption of zinc are shown in appendix tables 49, 50, and 51.

World mine output of zinc in 1952, totaling about 2.8 million tons, is the highest on record and reflects a steady upward growth in postwar years. Peak wartime output in 1942 and 1943 averaged about 

2.3 million tons annually. Although the United States is still the world's largest producer of zinc in ore, its share of the world output

has shown a generally downward long-term trend. Whereas in the prewar period 1937-38 the United States accounted for 29 percent of the world mine output of zinc, in 1951 the proportion had decreased to 27 percent, and in 1952 to 24 percent. In comparison with an increase of 44 percent in world mine output of zinc in 1952 over the average for 1937-38, the increase in mine output in the United States during the same period was only 17 percent. In 1953 domestic mine output was down 6 percent from the 1937-38 average. 

Mine output of zinc in Canada, Mexico, and Peru, the principal sources of United States imports of zinc, shows substantial gains in recent years as compared with the immediate prewar period. In 1952 

Canada ranked second in importance to the United States as a producer of zinc in ore, followed by Mexico, Australia, and the U. S. S. R. 

The position of the United States as a producer of zinc metal, unlike its position as a producer of zinc ore, has increased in relative importance since the prewar period. The United States is by far the world's largest producer of slab zinc, accounting for close to twofifths of the world output of slab zinc in 1952, as compared with 29 percent of world output during the period 1937-38. 

World smelter output of primary zinc increased steadily in postwar years, and in 1952 it was 38 percent larger than the annual average output in 1937-38. Smelter output of primary zinc in the United 

States in 1952 was 80 percent larger than the annual average output in the United States in 1937-38.

Canada ranked second in importance to the United States in 1952 as a producer of zinc metal, followed by Belgium, the U. S. S. R., and 

West Germany. 

Just as the United States is the world's chief producer of slab zinc, it is likewise by far the world's largest consumer of zinc. In contrast with the declining relative importance of United States production of zinc in ore, United States consumption of primary zinc metal in relation to world consumption has increased since 1937. Whereas in the period 1937-38 the United States accounted for about 30 percent of total world consumption of zinc, and for 29 percent of world mine output of zinc, in 1952 it accounted for about 39 percent of world consumption but for only 24 percent of world mine output.

United States consumption of slab zinc in 1952 showed an increase of 65 percent over average annual consumption in the period 1937-38, as compared with an increase of only 9 percent for all other countries combined during the same period. Total world consumption in 1952 was 26 percent greater than the annual average consumption for 1937-38.

Although consumption of primary zinc metal in Western Europe (excluding the Soviet Union and the satellite countries) has grown substantially in the postwar years, it still is less than in years immediately before the war.

Changes in supply and demand before 1952 As previously noted, United States imports of zinc before World War II accounted for only a small part of the country's total supply of zinc, net imports in 1937-39 accounting for only about 6 percent of the total supply (domestic production plus net imports). Beginning in 1940, sharply increased demands for zinc in the United States to meet mounting military and industrial requirements necessitated a

large volume of imports. Domestic mine production of zinc, which averaged 576,000 tons annually in 1937-39, was considered insufficient to meet the estimated military and essential civilian needs, and domestic smelting capacity similarly was inadequate at the time to meet expected demands upon it. Measures were, therefore, taken by the 

United States Government to increase imports, particularly of ore, to expand or at least maintain domestic mine production, to expand smelter capacity, to establish a stockpile, and to control consumption and exports. The expansion of imports was undertaken partly by purchase agreements and partly by agreement with certain allied countries to divert to the United States a portion of the exports from Canada and Australia which had normally gone to the United Kingdom and Belgium.

The Government put into effect the premium price plan beginning on February 1, 1942, and extending to June 9, 1947. The principal purpose of the plan was to increase production from marginal or lowgrade ores, and to encourage reworking of old tailings. Under this plan mining concerns were paid premiums for above-quota production, in addition to the ceiling price of 84 cents a pound for Prime Western zinc, f. o. b. East St. Louis, fixed by the Government during the war. 

Some of the mines, the output of which was thus subsidized, were old properties which had been idle for many years. During the period the plan was in operation premiums averaging 4.067 cents per pound were paid on about 58 percent of the zinc produced by domestic mines.⁹

Mine output of zinc reached a wartime peak of 768,025 tons in 1942, but declined thereafter to 614,358 tons in 1945. By the end of 1943, domestic zinc-smelter capacity had reached a total of a little over 1 million tons, and production of primary slab zinc in that year amounted to 942,000 tons.

Imports of unmanufactured zinc increased to 608,551 tons in 1943, equivalent to 74 percent of that year's production of 828,000 tons (mine output plus secondary zine from old scrap). Reported consumption in that year was a little over 1 million tons. The large excess of imports plus production over reported consumption reflected additions to the Government stockpile and increased stocks in private hands. As previously noted, most of the wartime imports of zinc were entered free of duty for United States Government use. 

Zinc consumption in the United States, as used throughout this report, is "reported" consumption that is, consumption based largely on reports by individual consumers (and published by the American Bureau of Metal Statistics for the years 1937-39 and by the U. S. Bureau of Mines for 1943 and the years beginning with 1946). 

It does not include quantities going into Government or private stocks. Reported consumption differs from "supply" or "apparent" consumption, such as might be calculated by adding imports to production and subtracting exports. Reported consumption for a given year indicates the quantity of zinc actually used by consumers in the United States in that year whether from that year's supply or from stocks accumulated in previous years. Apparent consumption, Previously, beginning on September 24, 1940, zinc producers stabilized zinc prices at 74 cents a pound. 

In an effort to expand production, the Office of Price Administration set the price ceiling on October 9, 1941, at 84 cents.

U.S. Bureau of Mines, History of Premium Price Plan for Copper, Lead, and Zinc, 1942-47 (Information 

Circular 7536, January 1950, p. 20).

as noted above, indicates supply in a given year, made available from that year's domestic production and imports, for distribution in the United States for consumption or for Government or private stockpiling.

At the end of World War II, the Government owned over 400,000 tons of zinc (about half in the form of ore and half as metal). Some of the metal was subsequently sold to private industry, such sales continuing through the first half of 1948. The greater part, however, was transferred to the strategic stockpile. 

In 1946, the first postwar year, United States consumption of zinc remained at the high level of about 1 million tons, a quantity only slightly less than that consumed during the wartime year of 1943. 

Mine output of zinc, however, continued the general decline which began after the peak wartime output in 1942, and was at a level about equal to the annual average of the prewar period 1937-39. There were a number of major causes restricting domestic mine output in 1946. The major one was prolonged work stoppages due to strikes. 

Another was the continuing general shortages of manpower, equipment, and supplies, and the necessity to devote more attention to mine development, which was to a considerable extent suspended during the war. A contributing factor was the release to private industry during the year of Government-owned zinc that had been accumulated mostly by imports free of duty during the war. About 

14 percent of the total imports of zinc in 1946 were also imported free of duty for United States Government use.

The price situation during the first half of the year also affected production to some extent. The ceiling price of 84 cents per pound was in effect during this period. It was removed on June 30 and reestablished on July 25, 1946, and continued to October 14, when it was increased to 94 cents. Ceiling prices were removed on November 

9, 1946, and almost immediately the price advanced to 10%½ cents where it remained to the end of 1947. 

Producers' stocks of slab zinc at the beginning of 1946 were at the high level of about 259,000 tons (declining to about 176,000 tons at the end of the year).

The general absence of labor strikes in 1947 as compared with 1946, together with an improved labor supply in mines and mills and the highest annual price for Prime Western zinc since 1917, combined to increase mine output by 11 percent over the 1946 output. Consumption of zinc declined in 1947 but was still at a high level of 981,000 tons. Imports in 1947 increased to 390,000 tons, of which imports free for United States Government use accounted for only 6 percent, compared with 14 percent in the preceding year. Imports free of duty for smelting, refining, and export amounted to 30 percent of the total imports. Producers' stocks of slab zinc declined from about 176,000 tons at the beginning of 1947 to about 69,000 tons at the end of the year.

In 1948 zinc consumption increased to 996,000 tons. Mine output was almost as large as in the preceding year. Imports, however, dropped to 290,000 tons, thus declining 26 percent from the 1947 rate; net imports accounted for 24 percent of the country's total supply. Entries of zinc free of duty for United States Government use declined to less than 7,000 tons, equivalent to only 2 percent of total imports in 1948. Imports free of duty for smelting, refining, and

export amounted to 18 percent of total imports. Producers' stocks of slab zinc declined from about 69,000 tons at the beginning of 1948 to about 21,000 tons at the end of the year. 

A growing zinc shortage became most pronounced toward the end of 1948. After about the middle of 1948, the Government discontinued the release of certain of its war-accumulated zinc stocks, which release had helped to alleviate the shortage in the United States up to that time. During the last half of the year, after the Government ceased releasing stocks, the price of zinc rose sharply to 17%½ cents in 

November, the average price for the year having been 13.589 cents per pound.

Reflecting the general recession in industrial activity in 1949, zinc consumption in that year declined to 826,000 tons, showing a decrease of 17 percent from the 1948 level. Mine production declined by 6 percent to 593,000 tons in 1949. Imports, of which 28 percent were free of duty, increased by 2 percent. Of the total imports, 7 percent were entered free for Government use, and 19 percent were free of duty for smelting, refining, and export. The supply of zinc in the 

United States exceeded consumers' needs during most of the year, and producers' stocks of slab zinc rose from about 21,000 tons at the beginning of 1949 to 94,000 tons at the year's end.10 The price of zinc in the United States declined from 172 cents per pound on 

March 22, 1949, to 9 cents on June 15, 1949 (see table Z-7), and with minor fluctuations the price remained relatively low throughout the year.

Part of the reduced demand for zinc in the latter part of the year may be attributed to the 6-week steel strike which affected in turn the demand for zinc for galvanizing at steel plants. However, in 

December 1949, consumption of slab zinc turned upward. 

In response to increased requirements for zinc with the outbreak of hostilities in Korea in mid-1950 and the acceleration of the nationaldefense program, mine output of zinc in the United States rose 5 percent to a total of 623,000 tons in that year. Total consumption of zinc in the United States in 1950 rose sharply to 1,149,000 tons, an increase over the preceding year of 39 percent. Imports in 1950 reached the high level of 407,000 tons, 38 percent above the 1949 level; net imports accounted for about 36 percent of total zinc supply. 

No imports free for Government use were recorded; imports free for smelting, refining, and export accounted for 3 percent of total imports. 

Producers' stocks of slab zinc declined from about 94,000 tons at the beginning of 1950 to less than 9,000 tons at the year's end. Despite the high level of imports, the gains in domestic production, and use of stocked zinc, the slab-zinc supply in 1950 was insufficient to fill all requirements.
