Source: E & MJ Metal and Mineral Markets. 

NOTE.-Price ceilings on sales of zinc in the United States were imposed on Jan. 26, 1951; the price ceilings were increased by 2 cents a pound on Oct. 2, 1951, and, in order to prevent domestic buyers from buying zinc at higher prices in foreign countries (previously permitted), the Office of Price Stabilization prohibited any person in the United States from receiving foreign zinc at a delivered cost in excess of the ceiling price. 

All price ceilings on zinc in the United States were removed by the Office of Price Stabilization on Feb. 12, 1953.

In order to assure an adequate quantity of the limited zinc supply for military expansion programs and to provide for the most essential civilian requirements, the Government issued orders at the end of 1950 restricting the use of zinc for civilian products and limiting consumers' inventories. Reflecting the increasing volume of industrial activity during the year and the mounting zinc shortage, domestic zinc prices rose sharply from an average of 9.763 cents per pound in 

January 1950 to 17%½ cents at the end of the year. The price of foreign zinc had risen even more rapidly, however, and at the end of 1950 ordinary brands of Mexican zinc, f. a. s.11 gulf ports, were quoted at 

22 cents per pound, and up. Zinc imports declined toward the latter part of the year.

Government price controls were imposed on zinc, as on other metals, by the General Ceiling Price Regulation that went into effect on January 26, 1951; they were terminated February 12, 1953. For each seller the highest price at which he had sold zinc in the United States during the period from December 19, 1950, to January 25, 1951, inclusive, was fixed by the Office of Price Stabilization as the highest price at which he could sell zinc beginning on January 26, 1951. 

This regulation, in effect, resulted in a United States price of 17%2 cents a pound for domestic zinc and prices ranging from 184 to 18% cents a pound for foreign zinc sold in the United States. On October 

2, 1951, the Office of Price Stabilization increased the price ceilings by 2 cents a pound and, in order to prevent buyers from buying zinc at higher prices in foreign countries (as had been previously permitted), prohibited any person in the United States from receiving foreign zinc at a delivered cost in excess of the ceiling price. Because of the strong demand for zinc in relation to supply, these increased ceiling prices became the prices at which zinc was sold in the United 

States from October 2, 1951, through May 1952.

In 1951, mine output reached a postwar peak of 681,000 tons, 9 percent greater than in 1950. Imports in 1951 decreased to 334,000 tons, a tonnage 18 percent less than in 1950. Consumption of zinc, which had decreased somewhat from the 1950 level, amounted to 1,126,000 tons. Imports free for Government use totaled less than 

500 tons; imports free for smelting, refining, and export, which totaled about 41,000 tons, were equivalent to 12 percent of total imports.

The shortage of zinc in the United States continued critical in 1951, aggravated particularly by the reduced flow of supplies from foreign countries in the last half of 1951. The 18-percent decline in imports in 1951 as compared with 1950 (representing principally the reduced imports in the last half of 1951) is attributed largely to the fact that zinc was selling in foreign markets at prices substantially above the ceiling prices at which it could be sold in the United States. 

The disparity between the ceiling prices in the United States and the uncontrolled foreign prices became more marked after about mid- 1950. The disparity became greatest during the last half of 1951, when ordinary brands of Mexican zinc, f. a. s. gulf ports, considered by the trade to be representative of uncontrolled foreign prices at this time, were as much as 132 cents per pound above the United 

States ceiling price of 17%½ cents a pound for domestic zinc. (See table Z-8.) After the United States price ceiling was raised 2 cents

a pound on October 2, 1951, the foreign price was still as much as 11 cents above the United States price. Toward the end of the year, as declining demand reduced the uncontrolled foreign market prices, these price disparities diminished, although they did not entirely disappear until after the first quarter of 1952.

NOTE.-Price ceilings on sales of zinc in the United States were established by the Office of Price Stabilization effective Jan. 26, 1951; price ceilings were increased 2 cents a pound on Oct. 2, 1951, on which date the 

Office of Price Stabilization also prohibited any person in the United States from receiving foreign zinc at a delivered cost in excess of the ceiling price. All ceilings on zinc in the United States were removed on Feb. 

12, 1953.

At the end of September 1953 the freight and insurance cost of transporting zinc from gulf ports to New York was about 0.5 cent per pound and from London to New York, about 0.7 cent per pound. The New 

York delivered price for domestic Prime Western zinc at that time was 0.5 cent above the East St. Louis f. o. b. price for that grade of zinc.

The prices for foreign zinc are for slab zinc approximately equivalent in grade to domestic Prime Western zinc.

Slab-zinc supplies were placed under allocation control in the United States, effective August 1, 1951. The world shortage of zinc led also to international cooperation for the distribution and use of the free world supplies of primary zinc. The International Materials Con ference (which was formed early in 1951 to examine the critical situation in certain essential raw materials and to propose means of meeting it) made recommendations for international allocation of zinc for the fourth quarter of 1951 and the first two quarters of 1952. As the supply of zinc began to approach a balance with demand, however, international zinc allocations were discontinued in May 1952. 

For the most part, according to reports of the International Materials Conference, the recommended allocations were complied with by member countries.

The prolonged fighting in Korea and the possibility that the hostilities might spread and further aggravate the metal shortages had led to a Government policy of active encouragement of production of lead and zinc and other critical metals both in the United States and in foreign countries. In the United States the Government encouraged expansion of production facilities by allowing, for tax purposes, accelerated amortization of investments in such facilities; by contracting, in a few cases, for the long-term purchase of lead and zinc at fixed prices; by making loans for the expansion of production facilities; and by sharing in the expense of exploration projects for lead and zinc. The United States assisted lead and zinc producers in 13 foreign countries, both with development loans and with longterm contracts for purchases of lead and zinc at floor prices. These forms of Government assistance, together with the stimulus provided to private investors by the high market prices, resulted in the institution of many projects for the development and expansion of production facilities both in the United States and in foreign countries. (Table 69 in the appendix lists the major projects that have come to the attention of the Tariff Commission.) The long-term nature of some of the Government assistance projects, involving the purchase of metals at the relatively high prices that prevailed in 1951 and providing for deliveries extending into 1956 and 1959, suggests that the lead and zinc shortage was expected to last longer than it did. 

Changes in supply and demand since the beginning of 1952 The shortage of zinc was noticeably easing by the spring of 1952, and although in January 1952 the President had authorized the release of 15,000 tons of zinc from the strategic stockpile to consumers to augment supply, no zinc was actually so released. By about the end of April 1952 the price of Mexican zinc, f. a. s. gulf ports, which was 

30 to 31 cents a pound in mid-November 1951, had declined to the same levels as the price of Prime Western zinc, East St. Louis, 19%2 cents per pound. Zinc use and allocation controls were discontinued and inventory restrictions were liberalized in the United States on 

May 15, 1952; inventory controls were entirely removed on June 27, 1952.

The virtual disappearance of the disparity between the United States zinc prices and foreign zinc prices early in 1952 and the continued slack in European buying, together with the suspension of the import duties on zinc ore and slab zinc from February 12, 1952, to July 23, 1952 (Public Law 258, 82d Cong.), greatly stimulated United States

h imports in 1952. United States imports of zinc in 1952, which reached the record level of 699,000 tons, were more than double those of the previous year. Net imports of zinc in 1952 represented about 46 percent of the total supply of zinc. Imports free for Government use accounted for less than 1 percent of total imports, and imports free of duty for smelting, refining, and export accounted for 6 percent. 

Mine output declined by 2 percent to 666,000 tons in 1952. 

Producers' stocks of slab zinc rose generally during 1952 from about 20,000 tons at the beginning of the year to about 87,000 tons at the end. Stocks of zinc ore held by zinc smelters in the United States also increased generally during 1952 (although at a less rapid rate than those of slab zinc) and at the end of the year the stocks were about 38 percent greater than at the beginning of 1952 (see appendix table 36). 

Zinc stocks also accumulated outside the United States. Stocks of དྲ zinc metal in the United Kingdom (which were mostly British Government stocks) increased markedly from about 44,000 tons at the be- Sginning of 1951 to about 186,000 tons at the end of 1952. This increase reflected the general worldwide easing in zinc supply in addition to deliveries of zinc purchased in large quantities from overseas suppliers in earlier periods. el The decline of 103,000 tons in consumption of zinc in the United States in 1952, which was still at the very high level of 1,023,000 tons, was due in part to the steel strike of that year. 

The price of zinc (Prime Western slab at East St. Louis) first dropped below the established price ceiling of 19½ cents on June 2, 1952. The price drop of 2 cents a pound to 17%½ cents was followed by a 1½-cent drop on June 5 and a 1-cent drop on June 18, establishing the price at 15 cents a pound. The initial price declines were precipitated by the 2-month strike which began on June 2 in the United States steel industry. When the steel strike was called, it became apparent that the demand for zinc for galvanizing purposes, which normally accounts for one-third of the total zinc consumption, would be drastically reduced because of the shutdown of steel plants. The shortage of steel that resulted reduced the output of automobiles and other products and thereby also reduced demand for zinc for die castings used in making these products. By the end of 1952 the price of zinc had declined to 12½ cents per pound. 

In summary, the year 1952 represented a period of transition from scarcity of zinc to relative abundance. The supply and distribution of zinc in the United States in 1952 were as follows:

Estimated consumption of zinc in 1953 totaled 1,172,000 tons, an increase of about 15 percent over 1952. Mine output, which in March 

1953 began a steady decline, totaled 535,000 tons, or 20 percent less than in the preceding year.

Imports during 1953 were only slightly less than those in 1952 and totaled 698,000 tons. 

The quantity of zinc acquired for the strategic stockpile in the first half of 1953 totaled 25,000 tons. During the period January-September 1953 imports free for United States Government use totaled 20,910 tons (see appendix table 47). The Office of Defense Mobilization, which supplied the data on zinc acquisition for the strategic stockpile, informed the Tariff Commission on November 6, 1953, that- the current stockpile objective for *** zinc is completely on hand or on order and thatapproximately *** 20,000 short tons of zinc are to be delivered to the stockpile under existing contracts with foreign suppliers. 

The zinc, it was stated, is to be delivered by December 31, 1956. Additional quantities -the statement continuedof foreign *** zinc are expected to be delivered to the stockpile under development contracts of the Economic Cooperation Administration or successor agencies. 

However, the quantities to be delivered under these contracts are not firm, since the amounts due are based on the market prices at the time of delivery. 

According to data compiled by the American Zinc Institute, shipments of slab zinc for Government account totaled about 42,000 tons in 1953, compared with about 37,000 tons in 1952. These tonnages were equivalent to about 4 and 5 percent, respectively, of the total shipments of slab zinc (both primary and secondary) by domestic zinc smelters in 1952 and 1953.

21 tl 21 Producers' stocks of slab zinc continued to climb fairly steadily during 1953, rising from 87,160 tons at the beginning of the year to 180,620 tons at the year's end; at the end of January 1954, they had increased to about 199,000 tons, compared with about 22,000 tons at the beginning of 1952, and were at the highest level since 1946. 

Smelters' stocks of zinc ore similarly continued the climb which began in 1952, and at the end of 1953 they were 55 percent greater than at the beginning of 1952. 

Recent price changes

The price of Prime Western zinc-which began to decline in June 1952-continued the downward trend throughout 1953. On February 

12, 1953, all price ceilings on zinc were removed by the Office of Price 

Stabilization. From an average price of 12.588 cents per pound in

January 1953, the price fell to an average of 11 cents for the months of April through July; on September 2 the price fell to 10%½ cents, and on September 11 to 10 cents. On January 18, 1954, the price dropped further to 92 cents, at which level it remained through February 14, 1954. On February 15, 1954, the price was reduced to 94 cents, but on March 10 it was raised to 94 cents (see table Z-7). The decline in the price of zinc, from its 19½-cent level at the beginning of 1952 to its current level of 9% cents per pound, is much sharper than the decrease in the price of lead during the same period. The average price of domestic zinc in November 1953 (10 cents) was 49 percent below that in the first quarter of 1952. In comparison, the wholesale-price index of all commodities other than farm products, as reported by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, rose from an average of 114.1 in the first quarter of 1952 to 114.5 in January 1954. 

The current price of domestic zinc (94 cents) is 50 percent below the average price in the first quarter of 1952.

The price of Mexican zinc, f. a. s. gulf ports, followed a general downward trend in 1953, ranging from 10.625 cents per pound on 

January 28, 1953, to 9 cents at the end of December 1953 (compared with 10 cents for Prime Western, East St. Louis, at the end of the year) (see table Z-8).

Private trading in zinc on the London Metal Exchange (which had been suspended since December 1939) was resumed on January 2, 1953.

Nature of available market price quotations

The market prices of zinc in the United States referred to above are 

East St. Louis f. o. b. quotations for Prime Western zinc as reported by E & MJ Metal and Mineral Markets. They are based on actual firsthand sales of all grades of slab zinc by major primary producers or their agents in the United States on a flat or fixed-price basis. (Sales on the basis of average prices over some stipulated period or on the basis of the price prevailing on the date of shipment are not included in compiling the market prices.) The E & MJ daily price quotations are weighted by the quantities of zinc sold; the weekly,

F monthly, or annual averages are simple arithmetic averages of the weighted daily averages. 

The prices quoted for Prime Western zinc reflect sales by producers on a flat-price basis of other grades of zinc converted to Prime Western equivalent. Sales of other grades of zinc, which, as noted later, command established premiums over Prime Western zinc, are converted to the equivalent of Prime Western grade by subtracting the premium from the price at which the higher grade zinc was sold. Of the total production of slab zinc in the United States during the period 1948-52, 40 percent was Prime Western zinc (see appendix table 35). 

It may be noted that beginning on July 16, 1953, several major sellers of zinc offered Prime Western zinc on a delivered basis instead of on the customary f. o. b. East St. Louis basis. The delivered price (east of the Continental Divide) ranged from 0.25 to 0.5 cent per pound above the East St. Louis price. In August one major seller announced that it would hold to the East St. Louis basis but would absorb freight in excess of 50 cents per hundredweight (one-half cent per pound). In September 1953 sellers of zinc generally returned to the practice of pricing Prime Western zinc on the basis of f. o. b. East 

St. Louis; some, however, in order to meet competition, absorbed freight charges in excess of 0.5 cent per pound. Since that time the practice has generally been to quote prices of Prime Western zinc both on an f. o. b. basis East St. Louis and on a delivered basis, wherein the delivered price (representing the quotation on Prime Western zinc sold at centers where freight from East St. Louis exceeds one-half cent a pound) currently exceeds the East St. Louis price by one-half cent.

The price of Prime Western zinc generally determines the price of other grades of slab zinc, which usually carry established premiums over the price of Prime Western zinc. Premiums over Prime Western zinc in the East St. Louis market as currently quoted in the trade for the other grades are as follows (in cents per pound): Selected, 0.10 cent; Brass Special, 0.25 cent; Intermediate, 0.5 cent; High Grade (delivered), 1.35 cents; and Special High Grade (delivered), 1.50 cents.

The recent practice of pricing zinc both on an f. o. b. East St. Louis, basis and on a delivered basis, it may be noted, has applied to Brass Special and Intermediate grade zinc as well as to Prime Western zinc. 

Prices of High Grade and Special High Grade zinc have customarily been quoted on a delivered basis only.

The average delivered value of slab zinc shipped from domestic producers in 1952 ranged from 16.14 cents per pound (for the relatively small shipments to the West South Central area) to 17.76 cents per pound (for shipments to the Pacific area). The concentration of shipments of slab zinc to the East North Central and the Middle Atlantic areas reflects the use of slab zinc for its major use-galvanizing-in the principal iron- and steel-producing States, and the importance of zinc for die castings, which are used largely in the automobile industry located principally in the East North Central area. 

The average delivered value of shipments of imported slab zinc in 1952 ranged from 13.56 cents per pound (for the relatively small shipments to the New England area) to 18.22 cents per pound (for the small shipments to the West North Central area). As in the case of domestic producers' shipments, the East North Central and the Middle Atlantic areas accounted for most of the deliveries of imported slab zinc.

The average delivered values given above reflect shipments of slab zinc in fulfillment of sales contracts entered into at various times. 

Sales contracts concluded in the early part of 1952 or in 1951 were at higher prices than the contracts made later in 1952. The market price of zinc declined from 19½ cents per pound at the beginning of 1952 to 122 cents at the end of the year. In addition, the average delivered values probably reflect differences in the proportions of total shipments that constituted the various grades of slab zinc which command premiums over the price of Prime Western zinc.15 

The differences in delivered values of imported slab zinc shipped to the various consuming areas also probably reflect different proportions of shipments of metal imported during the period of duty suspension from February 12 to July 23, 1952. CHAPTER IV UNITED STATES FOREIGN TRADE IN ZINC 

Trend of imports As previously noted, United States imports of unmanufactured zinc before World War II were small, and during the period 1937-39 averaged 43,000 tons annually. Imports of zinc rose rapidly during the war and reached their wartime, peak of about 609,000 tons in 1943, when they were equivalent to over 80 percent of the domestic mine output of zinc in that year. During the postwar period 1946-51 imports remained at a relatively high rate, averaging 340,000 tons annually (a rate equivalent to 56 percent of the maximum wartime imports) and ranging from a low of 290,000 tons in 1948 to 407,000 tons in 1950. During 1952 (in which year zinc ore and slab zinc were free of duty from February 12 to July 23 imports of unmanufactured) zinc reached a record level of 699,000 tons. Imports of zinc in 1953, which totaled 698,000 tons and exceeded domestic mine output by 30 percent, were at virtually the same level as in the preceding year.

Sources of United States imports 

United States imports of unmanufactured zinc come principally from Canada and Mexico. Additional supplies of zinc come from a number of other countries, principally Peru, Bolivia, the Union of 

South Africa, Spain, and Guatemala.

The distribution of total United States imports of unmanufactured zinc during the 6-year period 1948 through 1953, by countries, is as follows (see table Z-13): 

Country Canada__

The United States is the market for most of the zinc produced in Mexico and Canada and for a substantial part of the output in Peru. 

During the 5-year period 1948-52 United States imports of zinc from Mexico were equivalent to 74 percent of Mexico's mine output of zinc, imports from Canada to 55 percent of that country's mine output, and imports from Peru to 25 percent of Peru's mine output. In total, United States imports of unmanufactured zinc from all countries during the period 1948-52 were equivalent to about 24 percent of the mine output of zinc in all foreign countries combined; in 1952, the ratio was 33 percent.

As described in greater detail in part IV of this report, United States firms in both the mining and smelting segments of the industry have substantial holdings in zinc-mining operations in foreign countries, including Canada, Mexico, and Peru as well as a number of others. It has been estimated that the output of zinc from those foreign mines largely controlled by United States companies was about 20 percent of world production in 1949.16

Canada and Mexico, which were the principal sources of zinc ores and concentrates imported into the United States in 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953, were also the leading sources of United States imports of zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs. Slab zinc, however, accounts for a larger proportion of the total zinc imports from Canada than of the total from Mexico. Imports of zinc from Bolivia, Guatemala, Spain, Australia, Peru, and the Union of South Africa have consisted wholly or largely of zinc ores and concentrates, whereas imports from Italy, West Germany, and Belgium-Luxembourg have consisted wholly or largely of zinc blocks, pigs, and slabs. 

The bulk of the total imports of slab zinc from Canada during the period 1952 through September 1953 (as reported by principal importers) consisted of Special High Grade zinc, and that country accounted for much the greater part of the total imports of Special High Grade zinc during the period. On the other hand, the bulk of the total imports of slab zinc from Mexico during the period 1952 to September 1953 consisted of Prime' Western zinc. Mexico was the source of most of the total imports of Prime Western zinc during that period.

Importers

The bulk of the United States imports of zinc ore and of slab zinc is accounted for by a relatively small number of concerns. Receipts of foreign zinc ore by 7 primary zinc-smelting concerns in the United States during 1952 and the first 3 quarters of 1953 were equivalent to about 80 percent of total United States imports of zinc ore during that period. Imports of slab zinc as reported to the Tariff Commission by 5 concerns for the period 1952 through September 1953 were equivalent to about 80 percent of the total United States imports of slab zinc during that period. Con- All primary zinc smelters in the United States, it may be noted, reported consumption of foreign zinc ore (some to a small extent) during 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953. A large part of the total imports of zinc ore was for the account of smelting companies which also produce a large part of the domestic mine output of zinc.¹7 cerns that operate zinc smelters and zinc-mining operations in the United States (either directly or through related or subsidiary companies) accounted for at least one-half of the total domestic mine output of recoverable zinc in 1952. 

Some of the principal importers of slab zinc during 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953 were concerns which (directly or through related companies) operate domestic primary zinc smelters; a few were also producers of domestic zinc ore.

United States exports United States exports of unmanufactured zinc have generally been small and have consisted principally of slab zinc smelted from ore imported free of duty for smelting, refining, and export. During the period 1937-39 they averaged about 4,000 tons annually and were equivalent to less than 1 percent of domestic mine production of recoverable zinc plus recoverable zinc content of old scrap processed. 

Exports of zinc increased sharply, however, during the war, chiefly as a result of lend-lease operations, and reached a peak of 134,000 tons in 1942. Exports declined thereafter to 47,000 tons in 1946, but in 1947 rose to 108,000 tons, over half of which went to the United Kingdom. During the years 1948-53, exports averaged 

47,000 tons annually, equivalent to about 7 percent of the average annual domestic mine output of recoverable zinc plus recoverable zinc content of old scrap (see table Z-6). Of the total domestic exports of unmanufactured zinc during the period 1949-52, 87 percent represented zinc slab, pigs, or blocks, 7 percent zinc scrap, and 6 percent zinc ore (data on exports of zinc scrap were not available separately for a period of years before 1949). 

During the period 1948-52, the value of domestic exports of unmanufactured zinc averaged about $16.7 million annually. Exports of the other items covered by this investigation were smaller. For zinc oxide and zinc lithopone, the average annual value of exports during 1948-52 was about $4.4 million, and that for zinc sheets was $1.8 million. The average annual value of exports of zinc dust during 1948-51 was $0.3 million (data for 1952 are not available). 

17 The zinc content of zinc pigments and salts produced by domestic manufacturers directly from foreign zinc ore (without the ore's having been converted to slab) probably did not average much in excess of 23,000 tons annually during the years 1946-51, a tonnage equivalent to about 10 percent of the average annual United States imports of zinc ore in that period.

In terms of quantity, exports in 1948-52 of zinc oxide and lithopone were equivalent to 6 percent of United States production of zinc oxide and lithopone during that period, and exports of zinc sheets were equivalent to about 22 percent of zinc-sheet production. 

Exports of zinc dust in 1948-51 were equivalent to about 2 percent of domestic production of zinc dust during that period. In contrast to the situation with respect to unmanufactured zinc, exports of zinc oxide and lithopone and of zinc dust and sheets have generally exceeded imports of such articles. 

The United Kingdom, France, Brazil, Canada, and India were the principal markets for United States domestic exports of unmanufactured zinc during 1952 and the first 9 months of 1953. These 5 countries in total accounted for 91 percent of the total value of exports during the period. As previously noted, the bulk of the domestic exports of unmanufactured zinc consists of slab zinc. The relatively small exports of zinc ore during the period all went to Canada.

Canada, Brazil, India, Cuba, and Mexico were among the principal markets for exports of zinc oxide, lithopone, zinc sheets, and zinc dust.

The zinc exported with benefit of drawback is contained in many different products and the exports of individual items have been erratic in recent years. CHAPTER V 

UNITED STATES CONSUMPTION OF ZINC 

The principal uses and properties of zinc, the forms in which it is consumed, the general trend in zinc consumption in the United States compared with that in other countries, and the distribution of zinc shipments by geographic areas were discussed generally in chapters I and III of part III of this report. As noted previously, the United 

States consumes far more zinc than any other country, and in 1952 accounted for about two-fifths of total world consumption. In this chapter, the trends in zinc consumption in the major uses are considered as well as some of the factors affecting these trends such as competition from substitute materials. 

Relative magnitude of uses As noted in chapter I of part III of this report, most of the zinc consumed in the United States is in the form of slab zinc as recovered from ores (by smelting or electrolytic refining and to a relatively small extent from zinc scrap). Of the total quantity of zinc consumed in the United States during the period 1948-52, about 87 percent was consumed in the form of slab (including primary and secondary slab zinc) and 12 percent represented the zinc content of zinc pigments and salts produced from ore without its first having been reduced to slab zinc. 

The proportion of the total output of slab zinc recovered from scrap is relatively small. During the period 1948-52, only about 6 percent of the total United States output of slab zinc represented redistilled secondary slab zinc (see appendix table 35), the balance representing primary slab zinc produced directly from ore. This output of secondary slab zinc accounted for only about 19 percent of the total recoverable zinc content of scrap processed in the United States during 194852. Except for such new zinc scrap as is consumed in the production of redistilled secondary slab zinc, secondary zinc recovered from new scrap is not included in the data on zinc consumption as used throughout this report, since (as noted in the discussion in connection with chapter III, pt. III) the inclusion of such new scrap would involve a certain amount of duplication. It may be noted, however, that the total annual recovery of secondary zinc from all sources (both old and new scrap) is substantial, although much smaller than the recovery of secondary lead. Secondary zinc recovered in all forms from all scrap processed in the United States in 1952 was equivalent to 34 percent of the total United States output of primary slab zinc in that year. 

Most of the secondary zinc recovered is from new scrap (about 76 percent in 1952) and represents in large part secondary zinc recovered in the form of brass and bronze (see appendix table 34). Unlike the situation with respect to the consumption of lead, wherein a large part represents lead which is recovered from secondary materials (chiefly because of the use of lead for battery plates), much of the total con sumption of zinc is not recoverable as secondary metal because, in part, of the large use of zinc for galvanizing. 

Consumption of unmanufactured zinc of all kinds for all uses in the United States in 1953 totaled 1,172,000 tons, representing an increase of 15 percent over that in 1952, and a tonnage 76 percent greater than the average annual consumption during the period 1937-39. Consumption of slab zinc in 1953 totaled about 978,000 tons, compared

with an annual average of about 552,000 tons in 1937-39 and 634,300 tons in 1929. The current capacity of the domestic primary zincsmelting industry, it may be noted, is in excess of domestic consumption of slab zinc. 

Foreign zinc ore has accounted for a substantial proportion of the total domestic output of slab zinc in recent years. During the period 

1948-52, 31 percent of the total output of primary slab zinc came from foreign ores, compared with 2 percent during the period 1937-39; in 

1952, the proportion was 36 percent.

The largest use of zinc is normally in the galvanizing of iron or steel in order to increase resistance to corrosion. As shown in the foregoing tabulation this use accounted for 45 percent of the total consumption of slab zinc during 1948-52, and for 41 percent of the total in 1953. Zinc coating or galvanizing is applied to a great tonnage of steel products of many types. The major applications of zinc coating on steel include roofing and siding sheets, tubes, pipe, wire and wire rope, chain, fencing, miscellaneous iron and steel fittings, poleline hardware, and a wide variety of miscellaneous products including boilers, pails, cans, tanks, and nails. 

Zinc-base alloys (which are those alloys in which zinc is the principal metal) accounted for the second largest use of slab zinc in postwar years (29 percent during 1948-52 and 31 percent in 1953). Zinc-base alloys are used predominantly in die-casting-the process of producing accurately dimensioned, sharply defined, smooth-surfaced parts by forcing the molten zinc-alloy metal under pressure into metal dies or molds. Die-casting is probably the fastest of all casting processes, and is often employed where large quantities of duplicate castings are involved and rapidity of production is important. The process permits the production of complex shapes. The automobile industry is the largest user of zinc-base alloys, principally for die-cast parts and assemblies for items such as fuel pumps, carburetors, radiator grills, windshield wipers, horns, heaters, speedometer frames, hardware, and instrument panels. Zinc die castings are used in a great many products of the electrical industry, including washing machines, oil burners, stokers, motor housings, vacuum cleaners, and electric clocks, and in the production of typewriters, picture projectors, cameras, vending machines, gasoline pumps, recording machines, tools, building hardware, padlocks, toys, and novelties.

Brass products accounted for the third largest use of slab zinc during the period 1948-52 and in 1953, or for 18 percent of the total in 1953. Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc (sometimes containing small amounts of other metals) commonly contains from 5 to 40 percent zinc. Brass finds a major wartime use in the production of cartridge and shell casings. It is used in large quantities in the manufacture of a wide variety of products including bearings, various castings and forgings, electrical fixtures, plumbing fittings and acces-

sories, clocks, instrument parts, miscellaneous hardware, pipe, sheets, rod, tubes, and wire.

In addition to the consumption of slab zinc for brass, substantial quantities of secondary zinc (as noted above) are recovered annually in the form of brass and bronze (see appendix table 34).

Rolled zinc, which accounted for about 6 percent of the total consumption of slab zinc in 1953, has many uses in the form of sheet, strip, and plate. Rolled zinc is used in the production of dry batteries, fruit-jar caps, weatherstrip, and photoengraving plates, and for heavy corrosion-resistant plates for steam boilers, ship hulls, and marine equipment. Rolled zinc is also used in building construction for roof valleys and flashing and other roof-drainage fittings. 

Zinc oxide ranked fifth among the uses of slab zinc in 1953, accounting for 2 percent of the total consumption of slab zinc. Zinc oxide is used largely in rubber for the manufacture of rubber tires and other rubber products and of paints and enamels, as a filler in floor coverings and textiles, and in products of the ceramics industry. Other uses are in pharmaceutical chemicals, printing ink, dental cement, soap, and glue. It may be noted that the total quantity of zinc in ore consumed directly plus slab zinc used in making zinc oxide (including leaded zinc oxide) has generally exceeded the tonnage of slab zinc consumed in making rolled zinc, and in some years has exceeded the tonnage of slab zinc consumed in making brass products. As noted, both rolled zinc and brass products rank ahead of zinc oxide as a consumer of slab zinc.

Other uses for slab zinc, which accounted for about 2 percent of total slab-zinc consumption in 1953, are in the production of wet batteries, various light-metal alloys, zinc dust, bronze powder, and various chemicals, and as cathodic protection against corrosion for pipelines and other underground iron and steel structures.

The most pronounced shift in the consumption of slab zinc has been in its increased use in zinc-base alloys (used largely for die castings) which in 1953 accounted for 31 percent of total slab-zinc consumption, compared with 13 percent in 1937-39 and 6 percent in 1929. As previously noted, zinc-base alloys ranked second in importance in 1953 as a consumer of slab zinc. As against the overall increase of 77

% percent in the consumption of slab zinc for all uses in 1953 as compared with 1937-39, and the overall increase of 54 percent as compared with 1929, the consumption of slab zinc for zinc-base alloys in 1953 was 316 percent greater than that in 1937-39 and 748 percent greater than that in 1929. Consumption for galvanizing, the major use of slab zinc, was 

66 percent greater in 1953 than in 1937-39 but only 39 percent greater than in 1929. Consumption of slab zinc for brass products was 19 percent greater in 1953 than in 1937-39 but 4 percent less than in 1929. 

Zinc (in the form of suitable alloys) possesses a number of qualities which make it particularly desirable for use in die castings; among these qualities are its relatively low melting point, good casting properties, suitability for plating, strength, and corrosion resistance. 

Zinc's major competition in die-casting applications is that offered by aluminum, which has found increasing acceptance in that field. 

Some of the features which make aluminum desirable for die castings are its light weight, high resistance to corrosion, qualities of heat dissipation, and the finishes which may be applied. 

Zinc and aluminum are by far the principal metals used for diecasting, and the two combined accounted for 96 percent of all nonferrous-metal die castings shipped by United States producers in 1953. The balance represented shipments of lead, copper, and magnesium die castings.

Shipments of aluminum die castings increased much more rapidly than those of zinc in postwar years. Shipments of aluminum die castings were 230 percent greater in 1953 than in 1946, compared with an increase of 38 percent in zinc die castings during the same period. 

On a tonnage basis, zinc die castings nonetheless still account for the larger part of all die castings shipped. 

Of the total shipments of all die castings in 1953, those of zinc accounted for 65 percent, compared with 79 percent in 1946. 

Aluminum die castings accounted for 31.0 percent of the total shipments in 1953, compared with 16 percent in 1946. 

Taking into account the fact that the weight of zinc, per unit of volume, is about two and a half times that of aluminum, shipments of aluminum die castings exceeded those of zinc in 1952 and 1953 on a volume basis.

The manufacture of zinc die castings generally employs Special High Grade zinc only, other grades not being suitable for such use.

During the period 1946-50, annual average consumption of Special High Grade zinc exceeded annual domestic production of that grade by about 22,000 tons. In 1951, consumption exceeded production by about 71,000 tons. In 1952, when production and consumption of

In general, the materials suitable for substitution for zinc in its major uses are relatively few. Aluminum is a major competitor of zinc in a number of its applications. Like the other major nonferrous metals, aluminum was in short supply during much of the postwar period. The shortage of aluminum eased considerably during 1953, however, and supplies of aluminum for civilian purposes have become increasingly available. Domestic production of aluminum reached a record high in 1953. Among the characteristics of aluminum are those of light weight (the weight of zinc per unit volume being about two and one-half times that of aluminum), good workability, high electrical and thermal conductivity, high resistance to corrosion, and pleasing appearance.

The price of aluminum has increased much less sharply since prewar years than has the price of zinc. The current price of aluminum, 21½ cents per pound, is about 7 percent greater than the average price in 1937-39. The current price of zinc, 94 cents per pound, is about 

80 percent greater than the average for zinc in 1937-39. In the first part of 1952, the price of zinc exceeded that of aluminum. Prices of zinc have been characterized by much greater fluctuations than those of aluminum.

Aluminum sheet for such uses as roofing and siding products is a strong competitor of galvanized sheet metal. Other uses of aluminum. which are competitive with galvanized products include those for aluminum-clad steel and aluminum nails. Both aluminum and magnesium are probably replacing substantial quantities of brass. Aluminum is being used extensively to replace brass for lamp-bulb bases. 

Magnesium may replace substantial quantities of zinc in the manufacture of dry-cell batteries, and is being used to an increasing extent in cathodic protection against corrosion. Magnesium is reported to have certain advantages over zinc in the production of photoengraving plates. Aluminum and magnesium could replace zinc to some extent as reducing agents in chemical reactions.

PART IV INFORMATION PERTAINING TO BOTH LEAD AND ZINC 

195

CHAPTER I GENERAL FEATURES OF THE UNITED STATES  

This part of the report is devoted principally to the mining and milling segments of the lead and zinc industries, although smelting and refining and transportation are also considered in certain of their aspects. The discussion relates primarily to the lead and zinc industries in the United States, but the industries in the principal foreign countries exporting lead and zinc to this country are also discussed briefly. Lead and zinc are considered together because they are produced to a large extent from complex ores containing both metals in recoverable quantities and because in this way comparisons of changes in the two industries are facilitated. 

As indicated by the information contained in this part of the report, most of the cost of producing primary lead and zinc and most of the employment in the lead and zinc industries are in the mining and milling stages of production. Also, mining and milling, especially mining and milling of ores valued primarily for their content of zinc, have suffered most from recent declines in market prices-as indicated by reductions in employment, production, and profits. 

The information on which this part is based was obtained mostly through the Tariff Commission's questionnaire surveys. It permits a comparison of data on employment and other economic aspects of the industries in 1952 with similar data for 1939; it also permits comparison of changes in the lead and zinc industries during the period since the beginning of 1952-a period marked by sharp declines in lead and zinc market prices and greatly increased imports. 

Major industry segments and production operations Lead or zinc metal is generally produced either from ore or from scrap. Metal from ores is known as primary metal, and that from scrap, as secondary metal.

The production of primary lead or zinc metal involves mining crude ore (after the necessary exploration and development work), milling the ore to produce concentrates, and smelting and refining to produce refined metal. Some of the ores or concentrates, especially of zinc, are used directly in making pigments and salts (about 15 percent of the recoverable zinc in ores mined in the United States is so used). 

Lead concentrates produced from the complex ores of the Western States must first be smelted to produce lead or base bullion, and the bullion must be further refined. Some lead plants treating complex ores combine the smelting and refining operations in the same plants while others specialize in smelting ores to produce lead bullion or in refining lead bullion to produce refined lead. Lead concentrates from the West Central States are relatively free of impurities and of precious metals; hence in those States smelting and refining are usually combined in the same plants. 197

Refined zinc (slab zinc) is produced directly from zinc concentrates by distillation processes in horizontal or vertical retorts at plants known as zinc smelters and by electrolysis in electrolytic plants.

The number of mines engaged in producing crude ores is relatively large. The number of mills (located near the mines) that concentrate the ores is smaller and the number of primary smelters or refineries is still smaller.

In the production of secondary lead or zinc, the mining and milling functions are replaced by scrap collecting, sorting, and segregating, and the smelting and refining operations are performed in the same plants. Secondary smelters and refiners generally smelt and refine several kinds of nonferrous scrap metals. A large part of their product is in the form of metal alloys.

Lead 

In 1952 there were 912 lead and zinc mines in the United States (counting all units regardless of size of output), but only 193 of them accounted for 95.4 percent of the aggregate mine output of lead and zinc. Lead and zinc ores were concentrated by some 120 mills. and zinc were mined and milled in 22 States. Lead concentrates and lead bullion (from both domestic and foreign sources) were smelted or refined in 13 plants located in 8 States.¹ Zinc concentrates (foreign and domestic) were smelted or refined in 18 plants, located in 8 States." 

Some of the lead and zinc scrap was processed by primary lead and zinc smelters and refineries, but the bulk of the scrap containing lead and zinc was smelted and refined in several hundred plants which processed scrap exclusively. However, a small number of the secondary plants account for the bulk of the secondary lead output. 

The control of each segment, described above, of the lead and zinc industries in the United States is concentrated, to a substantial degree, in relatively few companies. In 1952, based on reports to the Tariff 

Commission, the 10 companies (including their subsidiaries) which were the largest producers of newly mined lead accounted for 65 percent of the total United States output, and the 10 largest zincproducing companies produced 62 percent of the total mine output of zinc. Seven of the companies in these two groups are the same, and these seven accounted for 55 percent of the lead, 51 percent of the zinc, and 52 percent of the lead and zinc combined. 

Concentration is more pronounced in primary smelting and refining of lead and zinc than in mining and milling these metals. The 13 primary lead smelters and refineries are controlled by 6 companies (subsidiaries not counted separately) and the 18 primary zinc smelters are controlled by 12 companies including 4 of the companies that control lead smelters and refineries.

A large part of the crude lead and zinc ore is milled or concentrated by companies that, in addition to processing ore produced by their own mines, process purchased ore or treat, on a toll or custom basis, ore owned by others. Similarly, an even larger part of the lead and zinc concentrates is smelted or refined by companies that purchase the concentrates or process them on a toll basis. Smelting companies that smelt mostly purchased ores or that treat, on a toll basis, ores owned by others are known as custom smelters. 

The activities of some of the large companies also include secondary smelting and fabricating operations. Some of the companies produce metals other than lead and zinc and some of them control similar activities in other countries.

In 1952, primary lead refineries produced 472,852. tons of refined lead from primary sources, 383,358 tons from domestic ores and base bullion, and 89,494 tons from foreign ores and base bullion. (See appendix table 5.) In addition, primary refineries produced 3,070 tons of refined lead from scrap. The total quantity of refined lead produced by primary refineries was 475,922 tons. Primary lead refineries also produced 58,203 tons of antimonial lead in 1952. 

According to the American Bureau of Metal Statistics, primary lead refineries in the United States at the end of 1952 had annual capacity to produce 870,000 tons of pig lead and refined lead. Assuming that this includes capacity to produce antimonial lead, total primary refinery production in 1952 was equal to about 61 percent of capacity. 

Primary zinc smelters and electrolytic plants in 1952 produced 904,479 tons of slab zinc from primary sources, including 575,828 tons from domestic ores and 328,651 tons from foreign ores. (See appendix table 34.) In addition, they produced 18,861 tons of redistilled zinc, or a total of 923,340 tons from all sources. Primary zinc smelters and electrolytic plants had the capacity to produce 1,014,000 tons of slab zinc at the end of 1952. Thus the 1952 output amounted to 91 percent of capacity.

In order to determine approximately, for purposes of comparison, the number of employees at mines and mills producing principally recoverable lead and the number at operations producing princi pally recoverable zinc, the reports for mines and mills were classified as predominantly lead or predominantly zinc and chiefly lead or chiefly zinc. Reports were classified as "predominantly" lead, or zinc, when they covered operations producing ores in which the gross market value of the recoverable lead content, or that of the recoverable zinc content, was 75 percent or more of the total gross market value (at average market prices in 1952) of all recoverable metals contained. 

Other data, such as those from the 1939 census of mineral industries (see appendix table 63), indicate that about one-fifth of the employees at mines and mills are at the mills.

The remaining reports were classified as chiefly lead or chiefly zinc, being classified as "chiefly" lead, or zinc, when they covered operations producing ores in which the gross market value of the recoverable lead content, or that of the recoverable zinc content, was greater than the gross market value of the recoverable content of any other single metal. 

A summary of employment data from reports classified as indicated above shows that a considerably larger number of employees were engaged in mining and milling for zinc than in mining and milling for lead. The number of employees accounted for by reports classified as predominantly zinc and chiefly zinc represented about two-thirds of the total number of employees. Total mine output of zinc in the United States represents about two-thirds of the total mine output of zinc plus lead. The number of employees tabulated from reports classified as chiefly lead exceeded somewhat the number of employees classified as predominantly lead; likewise, the number of employees from reports classified as chiefly zinc exceeded by a small margin the number of employees from reports classified as predominantly zinc.

The average number of employees in primary smelting and refining of lead and zinc was almost 17,500 in 1952. The number of employees at zinc smelters and refineries accounted for 73 percent of the total employment at both lead and zinc smelters and refineries. The proportion (73 percent) of the total number of workers in primary smelting and refining that were employed at zinc plants is larger than the proportion (about 66 percent) of all workers in mining and milling lead and zinc that were employed at predominantly or chiefly zinc mines and mills. Zinc ores and concentrates are more difficult to smelt than lead ores and concentrates. Also, the primary zinc smelters in the United States are engaged in smelting foreign ores to a much greater extent than are primary lead smelters. It may be recalled that about 83 percent of the United States imports of unmanufactured zinc in 1952 were in the form of zinc-bearing ores and concentrates, while lead-bearing ores and concentrates accounted for only 17 percent of the total imports of unmanufactured lead in that year.

3,557. Primary zinc smelters and refineries employed 2,717 persons at plants processing mostly foreign materials, compared with 10,010 at plants consuming mostly domestic materials.

The mine value of the crude ores (and tailings) produced by these operations plus the value added in milling, (value of the concentrates produced minus the value of ores milled) in 1952 aggregated $225,384,000 (see appendix table 60). This represented almost 68 percent of the gross market value of the recoverable metals produced from the ores mined (and old tailings reclaimed) at average market prices prevailing in 1952.6

If this mine or mill value of all products, $225,384,000, is apportioned among the individual recoverable metals contained in the ores mined and tailings reclaimed, according to their gross market value (the quantity of each recoverable metal multiplied by its average market price), and the total mine or mill value of each metal thus obtained is divided by the units of recoverable metal contained in the ores and tailings reclaimed, approximate unit values at the mines or mills are indicated. Such unit values are not precise, because the recoverable contents of the ores produced are not necessarily the contents paid for, and because this method of computation apportions the smelting charge paid by the mines according to the market value of each metal although the cost of smelting some metals, such as zinc, is higher than the cost of smelting lead. The unit values thus computed tend to overstate the average mine or mill value of a pound of zinc and to understate the average mine or mill value of a pound of lead. Nevertheless, the computation indicates approximately the unit values of recoverable metals at mines and mills, the first stage of production.

The annual averages, however, do not indicate the full extent of the fluctuations as shown by daily price changes which are given in table L-7 in part I and table Z-7 in part III. For example, the market price of lead changed from 15 cents a pound at the beginning of 1948 to 21%½ cents at the end of that year and then went down to 

12 cents in 1949; other examples of large price changes in lead are those from 102 cents on March 14, 1950, to 19 cents at the end of 1950 and down again to 12 cents on April 20, 1953. Some of the leadprice changes, like those on March 8, 1949, and October 2, 1951, were as much as 2 cents in a single day. Similarly, the market price of zinc changed from 10½ cents a pound at the beginning of 1948 to 17%½ cents at the end of that year and then declined to a low point of 9 cents on June 15, 1949; later, the price of zinc rose from 

9% cents on January 18, 1950, to 19½ cents on October 2, 1951, and then declined to 94 cents on February 15, 1954. Just as for lead, some of the changes in the price of zinc in a single day were as much as 3 cents (on July 28, 1948) and 2 cents (on October 2, 1951, and 

June 2, 1952).

Sharp fluctuations in the market prices of lead and zinc result in fluctuating income for the lead and zinc industries (especially for the mining and milling segment), particularly for concerns with limited. financial resources that cannot long endure a period of very low prices. They also result in instability in the cost of raw materials for manufacturers of lead and zinc products and hence in a narrowing of the competitive advantage of lead and zinc over substitute raw materials, such as aluminum, which are not characterized by such

price instability. Market prices of zinc, which enters directly into military products (mainly for cartridge cases) in greater quantities than lead, have been stimulated upward to a greater extent than those of lead by war conditions this notwithstanding the great need also for lead in wartime. This effect was especially apparent during World War I, when the prices were not limited by price ceilings, but it was also apparent during World War II and the Korean emergency when the prices were subject to Government price control. 

The market prices of zinc have also been more sensitive than those of lead to declines in general business activity. 

Historically, the market price of zinc generally exceeded, by a substantial margin, the market price of lead, until the early 1920's. 

Since then, however, the price of lead has generally exceeded the price of zinc, except during the periods of World War II and the Korean emergency. The development of selective flotation, whereby most of the zinc content of the more abundant lead-zinc or zinc-lead ores could be recovered, may have had a bearing on this trend. 

Also, ores containing both lead and zinc are found to be richer in zinc than in lead as mining progresses to deeper underground levels. The ratio of recoverable zinc to recoverable lead produced from mines in this country has increased substantially, from 1.1-1 in 1926-30 to 

1.7-1 in 1952 (see appendix table 66).

In the 28 years 1926-53 the price of lead on the average exceeded the price of zinc by about 0.2 cent per pound. If for this period the prices during the war years 1941-45 are excluded from consideration, the average price of lead exceeded the average price of zinc by about 0.6 cent per pound.

Thus, when at the beginning of 1952 the price of zinc was 19½ cents a pound and the price of lead 19 cents, the price of zinc in relation to that of lead was abnormally high; and as of March 10, 1954, with the price of zinc at 94 cents and that of lead at 13 cents, the price of zinc was abnormally low in relation to the price of lead. 

From the beginning of 1952 to March 10, 1954, the price of zinc in the United States dropped 50 percent, while the price of lead declined 

32 percent.

CHAPTER II LEAD AND ZINC RESOURCES AND GRADE OF ORE MINED IN THE UNITED STATES 

Ore reserves

Lead and zinc ore deposits are widely distributed in the United States and throughout the world. The deposits vary greatly as to size, richness, and accessibility. Usually the sulfide minerals galena, the principal lead mineral (86 percent lead), and sphalerite, the principal zinc mineral (67 percent zinc), are contained in the same ore, although in widely varying proportions. An important exception to this in the United States is the zinc ores in northern New Jersey which do not contain any lead. Lead is also commonly associated with silver in the same ore, and zinc (with or without lead) is often found in the same ore with copper. Many of the complex ore deposits in the Western States contain appreciable quantities of silver, copper, and gold in addition to lead and zinc.

The latest estimates of known lead and zinc ore reserves in the United States and in the world, by continents, as estimated by the United States Geological Survey, are shown in table LZ-3. The estimates give the aggregate lead and zinc content of ore deposits that were considered to be minable at a profit at metal prices and costs prevailing at the end of 1949. (At the end of that year the market price of lead in the United States was 12 cents a pound, and that of zinc, 9% cents.) The estimates show the lead and zinc content (not all recoverable) of measured (or proven) and indicated ore. "Measured" ore is that proven by sufficient development work to leave little doubt as to its limits and grade. "Indicated" ore is that shown to exist by development work which was not extensive enough to determine the exact size and grade of ore deposits. The statistics do not include "inferred" ore, the figures for which are usually estimated from preliminary development and geological work and are, therefore, less accurate. 

At the end of 1949, the estimated reserves of lead in measured and indicated ore deposits in the United States (as shown in table LZ-3) were 2,900,000 tons, or 7.5 percent of the world total; estimated reserves of zinc in measured and indicated ore were 8,500,000 tons, or 12.5 percent of the world total. Only between 80 and 90 percent of these reserves of lead and about 75 percent of the reserves of zinc are estimated as recoverable owing to mining, milling, and smelting losses. Measured lead reserves in the United States were smaller than those in other North American countries (taken together), in Europe, Australia, or Africa; they were larger than the lead reserves in either South America or Asia. Measured and indicated zinc reserves in the United States were not so large as those of South America, Europe, or Australia, but they were larger than those of other North American countries combined, and larger than those in 

Asia or Africa. or 7 It has been estimated by the U. S. Geological Survey that of all the elements in the earth's crust lead and zinc constitute about 0.0001 percent, compared with 8.0 percent for aluminum, 4.5 percent for iron, 2.5 percent for magnesium, 0.02 percent for nickel, and 0.002 percent for copper. Of all metals contained in the world's igneous rocks (rocks produced by the cooling of molten or plastic material), about 0.004 percent is comprised of zinc and 0.002 percent of lead. In addition, sea water carries perceptible quantities of lead and zinc as well as other metals. 

The ore minerals in northern New Jersey are zincite (a zinc oxide containing about 80 percent zinc), willemite (a zinc orthosilicate, containing about 59 percent zinc), and franklinite (an ore containing iron, zinc, and manganese in varying proportions and used to some extent for making spiegeleisen).

NOTE. This tabulation shows the lead and zinc content (not all recoverable) of measured or proven lead, zinc, and lead-zinc ore (that is, ore measured by sufficient development work to leave little doubt as to its limits and grade) plus indicated ore (that is, ore shown to exist by development work which, however, was not extensive enough to determine the exact size and grade of ore deposits). The statistics do not include inferred ore, which is usually estimated from preliminary development and geological work. The figures shown for lead and zinc content apply to deposits that were considered to be minable at a profit at metal prices and costs prevailing at the end of 1949. 

The ore reserves given in this table should be regarded as minimum reserves that will be augmented as further exploration and development work is undertaken. Mining companies, owing to the expense involved and to other considerations, usually do not develop ore bodies to an extent greater than would be necessary to carry on mining operations for about 4 to 5 years. 

It should be realized that these estimates of lead and zinc in ore represent only the reserves shown by development work. Mining companies usually do not develop ore bodies for more than 4 to 5 years ahead of mining because of the expense involved and for other reasons. Also the reserves are those regarded by the estimators to be minable profitably at metal prices and costs prevailing at the time the estimates were made. The estimates depend upon the status of development work and the economic conditions prevailing at the time of the estimates. Thus in January 1944, under conditions then prevailing, the United States Geological Survey and the United States Bureau of Mines estimated the lead content of measured and indicated ore reserves in the United States at 2,090,000 tons (compared with 2,900,000 tons at the end of 1949). Similarly, the estimate of zinc. contained in such ore reserves in the United States in January 1944 was 6,957,000 tons (compared with 8,500,000 tons at the end of 1949). 

United States ore reserves of lead and zinc have been sufficient to enable this country to produce much more lead and zinc than any other country for a great many years. (See appendix tables 20 and 

49.) Although the aggregate mine output of lead and zinc-especially of lead-in the United States has declined from the peak level of the late 1920's, the trends for individual mining districts show wide differences reflecting depletion of commercial lead and zinc ore deposits in some areas and the discovery and development of new ore bodies, or extension of known ore bodies, in other areas. Between 1926-30 and 1952, annual mine output of lead in the United States declined 39 percent, while zinc output declined 5 percent and lead-plus-zinc output decreased by 21 percent. (As previously noted, the ratio of zinc to lead produced by mines during this period increased, owing partly to the fact that ore deposits at deeper levels contain more zinc in relation to the lead content than at levels nearer to the surface.)

Among the more important mining districts that have shown the largest net declines in mine output between the level of 1926-30 and 1952, in terms of tons of recoverable lead plus zinc, are the following: 

Tri-State district (embracing the adjacent corners of Kansas, Missouri, and Oklahoma), where the drop in annual tonnage produced has amounted to 271,000 tons (mostly zinc); Southeastern Missouri (decline of 71,000 tons, mostly lead); Park City, Utah (decline of 45,000 tons lead and zinc); New Jersey (decline of 36,000 tons, all zinc); 

Tintic district in Utah (decline of 35,842 tons, lead declined more than zinc increased); Coeur d'Alene district in Idaho (decline of 30,000 tons, lead declined more than zinc increased); and Animas district in 

Colorado (decline of 28,000 tons, lead and zinc). Several smaller mining districts discontinued production of lead and zinc altogether owing to exhaustion of ores. Among these are the Willow Creek district in New Mexico, where operations were suspended in 1939, and the Old Hat district in Arizona, where mining for lead and zinc ceased after 1952. (See appendix table 66.)

On the other hand, several mining districts in the United States have substantially increased their production of lead and zinc since the late 1920's through the discovery and development of newly found ore bodies. Production (mostly zinc) in the Central district of New 

Mexico in 1952 was 41,000 tons larger than the average in 1926-30 principally because of exploration and development work begun in 1940. Production of lead and zinc (mostly zinc) in the State of 

Washington was larger by about 30,000 tons in 1952 than in the late 1920's, owing to the discovery and development of sizable low-grade ore bodies in the Metaline Falls district in the last 15 years. Similarly, production in 1952 as compared with the average for 1926-30 was about 25,000 tons higher in the Summit Valley (Butte) district of Montana, 14,000 tons higher in northern Illinois and Wisconsin, 12,000 tons higher in California, and 10,000 tons higher in the Pioche district of Nevada. 

Recent mine developments

Under the stimulus of recent high lead and zinc prices and Government encouragement (1950-52), numerous exploration projects were undertaken both in the United States and in foreign countries; some of them have resulted in important ore discoveries and have led to the development of new mines and expansion of old ones. Some of the major projects in the United States and foreign countries are listed in appendix table 69.

Among the more important developments in the United States are those in Washington County, in Southeastern Missouri, where 2 new mines are being developed with annual capacity to produce more than 30,000 tons of lead (with some zinc). One of the large mining companies announced in 1952 the discovery of a large zinc ore body in eastern Tennessee that may contain over 1 million tons of zinc, and a shaft is being sunk to develop this ore body. Mine-development work is in progress in Pennsylvania, a State not listed as a zinc producer in recent years, from which 39,000 tons of zinc per year are expected in the near future. Other important mine developments as well as mill-construction projects when completed may increase the production of lead and zinc in Idaho, Colorado, Washington, and other States, and the production of zinc in New Jersey, Virginia, Montana, 46566-54-15

and other States. Most of these developments were undertaken before the recent declines in prices of lead and zinc; but a considerable amount of such development work is continued even when prices are temporarily unfavorable. These developments, involving the investment of many millions of dollars, may in the future offset the effect on mine production of depletion of ore deposits in older mines. 

New and improved scientific methods of exploration are being applied to an increasing extent to locate ore bodies below the earth's surface, the presence of which are not revealed by outcrops that have guided prospectors in the past. Some of the recent discoveries have employed geophysical and geochemical procedures-methods that may provide much more knowledge than is now available as to the actual extent of the lead and zinc ore resources of the United States. 

The resource of lead and zinc metals in use A growing share of United States supply of lead and to a lesser extent of zinc is obtained from old scrap. The increase in lead production from old scrap has become so large in recent years that it has exceeded mine production. With a steady growth in the country's stock of lead- and zinc-containing articles from which these metals are salvageable after use (including lead-acid storage batteries, lead cable coverings, brass articles, and zinc die castings), the increase in secondary production of lead may be expected to continue and there may also be somewhat increased recovery of zinc from old scrap.

The grade of ore mined, more particularly the recoverable content of metals in ore, is a key determinant (along with market prices of the metals, milling and smelting charges, and transportation costs from mines to smelters) of the income received for the ore mined. Detailed data on the recoverable grade of ore mined in the United States among the principal mining districts in 1939, 1942, and 1952 are shown in appendix tables 67 and 68.

This tabulation of grade of ore mined in 1952 is based on all ores mined in the United States (excluding old tailings and material from old slag dumps) that were valued chiefly for their content of lead and zinc. It includes ores mined by all lead and zinc mines as reported to the United States Bureau of Mines including ores produced by some mines that were not covered in the Tariff Commission's questionnaire survey of mines."

The grade of ore mined as given in the above tabulation is in terms of recoverable metal content rather than gross metal content often referred to in the mining industry. The grade of ore mined, as measured by recoverable metal content rather than as measured by gross metal content, is presented here because it is more closely related to the value of the ores than is their gross metal content. The recoverable metal content is of crude ore mined, not of concentrates produced. 

In 1952 lead and zinc mines in the United States produced a total of 25,086,000 tons of crude ore, not including old tailings or material from old slag dumps reclaimed for re-treatment (which are discussed later). The recoverable metal content of this ore averaged 1.4 percent lead (by weight), 2.5 percent zinc, and 0.1 percent copper, in addition to 0.73 ounce of silver and 0.006 ounce of gold per ton of ore. On the basis of average market prices prevailing in 1952, the silver, copper, and gold content amounted to less than 10 percent of the gross market value of all recoverable metals contained. The gross metal content of the ores mined in the United States, which includes metal lost in milling and smelting the ores, was 1.7 percent lead, 3.2 percent zinc, 0.1 percent copper, and 0.91 ounce of silver and 0.007 ounce of gold per ton. Thus, of the total metal contained in the ores mined in 1952, The Commission's survey, however, covered such a large percentage of production from lead and zinc mines in the United States in 1952 that the recoverable grade of ore mined based solely on reports to the Commission was virtually the same as that based on output from all mines.

about 87 percent of the lead and 79 percent of the zinc was recoverable. The remainder was lost in milling and, to a lesser extent, in smelting.

The recoverable grade of ore mined in the United States in 1952 varied widely among the mining States or districts both with regard to the total quantity of metal contained per ton of ore and with regard to the kinds and relative amounts of the metals contained. The lowest grade of ore mined, in terms of percentage of lead-plus-zinc content, was in the Tri-State district (0.4 percent lead plus 1.4 percent zinc). 

The recoverable grade of ore mined in Southeastern Missouri was almost as low (1.8 percent lead plus a very small amount of zinc).

Southeastern Missouri ores, however, were almost entirely of lead (prices of which are currently higher, relatively, than are those of zinc), whereas in the Tri-State ores the zinc content was 3½ times that of lead. Moreover, Southeastern Missouri ores contained a little silver. The grade of ore mined in the Upper Mississippi Valley district including northern Illinois and Wisconsin was also quite low (0.3 percent lead and 2.7 percent zinc).

The recoverable grade of ore mined in 1952 was generally highest in the Western States, where the ores contained not only relatively high percentages of lead and zinc but also appreciable quantities of silver, copper, and gold. Among Western States the average recoverable grade of ore mined in terms of lead-plus-zinc content was highest in 

Utah (11.9 percent) and almost as high in California (10.6 percent).

The ores produced by lead and zinc mines in these two States also contained relatively large quantities of silver, gold, and copper. The recoverable grade of ores mined in Washington, which averaged 1.5 percent lead and 2.6 percent zinc (with very small additional content of silver, gold, and copper), was lowest among the Western States.

The grade of ores mined in Montana, 4.3 percent combined lead and zinc, was not much higher than that of those mined in Washington, but these ores contained somewhat larger quantities of silver, gold, and copper than the ores mined in Washington. The combined recoverable content of lead and zinc in the ores mined in other Western States averaged 5.9 percent in Arizona, 6.8 percent in Colorado, 7.2 percent in Idaho, and 8.1 percent in Nevada.

The recoverable grade of ore mined in the group of Eastern States, including New York, New Jersey, Tennessee, and Virginia, averaged 

5.1 percent zinc and 0.2 percent lead. The average grade of ore mined among the Eastern States included in this group varied widely-with the highest average exceeding that in the Western States. 

As indicated by the data for 1952, the Eastern States produce zinc almost exclusively. Zinc is also the predominant metal in ores mined in northern Illinois and Wisconsin and in New Mexico, although the ores mined in these States contain appreciable quantities of lead. Zinc is the more important metal in ores mined in the Tri-State district and in Montana, Arizona, Colorado, and Nevada, although not to so large an extent as in the States previously named. 

The number of States mining ores in which lead predominates is smaller than the number mining predominantly zinc ores. Southeastern Missouri is the outstanding producer of predominantly lead ores. The ores mined in Utah contained 1.5 times as much lead as zinc, and the ores mined in California contained 1.2 times as much lead as zinc. Idaho, which is the largest producer of lead and the

second largest producer of zinc among the Western States, produces about equal tonnages of lead and zinc. 

Re-treatment of old tailings and smelter slag.-"Old mill tailings" i refers to material that was rejected during the milling (or concentration) of crude ores in past years. Milling methods have improved over the years, especially with the development of selective flotation techniques in the 1920's. As a result, less metal is lost in milling than formerly. Some of the older mining districts, especially the Tri-State and Southeastern Missouri districts, had accumulated large piles of old tailings, the metal content of which can be profitably extracted with i improved methods when metal prices are favorable. Most of the dold-tailings dumps in the Tri-State district have been re-treated (some of them twice). In 1952 a total of 2,679,000 tons of old tailings were re-treated in Southeastern Missouri, in the Tri-State district, in Idaho, and in a few other States. No old tailings were re-treated in the Tri- 

State district in 1953. These tailings include a very small quantity of mine tailings (boulders and the like rejected in mining) in addition to mill tailings. The recoverable metal content of these tailings averaged 0.6 percent lead and 0.3 percent zinc.

Improved metallurgical techniques have also permitted larger recoveries of metals in smelting. Older lead-smelting processes did 

Tea not recover zinc contained in lead concentrates; such zinc was in the slag removed from the blast furnaces of lead smelters. Beginning in World

War II, some companies added zinc-fuming facilities to the lead smelters to recover the zinc contained in blast-furnace slags. The addition of such zinc-fuming facilities to lead smelter works has been accelerated in recent years both in the United States and in foreign countries. In 1951, according to the United States Bureau of Mines, the four slag-fuming plants at lead smelters treated 606,000 tons of hot and cold slag which yielded 108,000 tons of oxide fume containing 74,672 tons of recoverable zinc (12.3 percent of the weight of the slag). Changes in the grade of ore mined. Changes in the grade of ore mined have an important bearing on both the income received and the expenses incurred in mining. Low-grade ore, in comparison with highgrade ore, necessitates breaking, loading, hoisting, and milling a larger tonnage of material to obtain an equivalent quantity of incomeyielding recoverable metal. As indicated later, however, some companies have been able to keep costs down despite mining low-grade ore, by mechanization and improved mining methods. 

In order to determine how the average grade of the ore mined by lead and zinc mines has changed in recent years the Commission supplemented the data for 1952, discussed above, with similar information developed from data compiled in the 1939 census of mineral industries 10 and data for 1942 from the United States Bureau of Mines.
