The general decline in the average grade of crude ore produced at lead and zinc mines in the United States for the years indicated is the net effect of the closing or curtailment of operations at some mines and the opening or expansion of other mines. Depletion or exhaustion of high-grade ore bodies is probably one of the influencing factors but not necessarily the most important one. Mining companies seek to produce the most income with the least cost. Often the highest grade ore is least accessible and most costly to mine. 

This is indicated by the relatively high costs per ton of the high-grade ore produced in some of the Western States discussed in the next chapter.

Improvements in mining equipment and techniques for handling large masses of low-grade ores are probably an important factor in the general trend toward the mining of lower grade ores. 

Prices obtainable for the product mined are, of course, another factor considered by mine operators. Orderly exploitation of a developed ore body requires the removal of lower grade ore whenever it can be mined without loss. Ore bodies are usually not uniform in grade throughout. Some companies have deliberately turned to mining their lower grade ore when the prices of lead and zinc were favorable. Average market prices of lead and zinc in the United

CHAPTER III VALUE OF PRODUCTS, PRINCIPAL EXPENSES, AND PROFIT OR LOSS IN PRIMARY LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES 

This chapter is devoted principally to the discussion of value of products, principal expenses, and profit or loss in the mining and milling segment of the lead and zinc industries. Some information, however, is also presented at the end of the chapter on profit or loss in primary smelting and refining. 

Before considering the changes in the conditions prevailing in the lead- and zinc-mining industries in the United States associated with the sharp declines in prices and greatly increased imports since the beginning of 1952, it is desirable to consider broadly previous changes. 

A comparison of data for 1939 and 1952 shows some of the earlier changes. The calendar year 1952 is the latest year for which data could be assembled, and although market prices began to decline after the first part of the year, the average prices for the year were still relatively high-16.467 cents a pound for lead, and 16.215 cents a pound for zinc. The average price of lead exceeded the average for zinc by 0.252 cent, close to the average difference of 0.2 cent for the last 28 years. The year 1939 is the latest prewar year for which substantial data bearing on the economic condition of the industries are available-largely because a census of mineral industries covered that year. The average market price of lead in 1939 was 5.053 cents

a pound and that of zinc, 5.110 cents. The price of zinc, perhaps already stimulated by the imminence of war in Europe, was slightly higher than that of lead.

Income received from the products of mining and milling in 1939 and 1952 The crude ores mined (exclusive of tailings) by all lead and zinc mines in the United States in 1939 contained, on the average, the following approximate content of recoverable metals per ton of ore: 

44.3 pounds of lead, 56.4 pounds of zinc, 0.7 pound of copper, 0.71 ounce of silver, and 0.004 ounce of gold in addition to some miscellaneous products. At the average market prices of these metals prevailing in the United States in that year, the gross market value of these quantities of metal plus the miscellaneous products was $6.07. 

The value of all products at mines and mills-that is, the total net income received from mining and milling per ton of crude ore mined in 1939 amounted to $3.84, which was 63.3 percent of the gross market value of the recoverable metals contained in the ores and concentrates produced." (See appendix table 59.) 

By a similar computation, a ton of ore mined (exclusive of tailings) by lead and zinc mines in the United States in 1952 contained the following approximate content of recoverable metals: 28.9 pounds of lead, 50.7 pounds of zinc, 1.2 pounds of copper, 0.73 ounce of silver, and 0.006 ounce of gold. At the average market prices of metals in the United States in 1952, the above recoverable metal content plus some miscellaneous products per ton of ore mined had a gross market value of $14.53. Reports to the Tariff Commission of mining companies that produced 93 percent of all lead and zinc mined by all lead and zinc mines indicated that the value of all products at mines and mills amounted to $9.83 per ton of crude ore mined, or 67.7 percent of the gross market value of the recoverable metals contained in the ore mined.12 (See appendix table 60.) This percentage is slightly higher than that for 1939. 

The average mine or mill value of products per ton of crude ore mined in 1952 was 156 percent higher than the average for 1939. By comparison, the market price of lead increased by 226 percent during the same period, and the market price of zinc by 217 percent.

The relatively smaller increase in the average value of products per ton of ore mined reflects the lower grade of ore mined (as measured by the content of recoverable metals) in 1952 as compared with that in 1939. 

11 The value of products-and the principal expenses discussed later in this chapter-are related to crude ore mined exclusive of old tailings. This value of products at the mines or mills excludes costs of transportation from mines or mills, smelting charges, etc. The value of all products at mines and mills is not necessarily the same as net sales, which are also discussed in this report. The aggregate sales of more than one company involve duplications insofar as the value of ore sold by one company reappears as part of the sales value of concentrates produced from such ores and sold by another company. The subtraction of the value of ores milled from the value of concentrates produced avoided such duplication in aggregating the value of all products at mines and mills or the mine or mill value of all products as used in this report. 

Some of the companies that have integrated operations wherein the ore mined and milled is also smelted at other works of the same company, could supply only an estimate of the mine or mill value of the ores and concentrates produced. To get at the mill value of concentrates produced, these companies generally estimated the market value of the recoverable metal content of the concentrates and deducted therefrom smelting and refining charges and costs of transportation of concentrates from mills to smelters. Where it was necessary also to determine the value of milling ore (before milling), the companies subtracted from the value of the concentrates the costs of milling the ore. For one of the important mining companies such estimates were prepared by the Commission's staff on the basis of other available data.

NI 2-8 The average value of all mine and mill products per ton of crude ore mined varied widely from one mining district to another in both 1939 and 1952. This value is directly related to the grade of ore mined, which, as previously noted, varies widely among the districts.

Method of determining the price received for ores and concentrates.— 

The amount received by mining companies per unit of their products fluctuates with changes in market prices of metals to a greater extent than the income received per unit of products of smelting and refining companies. In order to understand why this is so, it is necessary to consider how the price paid for ores and concentrates is determined. 

A large part of the ores and concentrates produced, probably nearly one-half of those produced in 1952, are processed by custom smelters. 

These smelters purchase ores and concentrates from large ore producers on the basis of negotiated contracts covering several years, or from small or irregular producers on the basis of "open" schedules (standing offers to buy ores under terms specified by the smelter) subject to change on relatively short notice. Although the contract terms differ in many details, the net amount paid to the seller for the ores and concentrates is generally based on their metal content 13 multiplied by the prevailing market prices, from which deductions are made (in various ways) to cover losses in smelting, costs of smelting, refining, and marketing, the cost of transporting the ores from the mine to the smelter, the cost of transporting lead bullion from smelters to refineries, and the smelter's profit. The seller of the ore is usually paid for it at the time he delivers the ore to the smelter. 

Smelter purchase contracts vary in many details to take account of the size and regularity of the ore supply anticipated from the producer, the kind and grade of that ore supply, and other factors that affect the costs of smelting and refining. Elements in the ores that increase smelting costs, such as arsenic, antimony, tin, bismuth, and zinc (if in lead concentrates) and insoluble elements, are penalized if carried in the ores and concentrates in excess of prescribed minimum percentages. On the other hand, elements that facilitate processing, such as iron and fluxing materials, are sometimes given a credit. 

Also premiums are paid for the content of silver and gold. Some smelter contracts have escalator clauses in them providing for increases in smelter charges with increases in important smelting cost elements, such as wage rates. 

Smelters generally offer more favorable terms to ore producers who can assure a large and regular flow of ores and concentrates than to those who can furnish only small or irregular supplies. The market for the ores or concentrates produced at a given locality is generally limited to the nearest smelter, for, as noted below, the cost of transporting ores and concentrates is substantial in relation to their value at mines or mills. 

13 The amount to be paid for ores depends to a large extent upon their metal content. Usually both buyer and seller agree to settle on the average of their separate assay analyses if the two are within 0.5 percent. If not, a sample of the ore is usually sent to a mutually acceptable public chemist or "umpire" and his analysis is then averaged with that of either the buyer or the seller, whichever analysis is closest to that of the "umpire."

Custom smelters derive their income principally from the profits of processing the ores or concentrates. Increases in the market prices of the metals produced are usually and in large degree offset by increases in payments for ores or concentrates, the prices of which are based on the market prices of the metals. Similarly, Similarly, decreases in the market prices of metals produced by smelters are generally largely offset by reductions in the payments for ores or concentrates purchased.

Smelters, however, generally reduce smelting charges when the market prices of metals decline, thereby reducing their profit from smelting; and they increase the charges when the market prices of metals advance. These increases and decreases are, however, much smaller than the changes in prices in response to which they are made. 

The extent of this variation in smelting charges is not the same for all the smelters. For smelting most zinc concentrates, the charges are increased or decreased about $1 to $2 per ton of concentrates for each 1-cent-per-pound change in zinc market prices. Some smelter contracts have lower limits below which smelter charges are not reduced. In 1952, mining and milling companies that reported to the Tariff Commission produced a total of 1,179,000 tons of zinc concentrates with an aggregate value at mills of $132,869,000 or about $113 per ton. These concentrates contained an average of 54 percent zinc. A decrease of $1 to $2 per ton of zinc concentrates in the smelter's charge would have been equivalent to reduction of 0.09 to 

0.18 cent per pound of zinc content in the price paid by the smelters for concentrates. This indicates that even if none of the smelting contracts imposed a lower limit to the reductions in smelting charges, a 10-cent drop in the market price of zinc would have resulted in a decrease of only 0.9 cent to 1.8 cents in smelting charges per pound of zinc contained in concentrates.14 

The cost of transporting ores and concentrates, as explained above, is a cost borne by the ore producer. In most areas this cost, in accordance with railroad practice, is based on tonnage moved, and in others, principally in the Northwestern States, on the value of the ores and concentrates moved. In the latter States the cost of transporting the ores is thus reduced somewhat by reductions in the market prices of metals contained in the ores. 

Except for the adjustments in smelting charges and transportation costs explained above, the mine operator bears most of the impact of each reduction in the market prices of the metals contained in the ores mined.

Cost of transporting ores and concentrates from mines and mills to smelters.-The Tariff Commission's questionnaires distributed to primary smelting and refining companies requested these companies to report the average costs of transportation, insurance, and other handling charges for lead and zinc ores and concentrates from principal mining districts to the smelters regardless of who paid these costs. 

These data for 1952 are summarized in appendix table 23 for lead, and in appendix table 52 for zinc. The cost of transporting lead

As noted in chapter I of part IV, in 1952, for the United States as a whole, the cost of transporting lead ores and concentrates from mines and mills to smelters, combined with the cost of transporting lead bullion from smelters to refineries, averaged 1.2 cents per pound of recoverable metal contained in lead ores and concentrates produced in that year. This cost amounted to about 11 percent of the estimated value of recoverable lead produced at mines and mills. 

Similarly the cost of transporting zinc ores and concentrates from mines to smelters in the United States in 1952 averaged 0.8 cent per pound of recoverable zinc, or about 7 percent of the estimated mine or mill value of recoverable zinc produced.

The average costs given above were computed by obtaining arithmetic (unweighted) averages of costs of moving ores and concentrates (per pound of lead or zinc content) from principal mines or mills to each smelter and by weighting these arithmetic averages by the total lead or zinc content of ores and concentrates from domestic sources consumed by each smelter in 1952. The average was then adjusted to represent cost per pound of recoverable metal. The average cost of transporting lead in ores and concentrates from each shipping point to each destination ranged from 0.1 cent to 2.1 cents per pound of lead content, and that of transporting lead in bullion, from 0.7 cent to 1.3 cents. The average cost of transporting zinc in ores and concentrates over each principal route varied from 0.1 cent to 1.5 cents per pound of zinc content.

Freight rates for rail transportation of lead and zinc ores and concentrates in the United States have increased substantially since 1946. 

Rail freight rates, on carload lots, per ton of ores and concentrates in 1939, 1946-49, and 1952 over typical routes from mines to smelters are summarized for lead ores and concentrates, in appendix table 25, and for zinc ores and concentrates, in appendix table 53. These tables were compiled from information supplied to the Tariff Commission by the American Zinc Institute. Rail freight rates on both lead and zinc ores and concentrates increased in each of the postwar years 1947, 1948, 1949, and 1952. The rates prevailing at the end of 1952 on lead and zinc ores and concentrates were from 36 to 80 percent above the rates prevailing at the end of 1946.

The ratio of principal expenses to value of products was higher in 1952 than in 1939 for all the mining areas shown except for New York, New Jersey, Tennessee, and Virginia combined, where the ratio declined. The decrease shown for this group was the result of a more-than-average rise in value of products per ton of crude ore mined accompanied by a less-than-average increase in principal expenses per ton of ore mined. The increase in the value of products per ton of ore mined in these States was substantially less than the rise in principal expenses per ton of ore. Although labor requirements per ton of ore mined in these States as a group were reduced substantially, this reduction was not sufficient to offset the effect of a more rapid rise in hourly wage payments than in value of products per ton of ore mined.

The outstanding fact shown by the above tabulation is that in the Western States the mining and milling of lead and zinc ores requires much more labor than it does in the other areas. Unit labor requirements are lowest in the Tri-State and the Southeastern Missouri districts; the large open stopes and other physical conditions in these districts permit the use of mining methods and large-scale mechanization that cannot be as effectively employed in mining the richer but smaller and less accessible ore bodies in the Western States. 

Man-hour requirements per ton of ore mined in the United States as a whole declined by only 4 percent between 1939 and 1952. 

Unit labor requirements increased by 5 percent in the Eastern States and by 10 percent in Southeastern Missouri. These increases may reflect more development work in 1952 than in 1939; several new mines are being developed in these areas. 

The Tri-State district shows an unusually large reduction in manhours required per ton of ore mined. Some of the largest and more progressive companies in this area have introduced new and improved mining methods in recent years including the use of diesel-powered truck haulage underground, improved trackless loading equipment, and mobile drill jumbos.

Recent changes in operating profit or loss in primary lead and zinc industries Nature of data on profit or loss.--The questionnaire distributed by the Tariff Commission to mining and milling companies called for information on total net sales, operating expenses, and profit or lossbefore and after income taxes for operations engaged in mining and milling ores or concentrates valued chiefly for their content of lead plus zinc. Similar data (discussed later) were also requested in the questionnaire distributed by the Tariff Commission to primary lead and zinc smelting and refining companies.

The Commission did not attempt to make a detailed accounting study of sales income, operating expenses, and profit or loss. No attempt was made, nor could any have been made within the limitations of time and staff, to obtain reports of the financial data in accordance with uniformly defined concepts of such items as depreciation, amortization, and depletion. The companies were asked only to report data summarized from their audited profit-and-loss statements.

ti

Some check on the accuracy of profit-and-loss data reported was afforded by information reported in other parts of the questionnaires, and some obviously incorrect reports were rejected as a result. By and large, however, the completed reports were summarized and tabulated as reported.

Profit-and-loss data were requested for 1939, 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953. Very few of the companies could report data for 

1939, and very few reported data on income taxes paid and net profit or loss after income taxes. Some of the large concerns have integrated operations extending into smelting, refining, fabricating, and other activities as well as mining and milling; some are engaged in producing metals other than lead or zinc; and some have operations in foreign countries as well. A few of these companies stated that they could not report financial data segregated in the manner called for, especially with respect to income taxes paid. A few integrated concerns submitted reports in which the data requested had been partly estimated.

Profit or loss from mining and milling in 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953. After the elimination of reports that were incomplete or that were obviously in error and could not be corrected by correspondence without unduly delaying the summation of returns, financial data from mining and milling companies were summarized for 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953 from 95 reports covering 185 mines and 67 mills. (See table LZ-5.) In 1952 these mines and mills produced 79 percent of the mine output of recoverable lead and 56 percent of the recoverable zinc produced by all lead and zinc mines in the United States. This is considerably less than the lead and zinc accounted for (92 and 93 percent, respectively) by the operations covered by the 211 reports from which data (previously discussed) were tabulated on quantity and value of products, principal expenses (labor, supplies and materials, fuels, and purchased electricity), and employment."

River, and Colorado, and especially California and Montana, are poorly represented. The average output per mine of lead plus zinc. in 1952 by the 185 mines covered by the 95 reports was about 3,550 tons, compared with an average output of 3,000 tons by the 313 mines covered by the 211 reports.

In the first two columns of the tabulation (based on 1952 data from the 95 reports) the ratio of all expenses (except income taxes) to net sales is compared with the ratio of principal expenses to value of products. "Principal expenses" as used in this report include only expenditures for salaries and wages, supplies and materials, fuels, and purchased electricity. "Net operating profit (or loss)" refers to total net sales (receipts from sales of all mine and mill products) minus all expenses (including cost of labor, supplies and materials, fuels, and purchased electricity, and also depreciation of plant and equipment, amortization, depletion or royalties, taxes other than income taxes, other mining and milling expenses, and administrative and selling expenses).

Labor cost, the principal element in the cost of mining and milling, probably increased between 1950 and 1952. Average hourly earnings of production and related workers in lead and zinc mining and milling as reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics increased by 20 percent from an average of $1.60 in 1950 to an average of $1.92 in 1952. 

The ratio of net operating profit before income taxes to net sales varied widely for operations covered by individual reports. (A separate report was requested from each company for its lead and zinc mining operations in each State.) This is indicated by table LZ-6, which shows the distribution of the 95 reports and the 1952 output of lead and zinc produced by the operations covered, according to the ratio of net operating profit to net sales in 1950, 1952, and the first half of 1953. In each of the periods a number of operations show very high ratios of losses to net sales. Some of these include nonproducing or virtually nonproducing operations that (in 1 or more of the 3 periods considered) were either engaged in development work only or were inactive and incurred expenses in the maintenance of production facilities.

Financial data on profit and loss, similar to that for mining and milling presented above, were obtained for 12 out of the 18 primary zinc smelters and refineries and for 5 out of the 13 primary lead smelters and refineries. The 12 zinc plants included in the tabulation presented in table LZ-7 accounted for 72 percent of total slab-zinc shipments in 1952 from all primary zinc smelters and refineries. The 6 zinc plants excluded from the tabulation for zinc smelters included a smelter in each of the States of Illinois, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, and Oklahoma, and 2 plants in Texas.

Most of the data submitted for primary lead smelters and refineries proved to be defective, mostly because of incomplete data on costs of materials. The 5 reports that were complete included 3 plants smelting only, 1 plant smelting and refining, and 1 plant refining only.

CHAPTER IV RECENT CHANGES IN PRODUCTION AND EMPLOYMENT IN THE PRI- MARY LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES IN THE UNITED STATES 

Changes in mine output of lead and zinc since the beginning of 1952 Overall changes in the United States. 18-Monthly mine output of both lead and zinc in the United States showed a sharp downward trend from the early part of 1952 to the end of 1953. The decline in output during this period was substantially greater for zinc than for lead. 

Mine production of 37,745 tons of recoverable zinc in December 1953 was 37 percent below the monthly average for the first 3 months of 1952, while the December 1953 output of lead (revised), amounting to 27,107 tons, was 21 percent below the level of lead production in the first quarter of 1952 (see appendix tables 12, 13, 41, and 42). For

E the year 1953 as a whole, zinc output (534,730 tons) was 20 percent lower than in 1952, and lead output (337,204 tons) was down 14 percent.

In comparison, the Federal Reserve Board index of physical volume of industrial production (adjusted for working-day and seasonal variations) showed a general increase from the middle of 1952 through July 1953 (the month of the Korean armistice), and although it declined from July 1953 through December 1953, it nonetheless was 5 percent greater in December 1953 than in the first quarter of 1952. 

Mine output of lead and zinc in the United States is usually not subject to important seasonal variations. Virtually all of the mining 

18 Some minor revisions of data on mine output of lead for December 1953 (particularly for the West Central States) and the total for 1953 were published by the Bureau of Mines toward the end of March 1954. 

Although these revisions are taken into account in the discussion of mine-production changes in this chapter, the data were received too late to be incorporated in basic tables and other sections of this report.

is underground and not greatly affected by weather conditions, although on occasion unusually severe weather conditions may affect power supply and transportation of ore and supplies. 

The reduction of about 53,000 tons in the mine production of lead in the United States in 1953, as compared with output in 1952, was greater than the reduction between any other 2 successive calendar years in the postwar period. The decline of 131,271 tons in the mine production of zinc in 1953 as compared with the output in 1952which in part reflected curtailed output owing to labor disputes-was greater than that between any 2 successive calendar years since the severe depression of the early 1930's. 

Mine output of lead in January 1954, the last month for which data are available, reflected a continuation of the general downward trend in production and was 8 percent below the December 1953 level. 

Mine output of zinc in January 1954, however, was 3 percent above the December 1953 rate, an increase due in large part to the resumption of mining and milling activities at operations of one of the major producers in the Tri-State area. 

Mine output of lead in January 1954 (24,978 tons) was 11 percent below the monthly average of 28,100 tons for 1953 and 23 percent below the monthly average of 32,513 tons for 1952. Mine output of zinc in January 1954 (38,717 tons) was 13 and 30 percent below the monthly averages for 1953 (44,561 tons) and 1952 (55,500 tons), respectively.

Changes in mine output by principal regions or States. While the rate of mine production of lead and zinc in the United States as a whole declined 21 and 37 percent, respectively, between the first quarter of 1952 and December 1953, the extent of the decline in the individual States varied widely (see appendix tables 12, 13, 41, and 42). Although December 1953 mine output of lead and zinc was nil, or almost nil, in some States, it had increased somewhat in a few States. 

The production of lead from Oklahoma mines in December 1953 was 73 percent less than the monthly average production in the State in the first quarter of 1952. In Arizona, output of lead dropped 56 percent during the same period; in Colorado it declined 26 percent; in Utah, 23 percent; in Idaho, 20 percent; and in 

Montana, 9 percent. Lead output in New Mexico declined by 77 percent; that in Washington by 44 percent; and that in Kansas by 

91 percent. However, December 1953 output in Missouri, the major lead-producing State, was only slightly below the average for the first quarter of 1952; average monthly output in that State in the last quarter of 1953 as a whole, however, was 6 percent below the average for the first quarter of 1952. The relatively small production of lead in northern Illinois and Wisconsin, combined, increased 18 percent during the period. For the group of States east of the Mississippi 

River as a whole, output of lead decreased by 16 percent, while that in the West Central States declined by 27 percent, and that in the 

Western States by 27 percent. Mine output of lead in January 1954 in each of the three major geographic divisions (Western States, West Central States, and States east of the Mississippi) was below that in 

December 1953.

Mine output of zinc in the Western States (not including the West Central States) and in the States east of the Mississippi River was lower in January 1954 than in December 1953. Production in the 

West Central States increased from 1,646 tons of recoverable zinc in December 1953 to 4,139 tons in January 1954, largely as a result of resumption of production at some of the mines following settlement of labor disputes.

Many reports to the Tariff Commission from lead and zinc producers, periodic publications of the United States Bureau of Mines, and trade-paper reports attribute the fall in output of both lead and zinc in the United States during the period 1952-53 largely to the sharp decline in the prices of these metals. As previously noted, the price of lead in December 1953 was 29 percent below the average for the first quarter of 1952 and the price of zinc in December 1953 was 49 percent below the average for the earlier period. The current (March 10, 1954) prices, 13 cents a pound for lead and 94 cents a pound for zinc, are one-half cent and one-quarter cent, respectively, below their December 1953 levels.

In addition to the direct influence of changes in the prices of the metals, many other influences (which may be affected by the prices of the metals but which are in substantial degree or wholly independent of such prices) affect mine output. Among these are influences tending to decrease output, such as mine or mill shutdowns owing to labor disputes, exhaustion of ore reserves, increased costs of production, power shortages, unusually severe winter weather conditions, lack of market for ores due to mill or smelter shutdowns, and reduced length of workweek; and influences tending to increase output, such as the opening of new mines, the completion of development and expansion projects, and the resumption of operations after labor disputes. Perhaps the most important of these influences in recent periods, other than reduced prices, were the mine shutdowns, owing to labor disputes, in Utah, Colorado, the Tri-State district, southern

Illinois, Kentucky, and New York. Power shortages also reduced production in the Pacific Northwest.

Mine closures or curtailments.-A total of 179 lead and zinc mine or mill closures or major curtailments of mining and milling operations that occurred from the beginning of 1952 through November 1953 came to the attention of the Tariff Commission through information supplied in the reports to the Commission, the hearings held in connection with the investigation, trade publications, Bureau of Mines reports, correspondence, and other sources.19 These closures and curtailments probably resulted in the removal of over 9,000 employees from the payrolls of these operations. However, because of the completion of some development on other projects and some expansion in other mines, the net decline in total employment was less. 

The cessation of production at lead and zinc mines does not eliminate the cost of their maintenance and upkeep to prevent serious damage to the properties and to safeguard investments. Some mining companies reported to the Tariff Commission that large expenditures for pumping, retimbering, and other maintenance were needed to prevent excessive damage to mine equipment and installations and to underground workings from mine flooding and cave-ins. These maintenance costs are frequently the only alternative to permanent closure of the mines and loss of ore reserves because of the high costs that would otherwise be involved in restoring the mines to production. 

Curtailments in zinc smelter output

Smelter output of slab zinc from foreign and domestic sources (including primary and redistilled secondary) which in 1953 totaled 971,000 tons, slightly larger than in 1952, was the second highest on 

How record, being only 20,000 tons below the peak output in 1943. ever, slab-zinc output began to decline in November 1953. Output in February 1954 (68,020 tons) represented the lowest monthly output since November 1949 and was 12 percent below the total produced in February 1953. This reduction reflects a general cutback in production by a number of zinc smelters toward the end of 1953, as well as the closing of one primary zinc smelter in February 1954.20 

Curtailment of production facilities has been accompanied, at some operations, by a reduction in length of workweek. Total curtailment in slab-zinc output since the late part of 1953 has been reported by trade publications as aggregating about 14,000 tons per month, which is equivalent to about one-sixth of the total domestic primary smelting capacity. According to trade-paper accounts, most of these curtailments in slab-zinc output were attributed by smelting concerns to the decline in the price of zinc. As previously noted in part III, smelters' stocks of slab zinc showed a general upward trend from the beginning of 1952 and at the end of January 1954 had reached the relatively high level of close to 200,000 tons. 

19 According to the Bureau of Mines, from the beginning of 1952 through January 1954 more than 40 majo zinc or lead mines had shut down and an additional large zinc mine was scheduled to close in March 1954. 

20 One of the major zinc smelters (in Oklahoma) was shut down from early November 1953 to the end of the year as the result of strikes at mining operations. This smelter, however, had resumed operations in 

January 1954 following the settlement of these labor disputes.

Distribution of production by size of mine The lead and zinc mining industry is comprised of a large number of mines with production concentrated largely in a small number of very large mines. This is shown by an analysis of the records of the te Bureau of Mines for 1952 as summarized in table LZ-8 and appendix table 65. ​te The Bureau of Mines compiles mine-production data for every known operation, no matter how small. Data for 1952, for example, include production from 43 mines that produced less than 1 ton each of recoverable lead or zinc. The total number of lead and zinc mines, as recorded by the Bureau of Mines for 1952, was 912, of which 305 were classified as lead mines, 242 as zinc mines, and 365 as lead-zinc mines (see table LZ-8). 

Of the total of 912 mines, the 55 largest ones, each producing 4,000 or more tons of recoverable lead plus zinc, accounted for about fourfifths of the total mine production of lead and three-fourths of the ti total mine output of zinc. At the other extreme, 512 of the mines, each producing less than 50 tons of lead plus zinc, accounted for only 0.8 percent of the total lead production and 0.4 percent of the total zinc production. Most of the mines in this small-size category did not respond to the Tariff Commission's questionnaires; many of them have ceased production since the beginning of 1952. ​19 The Bureau of Mines recorded 193 lead and zinc mines in 1952 that produced 500 or more tons of lead plus zinc. These 193 mines accounted for 95.2 percent of all the lead and 95.5 percent of all the zinc produced by all lead and zinc mines. The number of producing mines in this size category remains relatively constant from year to year, whereas the number of smaller mines fluctuates widely from year to year (see appendix table 64). In general, the annual number of producing mines varies with the market prices of the metals. 108

The data on employment at mines and mills as shown in the above tabulation were adjusted upward to represent all lead and zinc mines as indicated by the production coverage of operations reported. 

The total number of employees in lead and zinc mining and milling and in primary smelting and refining in the United States declined by about 8,650, or 20 percent, from 43,200, the monthly average for the first quarter of 1952, to 34,550 in October 1953.

Although employment declined generally throughout the period considered, the sharpest declines occurred in 1953. Between January 

1953 and October 1953 employment declined 13 percent, compared with a decline of 7 percent between January and December 1952. 

Activity in the primary lead and zinc industries is usually not subject to large seasonal variations. 

On the basis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (which show the same percentage decline in employment at lead and zinc - mines as that shown by the Commission's survey for earlier months), mine and mill employment in December 1953 was 3 percent lower than that in October, and employment in January and February 1954 was probably still lower as a result of additional mine closures and zinc-smelter cutbacks. It may also be noted that in recent months a number of mining and milling and primary smelting and refining concerns have announced reductions in the length of their workweek.

The great bulk of the total decline in employment in the primary lead and zinc industries since the early part of 1952 was in the mining and milling segment. Smelter and refinery output, as previously noted, was generally maintained at a fairly high level through 1952 and most of 1953, reflecting a continued high rate of processing of imported ores. 

Changes in employment in lead and zinc mining and milling.—In comparison with the overall decline of 20 percent in employment in the primary lead and zinc industries from the monthly average for the first quarter of 1952 to October 1953, employment in the mining and milling segment declined by 32 percent between the 2 periods.

This decline is somewhat greater than the 30-percent decline in the mine output of lead and zinc combined. Some mine operators reported to the Commission that in order to cut costs in the face of declining market prices for lead and zinc they cut back on develop- 46566-54--17

ment and exploration activities. The relatively sharper decline in mine employment than in mine output seems to confirm this. 

Much the greater part (about three-fourths) of the total decline in employment in the lead and zinc mining and milling segment occurred at zinc mines and mills, where, in October 1953, employment had dropped by 38 percent from the monthly average for the first quarter of 1952, compared with a decline of 21 percent for employment at lead mines and mills. Employment at mines and mills classified as predominantly zinc decreased between the 2 periods by 39 percent, compared with 37 percent for that of other zinc mines and mills. The decline in number of employees at mines and mills classified as predominantly lead was only 6 percent, compared with a drop of 34 percent for other lead mines and mills. 

Changes in employment in primary lead and zine smelting and refining. The decline of less than 3 percent in monthly employment at primary lead and zinc smelting and refining operations between the first quarter of 1952 and October 1953 was far smaller than the decline in employment at mines and mills during that period. Employment at operations processing mostly domestic materials showed a 4-percent decline (about the same for both lead and zinc operations) while employment at operations processing mostly imported materials increased by about 2 percent (see appendix tables 9 and 38). As noted above, substantial cutbacks in zinc-smelter operations are reported to have taken place since the last quarter of 1952, including the shutdown of one horizontal-retort zinc smelter in February 1954. 

Regional changes in mining and milling employment. This analysis of changes in employment in the principal mining areas is based on the data reported to the Tariff Commission by mining and milling companies. Although the operations covered by these data accounted for a high proportion of the total lead and total zinc production in the United States (92 percent for lead and 93 percent for zinc), the coverage was considerably lower than this in those States particularly Arizona, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, and the Tri-State and Upper Mississippi Valley districts-in which an appreciable proportion of the total mine output comes from relatively small mines. For example, mines producing less than 500 tons of lead and zinc in 1952 (although accounting for only 4.8 percent of the total United States output of lead) accounted for about 19 percent of the total mine output of lead in Nevada in that year, for 18 percent of the lead output in the Upper Mississippi Valley district, for 16 percent in the Tri-State area, for 12 percent in New Mexico and Colorado, and for 11 percent in Arizona. Similarly, mines producing less than 500 tons of lead and zinc in 1952 and which accounted for only 4.5 percent of the total 

United States mine output of zinc in that year, accounted for 16 percent of the mine output of zinc in the Tri-State area, for 8 percent of that in the Upper Mississippi Valley, and for 7 percent of the total in Arizona and Nevada. Many of the questionnaires were not returned from small operators in these areas because the mines had shut down. 

Thus the percentage declines in employment for these States and districts, as indicated by the Commission's survey, are probably understated.

Employment in October 1953, as compared with the monthly average for January-March 1952, declined most sharply in the Western States. The decline for the 9 Western States averaged 38 percent

and ranged from 26 percent for Idaho to 88 percent for New Mexico. 

Employment declined between these 2 periods by 45 percent in Arizona, 37 percent in California, 34 percent in Colorado, 29 percent in 

Montana, 58 percent in Nevada, and 31 percent in Washington.

In the West Central States, the number of employees on the payrolls of the lead and zinc mines and mills in October 1953 was about 28 percent smaller than that in the first quarter of 1952. The drop in employment in the predominantly zinc-producing Tri-State district between the 2 periods was 64 percent, whereas the decline in employment in the predominantly lead-producing Southeastern Missouri district was only 5 percent. 

200 In the States east of the Mississippi River, where zinc mining predominates, the drop in employment was most severe in northern Illinois and Wisconsin (the Upper Mississippi Valley district), where the decline was 40 percent, and much smaller in the States with larger zinc production New York, New Jersey, Kentucky, Pennsylvania (mine development only), Tennessee, and Virginia (the 6 States combined), where the decrease was only 6 percent. 

It should be noted that many of the lead and zinc mines, particularly in the Western States, are located in areas where other means of livelihood are limited or entirely nonexistent. Mine or mill shutdowns in such areas present a difficult problem both to the worker and his family and to the supporting service industries. In some areas the situation, if long continued, gives rise to so-called ghost towns with the consequent severe depreciation or total loss of realty holdings s in addition to the loss of income to the worker. The mine operator, be on the other hand, loses skilled workmen who may not be easily di replaced should economic conditions permit resumption of operations

CHAPTER V COST OF TRANSPORTING LEAD AND ZINC TO UNITED STATES MARKETS 

The cost of transporting ores and concentrates affects competition for the United States market among domestic producers, among foreign producers, and as between foreign and domestic producers. 

For this reason, the Commission made a special effort to obtain data on the cost of transportation. 

Nature of data assembled on transportation costs Data on the cost of transportation, insurance, and other handling of domestic and imported ores were obtained in a questionnaire survey of primary lead and zinc smelting and refining companies. These companies also provided data on the cost of transporting refined lead hand slab zinc from primary smelters or refineries to consumers in the United States. Information on the cost of transporting refined lead et and slab zinc from foreign sources to United States destinations was assembled by the Commission. 

The data on cost of transporting lead and zinc assembled for this report relate to such costs incurred for transporting lead and zinc in ores or concentrates and in metallic form from mines and mills to consumers. For zinc practically all the transportation costs consist i of (1) the cost of transporting concentrates from mills to smelters or refineries, and (2) the cost of transporting slab zinc from the smelters or refineries to consumers. With respect to lead, however, as already

indicated, the product of smelters is base or lead bullion which is always further refined, much of it by refineries distant from the smelters. For lead, therefore, the data include the cost of transporting bullion from smelters to refineries.

The data collected by the Commission regarding the cost of transporting lead-bearing ores and concentrates and tabulated below relate to the movement of 78 percent of such imported ores and concentrates in 1952. Similarly, the data on the cost of transporting zinc-bearing ores and concentrates relate to the movement of 58 percent of the total zinc imported in that form in that year; those for refined lead, to the movement of 51 percent of the total refined-lead imports, or 71 percent of imports of refined lead other than for United States Government use; and those for slab zinc, to the movement of 91 percent of all slab-zinc imports.21

你 ​20 18 享​飯 ​The average cost of transporting lead and zinc to the United States is determined not only by the actual rail and water freight rates but also by the routes over which the materials move and the quantities moved over each route. Complete data on the cost of transporting lead and zinc would have yielded somewhat different weighted averages, especially for zinc-bearing ores and for refined lead, the available cost data for which covered only a little more than half of the total imports. Sufficient information has been assembled, however, to indicate in a general way the broad differences in transportation costs.

From the data assembled, the indicated average cost of transporting lead and zinc in ores and concentrates from foreign countries to smelters in the United States in 1952 was higher than the cost of transporting lead and zinc metal from foreign sources to consumers in the United States.23 The lead content of lead-bearing ores and concentrates averaged 54 percent and the zinc content of zinc-bearing ores and concentrates averaged 55 percent. The cost of transporting lead in ores and concentrates from foreign countries averaged 1.93 cents per pound of lead content and the cost of transporting zinc in ores and concentrates averaged 1.35 cents per pound of zinc content. A larger percentage of imports of zinc in ores and concentrates than of lead in ores and concentrates comes from nearby sources in Mexico and Canada. The bulk of United States imports of lead-bearing ores and concentrates come from Peru, Bolivia, the Union of South Africa, Australia, and Canada, in the order named. The bulk of the very much larger imports of zinc-bearing ores and concentrates come chiefly from Mexico, Canada, and Peru, and to a less extent from Bolivia, the Union of South Africa, and Spain.

The cost of transporting refined lead from foreign countries to 

United States consumers in 1952 averaged about 1 cent per pound and the cost of transporting slab zinc from foreign countries to 

United States consumers in that year averaged 1.18 cents per pound.

The bulk of United States imports of refined lead in 1952 came from Mexico, Canada, Australia, Yugoslavia, and Peru. The bulk of the smaller imports of slab zinc came from Canada and Mexico. 

The weighted average costs of transporting lead or zinc in ores and concentrates were 0.93 and 0.17 cent per pound more, respectively, than the costs of transporting refined lead and slab zinc, while the import duty on refined lead exceeds that on lead in ores by 0.31 cent and the import duty on slab zinc exceeds that on zinc in ores by 0.1 cent.

The cost of transporting lead and zinc from individual foreign countries to the United States varies widely, not only from country to country but also for shipments along different routes from individual countries, depending upon the distances the materials are transported and the mode of transportation. It may be noted from the above that the costs of transporting lead and zinc from the less distant countries are not always the lower costs. 

For example, the average costs of transporting refined lead from Australia and Yugoslavia were lower than the average cost of transporting refined lead from Canada, and the average costs of transporting slab zine from the European countries of West Germany, Belgium, Italy, and Yugoslavia were lower than the average costs of transporting that metal from Canada and Mexico. The reason for these differences in costs is that a large part of the United States imports of lead and zinc from Canada and Mexico are shipped by rail rather than by water, and rail freight rates are higher. 

Cost of transporting foreign and domestic ores and concentrates to United 

Štates smelters

The data presented above indicate that in 1952 the average cost (per pound of lead content) of transporting lead-bearing ores and concentrates from foreign countries to United States smelters in 1952 varied from 1.10 cents for imports from Mexico to 2.99 cents for imports from the Philippine Republic, and averaged about 1.93 cents per

pound for imports from all countries combined.24 In comparison, the cost (per pound of lead content) of transporting lead in lead ores and concentrates in the United States from mining districts to lead smelters in 1952 varied from 0.06 cent to 2.13 cents, and the average is estimated at about 0.54 cent (see appendix table 23).25 Therefore, on the average, the cost of transporting lead in ores and concentrates from foreign countries to smelters in the United States in 1952 exceeded the cost of transporting lead in ores and concentrates from United States mines to United States smelters by about 1.39 cents per pound of lead content. However, substantial although undetermined quantities of lead ores and concentrates from United States mines located at greaterthan-average distances from smelters were transported at costs that were higher than the costs of transporting the ores from most of the foreign sources; in a few instances, this difference was greater than the United States import duty of three-fourths cent per pound of lead content of lead-bearing ores.

The average cost of transporting foreign zinc-bearing ores to United States smelters in 1952, as previously indicated, ranged from 1.08 cents per pound of zinc content for ores from Canada to 2.08 cents for ores from the Union of South Africa and to 5.11 cents for ores from the 

Philippine Republic,26 and averaged 1.35 cents for ores from all foreign countries combined. By comparison, the costs of transporting zinc ores and concentrates in the United States from mines to smelters in 1952 ranged from 0.07 cent to 1.49 cents per pound of zinc content, and the average cost of transportation from all mines to all smelters is estimated at 0.76 cent per pound of zinc content (see appendix table 52). The cost of transporting foreign zinc ores exceeded the cost of transporting domestic zinc ores to United States smelters by about 0.59 cent. The differential between the costs of transporting foreign and domestic zinc ores was thus much smaller than the previously. noted differential between the costs of transporting foreign and domestic lead ores (1.39 cents). In fact, the average cost of transporting the domestic zinc ores and concentrates received by 7 domestic smelters in 1952 apparently exceeded the average cost of transporting time zinc-bearing ores to United States smelters from all foreign countries; these 7 domestic smelters accounted for more than half of the total zinc content of domestic ores and concentrates consumed in the United States. Some of the domestic ores (quantities involved not determined) were transported to domestic smelters at costs that exceeded the average cost of transporting ores from foreign countries to United States smelters by amounts larger than the United States import duty on zinc-bearing ores of 0.6 cent per pound of zinc content.

The average cost of transporting refined lead from foreign countries to United States consumers in 1952, 1.00 cent a pound, was 0.61 cent higher than the average cost of transporting refined lead from primary domestic refineries to United States consumers in that year (0.39 cent a pound). Similarly, for slab zinc in 1952, the average cost of transportation from foreign countries to United States consumers, 1.18 cents per pound (higher than for lead), exceeded by 0.46 cent the average cost of transporting slab zinc from primary smelters and refineries in the United States to domestic consumers (0.72 cent per pound).

Changes in rail and ocean freight rates on lead and zinc materials The information on average transportation costs, summarized above, which was received by the Tariff Commission from primary smelting and refining companies and importers, was supplemented by data received from the American Zinc Institute, transportation com- 27 Details given for lead in appendix tables 27 and 29 and in table L-9 in part II, for zinc in appendix tables 55 and 57 and in table Z-9 in part III.

Ca panies, the Interstate Commerce Commission, the Federal Maritime

Board, and other sources on changes that have occurred in freight rates since 1939. Some of these data are summarized for lead, in appendix tables 25, 28, and 30, and for zinc, in appendix tables 53, 56, and 58.

Rail freight rates for hauling lead and zinc ores and concentrates in the United States have increased substantially since the end of World War II. The rates increased in each of the years 1947-49, and in 1952. At the end of 1952 the rates for hauling ores and concentrates (in carload lots) from individual mining districts to individual smelters were from 36 to 80 percent higher than the rates prevailing at the end of 1946.

Rail freight rates for hauling refined lead, lead bullion, and slab zinc. also increased in the United States in each of the postwar years 

1947-49, and in 1952. The rates at the end of 1952 for hauling refined lead and slab zinc (in carload lots) from individual smelters or refineries to individual consuming areas in the United States were from 59 to 118 percent above those prevailing at the end of 1946. 

Much of the lead and zinc from Canada and Mexico, the principal sources of United States imports, comes by rail. Changes in rail freight rates in Canada have been similar to such changes in the United States rates. Rail freight rates in Mexico have probably increased as much as or more than the rates in the United States. 

Ocean freight rates-unlike domestic rail rates, which are controlled by the Interstate Commerce Commission-rose sharply during World War II owing to the risks involved in ocean transportation and the increased demand for ocean shipping. Ocean freight rates at the end of World War II were substantially higher than in 1939. Although ocean freight rates were not increased in the postwar period as much as rail freight rates in the United States were changed during this period, the overall increases in ocean freight rates from 1939 to 1953 were generally larger. Ocean freight rates for hauling refined lead from Mexico, Peru, Australia, and Chile to Atlantic, gulf, or Pacific coast ports increased between December 1945 and September 1953 by from 11 to 49 percent; however, for the entire period from August 

1939 to September 1953 the increases ranged from 98 to 145 percent. 

Similarly, ocean freight rates for hauling lead-bearing ores from Peru, Australia, and Chile to Atlantic, gulf, or Pacific coast ports increased by 5 to 24 percent from December 1945 to September 1953, but by 

87 to 155 percent between August 1939 and September 1953.

Some countries, like Yugoslavia and the Union of South Africa, have become exporters of lead and zinc to the United States only in the last few years and there are no records of freight rates on shipments to the United States from these countries for earlier years. 

A smaller proportion of United States imports of zinc than of its imports of lead come from overseas, and a much larger proportion of its zinc imports than of its lead imports is in the form of ores. Ocean freight rates on zinc-bearing ores and concentrates from Peru and Chile to Atlantic and gulf coast ports declined 19 percent and 29 percent, respectively, between December 1945 and September 1953. During this period ocean freight rates on zinc ores from Australia to Pacific coast ports declined by 7 percent, and from Australia to Atlantic and gulf coast ports increased by 67 percent. Ocean freight rates on zincbearing ores, like those on lead-bearing ores, had increased sharply during World War II.

CHAPTER VI LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES IN FOREIGN COUNTRIES 

Material in chapter IV, part II, indicated the kinds, sources, and magnitude of United States imports of unmanufactured lead. Similarly, these aspects of United States imports of unmanufactured zinc were discussed in chapter IV, part III. It was indicated that the bulk of the imports of zinc come from Mexico and Canada, and that the bulk of the imports of lead come from these two countries, with substantial quantities also from Australia, Peru, and Yugoslavia. 

Financial interest of United States concerns in lead and zinc operations in foreign countries

A large part of the imports of lead and zinc are produced in foreign countries by companies owned by United States concerns or by foreign companies in which United States corporations have a substantial financial interest. Some of the more important of these corporate relationships are indicated below.

In Mexico, one of the principal sources of United States imports, virtually all the refined lead and slab zinc is produced by subsidiaries of the American Smelting & Refining Co. and the American Metals 

Co., Ltd.; these companies produce in Mexico lead and zinc metals from company-mined ores as well as from ores purchased from other Mexican producers. Other United States companies that produce lead and zinc in Mexico, mostly in the form of ores, include the Eagle- Picher Co., the Howe Sound Co., and the Fresnillo Co. The American 

Metals Co., Ltd., noted above, also has about one-third interest in 

San Francisco Mines, Ltd., a British-controlled company that accounts for approximately one-fifth of Mexico's lead-zinc mine output and that ships zinc concentrates to the United States for smelting. 

It is estimated that in 1952 well over one-half of United States imports of lead (mostly in pigs and bars) and almost two-fifths of the zinc imports (mostly in ores) from Mexico were produced by companies in which United States concerns have major interest. 

In Canada, the principal producer of lead and zinc that is owned by a United States concern is the Buchans Mining Co. This concern, a subsidiary of the American Smelting & Refining Co., produces lead and zinc ores in Newfoundland. Other United States concerns with interests in lead- or zinc-producing operations in Canada are the 

Howe Sound Co., the National Lead Co., the Pend Oreille Mines &

Metals Co., and the Newmont Mining Corp. The Howe Sound Co. has a 100-percent interest in the Britannia Mining & Smelting Co., which is a small producer of zinc in British Columbia; the Pend Oreille 

Mines & Metals Co. has a 60-percent interest in the Reeves Mac- 

Donald Mines, Ltd., which operates a lead-zinc property in British 

Columbia; and the National Lead Co. operates a secondary lead smelter at Toronto. The Newmont Mining Corp. has a small share interest in the Hudson Bay Mining & Smelting Co., Ltd., one of

Canada's principal zinc mines. In addition, the St. Joseph Lead Co., through a wholly owned subsidiary, the Leadridge Mining Co., Ltd., has a substantial interest in the newly discovered lead-zinc-silver ore deposit in New Brunswick. This deposit promises to become an important source of new production of these metals, and the St. Joseph

TH Lead Co. is furnishing substantial financial assistance for its development.

Of the total United States imports of lead and zinc from Canada in 1952, probably less than one-fifth came from operations owned by 

United States companies.

In Peru, the Cerro de Pasco Corp., a United States concern, accounts for a substantial part of the mine output of lead, most of the mine output of zinc, and virtually the entire output of refined lead and slab zinc. The bulk of the United States imports of zinc and lead from 

Peru are from Cerro de Pasco's operations.

In South-West Africa, 2 United States companies- the American Metals Co., Ltd., and the Newmont Mining Corp.-together have over one-half interest in the Tsumeb Corp., Ltd., which is the leading producer of lead and zinc in that country. United States imports from South Africa probably come from these operations; in 1952 these imports, all in ores, amounted to 16,000 tons of lead and 15,000 tons of zinc. 

In North Africa, the St. Joseph Lead Co. and the Newmont Mining

Corp. have substantial interests in Société Nord-Africaine du Plomb and Société des Mines de Zellidja, which are the principal lead-zinc producers in French Morocco. The United States imported 7,000 tons of lead from this country in 1952. 

The bulk of Argentina's mine production of lead (20,000 tons in 1952) and zinc (17,000 tons) is accounted for by Cía. Minera Aguilar, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of St. Joseph Lead Co. United

States imports of unmanufactured zinc from Argentina amounted to 4,000 tons in 1952; no imports of lead from Argentina were recorded in that year.

Several officials of a United States lead- and zinc-mining company have interests in lead- and zinc-producing operations in Guatemala. 

In 1952, Guatemala's mines produced about 5,000 tons of lead and 9,000 tons of zinc approximately equal to the content of these metals in ores imported into the United States from that country. 

In Australia, the American Smelting & Refining Co. has substantial share holdings in Mount Isa Mines, Ltd., and operates the lead and zinc properties of this company; it also has an interest in the Anglo- 

Westralian Mining Party, Ltd., which is a small producer of lead. 

E The Newmont Mining Corp. has financial interest in Broken Hill 

South, Ltd., and the Consolidated Zinc Corp., Ltd. These companies are large producers of lead and zinc in Australia, and an undetermined part of United States imports from Australia come from these operations.

Competitive position of United States and foreign producers of lead and zinc In order to provide information on lead and zinc mining and milling in foreign countries comparable to that for the United States, a number of important foreign producers of lead and zinc were requested to supply data similar to that obtained from the domestic industries. Reports were requested from the leading producers of primary lead and zinc in Canada, Mexico, Peru, and Australia. In response to these requests, reports were received from 3 Canadian companies, and from 2 Mexican companies. Some of the information which had been requested from Australian companies, principally

that relating to hours worked and wages paid, was received by cablegram in mid-March 1954.

The reports received for Canada covered 4 large mines and 3 mills that in 1952 accounted for 80 percent and 61 percent, respectively, of total recoverable mine production of lead and zinc in that country. 

Reports received for Mexico covered 15 mines and 12 mills that in 1952 accounted for a little more than 28 percent and 45 percent, respectively, of Mexico's mine production of lead and zinc. The data received from Australia were for 4 companies that in 1952 accounted for over 68 percent of that country's mine output of lead and zinc. 

The data for foreign operations were supplied to the Commission on a confidential basis. As a result, the Commission is not at liberty to disclose all of the details. The following material, except that on ore reserves, is a general summary of information obtained from the companies operating in foreign countries. 

Grade of ore mined and value of products per ton of ore mined.-One of the outstanding differences between the lead- and zinc-mining industries in the United States and in the foreign countries is the very much higher grade of ore mined in foreign countries. 

The latest available estimates of lead and zinc in ore reserves in the United States and foreign countries (as of January 1, 1950), as compiled by the United States Geological Survey were shown in table LZ-3 in chapter II, part IV, of this report. These data show that of the measured and indicated reserves of lead in ore, the largest reserves (12%½ million tons) were in Australia and the next largest (10 million tons) were in Europe, with the reserves in North America (7.9 million tons)-mostly in Canada-ranking third in size. largest reserves of zinc in measured and indicated ore (19%½ million tons) were in Europe, and the second largest reserves (16%½ million tons) were in North America, about equally divided between the United States and the rest of this continent. The reserves of zinc in ore in Australia and South America (14 million tons and 12 million tons, respectively) ranked third and fourth in size. The The estimated grade of the measured and indicated ore reserves in the foreign countries supplying the United States with the bulk of its imports of lead and zinc is shown in table LZ-9. These data, as estimated by the United States Geological Survey, like those on size of known reserves shown in table LZ-3, relate to reserves as of January 

1, 1950. As previously indicated in this report, "grade of ore" refers to the metal content of the ore. The grade of ore reserves shown in table LZ-9 is in terms of gross metal content. The grade of ore in terms of recoverable metal content is much lower, probably no more than about 85 percent of the gross lead content and about 75 percent of the gross zinc content-owing to losses in mining, milling, and smelting. 

In terms of gross metal content (especially of lead and zinc content), the average grade of measured and indicated ore reserves is highest in Australia, 12.2 percent lead and 13.5 percent zinc. Australia's ore reserves are probably larger and richer than those in any other major producing country supplying the United States with lead and zinc imports. The grade of ore reserves in Peru and Mexico is probably next highest, followed by Yugoslavia and Canada; the data on grade of ore reserves in Mexico, however, are less precise than the data for other countries. 18

Comparable data on grade of ore reserves in terms of gross metal content are not available for the United States. Data are available, however, on the grade of ore mined in 1952 in terms of recoverable metal content for United States companies and for some of the major producers in Canada, Mexico, and Australia. Data for the United 

States were discussed in detail in chapter II, part IV of this report. 

The recoverable metal content of lead and zinc ore mined in the 

United States in 1952 averaged 1.4 percent lead and 2.5 percent zinc, in addition to about 0.1 percent copper and about 0.73 ounce of silver, and 0.006 ounce of gold per ton of ore.

The annual reports of the major Australian companies and the reports to the Tariff Commission from some of the major producers in Canada and Mexico, noted above, indicated the grade of ore mined in these countries in 1952. The ore mined in that year in Canada, Mexico, and Australia had a much higher recoverable content of lead and zinc than that mined in the United States. In addition, the ore mined in these countries had a substantially higher recoverable content of silver and, in Canada and Mexico, of gold and copper as well. 

The average value of mine and mill products per ton of ore mined in 1952 by lead and zinc mines in Canada and Mexico for which reports were received by the Commission was very much higher than the average, $9.83 per ton, for mines and mills in the United States. 

Although data were not reported to the Commission on value of products per ton of ore mined in Australia, the high grade of ore mined in that country indicates that the value of the products per ton of ore mined at lead and zinc mines in Australia was probably as high as or higher than that in Canada or Mexico. 

Principal operating expenses.-Average labor costs per ton of crude ore mined by the 3 Canadian and the 2 Mexican companies that reported to the Commission were somewhat higher than the average, $4.35 per ton, for the United States companies as a whole. However, because of the much higher value of products per ton of ore mined in

Canada and Mexico, the labor cost per dollar's worth of products was much less than in the United States. 

Average hourly earnings of production and related workers at the Canadian mines and mills, taken as a group, were only slightly less than the average in the United States, whereas average hourly earnings of the Mexican workers were very much smaller than those of workers in either the United States or Canada. Data received from Australia show that average hourly earnings of production and related workers at the large lead and zinc mines in that country are similar to those in the United States and Canada. In this connection, however, it is noted that a substantial part of wage payments to employees at Australian mines is in the form of lead-bonus payments. Such payments consist of a weekly bonus that is based on the average price realized for lead sold by producing companies. The lead bonus thus provides for Australian producers some flexibility in wage costs present by reason of the fluctuation in total wage payments with changes in the market price of lead.28 In the United States, with some exceptions that exist in the Tri-State district, wage rates in lead and zine mining are not tied to metal prices. 

The average cost of supplies and materials per ton of crude ore mined at United States operations in 1952 was somewhat higher than that for the 3 Canadian operations, and was much lower than that for the 2 Mexican companies. However, relative to the value of products the cost of supplies and materials is much higher in the United States than in either Canada or Mexico. 

An outstanding difference between the cost of lead and zinc mining and milling in the United States and Canada, on the one hand, and in Mexico, on the other, is in the element of taxes other than income taxes. These taxes in Mexico consist largely of ad valorem taxes on exports and on production, described in appendix B of this report. 

Taxes other than income taxes (including these export and production taxes) per ton of crude ore mined in Mexico, as reported to the Tariff Commission, were very much higher than those in the United States and much higher than those in Canada. In fact, taxes other than income taxes per ton of ore mined in Mexico were, on the average, larger than the cost of labor plus the cost of supplies and materials per ton of ore mined. The amount of export and production taxes paid by Mexican producers fluctuates with changes in market prices of lead and zinc. The fluctuation in these taxes, like the lead-bonus payments in Australia, operates during periods of declining prices in such a way as to reduce any competitive disadvantage to Mexican producers attributable to the prevalence of higher taxes of this type in that country than in the United States. 

Net operating profit

Operating-profit data comparable with those obtained from United States concerns were reported for foreign lead and zinc mining and milling operations that accounted for about 12 percent of the recoverable lead and 38 percent of the recoverable zinc produced from all mines in Canada in 1952; such data were also obtained for similar operations in Mexico that accounted for 28 percent of the lead and 45 percent of 28 Although there is no zinc bonus in Australia, most operations in that country produce both lead and zinc, and hence lead-bonus payments affect average wage costs of most Australian producers.

the zinc produced from all mines in that country in 1952. The profit data on United States operations, it will be recalled, covered lead and zinc mines and mills that accounted for 79 percent of the total domestic production of lead, and 56 percent of the output of zinc from all lead and zinc mines.

The average ratio of net operating profit before income taxes to net sales for the operations covered in each of the three countriesthe United States, Canada, and Mexico was lower in 1952 than in 1950, and lower in the first half of 1953 than in 1952. For the Canadian companies reporting, the ratio of net operating profit to net sales (before income taxes) was very much higher than for companies in the United States, and the decline in the Canadian ratios from 1950 to the first half of 1953 was much less than that in the United States ratios. For the Mexican operations, the average ratio of net operating profit to net sales before income taxes was much higher than for the United States concerns in 1950; in 1952, the average ratio was about the same as for the United States; but in the first half of 1953, the average ratio for Mexico was substantially lower than the average ratio for the United States during this period. Comparable data are not available for Australian companies. 

Recent changes in mine output in foreign countries In other parts of this report it has been noted that the aggregate level of production of lead and zinc in foreign countries has, since the end of the war, been substantially higher than postwar consumption of lead and zinc in these countries. Thus, in most postwar years there has been a large excess of production over consumption in foreign countries that are the major suppliers of United States imports, and this surplus has increased in nearly every year since 1946. Moreover, the data indicate that most of this surplus has in recent years been shipped to the United States market. Here the discussion is confined to changes in mine production since the beginning of 1952-the period marked by sharp declines in the market prices of lead and zinc-in the principal foreign countries supplying United States imports of these products. Production of lead and zinc in these countries (Mexico, Canada, Peru, Australia, and Yugoslavia) is much larger than consumption, and a large part of their exportable surplus of these metals has been shipped to the United States. 

Data on the monthly output of lead in these five countries during 1952 and 1953 are shown in table LZ-10. For Mexico, Canada, and 

Australia, the data represent mine production of recoverable lead. 

For Peru and Yugoslavia, monthly data on mine output were not available, and for these countries, information on smelter production has been used to indicate changes in the rate of output during the 2-year period covered; the 1953 totals for Peru and Yugoslavia are [ annual rates based on production in the first 10 months of the year.

The aggregate level of production of lead in the five principal foreign countries, as indicated by table LZ-10, increased by about 7 percent in 1953 over the 1952 level. Canada's lead mine production increased by 28,000 tons, or 17 percent, and that of Australia increased 40,000 tons, or 18 percent, whereas estimated smelter output in Peru and Yugoslavia increased about 21 percent and 8 percent, respectively. 

From 1952 to 1953, mine production of lead in Mexico declined 27,000 tons, or 10 percent. In the same period United States output of lead declined 54,800 tons (from 390,200 tons to 335,400 tons), or about 14 percent.

Data on monthly mine output of zinc in Mexico and Canada, the principal foreign suppliers of United States imports of unmanufactured zinc, are shown for 1952 and 1953 in table LZ-11. Mexico's mine production of zinc was maintained in 1953 at about the same level (220,000 tons) as during 1952, whereas Canada's mine production in 1953 increased by 33,400 tons, or 9 percent. In the same period 

United States mine production of zinc declined by 131,300 tons, or about 20 percent.

Apparent consumption, such as might be calculated from data on production, changes in producers' and consumers' stocks (but not Government stocks, which are confidential), imports, and exports, would differ from reported consumption partly because such calculated data would include withdrawals for the strategic stockpile as well as lead actually consumed. Apparent consumption of lead, computed as indicated above, would also differ from reported consumption because available data on private stocks are incomplete, because computed data would be based in part on total lead content rather than recoverable lead content of some imports, and because production data exclude lead from new scrap (sometimes referred to as "runaround" scrap) whereas reported consumption data include consumption of lead recovered from new scrap.

Entries into bonded warehouses may subsequently be (a) withdrawn for consumption (when they would be recorded as withdrawals from bonded warehouses for consumption), (b) reexported in the same form (when they would be recorded as an export of domestic merchandise), or (c) smelted or refined in bond and the resulting metal exported (when the metal would be recorded as an export of domestic merchandise and the metal content and foreign value of an equivalent amount of imported raw materials processed-ores, concentrates, scrap, etc.-to obtain the quantity of metal exported would be recorded at virtually the same time as a withdrawal from bonded warehouse for consumption).
