NOTE. There is considerable variation among mine operators and others on what constitutes a single mine. Almost all lead and zinc mining is underground. Some operations have single openings or hoisting shafts, others have more than 1 such opening. Some operators may regard a group of openings as a single mine, whereas others may count each opening as a mine. Some operations, begun as separate establishments in a given locality and originally regarded as several mines, became interconnected after mine openings were extended and were subsequently regarded as single mines. Sometimes a given group of operations was regarded as more than 1 mine until a consolidation of ownership occurred, and thereafter the units merged under common ownership came to be regarded as a single mine. 

This analysis of the number of mines counted as 1 mine many groups of operations which were not easily identified as constituting more than 1 mine. It also counted as 1 mine in all years each group of operations identified as separate mines in the earlier years but which were later merged into single mines. Although the total number of mines thus counted may be subject to question, the operations were counted in the same way from year to year and the numbers indicate approximately the trend in the number of producing units. 

The count includes all operations, however small, producing ores or reclaiming old tailings or old slag dumps, valued principally for their content of recoverable lead or zinc. 46566-54--23

B. TAXES PAID IN MEXICO BY THE LEAD- AND ZINC-MINING INDUSTRY 

The principal taxes on Mexican mining operations are (1) the special export surtax imposed in addition to the regular export duties and (2) the Mexican production tax, a progressive tax based on the value of metals produced. Both taxes are levied in addition to Mexican national income taxes on corporate earnings and in addition to State or municipal taxes. 1 Export taxes.-The special export surtax, which is 15 percent ad valorem, was placed in effect in 1948, for the purpose of capturing "exchange profits" that were expected to accrue to mineral producers as a result of the devaluation of the Mexican peso. Both the regular export duty and the export surtax are levied on the invoice value of shipments or on the official peso valuation of the metal exported, whichever is higher.2 A mercantile tax of 2 percent is applied to the sum of the regular export duty and the special export surtax. 

In the export-tax schedule two basic tax rates are provided for lead and zinc ores. On ores produced by mines located more than 

1,000 kilometers from Mexican mills or smelters, a higher export tax is applied in order to encourage treatment of the ore in Mexico rather than in other countries. The export-tax schedule, in percent. ad valorem, for lead and zinc ores and concentrates early in 1954 is shown in the following tabulation:

1 Duty free. 

The total tax applicable to lead ore is 22.4 percent ad valorem, or 17.2 percent, depending on the distance of the mine from Mexican mills or smelters. The corresponding rates for zinc ores are 22.4 percent ad valorem and 15.3 percent. Exported lead concentrates are dutiable at 17.2 percent ad valorem, and zinc concentrates, at 

18.1 percent.

Production taxes.-Mexican production taxes are a severance tax imposed by the Government for the purpose of recovering, in the In 1948 the peso was devalued from 4.86 pesos to 6.85 pesos per United States dollar. A further devaluation in 1949 reduced the value of the peso to 8.65 pesos per United States dollar. 

2 For tax purposes, official peso valuations are set by the Mexican Government on the principal mineral and metal exports.

national interest, a portion of the value of minerals exploited by private producers. In effect, the tax consists of 3 parts: (1) A basic ad valorem rate applied to the official valuation of the metal as determined monthly by the Ministry of Finance on the basis of 

New York market quotations, (2) an additional ad valorem_tax based on the excess of the current prices of lead and zinc over fixed minimum prices, and (3) an additional tax equal to 10 percent of the first 2 taxes combined.

For lead ores the basic production tax rate is 3.7 percent ad valorem and for lead concentrates, 2.3 percent ad valorem. As noted above this tax is applied to the official valuation of the product as determined by the Ministry of Finance. An additional tax of 0.6 percent is payable for each 0.03 peso, or fraction thereof, by which the peso equivalent of the New York price exceeds 0.17 peso per pound. 

Finally, 10 percent additional is added to the 2 taxes mentioned above. 3 For zinc ore the basic production tax is 2.4 percent ad valorem. 

For zinc concentrates, it is 1.4 percent. An additional tax of 0.3 percent is levied for each 0.03 peso, or fraction thereof, by which the peso equivalent of the New York price exceeds 0.19 peso per pound. 

A further tax of 10 percent is added to the 2 foregoing taxes. 

Tax rebates.-A tax rebate of up to 75 percent of the production and export taxes paid is permitted at the discretion of the Minister of Finance. This rebate, however, is allowed only to producers whose production and export-tax payments do not exceed 200,000 pesos per month. For each 1,000 pesos by which tax payments fall below 

200,000 pesos per month, the producer is entitled to a rebate of 0.375 percent, but, as noted above, the allowable rebate cannot exceed 75 percent of taxes paid. Only small producers receive direct benefit. from this provision of law, and the large operations, many of which are owned by companies outside of Mexico, obtain no direct tax relief from the provisions of the law. 

Income taxes.-Mexican income taxes range from 3.8 percent on annual taxable profits of 2,000 pesos to a maximum of 30 percent on taxable profits in excess of 500,000 pesos. An additional tax of 10 percent is applicable to profits distributable as dividends. The 10percent tax is not applied when distributable profits are allocated to a reinvestment reserve by the company. An excess-profits tax, ranging from 5 percent to 25 percent, is payable on profits exceeding 15 percent of the working capital. The tax laws permit deductions of 

5 percent for real-estate amortization and deductions of 10 percent. for amortization of other immovable property. Under special circumstances the tax on immovable property may be increased to 20 percent. No deduction is permitted for depletion of ore reserves. 

Although the official rate of exchange is 8.65 pesos per United States dollar, the rate of 4.85 pesos per 

United States dollar is used by the Mexican Government for calculating these taxes. * For foreign companies, working capital is defined as 60 percent of total assets.

C. DOCUMENTS LETTERS TRANSMITTING RESOLUTIONS REQUESTING THE TARIFF COM- MISSION TO INVESTIGATE THE LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES Hon. EDGAR B. BROSSARD, UNITED STATES SENATE, COMMITTEE ON FINANCE, 

July 27, 1953.

Chairman, United States Tariff Commission, Washington, D. C. 

DEAR CHAIRMAN BROSSARD: The Senate Finance Committee today approved a resolution directing the Tariff Commission to make an investigation of the lead and zinc industries of the United States. A copy of that resolution is enclosed. 

You will note that the investigation is to be made pursuant to section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930. I trust that this investigation will in no way interfere with the prompt action of your Commission in concluding any other investigations of these products which may have been or may be applied for under any other sections of the law. 

It was the opinion of the committee that the situation with regard to the lead and zinc industries was such that any investigations concerning these industries should be concluded without undue delay. 

With very best regards, I am Sincerely,

EUGENE D. MILLIKIN, Chairman. 

COMMITTEE ON WAYS AND MEANS, HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, 

Washington, D. C., July 29, 1953.

Hon. EDGAR B. BROSSARD, Chairman, United States Tariff Commission, 

Washington 25, D. C.

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: At the direction of the Committee on Ways and Means, 

I hereby transmit to the Tariff Commission a resolution unanimously adopted this date by the committee. This action is taken pursuant to section 332 of the Tariff 

Act of 1930, as amended. 

Sincerely yours,

DANIEL A. REED, Chairman. 

RESOLUTIONS DIRECTING THE INVESTIGATION OF THE LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES ADOPTED BY THE SENATE COMMITTEE ON FINANCE AND BY THE COMMITTEE ON WAYS AND MEANS OF THE HOUSE OF REPRE- SENTATIVES RESOLUTION 

Resolved, That the Tariff Commission is hereby directed pursuant to section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (19 U. S. C. 1332), to make a thorough investigation of the domestic lead and zinc industries, including the effect of imports of lead and zinc on the livelihood of American workers, and to report the results of its investigation to the Senate Finance Committee on or before March 31, 1954. 

SEC. 2. Such investigation shall be made after due notice and opportunity for hearing is given to interested parties. The report of the Commission shall set forth the facts so determined relative to the production, trade, and consumption of lead and zinc in the United States, and shall take into account all relevant factors affecting the domestic economy, including the interests of consumers, processors, and producers. Such report also shall contain a statement of findings as to the effect upon the competitive position of the domestic lead and zinc industries of the present tariff status of imported lead and zinc, so as to assist the Congress in determining what changes, if any, should be made in that tariff status. 

Resolved, That the Tariff Commission is hereby directed, pursuant to section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (19 U. S. C. 1332), to make a thorough in-

ES the vestigation of the domestic lead and zinc industries, including the effect of imports of lead and zinc on the livelihood of the American workers, and to report the results of its investigation to the Committee on Ways and Means, on or before March 31, 1954. 

SEC. 2. Such investigation shall be made after due notice and opportunity for hearings is given to interested parties. The report of the Commission shall set forth the facts so determined, relative to the production, trade and consumption of lead and zinc in the United States, and shall take into account all relevant factors affecting the domestic economy, including the interest of consumers, processors and producers. Such report also shall contain the statement of findings as to the effect upon the competitive position of the domestic lead and zinc industries on the present tariff status of imported lead and zinc, so as to assist the Congress in determining what changes, if any, should be made in that tariff status.

THE TARIFF COMMISSION'S ANNOUNCEMENT OF ITS INVESTIGATION OF THE LEAD AND ZINC INDUSTRIES, AND OF THE PUBLIC HEARINGS TO BE HELD IN CONNECTION THEREWITH UNITED STATES TARIFF COMMISSION WASHINGTON PUBLIC NOTICE INVESTIGATION INSTITUTED AND HEARING SET LEAD AND ZINC 

(Investigation under section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930) Pursuant to a resolution of the Committee on Finance of the United States Senate on July 27, 1953, and of the Committee on Ways and Means of the House of Representatives on July 29, 1953, the United States Tariff Commission, on the 29th day of July 1953, instituted a general investigation under the provisions of section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, of the domestic lead and zinc industries, including the effect of imports of lead and zinc on the livelihood of 

American workers.

The purpose of the investigation is to determine the facts relative to the production, trade, and consumption of lead and zinc in the United States, taking into account all relevant factors affecting the domestic economy, including the interests of consumers, processors, and producers. Upon completion of the investigation the Commission will submit a report of the results thereof to the 

Senate Finance Committee and the House Committee on Ways and Means. 

Such report will include a statement of findings as to the effect upon the competitive position of the domestic lead and zinc industries of the present tariff status of imported lead and zinc.

Hearings. Public hearings, at which all interested parties will be given opportunity to express their views, will be held in connection with this investigation, beginning on November 3, 1953, with respect to lead and beginning November 5, 1953, with respect to zinc. Hearings will be open at 10 a. m. on the days fixed, and will be held in the hearing room of the Tariff Commission, Eighth and É 

Streets NW., Washington, D. C.

Requests to appear.-Interested parties desiring to appear and give testimony at the hearings should notify the Secretary of the Commission in writing, at its offices in Washington, D. C., in advance of the hearings. 

I hereby certify that the above investigation was instituted and hearings were ordered by the United States Tariff Commission on the 29th day of July 1953. 

DONN N. BENT, Secretary. 

Issued July 29, 1953.

THE TARIFF COMMISSION'S REQUEST TO THE COMMITTEES FOR AN EXTENSION OF TIME FOR COMPLETION OF ITS REPORT UNITED STATES TARIFF COMMISSION, 

Washington 25, March 11, 1954.

Hon. EUGENE D. MILLIKIN, Chairman, Committee on Finance, United States Senate. 

DEAR SENATOR MILLIKIN: Reference is made to your letter of July 27, 1953, transmitting to the Commission a copy of a resolution adopted by the Senate Finance Committee, directing the Tariff Commission to make an investigation under the provisions of section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930 of the domestic lead and zinc industries and to report the results of the investigation to your committee on or before March 31, 1954. A similar resolution was sent to the Commission by the chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee on July 29, 1953. 

As you no doubt are aware, the domestic lead and zinc producers filed an escape-clause application shortly after the Commission instituted the section 332 investigation, and both investigations have been conducted concurrently. addition to the independent investigation by members of the Commission's staff, extensive hearings were held and questionnaires were sent out to importers and to domestic and foreign producers. The task of digesting and analyzing the great mass of information obtained in these investigations has been going forward In

as rapidly as has been humanly possible. However, because of the great pressure on the Commission and the Commission's specialists and the great task which will be involved in the mechanical job of duplicating and assembling the reports in these investigations, the Commission is afraid that the requirement for the transmission of the section 332 report by March 31, 1954, will result in a report which would be much less satisfactory to us and much less helpful to your committee than one which could be prepared if we had just a short period longer to do the job.

Accordingly, the Commission is requesting your committee to grant it an extension of time, until April 20, 1954, within which to submit the report on the section 332 investigation on lead and zinc. 

Sincerely yours,

EDGAR B. BROSSARD, Chairman.

COMMITTEE ON WAYS AND MEANS, HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, Washington, D. C., April 6, 1954. 

Hon. EDGAR B. BROSSARD, Chairman, United States Tariff Commission, Washington, D. C. 

MY DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: This letter is written with respect to your request for an extension of time to permit preparation of a report to the Committee on Ways and Means by the Tariff Commission on the present status of our domestic lead and zinc industries.

Pursuant to the terms of the committee resolution directing this study the report was due on or before March 31, 1954, and was to be based on a thorough investigation of the domestic lead and zinc industries including the effect of imports of lead and zinc on the livelihood of American workers. 

You are hereby authorized an extension of time for filing this report to April 20, 1954. 

Sincerely yours,

DANIEL A. REED, Chairman.
